### (d) The five hard problems specific to Smartsheet's shape

These are the things to be visibly curious about. Each has a genuine tension; naming the tension is what makes it a senior answer rather than a component list.

#### 1. Permission-aware retrieval across two permission systems

Smartsheet has **two overlapping authorisation models**, and AI retrieval has to satisfy both at once. The first is the sharing hierarchy — workspace → folder → sheet, with roles (Owner > Admin > Editor > Commenter > Viewer) that **inherit downward**, plus item-level shares and published links. The second is **row-level scoping through Dynamic View and WorkApps**, where two users with identical sheet-level grants legitimately see *different rows*. Retrieval has to reflect both, per request, per user.

**The tension:** you cannot evaluate the full permission computation at query time — walking inheritance and applying row filters for every candidate document blows the interactive latency budget — but you cannot fully pre-materialise it either, because sharing changes constantly and a stale materialised ACL is a data-leak bug, not a freshness bug. Every player who has published on this resolves it the same way: **mirror ACLs into the index at ingest, evaluate the requesting user at query time, and reuse the product's existing authorisation libraries rather than re-implementing the rules in the AI path.** Slack states this explicitly and says only the invoking user ever sees the output. Glean runs a separate permissions crawl alongside the content crawl and syncs it near-real-time. Notion had to build a whole CDC data lake (Postgres → Debezium → Kafka → Hudi → S3/Spark) largely because computing a block's permission means walking its parent tree to the workspace root — and they say that project is what made the AI rollout possible. The Smartsheet parallel is exact.

**The design consequence people miss:** the ACL is part of the **retrieval key**, not a post-filter. Post-filtering a ranked list gives you an empty result set for a legitimate user (their permitted documents ranked 40th) *and* no protection at all if the filter is ever skipped on a fast path.

**The failure mode to name.** Microsoft 365 Copilot's "oversharing" story is the lesson worth citing: Copilot respects permissions correctly and still caused incidents, because it made *pre-existing* over-permissioning visible for the first time. Reported scale is 150–300 overshared SharePoint sites per enterprise tenant, with "shared with everyone except external users" as the invisible killer. Smartsheet's equivalents are a sheet shared to an entire workspace, and published links.

**And the metric.** Permission-violation rate is not a dashboard number. It is an alarm, and its target is exactly zero.

> **Say it like this:** "You've got two permission systems — sheet sharing and Dynamic View row filters — and they don't compose trivially. My prior is that the ACL belongs in the retrieval key rather than in a post-filter, evaluated as the requesting user using the existing authz libraries. What I'd want to know is whether you'd ship a sharing-assessment report *before* enabling workspace-wide AI search, because the Copilot lesson is that AI doesn't create over-permissioning, it exposes it."

#### 2. AI over user-defined schemas, where every tenant's schema is different

A warehouse team can build a semantic layer once, because there is one schema. Smartsheet has **100,000+ customers and 13.4 million collaborators** by their own AWS post, across **6 billion active tasks** — and every sheet is a schema its owner invented: column names in any language, types that only sometimes match what the name suggests, dropdowns with tenant-specific enumerations, cross-sheet references, and a row forest whose parent/child structure carries real meaning that `CHILDREN()` and `ANCESTORS()` depend on. The argument does not depend on the exact count; it depends on the fact that the count is large and the schemas are unrelated.

**The tension:** the semantic layer is what makes structured-data AI reliable, and you cannot author one per tenant. So you need a **schema-digest generator** that derives the semantic layer automatically per sheet — column name, type, allowed dropdown values, referenced sheets, hierarchy shape, and a handful of representative rows — plus a **curated cross-tenant metric vocabulary** (percent complete, days late, at risk, rolled-up health) that the model selects from rather than re-deriving.

**The published evidence, stated at the confidence it deserves.** The semantic-layer benchmarks I have seen — dbt Labs published one in 2026 — all point the same direction: routing generation through a curated semantic layer beats raw text-to-SQL on the same schema by a wide margin, and improving the underlying models in that layer lifts both approaches while lifting the constrained one more. ⚠️ I have not re-verified the exact percentages, so **do not quote decimals**; quote the direction and offer to re-derive it on their data. The number you *can* quote is from the Spider 2.0 paper (arXiv 2411.07763), which I did verify this morning: the databases are sourced from real applications and *"often containing over 1,000 columns"*, and *"based on o1-preview, our code agent framework successfully solves only 21.3% of the tasks, compared with 91.2% on Spider 1.0 and 73.0% on BIRD."* That is the empirical argument against free-form generation over a customer's arbitrary sheet portfolio, and it is a paper you can cite by its own framing.

> **Say it like this:** "Semantic-layer failures are refusals; free-form query failures are confidently wrong numbers. A refusal costs a retry — a wrong number in a status rollup that a government PMO acts on is an incident. Spider 2.0 is the number I'd point at: enterprise schemas often over a thousand columns, and an o1-preview code agent solved 21.3% when the paper landed, against 91.2% on Spider 1.0. So on a product where every tenant invents their own schema, I'd spend the engineering on auto-deriving a per-sheet schema digest and a shared metric vocabulary, not on a bigger model."

#### 3. The recalculation and dependency graph

This one you open as a **question**, not an assertion — and it is the strongest question you have. smartsheet.com/ai says AI columns *"summarize, translate, and analyze sentiment in real time."* That wording is equally compatible with evaluation on save, evaluation on demand, and full participation in the recalculation graph. ⚠️ **Do not state that Smart Columns auto-recompute.** If the interviewer corrects the premise, the analysis below dies in its opening sentence — whereas asked as a question, the same analysis lands either way.

If they *do* sit in the recalculation graph, then an LLM call is inside a spreadsheet dependency graph, and spreadsheet dependency graphs have properties LLM calls do not: they are deterministic, they are effectively free, they are expected to converge, and they fan out. Change one cell and formulas, cross-sheet references, cell links and rollups cascade.

**The tension:** determinism versus cost versus freshness, and you cannot have all three. Recompute eagerly on every upstream change and a single paste of 5,000 rows becomes 5,000 model calls, turning a bounded per-seat entitlement into an unbounded bill — the arithmetic is in §(h). Recompute lazily and the sheet shows stale AI values sitting next to fresh formula values, so users stop trusting both. Recompute non-deterministically and a user who edits an unrelated column watches the sentiment score change, then files a bug you cannot reproduce.

**The design space worth naming out loud:** **content-addressed caching keyed on the exact input tuple** so an unrelated edit doesn't re-fire; **debounce and batch windows** feeding batched inference; **materialised results carrying a visible "computed at" provenance**; **dirty-marking with explicit refresh** rather than eager recompute; and a **per-tenant token budget that degrades the column to "stale — refresh?" instead of silently spending**.

⚠️ **On determinism, be precise, because this is catchable.** Temperature zero and a pinned model version *narrow* the variance; they do not make a hosted LLM deterministic — request batching, floating-point non-associativity on GPU, and MoE expert routing all produce run-to-run variation under greedy decoding. The thing that actually makes a Smart Column idempotent is the **content-addressed cache**: same input tuple, same stored result, no second call. Which also means a model upgrade is a **migration with a backfill and a diff**, not a config edit — every cached value in every tenant was produced by the old model.

> **Say it like this:** "The page says AI columns work in real time — does that mean they re-evaluate when an upstream cell changes, or on save, or on demand? Because if they're in the recalculation graph, you've put a non-deterministic, metered call somewhere users expect instant, free and reproducible. My instinct would be content-addressed caching on the exact input tuple, since that's what actually gives you idempotency — temperature zero only narrows the variance. And if that's right, swapping the model behind a Smart Column is a backfill with a diff, not a config change."

> **And if they say it's on-demand or on-save:** "Then the cost story is much easier and the interesting problem moves to batching and to what a five-thousand-row bulk operation does. Same cache, different trigger."

#### 4. Enterprise and government tenants constrain which models may be called at all

**Smartsheet Gov is FedRAMP authorised and runs in AWS GovCloud West (Oregon)** — their trust page names FedRAMP among SOC 2, ISO 27001 and ISO 27701, and names the GovCloud West region. ⚠️ **Do not say "P-ATO from the JAB."** The Joint Authorization Board was replaced by the FedRAMP Board under the FedRAMP Authorization Act and no longer issues P-ATOs; saying it in September 2026 dates your knowledge by two years, which is the opposite of what this section is for. Also drop the DISA IL-4 specific for Smartsheet Gov unless you can source it — the argument does not need it.

What their own whitepaper says, and this is the load-bearing line: *"Our AI tools are not currently available in Smartsheet Gov."* Meanwhile Bedrock in GovCloud reached FedRAMP High and DoD IL-4/5 in May 2025, initially with Claude 3.5 Sonnet v1 and Claude 3 Haiku plus Agents, Guardrails, Knowledge Bases and Model Evaluation, and added OpenAI GPT, gpt-oss and NVIDIA Nemotron models in June 2026. Azure OpenAI is authorised in Azure Government, but its model catalogue lags commercial badly. Residency is a third axis: US, EU and Australia exist as isolated environments, and residency-at-rest is not residency-of-inference — "global" deployment types on both Azure and Bedrock explicitly may process anywhere.

**The tension:** feature parity versus compliance boundary. If model choice is a per-feature constant, every feature is gated by the weakest environment it must run in, and the gov SKU holds the whole roadmap hostage. The clean design is a **capability tier in the router**: each feature declares a *minimum capability class*, each SKU and region declares an *allowed model set*, and the gateway enforces the intersection as a **route allowlist** — not a config flag an engineer can flip under deadline pressure. The product consequence has to be explicit rather than accidental: where no qualifying model exists, the feature is **visibly disabled with an explanation in the admin console**, never silently degraded. A gov customer quietly served a worse model is a compliance incident wearing a UX costume.

The second-order point, and the one most candidates miss: prompts and outputs are **stored alongside sheet data in the Smartsheet database**. That means the AI audit log inherits every retention, residency and deletion obligation of the source data it quotes. Your observability store just became regulated data.

> **Say it like this:** "Your whitepaper says AI isn't available in Smartsheet Gov, and Bedrock in GovCloud has had FedRAMP High since 2025 — so that reads like a roadmap item, not a permanent limit. The design consequence is that model choice can't be a per-feature constant: features declare a minimum capability class, SKUs and regions declare an allowed model set, and the gateway enforces the intersection as an allowlist. And the bit people forget is that you retain prompts and outputs next to sheet data, so the AI audit log inherits the same residency and deletion obligations as the sheet it quoted."

#### 5. Multi-tenant cost attribution

Three model providers, a per-seat P&L with **no separate AI SKU**, PE ownership, and a JD that says "design to cost" twice in different words. AI-native gross margins run roughly 50–60% against 80–90% for classic SaaS, and inference tends to grow as a *share* of spend as adoption grows, because usage outruns unit-cost declines. Their own April 2026 research release — "Traditional Thinking on Metrics is Holding AI Adoption Back" — says publicly that measuring AI value is unsolved, which is an unusually good opening for this conversation.

**The tension:** bounded per-seat revenue against unbounded per-seat cost. Power users run 10–100× the median, and request-count rate limiting does not contain it, because the unit of spend is the token, not the request. So: **meter tokens, not requests**; enforce budgets at the gateway in four scopes (per request, per session, per tenant, global) so an over-budget call is blocked *before* it reaches the provider; alert on 3× daily baseline, on a single tenant exceeding a threshold share of platform spend, and on estimate-versus-actual drift beyond 20%.

Then the attribution problem proper: you need cost per tenant *and* per feature *and* per accepted output, which means the gateway stamps every call with tenant, feature, model, cached-versus-fresh token split, and a **request lineage id** — and that telemetry must be joinable to acceptance events, or you can measure spend but never value. The event schema for this is in §(h)1, and typing it into the pad is worth more than describing it.

The honest product answer is that metering precedes pricing. Notion's version is the hard-edged one worth citing: credits priced per thousand, pooled per workspace, **non-rolling**, and Custom Agents **pause immediately at zero — scheduled runs are skipped, not retried**. That last clause is the design decision most teams avoid making, and it is the one that makes the budget real rather than decorative.

> **Say it like this:** "Cost attribution belongs at the gateway, not inside each feature — every call stamped with tenant, feature, model and the cached-versus-fresh token split, with budgets enforced in four scopes so an over-budget request never reaches the provider. The metric I actually care about isn't cost per token, it's **cost per accepted output**, which is a schema decision you have to make before you have the data. Is that something you can compute today?"

### (e) Why Smartsheet, and what to ask

#### Three genuine answers

Use one; hold the others in reserve. Each is specific enough that it could not be said about any other company.

**1. The Neptune post described your own bug, an order of magnitude larger.** Their published *before* state — Snowflake joins, migrated to DynamoDB by a Lambda, feeding models that needed constant retraining — is the canonical offline/online divergence problem, and you have shipped the fix for a smaller instance of it this year. That is not admiration, it is recognition, and it is the most credible form of interest you can express.

**2. Structured-data AI is a harder and more interesting problem than document RAG, and Smartsheet is one of the few places where it is the whole business.** Most AI platform roles are document retrieval behind a chat box. A grid product forces the interesting version: typed schemas, constrained generation, execution-based evaluation, a recalculation graph, and a validator that can be *deterministically right* before a model is ever graded. You can say honestly that you would rather work on generation that can be verified than generation that can only be judged.

**3. A platform team at the founding stage of a GCC with an explicit AI-first charter.** The Bengaluru site is being built to add 200+ people and become one of Smartsheet's largest engineering locations, with a stated mandate to be "a central source of AI innovation." Joining a platform team that early means writing the paved road rather than inheriting one — and your record is building roads, not just driving on them: the SageMaker MLOps platform for NatWest that AWS showcased at re:Invent, the shared multi-container endpoints at ResMed, the drift-monitoring utility that provisions Datadog dashboards from data-scientist-authored thresholds, and at TrueBalance the core pieces you built of the internal MCP developer assistant — the first Slack integration, the Google Docs skill, and the PR skill that writes titles and descriptions from the diff — inside a system that ties Jira, GitHub, Jenkins, AWS and Grafana behind one plain-English interface.

> **Say it like this (the 40-second version):** "Three reasons, in order. First, the Neptune post — the before state you describe, warehouse joins into a key-value store feeding models that needed constant retraining, is the exact class of bug I debugged this year at much smaller scale, and I'd rather work on that problem than talk about it. Second, structured-data AI is the version of this I find genuinely interesting, because a generated formula can be parsed, type-checked and executed before anyone judges it — you get determinism where most AI teams only get opinions. Third, the GCC is early enough that the paved road is still being laid, and building platforms other engineers depend on is what I've done at Tiger, at ResMed and now at TrueBalance. I'd rather write that road than inherit it."

#### Twelve questions to ask, ordered by what they reveal

Ask three or four. Choose by what the hour exposed. The first three carry the most information per second and work in almost any version of this round. Items marked ⭐ are questions only someone who has actually run an ML platform would think to ask.

| # | Question | What a good answer tells you |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | "Is this team building the platform that product teams ship AI features on, or the analytics and data-science platform inside BI & Ops? The JD reads like the second, the GCC charter reads like the first." | Resolves the biggest ambiguity in the whole role: internal-analytics customer versus product-engineering customer. Determines whether your work ever touches Smart Assist. **Have the branch ready either way — §(f), Plan B** |
| 2 | "How far along is the Snowflake-to-Databricks migration, and does the AI/ML platform get built on the destination or the source?" | Building on Snowflake means inheriting a migration mid-flight; building on Databricks means building on something the org is still learning. Either is workable — not knowing which is the risk |
| 3 ⭐ | "How is inference cost attributed today — per feature, per tenant, or just as one cloud line item? And **is cost per accepted output something you can currently compute?**" | The best single line you have. If it's one line item, the metering work is unstarted and that is a well-defined, high-visibility first project matching the JD's design-to-cost language exactly. It is a real diagnostic *and* it advertises the first thing you'd own |
| 4 ⭐ | "What does the path look like today for a data scientist going from a validated model to a served endpoint — how many hand-offs, and how long end to end?" | The honest answer *is* the job description. A long answer means obvious first wins; a short one means you would be optimising, not building |
| 5 | "The Neptune Knowledge Graph replaced a Snowflake-join to DynamoDB pipeline feeding constantly-retrained models. Is that graph a platform asset other teams build on now, or does it still belong to the recommendations team?" | Shows you read the deepest post in their corpus. The answer tells you whether "platform" is real here or aspirational |
| 6 | "AI columns work 'in real time' — does that mean they re-evaluate on upstream change, on save, or on demand? And what happens on a five-thousand-row paste?" | Their answer reveals the maturity of the cost and determinism story faster than any org-chart question. Note this is phrased as a question, not an assertion |
| 7 ⭐ | "Who owns rollback when a model behind a live feature regresses — the model owner or the platform? Is there an automated trigger, or is it a human decision?" | Distinguishes a real platform from a deployment script. Automated rollback implies genuine online guardrail metrics already exist |
| 8 ⭐ | "For generated formulas and automations, is there a shared eval harness — a golden set with execution-based scoring gating merges — or does each feature team run its own?" | Shared means a mature team you can contribute to immediately. Per-team means you have just found your highest-value first project |
| 9 ⭐ | "The monitoring line mentions Monte Carlo. Is data observability already in place, or is this the year you stand it up — and is it wired to model-level alerts or only table-level?" | Table-level only is the common state; connecting data incidents to model degradation is where platform value actually lives. Also gives you a clean, honest place to repeat that you haven't used the tool |
| 10 | "Prompts and outputs are retained alongside sheet data. Does the AI audit log inherit the same residency and deletion obligations as the source data, and who owns that today?" | A senior, compliance-aware question. The answer tells you how much governance debt exists behind the whitepaper |
| 11 | "Tool calls went from 42,000 to over 700,000 a week while weekly actives grew about 9x — so the average interaction got deeper. What broke first when writes became a third of the interesting traffic?" | Invites a war story, which is the most useful thing you can extract from an interviewer. Write-heavy agent traffic is where auth, idempotency and audit actually get tested. Uses their freshest published number |
| 12 | "The whitepaper says AI tools aren't available in Smartsheet Gov, but Bedrock in GovCloud has had FedRAMP High since 2025. Is closing that a roadmap item, and would this team own the routing constraints that make it possible?" | Proves you read past the marketing page, and tells you whether compliance-constrained model routing is in this team's scope |

**Two things to ask only if the room is warm:** whether the loop includes a second design round (reports conflict — some describe two design rounds for seniors, others one design plus one behavioural), and how the team is split between Bengaluru and the US after the 2025–26 reorganisation. Ask the first through the sourcing recruiter or the interview coordinator rather than the interviewer if you can.

**Never ask about:** layoffs, take-private economics, whether the Databricks migration is "worth it," or anything requiring them to comment on Blackstone or Vista.

### (f) Driving the hour

A design round grades how you scope and sequence at least as heavily as what you know. Chapter 54 covered pad mechanics; this is the arc.

#### The time budget

| Minutes | What | Your goal |
|---|---|---|
| 0–3 | Intro | The **30-second** version from Ch.54, not the 90-second one. Design rounds are short on airtime and you need theirs |
| 3–6 | The five-gaps disclosure, §(c) | Unprompted. Costs ninety seconds, buys the hour |
| 6–10 | Their framing, then your five clarifying questions | You must know which platform this is before you draw anything |
| 10–20 | Requirements, SLOs and non-functional constraints, written in the pad | The step candidates skip and interviewers grade |
| 20–40 | The design, one component at a time, checkpointing after each | Draw, then stop and ask |
| 40–50 | Their deep-dive, wherever they push | Follow them. Do not defend the drawing |
| 50–57 | Two or three questions from §(e) — lead with #3 | Q3 does double duty: diagnostic and pitch |
| 57–60 | Logistics: notice, next steps | Numbers from the consistency sheet, unchanged: 60 days, buyout discussable, [current CTC — private] current, [expected CTC — private] expected, no offer in hand |

#### The opening clarification checklist

Five questions, ninety seconds, before you draw a single box. Announce that you are going to ask them — the announcement is itself the signal.

> **Say it like this:** "Before I draw anything, five quick scoping questions, thirty seconds each — the design changes completely depending on the answers."

1. Who is the user of this platform: your data scientists, or product teams shipping customer-facing AI?
2. What is the traffic shape — batch scoring, interactive request/response, or agentic multi-step?
3. What latency is the worst-case user allowed to feel?
4. Multi-tenant with per-tenant isolation, or one internal tenant?
5. What already exists that I should build on rather than replace?

Then, before designing, **state the SLOs you are designing to as numbers, and say you are inventing them so they can correct you.** "I'll assume p99 under 400ms for interactive scoring, four nines on the serving path, and drift detection with a 24-hour worst-case time-to-detect. Push back on any of those."

#### The order to present components in

Never lead with the box diagram. Lead with the contract.

1. **The contract** — what a model owner hands the platform, and what the platform guarantees back.
2. **The data path** — where features come from offline and online, and how those two stay the same thing.
3. **The serving path** — packaging, promotion, traffic shifting, rollback.
4. **The observability path** — what is measured, at what cadence, who is paged.
5. **The cost path** — metering, attribution, budgets.
6. **The governance path** — versioning, lineage, approvals, retention.

Checkpoint after each with one sentence, then stop: *"That's the contract — want me to keep going, or go deeper here?"* Silence after a checkpoint is the interviewer choosing the next topic. Let them.

#### Stop signals

Stop talking when any of these is true:

- You have been speaking for **ninety seconds without asking anything**.
- You are describing a **tool** rather than a **decision**. "We'd use MLflow" is a tool. "Versioning lives next to the artifact so promotion can refuse" is a decision.
- You have named a trade-off and **not chosen a side**. This is the common senior failure: naming both options and declining to commit reads as evasion, not balance. Choose, then say what would change your mind.

#### Plan B: if question 1 resolves to "we are the analytics platform; we never touch Smart Assist"

Half of §(b) and §(d) becomes background rather than foreground. Do not abandon it and do not keep pushing it — reframe and pivot inside thirty seconds. What survives intact:

| Still fully relevant | Because |
|---|---|
| §(d)5, cost attribution | Internal analytics agents cost money the same way. Same meter, same four scopes, same lineage id |
| §(d)2, schema heterogeneity | It becomes internal: dbt models, Snowflake schemas, a lakehouse mid-migration. One tenant, same problem |
| §(c), the mapping table and the paved-road framing | This is literally the job description |
| The 4,001-vs-28 feature-parity story, and §(g)1 | Train/serve skew is platform-agnostic and it is your strongest single artefact |
| §(d)4, governance and retention | Unity Catalog exists because of exactly this. Your NatWest/FCA lineage story is the transferable half |
| §(h), every pad artifact and the arithmetic | All four are internal-platform artifacts. None of them assume a product surface |

> **Say it like this (the pivot):** "Then let me put the product surface aside — I read it because I wanted to understand what your data scientists will eventually ask you for, but it isn't today's problem. Today's sounds like a paved road for internal models, mid-migration, with the governance layer being chosen at the same time. That's closer to what I built at Tiger for NatWest than anything else on my CV. Can I ask what the current path looks like end to end, and where it hurts most?"

And the other branch — **"we are the product-AI platform"** — means everything in §(b) and §(d) is foreground, and §(d)1, permission-aware retrieval, is the first thing to raise, because it is the constraint every other component has to route around.

---

### (g) The two prompts you will almost certainly get

#### 1. "Design the platform that serves and monitors models for our feature teams"

Answer as a contract, then a path, then the failure modes. Twelve minutes if uninterrupted — and you will be interrupted, which is the point.

**The contract.** A model owner hands the platform four things and nothing else:

| Artifact | What it is | Why it is mandatory |
|---|---|---|
| Model artifact | Versioned, immutable, content-addressed | The only thing most platforms ask for, and the least interesting one |
| **Feature contract** | Exact feature names, types, allowed ranges, required/optional flags the artifact expects | This is the one that prevents the bug in your own story |
| Eval set + threshold | Frozen fixtures and the number below which promotion fails | Without a threshold, "the eval looked fine" is a vibe |
| **Rollback predicate** | The online metric and the value at which this model is pulled, written by the owner | Rollback that needs a human decision is not rollback |

If any of the four is missing, promotion is **refused**. That refusal is the platform's single most valuable behaviour, and it is the thing that distinguishes a platform from a deployment script.

**The path.**

```text
  register           build             gate                promote            observe
  ---------          ---------         ---------           ---------          ---------
  artifact      container image     offline eval        shadow  (0%)       drift / PSI
  feature   ->  pinned base,     -> vs frozen set    -> canary (1%)     -> p50/p95/p99
  contract      digest-pinned       + feature-contract   ramp (10/50%)      missing-rate
  eval set      deps                subset assertion     GA   (100%)        per feature
  rollback      SBOM                + latency budget     auto-rollback      cost/request
  predicate                         on a load fixture    on predicate       acceptance
                                                                            joined by
                                                                            lineage id
```

**The three failure modes to name, in this order — ranked by how often they actually happen, not by how interesting they are:**

1. **Train/serve skew.** Your own story: 4,001 offline features against 28 keys actually present in the real-time payload, defaults silently imputed, a near-constant served vector, and a model that still returned plausible scores. The platform fix is not "be careful" — it is a serialised feature contract shipped next to the artifact, a hard fail on missing required features, a CI subset assertion as a promotion gate, and a per-feature missing-rate metric emitted by the scorer itself. Code in §(h)2 and §(h)4.
2. **Silent degradation.** Nothing errors. Data drifts, the label distribution shifts, and AUC decays over a quarter. This needs an online guardrail metric with a named owner and a page — not a dashboard nobody opens.
3. **Deployment nobody can undo.** If rollback requires the model owner to be awake, you have a script. Rollback must fire automatically on the predicate the owner declared, and be reversible in one command.

> **Say it like this (three beats, then stop):** "The contract is four artifacts, and promotion refuses if any is missing. The path is register, gate, shadow, canary, ramp, with automatic rollback on a predicate the owner wrote. And the failure I'd design against first is train/serve skew — I shipped that bug this year, and the reason it's the dangerous one is that it doesn't error, it just returns plausible numbers."

#### 2. "Design the RAG stack behind Smart Assist"

Only if §(f) question 1 resolved to product-AI. The order that scores well:

1. **Permission first, not last.** The ACL is part of the retrieval key, not a post-filter. Post-filtering a ranked list gives you an empty result set for a legitimate user *and* no protection if the filter is ever skipped on a fast path. §(d)1.
2. **Top-level retrieval is structural, not semantic.** Find the *sheet*, then fetch the values live. Embedding numeric cells is how you get a confidently wrong rollup nobody can reproduce, because the embedding is stale the instant someone edits a cell.
3. **The chunk is the schema digest, not the rows.** Column names, types, allowed dropdown values, referenced sheets, hierarchy shape, and a handful of representative rows. That is what a model needs to decide *which* sheet and *what* operation.
4. **Generation targets a constrained DSL.** Formula language, automation DSL, or a curated metric vocabulary — not free text. Parse, type-check, sandbox-execute against sample rows, show a diff.
5. **Eval is execution-based** against frozen fixtures with `TODAY()` and `NOW()` pinned, not string similarity. §(h)3.
6. **The gateway meters and bounds it.** §(d)5 and §(h)1.

> **Say it like this:** "I'd put permission in the retrieval key rather than a post-filter, keep top-level retrieval structural — find the sheet, fetch the values live — and make the generation target a constrained DSL so I can execute the answer before anyone judges it. The part I'd want your input on is the chunk: I think it's the schema digest rather than the rows, but that depends on how much of Smart Assist is lookup versus analysis."

#### 3. "What would your first 90 days look like?"

Three phases, and the first has no deliverable other than a document. Say that out loud; it is the whole point.

| Days | What | Deliverable |
|---|---|---|
| 0–30 | Ship one real thing through the **existing** path, end to end, as a user of it. Interview every data scientist about their last incident and their last deploy. Write down every hand-off and every wait | A written map of the current path with hand-offs and wait times marked. **No new framework** |
| 30–60 | Fix the cheapest thing that removes a hand-off, and instrument what is currently unmeasured. My prior on this JD is that the unmeasured thing is **cost per feature per tenant**, because "one cloud line item" is the common state | Metering at the gateway or the serving layer, joinable to acceptance events. One hand-off removed |
| 60–90 | Propose the paved road with evidence from the map, and pick the first component to actually own. Land one promotion gate that refuses a real bad model | A gate in CI that has already blocked something, and a written proposal argued from the map rather than from taste |

> **Say it like this:** "Thirty days with no framework, because a platform team that ships a framework before it has used the current path builds the wrong one. I'd push something through the existing pipeline myself, write down every hand-off, then fix the cheapest one. My prior is that what I'd find unmeasured is cost per feature per tenant — but that's a prior, not a plan, and I'd rather be told I'm wrong in week two than in month three."

⚠️ Do not promise a migration, a re-platform, or a headcount ask in the first 90 days. In a cost-conscious year following two rounds of layoffs, "I'd spend the first month removing work from other teams" beats any architecture diagram.

### (h) The CoderPad surface: four things to type, and the arithmetic

In a design round the pad is a whiteboard. But typing something real, fast, is how you separate from a candidate who is merely fluent. Each artifact below is under three minutes and each makes an argument you have already made in words. Type one; do not type all four.

#### 1. The gateway metering event

The schema decision §(d)5 argues you must make *before* you have the data. Type this while saying "cost per accepted output" and it lands.

```json
{
  "event": "llm_call",
  "request_lineage_id": "01J8XW...ULID",
  "parent_lineage_id": null,
  "tenant_id": "org_84213",
  "plan": "enterprise",
  "residency": "eu",
  "user_id_hash": "sha256:...",
  "feature": "smart_columns.sentiment",
  "surface": "recalc",
  "provider": "azure_openai",
  "model": "gpt-4o-mini-2026-xx",
  "route_reason": "capability_class=text.classify; allowlist=eu",
  "tokens": { "prompt_fresh": 812, "prompt_cached": 2960, "completion": 24 },
  "cache": { "hit": true, "key": "sha256(input_tuple + prompt_ver + model_ver)" },
  "cost_usd_est": 0.00041,
  "latency_ms": { "ttft": 210, "total": 480 },
  "outcome": "ok",
  "accepted": null
}
```

Three things to say about it, in this order:

- `request_lineage_id` plus `parent_lineage_id` is what makes an agent's fan-out attributable to the request that started it. Without it, an agent loop is unattributable cost.
- `prompt_fresh` versus `prompt_cached` is the split that makes the caching lever **measurable** rather than believed. Their own Roo Code post claims ~70% of input served from cache; you cannot claim or refute that without this field.
- `accepted` is null at call time and backfilled by a separate acceptance event joined on the lineage id. That join is what turns cost-per-token into **cost per accepted output** — and it is a schema decision, not an analytics decision, which is why it has to be made now.

#### 2. The promotion gate

Reviewers grade this on one thing: whether the gate can **refuse**.

```yaml
# .ci/promotion_gate.yaml — evaluated in CI before any traffic shift
model: loan_withdrawal_propensity
version: "2026.09.04-a3f1"

require:                                   # missing any of these -> refuse
  feature_contract:    artifacts/feature_contract.json
  eval_set:            fixtures/oot_2026Q2.parquet
  rollback_predicate:  "auc_online_7d < 0.78 OR p99_ms > 400"

gates:
  - name: feature_contract_subset
    # every required serving feature must exist in the online payload schema
    assert: "required(feature_contract) is_subset_of keys(online_payload_schema)"
    on_fail: refuse          # this is the 4,001-vs-28 bug, caught in CI

  - name: offline_quality
    assert: "roc_auc(oot) >= 0.80 AND roc_auc(oot) >= incumbent - 0.01"
    on_fail: refuse

  - name: latency_budget
    assert: "p99_ms(load_fixture, rps=200) <= 400"
    on_fail: refuse

  - name: cost_budget
    assert: "usd_per_1k_predictions <= 0.35"
    on_fail: warn            # warn, not refuse — cost is a conversation, not a veto

rollout:
  - shadow: { traffic: 0,  duration: 24h, compare: incumbent }
  - canary: { traffic: 1,  duration: 24h, auto_rollback_on: rollback_predicate }
  - ramp:   [10, 50, 100]
```

Say: "The gate I care about is the first one. Everything else is standard; that one is the bug I actually shipped."

#### 3. The eval fixture with time frozen

The most convincing ten lines you can type in a *Smartsheet* design round, because it shows you know why date formulas flake.

```python
# Execution-based eval for generated formulas. String match is the wrong metric.
FROZEN_NOW = datetime(2026, 9, 4, 9, 0, tzinfo=ZoneInfo("UTC"))

def score(generated: str, fixture: Sheet, expected) -> Verdict:
    try:
        ast = parse(generated)                       # 1. syntactically valid?
    except ParseError as e:
        return Verdict.INVALID_SYNTAX(e)
    if not type_check(ast, fixture.schema):          # 2. do types match the columns?
        return Verdict.TYPE_ERROR
    with sandbox(now=FROZEN_NOW, locale="en-US", tz="UTC"):
        got = evaluate(ast, fixture.rows)            # 3. actually run it
    if got != expected:
        return Verdict.WRONG_VALUE(got, expected)
    return Verdict.PASS(complexity=len(ast.nodes))   # 4. right answer — but readable?
```

Say: "Four verdicts, not one score, because 'invalid syntax' and 'wrong value' need different fixes — one is a decoding-constraint problem, the other is a retrieval or schema-digest problem, and a single accuracy number hides which. And `FROZEN_NOW` isn't a detail: without it every `TODAY()` formula is flaky and the golden set rots inside a week."

#### 4. The drift-monitor stub

Ninety seconds, and the one place your ResMed work maps exactly.

```python
def emit_feature_health(batch: pd.DataFrame, contract: FeatureContract, ref: RefStats):
    for f in contract.required:
        col = batch.get(f.name)
        missing = 1.0 if col is None else col.isna().mean()
        emit("feature.missing_rate", missing, tags={"feature": f.name})
        if missing > f.max_missing_rate:            # threshold from the contract,
            page("feature_contract_violation",      # not a number I invented
                 feature=f.name, rate=missing)
        if col is not None and f.dtype == "numeric":
            emit("feature.psi", psi(col, ref[f.name]), tags={"feature": f.name})
```

Say: "Missing-rate per feature is the metric that would have caught my 4,001-vs-28 bug in an hour instead of a sprint. PSI is the slower one that catches the drift nobody notices. And the threshold comes from the contract the model owner wrote, not from me — the same pattern as the Datadog monitors I auto-provisioned at ResMed from data-scientist-authored thresholds and slice definitions."

#### The arithmetic, done out loud in ninety seconds

"Design to cost" is the JD's loudest repeated signal, and the way to prove you mean it is to do the sum in front of them. Round hard, say you are rounding, and use round numbers so the arithmetic is checkable in someone's head.

**Worked example: a 5,000-row Smart Columns paste.**

| Quantity | Assumption — state it as an assumption | Value |
|---|---|---|
| Rows pasted | one bulk import | 5,000 |
| Prompt tokens per row | schema digest cached, plus ~150 tokens of cell text | ~1,000 fresh-equivalent |
| Completion tokens per row | a sentiment label and a short reason | ~30 |
| Blended price, small model | order of $0.50 per million in, $1.50 per million out | — |

- Input: 5,000 × 1,000 = **5M tokens** → 5 × $0.50 = **$2.50**
- Output: 5,000 × 30 = **150K tokens** → 0.15 × $1.50 = **$0.23**
- **≈ $2.75 for one paste.** Trivial — *once*.

Now the two multipliers that turn it into a P&L problem:

- **Recompute.** If the column re-evaluates whenever any upstream cell changes, and a user edits that sheet twenty times a month, that is 20 × $2.75 = **~$55/month on one sheet** — unless the cache is keyed on the exact input tuple, in which case edits to unrelated columns cost **nothing**.
- **Seats.** Take a nominal $30/seat/month and a target 80% gross margin: the entire cost budget for everything — infrastructure, support and AI — is about **$6/seat/month**. If AI gets a third of that, the ceiling is roughly **$2/seat/month**. One uncached, frequently-edited sheet has eaten **twenty seat-months of AI budget**.

> **Say it like this:** "Round numbers, and tell me where I'm wrong. A five-thousand-row Smart Columns paste is about five million input tokens — call it three dollars. Trivial once. But if it re-evaluates on every upstream edit, one sheet is fifty-odd dollars a month, and against a seat price where AI probably gets a couple of dollars of margin, that single sheet has eaten twenty seats. Which is why I'd key the cache on the exact input tuple before I'd tune a prompt — the caching decision is worth more than the model choice."

⚠️ Every number in that paragraph except the token arithmetic is a **stated assumption**. Say "call it" and "order of" out loud, and say the price per million is from memory. The point is the shape of the curve, not the digits — and if the interviewer corrects your price, you have just got them designing with you, which is the best outcome available in a design round.


---

## 2. The flagship design — the AI/ML Ops platform

The prompt will arrive in one of three shapes: *"Design an AI/ML Ops platform for Smartsheet"*, *"How would you let ten product teams ship AI features on Smartsheet safely?"*, or *"We want to add AI across the product — what does the platform underneath look like?"* They are the same question. The answer below is one continuous 40-minute delivery with the spoken lines interleaved. Type the banners into the CoderPad **first**, then fill them; an outline visible at minute six converts the rest of the hour from rambling into executed plan.

This chapter assumes Chapter 54 has already been read and does not repeat it. In particular it assumes the 90-second intro has already been delivered (Ch.54, intro scripts), that the consistency numbers are memorised (Ch.54, consistency sheet — 8 years total, ~4.5 in ML engineer titles, ~1.5 years Azure Databricks, [current CTC — private] current / [expected CTC — private] expected, 60 days notice), and that the Smartsheet object model is already loaded (Ch.54, product primer — workspace/folder/sheet/column/row/cell, rows-as-forest with `parentId`, cell links versus cross-sheet references, the formula language, and the permission ladder Owner > Admin > Editor > Commenter > Viewer with Dynamic View and WorkApps for row-level scoping). That primer is not background colour here; it is the source of the hardest constraint in the design, and it is cross-referenced again at the permission-materialisation subsection.

```text
=== REQUIREMENTS === NUMBERS === ARCHITECTURE === PLANES === HARD CALLS ===
=== PHASING === FAILURE MODES === NOT DOING ===
```

### 2.0 The one page to hold if you hold nothing else

If the 40 minutes go sideways, everything below can be improvised from this card. Read it last before the call.

```text
=== TIMEBOX (rehearsed, not aspirational) ===
  0-3   open: three loops at three clock speeds + the disclosure
  3-8   clarify: 6-9 questions, then TYPE the assumptions
  8-14  numbers + one-screen architecture
 14-26  walk the planes (cut list below)
 26-33  three hard calls
 33-35  phasing + NOT DOING
 35-37  failure modes + on-call
 37-40  close: three decisions, one unknown, hand back

=== SIX NUMBERS I MUST PRODUCE WITHOUT NOTES ===
  1  28 RPS average, 170 peak      -> not a scaling problem
  2  ~4,000 tok in / ~350 tok out  -> per ask-portfolio request
  3  $1.24M/month naive -> ~$330k after routing, caching, output caps
  4  270M vectors, ~460 GB at int8 -> index is small; the pipeline is the cost
  5  12M sheets x 500 rows = 6B rows -> why the grid stays OUT of the index
  6  1 RU per GB of namespace, 0.25 RU floor -> namespaces are a cost choice

=== THREE HARD CALLS, COMMITTED, FOUR WORDS EACH ===
  (i)   FM runtime      -> "Managed models, our gateway."
  (ii)  Tenancy         -> "Tiered: namespaces, then dedicated."
  (iii) Feature store   -> "Contract now, store later."

=== THREE CLOSING DECISIONS ===
  1  The grid never enters the vector index.
  2  The gateway is ours, so the model is a config value.
  3  Permissions get a priority lane and a published revocation SLA.
```

### 2.1 Minute 0–3: open with the frame, not with a diagram

Do not draw anything yet. Say the sentence that tells the interviewer you hold both axes — the request path *and* the lifecycle that produces the thing on the request path.

> **Say it like this:** "Before I draw anything — there are three loops in this system running at completely different clock speeds. The inference loop in hundreds of milliseconds, the index-and-retrain loop in minutes to days, and the governance loop in quarters. Most ML platform designs fail because someone designs the first one and bolts the other two on. I'll design the serving path, then the pipeline that feeds it, then the controls around both. And I'll say up front where my hands-on experience stops, so you can weight what I say."

Then the disclosure, once, unprompted, flat and unapologetic. It is already in writing with the recruiter, so repeating it is *consistency*, not confession.

> **Say it like this:** "One thing I flagged to the sourcing recruiter and want to repeat to you directly: I have not run Unity Catalog, Mosaic AI Agent Framework, Databricks Vector Search, Monte Carlo or Bedrock in production. I've built the equivalent layers with other tooling — dataset ownership and PII classification over HIPAA-class data in Snowflake at ResMed, lineage from data snapshot through model to decision as an audit requirement on an FCA-regulated banking platform at Tiger, retrieval on pgvector and FAISS, hand-rolled data-quality monitoring with Deequ and Datadog, managed serving on SageMaker. My Databricks experience is about a year and a half of Azure Databricks, Spark and Deequ, and it was data-quality and ETL work, not Lakehouse platform ownership. So when a product name comes up I'll tell you what I know about the *category* and where my knowledge stops, and I'd rather do that than guess. Does that work?"

**The disclosure rule for the rest of the hour, and it is a rule, not a mood.** That was the full disclosure and it does not get repeated. Every later product he has not used gets *one clause*, pivoting inside the same sentence to what he has operated — "Not something I've run; the category question is X, and the equivalent I've operated is Y" — and then straight on. Eight separate disclosure moments across forty minutes reads as defensive no matter how well each one is built. One full disclosure, then clauses.

### 2.2 Minute 3–8: clarify — ten questions, and the assumptions to type anyway

Ask six to nine of these. Each is chosen because the answer changes the architecture, not because it sounds thorough. Prefer the assumption-plus-check form: *"I'll assume X unless you'd rather I design for Y."*

| # | Question | What the answer actually changes |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Is this a platform for N product teams, or one AI feature? | Platform ⇒ paved road, registry, quotas, per-team SLOs. Feature ⇒ none of that. Ask first; it changes everything. |
| 2 | Which features are in scope — formula/automation generation, summarisation, ask-your-portfolio, agents that write back into sheets? | Write-back agents pull in approval gates, idempotency and the whole injection surface. Read-only summarisation does not. |
| 3 | Does the AI operate over a single sheet's context, or across a workspace/portfolio? | Single-sheet is a prompt-engineering problem. Cross-sheet is a **permission-materialisation** problem, which is the real project. |
| 4 | Is Smartsheet Gov in scope for this platform, or is it a separate stack? | If it is in scope, the compliant model menu becomes a hard architectural constraint rather than a preference, and features need a capability tier. Asked this way he tells you the authorisation level rather than you guessing it. |
| 5 | What's the latency budget on the interactive surfaces, and is it time-to-first-token or full completion? | Sets model class and whether retrieval plus rerank fits at all. |
| 6 | Is there an AI cost target — per seat, per tenant, or as a % of AI-attributed ARR? | Determines whether routing and caching are optimisations or requirements. |
| 7 | Do we already have a lakehouse/CDC path off the production stores, or does the platform build it? | This is usually 40% of the effort and it is invisible on the architecture diagram. |
| 8 | Who owns model quality — the platform team or the product team shipping the feature? | Sets the on-call model, and therefore what the platform must expose. |
| 9 | Any residency commitment beyond data-at-rest — must *inference* stay in region? | Residency-at-rest ≠ residency-of-inference. Different answer, different vendor list. |
| 10 | Team size and shape that has to operate this on day 90? | Three people cannot run a streaming feature store and a self-hosted GPU fleet. Say so out loud. |

If they say "you decide", type this straight into the pad and keep moving. Stated assumptions beat open questions.

```text
=== ASSUMPTIONS (mine; challenge any) ===
tenants with AI entitlement          15,000
AI-active users/day                  300,000   (MAU-AI ~900,000)
AI interactions per active user/day  8
AI-indexable sheets                  12,000,000  (avg 500 rows x 12 cols)
comments / conversation messages     400,000,000 in corpus
list price anchor for the AI seat    ~$30/seat/month   <- LOAD-BEARING,
                                        challenge this one first
features in scope:
  formula-gen (inline), summarise sheet/report, ask-your-portfolio
  (cross-sheet RAG), at-risk project scoring (classical),
  ONE write-capable agent behind human approval
latency:  formula-gen      p95 <= 600ms end-to-end
          ask-portfolio    p95 TTFT <= 1.2s, full <= 6s
          at-risk scoring  nightly batch, freshness SLO 24h
cost ceiling: AI COGS <= 3% of AI-attributed ARR; alarm at 5%
gov SKU in scope; residency = EU + US + AU minimum
platform team: 6 engineers by month 6
```

Now the arithmetic. Do it out loud, in round numbers, and let it *derive a constraint* — that is the move that reads as staff-level.

```text
=== NUMBERS ===
REQUESTS
  300k users x 8            = 2.4M AI requests/day
  avg RPS = 2.4M / 86,400  ~= 28 RPS
  peak 6x (US/EU overlap)  ~= 170 RPS
  --> THIS IS NOT A QPS PROBLEM. 170 RPS is one modest service.
      The problems are tokens, permissions, and cost.

TOKENS (per ask-portfolio request, budgeted)
  system + tool defs     600
  sheet schema digest    900   <- STABLE per sheet -> cacheable prefix
  retrieved context    2,000   <- 8 chunks x ~250 tok
  user turn + history    500
  = ~4,000 in ; ~350 out
  2.4M x 4.0k = 9.6B  input tok/day
  2.4M x 350  = 0.84B output tok/day

COST, NAIVE (all frontier; $3/1M in, $15/1M out -- ILLUSTRATIVE shape
             anchor, I would verify on the live pricing page)
  in  :  9,600 x $3  = $28.8k/day
  out :    840 x $15 = $12.6k/day
  = $41.4k/day = ~$1.24M/month     <-- NOT SHIPPABLE. Design must change.

LEVER 1  route: ~70% of traffic is cheap-model-shaped
         (formula gen, single-sheet summarise, classify, extract)
  frontier 30%  in 0.30 x 28.8 = $8.6k   out 0.30 x 12.6 = $3.8k
  small    70%  in 0.70 x 2.88 = $2.0k   out 0.70 x 1.26 = $0.9k
                 --------------------------------------------------
                 input $10.7k/day  +  output $4.7k/day = $15.3k/day

LEVER 2  prompt-cache the stable prefix (1.5k of the 4k input tokens)
         cache read ~0.1x input, write ~1.25x; assume 70% warm hit
         INPUT ONLY -- caching does not discount output tokens
         input multiplier ~= 1 - 0.70 x (1500/4000) x 0.9 = 0.76
                 input $10.7k x 0.76 = $8.1k ; output unchanged $4.7k
                                              = ~$12.8k/day

LEVER 3  output discipline (350 -> ~220 median: terse + structured out)
         OUTPUT ONLY -- multiplier 220/350 = 0.63
                 output $4.7k x 0.63 = $2.9k ; input unchanged $8.1k
                                              = ~$11.0k/day

  = ~$330k/month  =  ~$0.0046 per AI request
  = $330k / 900k AI-MAU = ~$0.37 per AI-active user per month

SANITY (and the sensitivity, because the seat price is my assumption)
  at ~$30/seat list  -> ~1.2% of ARPU   (ceiling 3%)  PASS
  at ~$15/seat list  -> ~2.5% of ARPU                 STILL PASS
  WITHOUT levers 1-3 -> $1.38/user/mo = 4.6% at $30, 9.2% at $15
  --> the conclusion survives halving my price assumption.
      It does NOT survive dropping the levers, at any price.

INDEX
  Do NOT embed rows. 12M sheets x 500 rows = 6B rows, and row-level
  sharing means chunk granularity must be <= permission granularity.
  6B ACL-scoped vectors is not a design, it is a surrender.
  Embed the TEXT surfaces only:
    12M sheets x ~6 chunks (title, description, column digest,
      recent comment threads, attachment text)      =  72M
    comments / attachment text chunked              = ~200M
    total                                           = ~270M vectors
  storage: 1024-dim int8 = 1KB/vec, HNSW overhead ~1.7x
           270M x 1KB x 1.7 = ~460 GB
    (float32 1536-dim would be 1.6TB raw, ~2.8TB indexed -> quantize
     with rescoring instead of buying RAM)
  backfill embed cost: 270M x ~150 tok = 40.5B tok
           at ~$0.02-0.10 per 1M  = $0.8k - $4k ONE-OFF
           --> embedding is cheap; the PIPELINE is the cost
  incremental: ~3% of the INDEXED CORPUS changes/day
           270M x 0.03 = ~8.1M chunks/day
           = ~94 index writes/sec sustained. Trivial.
```

> **Say it like this:** "Two things fall straight out of that arithmetic and they set the whole design. First, at 170 peak RPS this is not a scaling problem — if I spend the hour on Kubernetes autoscaling I'm designing the wrong system. Second, the naive token bill is $1.2 million a month against roughly $0.4 million of margin headroom, so routing, prompt caching and output discipline aren't optimisations for year two — they're load-bearing, and the gateway that enforces them is a day-one component. And the row-count line tells me the third thing, which is the most consequential: I should not put the grid in a vector index at all."

> **Say it like this:** "Two things on this board are load-bearing and everything else is replaceable. The left side has two arrows, deliberately, and they point in opposite directions. (A) goes down — permission events on a priority lane, separate from and faster than content, feeding a denormalised projection. (B) goes up — after retrieval and before generation, the policy plane re-checks the top eight document IDs against the system of record. (A) is a cache, so it will be wrong for a window; (B) is what makes that window survivable. And every serving path passes through the policy box. If I get those wrong, nothing else matters, because the failure mode isn't a bad answer, it's one customer seeing another team's headcount plan."
