#### Data plane and contracts

CDC off the production stores into bronze, contract-checked at ingest. A contract is a versioned schema per producing team, semantics owned by the producer, additive-only changes, breaking change ⇒ new version plus a dual-write window, and an SLA per feed on freshness, row volume and null rate.

The enforcement rule is the one worth saying aloud: **quarantine, never coerce.** A pipeline that silently defaults a missing field is exactly how a model dies quietly. At TrueBalance the offline pipeline produced 4,001 features while the real-time payload carried 28 keys; the transform imputed defaults for the rest, so the served vector was near-constant and every dashboard looked healthy. The fix — a serialised feature contract shipped next to the artifact, a hard fail on any missing required feature, a CI subset assertion as a promotion gate, and a per-feature missing-rate metric emitted by the scorer itself — is the shape of every data contract on this platform.

The Smartsheet-specific hard part is the **gold-layer `effective_principals` table**. A sheet's readability is not a column: it derives from workspace membership, folder inheritance, direct shares, nested group membership (so you need transitive closure and cycle detection), report and dashboard reach, and published links. Walking that tree per query is the same expensive traversal Notion described before they built their data lake to make AI viable. So materialise it: `share_edge` and `group_member` in silver, a transitive-closure job in gold, and a per-user principal set resolved at query time and cached 30–120 seconds keyed on a membership version.

If the pad is open, write it. This is the query the whole design rests on, and it is the one place the interviewer is most likely to say *show me*.

```sql
-- gold.effective_principals : who can actually read a sheet, and how strongly.
-- Fed by PRIORITY LANE (A). membership_version is the value the 30-120s
-- query-time principal-set cache is keyed on, so a revoke invalidates
-- the cache rather than waiting it out.
WITH RECURSIVE closure (principal_id, sheet_id, path, depth, grant_rank) AS (

    -- BASE: direct grants on the sheet, already flattened from workspace
    -- and folder inheritance by the silver conformance job.
    -- grant_rank: 5=OWNER 4=ADMIN 3=EDITOR 2=COMMENTER 1=VIEWER
    SELECT e.principal_id,
           e.sheet_id,
           ARRAY[e.principal_id]              AS path,
           0                                  AS depth,
           e.grant_rank
    FROM   silver.share_edge e
    WHERE  e.revoked_at IS NULL

    UNION ALL

    -- RECURSE: expand group -> nested group -> user.
    -- Along a single path, the WEAKER grant wins (least privilege).
    SELECT m.member_id,
           c.sheet_id,
           c.path || m.member_id,
           c.depth + 1,
           LEAST(c.grant_rank, m.grant_rank)
    FROM   closure c
    JOIN   silver.group_member m ON m.group_id = c.principal_id
    WHERE  m.revoked_at IS NULL
      AND  c.depth < 12                          -- depth bound (belt)
      AND  NOT (m.member_id = ANY(c.path))       -- cycle guard (braces)
)
SELECT c.sheet_id,
       c.principal_id,
       MAX(c.grant_rank) AS effective_grant_rank,   -- ACROSS paths, STRONGEST wins
       MIN(c.depth)      AS shortest_path_depth,    -- debugging: why can they see it
       w.membership_version
FROM   closure c
JOIN   silver.user u             ON u.user_id = c.principal_id  -- users only
JOIN   silver.membership_watermark w USING (principal_id)
GROUP  BY c.sheet_id, c.principal_id, w.membership_version;
```

Three lines in that query are the interview. The `path` array is a cycle guard — group A inside group B inside group A is a production reality in every large tenant, not a hypothetical, and without it the query does not terminate. `LEAST` inside the recursion and `MAX` in the outer aggregate are deliberately opposite: least privilege *along* a path, most privilege *across* paths, which is the semantics every real ACL system has and the thing that either leaks or over-restricts if you get it backwards. And `revoked_at IS NULL` rather than a hard delete, because you need to answer "who could see this on 14 March" for an audit.

Note what this table does *not* solve, and say so before they ask: it is sheet-level. Row-level sharing and Dynamic View scoping (Ch.54, permission model) sit *below* this grain, which is precisely the constraint that pushes the grid out of the vector index later in this delivery. `effective_principals` decides which sheets a principal may retrieve from at all; row visibility is then applied inside the data layer at query time, where the rows actually live.

> **Say it like this:** "I'd treat the denormalised ACL projection as an eventually-consistent cache with a **published revocation SLA**, separate from and much tighter than content freshness. A document appearing late is an inconvenience; a document disappearing late is an incident. So permission events get their own priority lane ahead of content events. And because a projection can be wrong, I keep a second, authoritative check: after retrieval and before generation, re-verify the top-8 document IDs against the system of record. That's eight cheap ID checks, not a re-crawl, and it turns a silent leak into a caught one."

Where the JD says Unity Catalog, describe the category honestly in one clause and keep moving: not something I've run — the category is the layer owning a three-level namespace, column classification, grants that inherit downward, and lineage from table to model to decision, and the differentiator I understand it has over a plain catalogue is that it governs models, functions and volumes as first-class securables alongside tables, which matters for agents because a tool backed by a catalogue function inherits its permissions from the same place its data permissions come from rather than needing a parallel authorisation system. The equivalent boundary I have actually built is dataset ownership and PII classification over HIPAA-class data in Snowflake at ResMed, and lineage from data snapshot through model to decision as an FCA audit requirement on the NatWest platform at Tiger. What I'd need is three or four weeks against a real workspace to learn how grants inherit in practice, what breaks on a Hive-metastore migration, and where lineage goes blind — path-based reads and UDFs, per the documentation.

#### Where Databricks actually fits

The architecture above says "one governed catalog" and not "Databricks" on purpose, but vendor-neutrality is not the same as having no opinion, and the JD is Databricks-centric enough that the question is coming. Have the answer ready and volunteer it.

| Put it on Databricks | Keep it off Databricks | Why the line is here |
|---|---|---|
| Medallion bronze/silver/gold, Spark transforms, the `effective_principals` closure job | The FM gateway | The gateway is the one place the model is a config value; coupling it to a data platform is how you end up unable to switch models |
| Data-quality and drift jobs (this is Deequ-on-Spark work, and it is the part I have actually done) | The serving plane — interactive endpoints, RAG service, agent runtime | Latency-bound request paths belong next to the product's own networking and egress controls |
| Batch training and nightly batch scoring for the classical models | The policy/authz plane | Authorisation must be one system for the whole product, not one per data platform |
| Notebook and exploration surface for data scientists | The vector index for multi-tenant customer content | See hard call (ii); tenancy boundary decides this, not platform preference |

> **Say it like this:** "If you're a Databricks shop, the medallion, the Spark transforms, the data-quality jobs and batch training go on it — that's the half closest to the eighteen months of Azure Databricks, Spark and Deequ I've actually done. What I'd keep off it is the gateway, the serving plane and the policy plane, and the reason isn't a view about Databricks, it's that those three are the parts I want portable across a model market that reprices every few months. On packaging: Asset Bundles are the Databricks-native deployment unit for jobs and pipelines, and I have not shipped with them — I'd expect the paved road to emit a bundle for the lakehouse-side assets and Terraform for everything else, rather than pretending one tool covers both."

#### Training, fine-tuning and automated retraining

Classical models — at-risk project scoring, duplicate-row detection, auto-categorisation — train on a snapshot with a recorded `data_snapshot` ID and **point-in-time-correct joins on event timestamps**. That phrase is non-negotiable: the label "this project slipped" is only usable joined to features as they existed *before* the slip. Everything else is leakage wearing a metric.

**Automated retraining is an explicit subsystem, not a cron job.** Four trigger classes, and they are not equivalent:

| Trigger | Condition | Why it exists |
|---|---|---|
| Scheduled floor | Monthly, unconditional | Catches slow covariate shift no monitor is watching for; also proves the pipeline still runs |
| Drift-triggered | PSI > 0.25 on any feature in the model's top-10 by importance, or prediction-distribution shift beyond the calibration band | Input world changed; the model may not have degraded yet, so this trains a challenger, it does not promote one |
| Performance-triggered | Rolling AUC on a **matured** label cohort drops below the promotion baseline by more than the noise band | The only trigger that measures the thing we actually care about, and the slowest — a "project slipped" label matures over weeks, so this runs on a lagging cohort and you must say so |
| Data-availability | A new material segment appears (new region, new SKU, new plan tier) with enough volume to model | Prevents the silent failure where the model is fine on aggregate and useless on the newest 8% of tenants |

The retrain runs automatically. **The promotion does not.** For customer-facing models the gate is: offline eval against the incumbent on the frozen versioned eval set; a slice check so no material segment regresses even where aggregate improves; a train/serve parity replay on the challenger's transform; calibration check, because a retrain that improves ranking and wrecks calibration breaks every downstream threshold; and a cost delta, because a bigger model that scores 0.4% better and costs 3× is not an improvement. Pass all five and the challenger goes to shadow — scored on live traffic, decisions logged, nothing served — then a 5 → 25 → 100% canary with the incumbent kept hot. Rollback is an alias flip, not a rebuild, target under sixty seconds.

> **Say it like this:** "Retraining is auto-triggered and promotion is not auto-approved, and I'd hold that line hard for anything customer-facing. The reason is that the failure mode of automated promotion isn't a bad model, it's a bad model that nobody can explain three weeks later. I built exactly this loop at Tiger on the NatWest platform — SageMaker training, inference, drift detection, CI/CD and automated retraining for an FCA-regulated bank, which is an environment where 'the pipeline promoted it' is not an acceptable answer to a regulator. What I'd add here that I didn't have there is the cost delta in the gate, because in 2026 that's a real dimension of regression."

Fine-tuning foundation models: **no, not in year one, and probably not in year two.** The case is economic before it is technical — no task moat, no eval set yet, and a permanent migration liability every time a better base model ships. A mid-size SaaS that fine-tunes buys an eval burden it does not yet have the golden set to carry. The industry pattern corroborates it: ServiceNow, a company with StarCoder, BigCode and its own research lab, moved away from defaulting to its in-house model in favour of frontier models — I'd want to double-check the specifics of that before leaning on it, but the ROI sequence is what carries the argument: **prompt → retrieval → routing → distillation**, in that order. The one exception worth naming is a small distilled model for a single very high-volume, very narrow task (formula-intent classification), *after* there is a stable eval set and enough volume to amortise it.

There is a trap here worth volunteering, because it is where the platform collides with the trust story. The highest-quality preference data this product will ever have is the accepted-then-edited formula pair — what the model suggested versus what the user shipped. Harvesting it turns customer content into training data, which collides head-on with *"customer data is never used to train third-party foundation models."* The correct answer is aggregate, de-identify, and make it an explicit opt-in data-contribution setting with an admin toggle — the narrow carve-out Atlassian publishes — not a quiet telemetry pipeline that someone discovers in a security review.

#### Registry and lineage

One registry, and it holds more than models. Models, **prompts**, agents, tool schemas, eval datasets and **index versions** are all versioned artifacts with the same promotion semantics. A prompt change is a code change: it gets a version, it goes through the pipeline, and it appears in every trace.

The manifest that must still be reproducible fourteen months later, when someone asks why a decision was made:

```yaml
# ILLUSTRATIVE manifest for a hypothetical Smartsheet model.
# Every value below is a placeholder; none of these are my numbers.
artifact:          at_risk_scorer
version:           v14
git_commit:        a3f9c1e
git_dirty:         false                  # refuse to promote a dirty tree
image_digest:      sha256:9b2f...         # never a tag
lockfile_hash:     sha256:41cd...
data_snapshot:     silver.sheet_events@version=1182
feature_contract:  sha256:77ab...         # the serialised required-feature set
prompt_version:    ask_portfolio@v9       # for LLM artifacts
model_id:          pinned, dated, never a floating alias
eval_set:          golden_portfolio@v6    # immutable version
metrics:           {auc: <measured>, ci95: [<lo>, <hi>]}
retrain_trigger:   drift|scheduled|performance|data_availability
approver:          <named human, for customer-facing promotions>
```

Two honest caveats to state rather than be caught on. Bit-exact retraining on multi-GPU is not achievable — non-deterministic reductions, cuDNN autotuning, NCCL ordering — so the goal is **statistical reproducibility plus complete lineage**: a re-run lands inside the noise band, and you can always answer *what went in*. Claiming bit-exactness is a tell that someone hasn't done it. Second, retention: if the pinned data snapshot sits on a table with a seven-day vacuum window, the "reproducible" pipeline breaks in a week. Pin the snapshot and extend retention for anything a production model references.

I have used MLflow for tracking and registry work; not the Unity-Catalog-backed registry. Two things I'd check on day one: that stages are replaced by aliases and the three-level namespace — the documentation is unambiguous that stages are not supported there — and *how hard the signature requirement actually bites*. The docs say model versions in UC must have a model signature, but they also document the behaviour of versions that do not have one: no input enforcement at inference, no use with AI functions without an explicit schema, no auto-generated input examples in serving. Whether that is a registration failure or a set of serving-time limitations changes whether I can make it a CI gate, and I'd rather find out than assume.

#### Deployment: what runs where

| Workload | Target | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Inline formula suggestion | Managed FM endpoint via our gateway; small model; grammar-constrained decode | 600 ms p95; no infra to own; cost per call is the only variable |
| Ask-your-portfolio | Stateless service on K8s + FM gateway | Retrieval and policy logic is real code; needs the cluster's networking and egress controls |
| At-risk scoring (nightly, 12M sheets) | Batch on spot with checkpointing | No latency requirement; 60–90% cheaper; an interruption is a retry, not an incident |
| Online classical scoring (dedupe, auto-tag) | Container endpoint, ARM64 image, scale-to-zero for low-QPS models | Exactly the Lambda + SQS + ECR ARM64 shape I own today, and the multi-container shared-endpoint pattern I ran on SageMaker at ResMed to hold per-model SLAs while sharing infrastructure |
| Anything GPU-resident | **Nothing, in year one** | See hard call (i) |

> **Say it like this:** "The default is managed. I'd only own a GPU when the arithmetic says so, and I'll show you the arithmetic — but the short version is that self-hosting wins on duty cycle, not on price, and at 170 peak RPS with a 6× diurnal swing across three regions we don't have the duty cycle."

**Held in reserve: the 60-second Kubernetes answer.** Do not put this in the narrative — deprioritising K8s is the correct call and saying "if I spend the hour on Kubernetes autoscaling I'm designing the wrong system" is the stronger move. But the JD names Kubernetes under both infrastructure management and modern engineering practices, so the rubric probably has a line for it, and the deprioritisation only reads as a decision if you can produce the answer on demand.

> **Say it like this (only if probed):** "Namespace per team with resource quotas and limit ranges, so one team's runaway batch job can't starve the gateway. HPA on CPU is the wrong signal for this workload — the work is IO-bound waiting on model providers — so KEDA scaling on queue depth and in-flight request count instead. Pod disruption budgets and topology spread constraints on the gateway specifically, because it's now in every request path and a node drain shouldn't be a partial outage. Separate node pools with Karpenter for the batch and spot work so evictions land where an interruption is a retry. And no GPU node pool at all, which is hard call (i) rather than an omission."

#### The foundation-model gateway — the highest-leverage single component

One proxy; every application call goes through it. Six functions, all cheaper to build once than ten times:

1. **Routing** by feature, cost tier, latency budget and **region** — this is the residency enforcement point, and it should be a route table, not a config flag.
2. **Caching** — prompt-prefix caching on the stable system prompt plus schema digest, and optionally a semantic cache whose key includes tenant ID **and a hash of the caller's effective principal set**. Keying a semantic cache on query text alone in a multi-tenant product is a leak generator: a cached answer built from a document the next caller can no longer see.
3. **Budgets** — token budgets at per-request, per-session, per-tenant and global levels, enforced *before* the call leaves for a provider. Request-count rate limiting is useless here, because one request can burn 100k tokens. Meter tokens.
4. **Fallback and circuit breaking** — a designated backup model per feature, with the breaker tripping on TTFT, error rate and p90 latency. Slack has written publicly about routing per feature rather than picking one model globally, with a designated fallback per feature, and reported meaningful quality gains on the hard reasoning surfaces and a large latency reduction on the high-volume short ones. I would not quote their numbers without checking them, but the shape is the point: **the router is a product decision per feature, not a global model choice.**
5. **Guardrails** — content filtering and PII handling applied to input *and* output at the platform layer rather than in every app. Output-only filtering does not protect against an injected instruction reaching a tool call.
6. **Observability with cost attribution** — tokens and dollars tagged with tenant, feature, prompt version and model version on every single call.

The caveat to volunteer before they raise it: the gateway is now a single point of failure in every request path, so it needs its own SLO, multi-region deployment and a documented bypass path.

Bedrock, which the JD names as preferable: not something I've run — the primitives map onto things I have, namely a managed endpoint inside your own network boundary with IAM auth, request/response logging, guardrails as a platform filter, and the on-demand versus provisioned-throughput decision, which is the same commitment-versus-burst trade I made sizing SageMaker endpoints. The operational details I would have to learn are the ones that actually bite: output-token burndown multipliers, the fact that an oversized `max_tokens` is reserved up front and throttles you at a fraction of your quota, and how cross-region inference profiles interact with a residency claim — a geographic profile keeps processing in the geo, a global one explicitly does not.

#### RAG and the vector index lifecycle

The most important decision in this section is a deletion. **The grid does not go into the vector index.**

> **Say it like this:** "Chunk boundaries must never cross ACL boundaries. If a chunk has two owners, there is no filter that makes it safe. In this product permissions are row-level — a user can see forty of five thousand rows through row-level sharing or a dynamic view — so embedding a sheet as one chunk is a leak by construction, and embedding per row is six billion ACL-scoped vectors. So the grid gets a *query* path, and only the text surfaces get an *embedding* path."

That splits into a router, and the router is the design:

| Question shape | Path | Why |
|---|---|---|
| "What's the total budget across my projects?" | Semantic/metric layer → typed query; aggregate computed **after** the ACL filter, in the data layer | Vectors cannot count, and an aggregate over rows the user can't see is a breach with a number attached |
| "Show me task 4821" / "invoices over $10k last quarter" | Direct query | Semantic search over structured data is a category error |
| "Which projects are blocked by a task owned by someone who left?" | **Graph traversal** over the curated entity graph | Multi-hop; no single chunk contains the answer. See below — this is its own path, not a footnote |
| "Summarise the discussion on the Q3 migration" | Hybrid dense + BM25 retrieval over comments and attachment text | Genuinely prose |

The structured half has the strongest published evidence behind it, and it is worth bringing into the room precisely. Sequeda, Allemang and Jacob's enterprise SQL benchmark (the one data.world published, and the one dbt's semantic-layer work builds on) measured GPT-4 answering business questions over enterprise databases at roughly **16% accuracy against a raw SQL schema, rising to roughly 54% when the model generated against a knowledge-graph representation of the same data**. dbt's own semantic-layer replication has reported a figure in the low eighties — verify that number on the live source before quoting it; the 16-to-54 result is the one I would stake an argument on.

The operational half of the argument is mine rather than anyone's published finding, and it is the half that matters more: **a constrained generation target fails closed; free-form SQL fails open.** When the model cannot express a question in a curated metric layer, it refuses, and a refusal costs a retry. When it cannot express a question in raw SQL, it emits a plausible query with a wrong join and returns a confidently wrong number. A wrong number in a portfolio rollup that a government PMO acts on is an incident, not a retry. Smartsheet has no dbt, but a sheet *is* a schema and the formula language *is* a constrained DSL (Ch.54, formula primer), so the equivalent is a curated metric layer — "% complete", "days late", "at risk" — plus generation into the formula grammar, never into free-form code.

#### The knowledge graph, and why it is not GraphRAG

The JD names Knowledge Graph twice, and it is the one AI/ML keyword on the list where the honest answer is *yes, in production, with numbers*. It also happens to be the right architecture here for reasons that have nothing to do with the JD.

The distinction to lead with: **GraphRAG infers a graph from prose; a curated entity graph reads one that already exists.** GraphRAG's whole cost structure comes from asking an LLM to extract entities and relations out of unstructured text, because in a corpus of documents there is no schema to read. Smartsheet is the opposite situation. The entities and the predicates are already declared — by the object model, by column types, by the dependency and predecessor columns, by cell links and cross-sheet references, by the sharing tables. Running an LLM over that to *guess* the relations is paying to reconstruct, lossily, something the foreign keys already state exactly.

So the gold layer carries a typed entity graph alongside `effective_principals`:

```text
ENTITIES     sheet, row, cell, column, user, group, workspace, folder,
             report, dashboard, attachment, comment, automation
PREDICATES   owned_by            row/sheet -> user
             assigned_to         row -> user
             parent_of           row -> row      (the row forest, Ch.54 parentId)
             depends_on          row -> row      (predecessor / dependency cols)
             blocks              row -> row      (derived: depends_on + status)
             linked_to           cell -> cell    (cell links, cross-sheet refs)
             rolls_up_to         sheet -> report/dashboard
             shared_with         sheet -> principal   (grant_rank on the edge)
             member_of           user -> group -> group
             approves            user -> automation/request
             commented_on        user -> row/sheet
             attached_to         attachment -> row/sheet
```

That answers the multi-hop row in the router table directly. *"Which projects are blocked by a task owned by someone who left?"* is `user WHERE deactivated → assigned_to⁻¹ → row → blocks⁺ → row → parent_of* → sheet`, intersected with `effective_principals` for the asking user. No chunk contains that answer; no amount of retrieval quality produces it; and critically, the traversal is a typed query the ACL filter composes with, so the aggregate is computed after the filter exactly as in the structured path. Embedding this data would have thrown away the only thing that makes the question answerable.

> **Say it like this:** "I built exactly this at TrueBalance, and it's the piece of my work that maps most directly onto the Knowledge Graph line in your JD. We had a regex SMS parser that was silently dropping fields — not failing, dropping — so I replaced it with a domain knowledge graph: seven entity types, twenty-nine predicates, and eighty-five-plus canonical field mappings. It got to 100% field coverage on a hundred thousand production messages — a hundred sixty-nine thousand eight hundred seventy-nine fields out of a hundred sixty-nine thousand eight hundred seventy-nine — with a hundred and seven tests, and I migrated it into a standalone CI-guarded ML repo so it wasn't living inside a feature branch. The transferable lesson is the one that applies here: the moment your predicates are defined by a schema instead of inferred by a model, your failure mode changes from a silent wrong answer to a query that returns nothing, and that is a trade I will take every time."

Retrieval mechanics for the prose path, briefly, because depth means mechanism:

- Hybrid dense + BM25 fused with reciprocal rank fusion at k = 60. BM25 carries the exact tokens embeddings lose — task IDs, error codes, SKUs, proper nouns, rare acronyms.
- Rerank top-50 down to top-8, with a hard timeout and a "skip rerank, return fusion order" fallback, so an external reranker cannot take the feature down.
- **Pre-filter on tenant and principal set; never post-filter.** Post-filtering means the model has already read it, and it silently under-returns: on pgvector at the default `hnsw.ef_search = 40`, a filter matching 10% of rows returns roughly four rows for a top-10 request, with no error. Iterative index scans were added in 0.8.0 to fix exactly that, they are opt-in, and they must be bounded (`hnsw.max_scan_tuples`) or a selective filter becomes an unbounded scan.
- **Alert on `returned < requested`.** That condition must never be invisible.

Index lifecycle: content-hash comparison to skip unchanged documents (this is where the cost saving lives); **delete-then-insert by document ID**, never upsert-by-chunk-ID, because chunk boundaries shift and orphaned chunks from an old chunking of a since-edited document are exactly how "the AI quoted a policy we deleted" happens; tombstones propagated to the index *and* the cache; and a nightly reconciliation job diffing the source document set against the index. Rebuilds are blue/green behind an alias, validated on a golden query set before any traffic, then shadow-read, then canaried 5 → 25 → 100% with the old index kept hot for 24–72 hours — plus a replay of the change log onto the new index before the swap, because writes land during the build.

And the tax to budget for explicitly: **an embedding model upgrade is a data migration, not a config change.** Store `embedding_model` and `chunk_strategy_version` on every chunk and assert at query time that the query model matches the index model. That single assertion prevents the most common self-inflicted RAG outage — a silent quality collapse after someone bumps a model string.

Databricks Vector Search / AI Search, which the JD names: not used it — my mental model of any managed index is an ANN structure over a source table that must stay in sync, and the questions are the ones I'd ask of any index: sync lag on updates and deletes, HNSW tunables, how filtering interacts with the ANN traversal, and whether the index inherits the source table's row filters. My reading of the documentation is that it **does not**: it states plainly that row and column level permissions are not supported and points you at application-level ACLs through the filter API, and production queries typically run as a service principal rather than as the end user. If that is right, multi-tenant RAG on it needs query-time tenant filters or per-tenant indexes, and I'd verify it before designing around it.

#### The agent runtime

Exactly one write-capable agent in year one, and it is fenced. Three rules, borrowed from Asana's published framing because they are correct:

1. Agents run at the **intersection** of the agent's permissions and the requesting user's — never the union, never a service account.
2. **Model output is untrusted input.** Anything the model emits that is acted on downstream goes through the same server-side validation and rendering path as user-generated content. The model is an untrusted client.
3. **Human approval is mandatory** for permission-elevating and destructive actions, regardless of model confidence.

Plus the operational bounds, all of them, enforced at the gateway so no code path can skip them: `max_steps`, `max_tool_calls`, per-run and per-tenant dollar caps, wall-clock timeouts, a repeated-failure rule (same tool, same arguments, failing twice ⇒ terminate, don't retry), and no-progress detection on a hash of `(tool, args)`. Every mutating tool takes an **idempotency key** generated once per logical intent, so a retry is a no-op rather than a second ticket. Tools return structured errors — `{"error": {"code": "TOOL_TIMEOUT", "message": "upstream 504 after 30s", "retryable": true}}` — never an empty success, because a tool that returns `{"results": []}` on failure is precisely how an agent makes four hundred calls in five minutes.

**On orchestration frameworks**, since the JD names LangChain and LangGraph and this is the obvious probe: framework-light by default, and the reason is architectural rather than taste. The agent loop *is* the state machine the platform must own, because the caps, the idempotency keys, the egress policy and the approval gate have to be enforced somewhere no application code path can skip — and the moment that logic lives inside a framework's control flow, "skip it" is one library upgrade away. LangGraph earns its place where its distinctive features are actually needed: durable checkpointing and human-in-the-loop interrupts, which is *precisely* the write-capable approval agent in Phase 3 — an agent that pauses for hours waiting on a human approval needs its state persisted and resumable, and that is a real problem I would rather not hand-roll. LangChain I'd use for retrieval glue where it saves a week, and never as the thing that owns policy. I have used both, and the honest summary of that experience is that they are excellent for getting to a prototype and dangerous as a place to put the security boundary.

And the containment control that works when everything else fails: **no open-ended outbound HTTP from the agent's execution environment.** An egress allow-list. The Notion 3.0 exfiltration bug was hidden white-on-white text steering an agent to concatenate private data into a URL; model behaviour was never going to stop that, and a network policy would have. Say the RAG-specific version of the threat too, because it is the one that matters in a collaboration product: *any user who can type into a shared sheet or a comment can attempt to steer another user's agent, and that injected instruction executes with the victim's permissions.*

For the tool surface, MCP is the right protocol choice. My understanding is that you already ship an MCP server — if it scopes to the caller's existing permissions and plan entitlements, then the platform's job is to make agent tool access inherit from that same authorisation system rather than reimplement it, which is a much better position than most companies are in. Is that how it works today? Either way, treat MCP as a supply-chain surface: pin server versions, review tool descriptions as code (a tool description is untrusted text entering the model's context), scope tokens narrowly per server, log every call with arguments and results.

I have built the client side of this — the MCP-based internal developer assistant at TrueBalance, where each task runs in an isolated Git workspace and the tools tie Jira, GitHub, Jenkins, AWS, Grafana and Slack behind one plain-English interface. The isolation-per-task decision there is the same instinct as sandboxing here.

#### Monitoring, data observability and evaluation

Four layers, and only three things page.

| Layer | Signals | Page? |
|---|---|---|
| Infra | latency p50/p95/p99, error rate, saturation, queue depth, gateway breaker state | Yes — availability |
| Data | freshness per feed, row volume, null/duplicate rate, schema change, feature-store hit rate, `returned < requested` | Yes — freshness SLO breach and the retrieval under-return |
| Model | input drift (PSI per feature), prediction-distribution drift, calibration, rolling quality on delayed labels, scheduled scorers on sampled production traces | No — ticket. A paging drift alert trains people to ignore drift alerts |
| Business & cost | acceptance and **accepted-and-retained** rate, cost per accepted outcome, tokens per tenant, permission-violation counter | Yes — canary guardrail breach, and the permission counter |

**PSI, since it is the one named metric and "what is it, how do you compute it, where's the alarm" is a standard follow-up.** Population Stability Index is `Σ over bins (actual% − expected%) × ln(actual% / expected%)`, computed against a **frozen** binning of the training distribution — typically ten deciles of the training data, with a small epsilon floor so an empty bin doesn't send the log to infinity. Conventional bands: below 0.1 no meaningful shift, 0.1–0.25 moderate and worth a ticket, above 0.25 significant. The senior caveat matters more than the formula: **PSI on a low-cardinality or heavily-imputed feature is noise**, which is exactly why the TrueBalance parity failure was caught by a missing-rate metric and not by a drift score — the served features weren't drifting, they were *absent*, and an imputed constant is perfectly stable.

That is a fifteen-line monitor, and it is worth writing on the pad because it makes the argument concrete:

```python
import numpy as np

def psi(edges: np.ndarray, expected_pct: np.ndarray,
        actual: np.ndarray, eps: float = 1e-4) -> float:
    """PSI against a FROZEN training binning. edges/expected_pct come
    from the artifact, never recomputed from the live window."""
    counts, _  = np.histogram(actual, bins=edges)
    actual_pct = np.clip(counts / max(counts.sum(), 1), eps, None)
    exp_pct    = np.clip(expected_pct,                  eps, None)
    return float(np.sum((actual_pct - exp_pct) * np.log(actual_pct / exp_pct)))

def emit_feature_health(name, values, ref, statsd) -> None:
    arr     = np.asarray(values, dtype="float64")
    missing = float(np.isnan(arr).mean())
    statsd.gauge(f"feature.missing_rate.{name}", missing)   # the one that catches parity
    if missing > ref["max_missing_rate"]:
        raise FeatureContractViolation(f"{name}: {missing:.3f} missing")  # fail closed
    present = arr[~np.isnan(arr)]
    if present.size < 500 or ref["distinct_count"] < 5:
        return                    # PSI on sparse or low-cardinality data is noise
    statsd.gauge(f"feature.psi.{name}", psi(ref["edges"], ref["pct"], present))
```

Two points to make deliberately. First, the metric trap. GitHub moved off raw suggestion acceptance rate as the headline Copilot measure — it rewards a high volume of short, easy suggestions — toward how much of the accepted code actually survives in the file. For formula generation the equivalent is "did the formula survive seven days in the sheet", not "did they click accept."

Second, evaluation is layered and reported separately: retrieval metrics (recall@k, nDCG) with no LLM in the loop so they can gate every pull request; generation metrics (faithfulness, answer relevance, and **refusal correctness**, which almost nobody measures and is how teams ship a confident hallucinator); and end-to-end task success. Golden set of 200–500 real queries, versioned in git, owned by a named person, and grown exclusively from production failures — an eval set that is a graveyard of every bug you've shipped. LLM judges pinned to a specific model version and calibrated against human labels (Cohen's κ > 0.6 to be usable), both orderings run to cancel position bias, and judged from a different model family than the generator.

For the formula and structured path there is something better than a judge: **execution-based scoring**. Run the candidate against fixture sheets and compare result sets, with `TODAY()` and locale frozen or every date formula flakes. Report exact-match and execution-accuracy separately — a large gap means the model is right but unidiomatic, which is a trust and maintainability problem, not a correctness one.

Monte Carlo, which the JD names as preferable: no hands-on — I've implemented the same function by hand (freshness, volume, schema, distribution, lineage), and at ResMed I built a drift-monitoring utility that ingested data-scientist-authored thresholds and slice definitions and auto-provisioned the Datadog dashboards and alerts from Snowflake feature statistics, which is the same idea with the configuration surface handed to the people who actually know the data. What a product like Monte Carlo adds over my version is automatic monitor generation across thousands of tables and lineage I don't maintain. The trap I'd watch for is the one my own version had: thresholds generating alerts nobody owns. Day-one question would be what fraction of alerts get actioned, and who is on the routing rule.

#### Governance, tenancy and compliance

- **Tenant ID comes from the authenticated token. Never from a request parameter.** This is the number-one real-world multi-tenant bug and it is worth stating flatly.
- Mandatory tenant scope injected in middleware that application code cannot bypass; missing tenant ⇒ deny, not "search everything."
- **Fail closed on authorisation, degrade gracefully on enrichment.** If the policy service is unavailable, refuse. If the reranker is unavailable, return fusion order. Have a position on this; they may ask.
- Every AI interaction produces an audit record: actor, tenant, query, document IDs retrieved, policy version, prompt version, model version, tools invoked, actions taken, human approval. Then the point most candidates miss — **that audit log now contains customer data, so it inherits every retention, residency and erasure obligation of the source.** Right-to-erasure must fan out to source, index, cache, traces, agent checkpoints and eval datasets, and the fan-out is built before the first request arrives.
- A **nightly cross-tenant probe test**: as tenant A, attempt every known path to tenant B's data — filter tampering, prompt injection, cache-key collision, group-expansion abuse, a revoked-then-queried document. It fails the build, and it is the artefact you hand a customer's security team.
- Gov SKU: features declare a **minimum capability class**, SKUs declare an allowed model set, and a feature with no qualifying model is *visibly disabled in the admin console* rather than silently degraded. Checked against AWS's own services-in-scope pages: Bedrock is listed in scope for FedRAMP in GovCloud at the High baseline (AWS has relabelled these Class C / Class D) and for DoD CC SRG IL4 and IL5 in GovCloud, alongside IL2 commercial and IL6 in the Secret Region. Service-level scope changes often enough that I'd re-check the page rather than trust a memorised list, and the architectural point holds regardless of what the table says on the day: **the compliant model menu differs per SKU, so a feature has to declare a minimum capability class and be visibly disabled where no qualifying model exists.**
- The pre-launch move worth proposing unprompted: **a sheet-sharing assessment before enabling workspace-wide AI search.** The Microsoft 365 Copilot lesson is that AI does not create over-permissioning, it makes existing over-permissioning legible — organisations discovered large numbers of sites shared to "everyone except external users" only once Copilot started surfacing them. Shipping the assessment first turns a support crisis into a product feature.

#### Cost control and unit economics

The dashboard metric is **cost per accepted AI outcome, by tenant** — not cost per call, because retries and abandoned answers are pure waste that a per-request number hides. Levers in ROI order: cut context tokens (better reranking ⇒ fewer chunks) → prompt-prefix caching → route small-first with escalation → cap output length and prefer structured output over prose → batch anything not latency-bound → quantize vectors rather than buying RAM → never re-embed unchanged documents.

Frame this deliberately as gross-margin protection rather than as engineering hygiene. Smartsheet has been privately held since Blackstone and Vista took it private in January 2025, and under that ownership a new feature line that quietly compresses gross margin is not a tolerable trade — **AI COGS as a percentage of AI-attributed ARR, measured per tenant, with a hard ceiling** is the metric that survives an owner conversation, which is why it is in the assumptions block rather than in a footnote. (Say the ownership fact once, in passing, and say nothing that implies public reporting or guidance.)

Two guardrails on the routing lever, because it is the one people get wrong. A router that escalates 60% of the time costs *more* than the frontier model alone, since you pay twice — so the escalation rate is itself a monitored metric with a budget. And the cheap tier needs the same eval gate as the frontier tier, or "we saved 70%" quietly means "we shipped a worse product to 70% of users."

Meter before you price. Notion's model is the honest one to borrow: pooled workspace credits that do not roll over, and agents that **pause immediately when credits run out** — scheduled runs skipped, not silently retried later. Most teams avoid that hard edge and end up with unbounded per-seat cost against bounded per-seat revenue.

#### The paved road — the developer interface

This is the half that makes it a *platform* rather than a feature.

A product team gets `mlp init <feature>` → a repo from template with the eval harness, the gateway client, the tracing decorators and the IaC module already wired; a CI pipeline whose gates are non-negotiable (data contract, offline eval versus the incumbent, slice check so no material segment regresses even when the aggregate improves, **train/serve parity replay**, red-team suite, cost-per-call budget); a canary with automatic rollback on guardrail breach; and a dashboard that exists on first deploy. Infrastructure comes from versioned Terraform modules that expose *intent* rather than resources —

```hcl
module "ai_feature" {
  source           = "git::https://github.example.com/infra//modules/ai-feature?ref=v3.2.0"
  name             = "ask_portfolio"
  tier             = "interactive"          # sets model class + budget
  region_set       = ["us", "eu"]
  budget_usd_month = 4000
  data_class       = "customer-content"     # drives retention + residency
  team             = "ai-search"
}
```

— with policy-as-code on the plan (OPA/Conftest) rejecting anything untagged with team, cost-centre and data-classification, and a plan-assertion gate that fails on a `delete` of any resource tagged `stateful=true`. On a Databricks-heavy estate the same `mlp init` emits a Databricks Asset Bundle for the lakehouse-side jobs and pipelines and Terraform for everything else; two deployment units is honest, one pretending to cover both is not.

Self-service with a bounded blast radius: namespace quotas, hard TTLs on anything experimental so sandboxes expire rather than accumulate, and the price shown in the same UI where the resource is requested. The reason data scientists go around IaC is never laziness — it's that the feedback loop is forty-five minutes and the experiment is five, and the console never says "this is $28k a month." Fix both. Off-road is allowed and explicitly unsupported; that honesty is what keeps the paved road honest.

> **Say it like this:** "My success metric for the platform isn't uptime, it's **median time from 'a team has a working prototype' to '1% of production traffic'**, and the number of teams doing that without me in the room. If that number isn't falling quarter on quarter, I've built a service, not a platform."

### 2.5 Minute 26–33: the three hard calls

These are the decisions where a reasonable engineer could go either way. Present the options, commit, and state the trigger that would change your mind.

#### Hard call (i): where do foundation models run?

| Criterion | A. Managed FM API behind our gateway | B. Databricks Model Serving | C. Self-hosted vLLM on EKS |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ops burden | Lowest — no GPU on-call | Low, but couples serving to one platform | Highest: capacity, drivers, KV-cache tuning, CVE patching |
| Cost at our duty cycle | Per-token; never idles | Per-token or provisioned; same shape | Per-GPU-hour; idles brutally |
| Frontier model access | Yes | Yes, plus provisioned throughput for fine-tunes | Open weights only |
| Gov / FedRAMP | Bedrock is in scope for FedRAMP High in GovCloud and DoD IL4/IL5 (checked on the AWS services-in-scope pages; re-verify, scope changes) | Would need verification | You own the accreditation |
| Residency | Geographic routing at the gateway | Workspace-region bound | Wherever you put the cluster |
| What we lose | Some control of p99 tail | Portability | Guardrails, invocation logging and managed evals unless rebuilt |

The arithmetic that settles it, done out loud:

```text
SELF-HOST BREAK-EVEN (illustrative rates)
  4xH100 reserved ~ $2.50/GPU-hr effective = $10/hr = ~$7.2k/month
  managed blended ~ $5 per 1M tokens
  tokens/hr needed just to match the GPU bill: $10 / $5 = 2M tok/hr
                                             = ~555 tok/s SUSTAINED
  rig peak ~3,400 tok/s -> break-even ~16% sustained on hardware alone
  add ~0.5 FTE of platform ownership -> ~35-40% sustained utilisation

  CAVEAT I SAY OUT LOUD: I am blending input and output here. Prefill
  is far cheaper per token than decode, and 3,400 tok/s is model-size
  dependent -- roughly right for a ~70B at high batch, an order of
  magnitude low for an 8B. A real sizing separates prefill from decode
  and comes off a single-replica load test, not off this block.

OUR PROFILE: 28 avg RPS, 170 peak -> 6x diurnal swing, three regions.
             Sustained utilisation would sit well under 20%.
             The verdict survives any reasonable substitution above.
```

> **Say it like this:** "A — managed models behind our own gateway. Self-hosting doesn't win because GPUs are cheap; it wins when you can keep them above roughly a third of the clock, and with a 6× diurnal swing across three regions we can't. What I'd insist on is that the *gateway* is ours, not a vendor's, so the model is a config value and we're never held by a multi-month capacity commitment while a better model ships — that was Slack's explicit motivation for going multi-cloud. **What changes my mind:** if one narrow, high-volume task — formula-intent classification at hundreds of QPS around the clock — grows to where a distilled small model on shared inference makes the arithmetic work, or if a gov or residency requirement leaves no compliant managed model. Then I self-host that one workload, not the platform. And I'd keep the platform guardrail in front of it either way, because losing content filtering and invocation logging is the hidden cost of self-hosting that nobody prices."

Say plainly, once: I have not sized a production GPU fleet. I can do the arithmetic and read the roofline, but I'd want a load test on a single replica before committing a number to a capacity plan.

#### Hard call (ii): shared multi-tenant index with ACL filters, or index-per-tenant?

| Criterion | A. One shared index, metadata ACL filter | B. Index per tenant | C. Tiered: namespaces for the long tail, dedicated for the top |
|---|---|---|---|
| Isolation | Weakest — one bad filter is a breach | Strongest, physical | Strong logical, physical where it's bought |
| Query cost | Worst — you pay for the whole namespace on every query | Best per query, worst in fixed overhead | Best overall |
| Ops at 15,000 tenants | Trivial | 15,000 indexes to build, migrate, monitor | Two operational modes, and worth it |
| BYOK / residency | Cannot satisfy per-tenant | Native | Native for the tenants that need it |
| Idle tenants | Free | Expensive | Offload inactive tenants to cold storage, rehydrate on access |

The number that decides it, and the mechanism matters as much as the number: **query cost tracks the size of the namespace you query, not the amount of data returned.** Pinecone's serverless pricing is 1 read unit per GB of namespace size with a 0.25 RU floor per query, and the docs are explicit that `top_k`, `include_metadata` and `include_values` are irrelevant to cost — only namespace size counts. So: query one 1-GB tenant namespace and you pay 1 RU; run the same query as a metadata filter across a single 100-GB namespace and you pay 100 RU. The floor caps the saving at 4× for tenants under a quarter-gigabyte, which at 15,000 tenants is most of them — but for anything above a gigabyte, **namespaces are a two-orders-of-magnitude cost choice as well as a security boundary.** That is the sentence that ends the debate.

> **Say it like this:** "C, tiered. Namespace-per-tenant as the default, because it is simultaneously the safer boundary and the cheaper query; dedicated indexes for enterprise, gov, BYOK and residency tenants, where logical isolation isn't an acceptable answer to a security review; and inactive tenants offloaded to cold storage, because at fifteen thousand tenants most are idle in any given week. **What changes my mind:** if cross-tenant retrieval becomes a product requirement — benchmarking, or template discovery across the estate — that breaks the namespace model, and I'd build a separate, deliberately consented corpus rather than loosen the boundary on the customer one."

#### Hard call (iii): build a feature store, or enforce a feature contract?

| Criterion | A. Feature contract + shared transform library | B. Full feature store (offline + online + point-in-time) | C. Adopt the platform's managed feature store |
|---|---|---|---|
| Solves train/serve skew | Yes, *if* the transform is genuinely shared | Yes, and adds point-in-time joins | Yes |
| Time to value | Weeks | Quarters | Months, plus platform coupling |
| On-call surface added | Almost none | A 24/7 online store | Mostly the vendor's |
| Pays off when | 1–3 models, few shared features | Many models sharing features, sub-hour freshness | Already all-in on the platform |
| Our situation | 3–4 classical models, mostly batch, 24h freshness SLO | — | — |

> **Say it like this:** "A, for year one. The problem a feature store exists to solve is skew, and skew is only removed if both paths share the *transformation code* — plenty of teams buy two stores and still run two implementations, which is a more expensive way to have the same bug. So I'd ship the cheap version of the guarantee: one transformation definition, a serialised feature contract next to every artifact, hard-fail on a missing required feature, and a CI subset assertion as a promotion gate. **Those four are exactly what I built at TrueBalance** after a train/serve parity collapse — four thousand and one offline features against twenty-eight keys in the real-time payload, silently imputed, the served vector near-constant, and every dashboard green. **The fifth one I'd add here and did not have there** is a nightly replay test: recompute yesterday's online features from the logged raw payloads, diff against what training would have produced, and alert on the p99 of the diff rather than the mean, because a mean diff hides a small number of catastrophically wrong rows. That is the control that would have caught my incident on day one rather than months in, and it's the first thing I'd build that I've never operated. **What changes my mind:** more than three consuming teams sharing features, or a freshness requirement under an hour. Either one and the coordination cost exceeds the on-call cost, and I'd build B — starting with the offline point-in-time-correct join, which is the half that actually prevents leakage. I'd build the online store last, not first, which is the opposite of how most teams do it."

### 2.6 Minute 33–35: phasing

```text
PHASE 1  (0-90 days)  "make ONE feature safe and measurable"
  - CDC -> bronze/silver for sheets, comments, share_edge, group_member;
    contract gate with QUARANTINE semantics
  - effective_principals materialisation + revocation PRIORITY LANE
  - FM gateway: routing, prompt caching, token budgets, tracing, breaker
  - ONE feature end to end: single-sheet summarise (read-only, no agent)
  - golden eval set v1 (200 real queries) + CI gate + cross-tenant probe
  - cost dashboard: tokens and $ per tenant / feature / prompt-version
  DONE = one feature at 5% canary, cost per request known, probe green

PHASE 2  (3-6 months)  "make it a platform"
  - registry for models/prompts/agents/indexes + lineage manifest
  - RAG service: hybrid + rerank + pre-filter + authoritative re-check
  - gold entity_graph (typed edges) + graph-traversal router path
  - blue/green index build, alias swap, change-log replay before swap
  - semantic/metric layer + formula-DSL generation with 4 validation
    gates: parse -> type & permission check -> sandbox execute -> diff UI
  - AUTOMATED RETRAINING: drift + scheduled + performance triggers wired
    to a challenger run; promotion gate (eval vs incumbent, slice check,
    parity replay, calibration, cost delta); shadow -> canary -> alias
    flip; promotion stays HUMAN-APPROVED for customer-facing models
  - paved road: repo template, IaC module, CI gate pack; 2 more teams on
  - at-risk classical scorer on the batch path
  DONE = 3 teams shipping without the platform team in the room

PHASE 3  (6-12 months)  "agents, tiering, gov"
  - write-capable agent behind approval + egress allow-list + idempotency
    (LangGraph here specifically, for durable checkpointing across a
     human approval that may take hours)
  - tiered multi-tenancy: dedicated indexes for enterprise / gov / BYOK
  - gov SKU capability tiering and model allow-list enforced in routing
  - metered AI credits wired to billing; showback for a quarter, then
    chargeback (never chargeback on numbers you haven't debugged)
  - scheduled scorers on sampled PRODUCTION traces, not just CI
```

The block that earns disproportionate credit, because almost nobody writes it:

```text
=== NOT DOING IN YEAR ONE (and why) ===
  x Fine-tuning or training a foundation model
      no task moat, no eval set yet, and a permanent migration liability
      every time a better base model ships. Industry pattern agrees --
      ServiceNow moved off defaulting to its in-house model -- but the
      economics carry it without the citation.
  x Self-hosted GPU inference
      duty cycle ~<20%; break-even needs ~35-40% sustained
  x Streaming feature store
      freshness SLO is 24h; it adds a 24/7 on-call surface a six-person
      team cannot carry. Revisit at >3 consuming teams or <1h freshness.
  x Embedding the grid / a row-level vector index
      6B ACL-scoped vectors; the grid gets a query path instead
  x Full GraphRAG over the corpus
      the graph we need ALREADY EXISTS as foreign keys between sheets,
      rows, owners and workspaces -- paying an LLM to infer relations
      from prose reconstructs, lossily, what the schema states exactly.
      (Published GraphRAG indexing runs have been reported in the tens
      of thousands of dollars at corpus scale; I'd want the corpus size
      before quoting a figure. The schema argument stands alone.)
      Revisit if >20% of the query log turns out to be multi-hop.
  x Multi-region active-active for AI features
      degrade to a smaller model or a cached answer instead; revisit
      when an enterprise contract puts an availability number on it
```

**On-call model.** The platform team owns *substrate* SLOs — gateway availability, index freshness, feature-pipeline freshness, registry integrity, policy-service availability. The model-owning product team owns *quality* SLOs — acceptance-and-retention, faithfulness, cost per accepted outcome — and gets paged for them. The platform's job is to make that page land on one dashboard link with the trace ID already filtered. If the wrong team is getting paged, that is a platform defect, not a rota problem.

**SLOs to write on the board:**

| SLI | SLO | Page? |
|---|---|---|
| Gateway availability | 99.9% over 28 days | Yes |
| Ask-portfolio p95 TTFT | ≤ 1.2 s | Yes on sustained breach |
| Permission-violation events | **exactly 0** | Yes, immediately |
| Revocation propagation | p99 ≤ 60 s | Yes |
| Index freshness (content) | p95 ≤ 15 min | Ticket |
| Feature-pipeline freshness | ≤ 24 h | Yes |
| Faithfulness on the golden set | ≥ baseline − 2% | Blocks the merge; not a page |
| Cost per accepted outcome | within budget; 3× anomaly | Ticket, unless 3× |

**What the runbook contains,** because "we have a runbook" is not an answer: for each failure mode — the exact first query to run, the dashboard link, the rollback command (which for a model or a prompt is a config flip, target under sixty seconds, never a rebuild), the per-feature and per-tenant kill switch, the escalation path, and the customer-communication template for a permission incident. Plus the quarterly game day: revoke access in a staging tenant and assert the chunk is unreachable through search, chat, cache and conversation history inside the SLA. An untested rollback is a hypothesis; an untested revocation is a claim.

### 2.8 Minute 37–40: the closing 90 seconds

Do not summarise everything. Name the three decisions that carry the design, the one thing you'd change with more information, and hand back. Do **not** re-run the disclosure here; it was made at minute zero and repeating it at the end makes the disclaimer the last thing they remember.

> **Say it like this:** "Let me close in about a minute. Three decisions carry this design. First, **the grid never goes into the vector index** — permissions here are row-level, chunk boundaries can't cross ACL boundaries, and six billion ACL-scoped vectors isn't a design. So structured questions get a semantic layer and a typed query where the aggregate is computed *after* the filter, multi-hop questions get the entity graph that already exists as foreign keys, and only the text surfaces get embeddings. That's also the decision that makes the numbers honest rather than merely plausible. Second, **the gateway is ours** — routing, prompt caching, token budgets, guardrails, per-tenant cost attribution and the per-SKU model allow-list all live in one place, because that's what takes a naive $1.2 million a month token bill down to roughly $330k, and it's what stops a capacity commitment pinning us to a model we've outgrown. Third, **permissions get their own priority lane and a published revocation SLA**, with an authoritative re-check on the top eight document IDs before generation, because the projection is a cache and caches are wrong for a window — the only question is whether you publish that window or discover it.
>
> The thing I'd most want to change with better information is the tenancy tier boundary. I've assumed namespace-per-tenant with dedicated indexes for enterprise, gov and BYOK, but that line should be drawn from your actual tenant size distribution, not from my guess at it.
>
> What I've actually operated, so you can weight the rest: an end-to-end MLOps platform on SageMaker for an FCA-regulated bank, with drift detection and automated retraining in it; multi-container shared endpoints holding per-model SLAs; feature contracts and train/serve parity gates built after a real production failure; a production knowledge graph that replaced a silently-lossy parser and hit full field coverage on a hundred thousand real messages; Deequ-based data quality on Spark; and drift monitoring that auto-provisions its own dashboards from feature statistics. I'd expect to be productive on the design questions from week one, and to need three or four weeks against a real workspace before I'd trust myself on Databricks-specific operational detail.
>
> Where would you like me to go deeper — the permission materialisation, the eval and promotion gate, or the cost model?"

That last question matters more than it looks. It converts the end of the design into the start of the next conversation, and it hands the interviewer the three places you are strongest.
