### D4. Monitoring and data observability for the whole platform

> *"Post-deployment monitoring for model performance, data drift and latency. Design the observability layer. Where does a tool like Monte Carlo fit?"*

#### If you only have eight minutes

**Crux sentence:** "Design the monitoring around which signal fires *first* for each failure class, because ML systems fail silently at 200 OK."

**Draw:** the five-layer stack, L1 to L5, with the arrow annotated "fastest, least meaningful" at the bottom and "slowest, most meaningful" at the top. That single diagram carries the whole argument.

**The one senior thing:** the detection-order table — per failure class, which layer catches it and why the others do not — and the refusal to page on model accuracy when labels lag 21 days.

**Do not skip the Monte Carlo disclaimer even at eight minutes.** It is two sentences and it is the reason the rest is credible.

Open with the honesty, immediately, because the JD names Monte Carlo and the recruiter has already been told in writing.

> **Say it like this:** "I should say up front: I haven't used Monte Carlo. I've built the equivalent with different tooling. At ResMed I wrote a Python and IaC drift-monitoring utility that ingested data-scientist-authored thresholds and slice definitions and auto-provisioned Datadog dashboards and alerts from Snowflake feature statistics. At Tiger I did two separate things that are both relevant: I designed the end-to-end MLOps platform on SageMaker for NatWest, an FCA-regulated bank, and that included drift detection and automated retraining; and separately, on a different engagement, I built large-scale data-quality checks with Deequ on Azure Databricks with the drift jobs orchestrated through Azure Data Factory. Different clouds, same problem shape. So I know the shape well and I'd be quick on the tool — let me design the layer and then tell you exactly where I'd buy versus build."
>
> **Cut to these two if you are short:** "I haven't used Monte Carlo — I've built the equivalent with Datadog and Snowflake at ResMed, and with Deequ on Azure Databricks at Tiger." / "Let me design the layer and then tell you where I'd buy versus build."
>
> ⚠ Keep the two Tiger engagements separate in speech. NatWest was **AWS SageMaker**. Deequ and Data Factory were **Azure Databricks**. Merging them invites "you ran ADF against SageMaker?" and there is no good answer to that.

#### Clarifying questions

1. **What is the label latency per model?** This is the first question, not the fifth.
2. **Who is on call, and for what?** If a data engineer gets paged for a model-quality regression they cannot fix, the alert is wrong.
3. **What is already instrumented** — do we have request/response logging, and is it sampled or complete?
4. **Do we monitor per tenant?** In multi-tenant SaaS, a platform-level aggregate hides everything that matters.
5. **What is the compliance requirement on retention** of prediction logs?

#### Assumed numbers (state them, invite correction)

| Assumption | Value | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Models under monitoring | 20–50 in production, ~10 carrying most of the traffic | Decides whether monitoring is per-model bespoke or a platform capability with a config |
| Features per model | 50–500 typical, one outlier in the thousands | The thousands case is what makes cardinality a budget problem rather than a detail |
| **Series cardinality** | features × slices × model versions × tenants ≈ **10^5–10^6 active series** | This is the monitoring bill. It has to be a designed number, not an emergent one |
| Label latency | Bimodal: a subset resolves <24 h, the median lands 7–60 days out | Decides that accuracy is a *review* signal and proxies are the *paging* signal |
| Prediction volume | 10^6–10^8 predictions/day platform-wide | Sets the sampling rate for raw prediction logs versus aggregated metrics |
| Prediction-log retention | 13 months for regulated tenants, 90 days hot elsewhere | Retention is a compliance liability and a storage line at the same time |
| Slice count | 20–50 explicitly defined slices per significant model | Deliberately capped; automated discovery is a weekly report, never a paging path |
| Baseline window | Training/validation set, pinned and versioned; plus a rolling 30-day window | Two different questions, so two baselines |

> **Say it like this:** "The number I'd most want corrected here is series cardinality. Everything else scales gracefully; that one is the difference between a monitoring bill that's a rounding error and one that's a line item somebody asks about. If I'm wrong by an order of magnitude on slices-times-features-times-tenants, the design changes."

#### The layered model, and which layer detects what first

```text
  L5 BUSINESS      conversion, task completion, escalation rate,
                   cost per successful task            <- slowest, most meaningful
        ^
  L4 MODEL         accuracy / AUC / calibration on delayed labels;
                   prediction distribution (PSI), confidence histogram
        ^
  L3 FEATURE       per-feature null/missing rate, range violations,
                   cardinality, freshness, train/serve skew
        ^
  L2 DATA          table freshness, row-count volume, schema change,
                   upstream job success, lineage       <- the Monte Carlo layer
        ^
  L1 INFRA         p50/p95/p99 latency, error rate, saturation,
                   GPU/CPU utilisation, queue depth    <- fastest, least meaningful
```

The insight to state plainly: **the layers are ordered by detection speed and inversely ordered by business meaning.** L1 tells you in seconds and tells you almost nothing about correctness. L5 tells you the truth and tells you in weeks. Everything in between is a bet on which proxy fires soonest for the failure you actually get.

| Failure | Detected first by | Why not the others |
|---|---|---|
| Upstream ETL job didn't run | **L2 freshness** (minutes) | L1 is green; the model happily serves stale features |
| A feature column renamed upstream | **L2 schema** / **L3 null rate spike** | L4 drifts only after enough traffic; L5 takes weeks |
| Serving code deployed with a different transform | **L3 train/serve skew** and the per-feature missing-rate metric | This is the TrueBalance failure — nothing else catches it, it returns 200s |
| Genuine population shift (new market, seasonality) | **L4 prediction PSI**, then L4 accuracy when labels land | L2/L3 are clean; the data is *valid*, just different |
| Model artifact rolled back but config didn't | **L4 prediction distribution step-change** + `model_version` cardinality | L1 green, L2 green |
| Adversarial or bot traffic | **L4 confidence histogram** collapsing to the tails | Volume looks normal at L2 |
| Cost blowout | **L1 token/GPU-hour per tenant** | Nothing else moves until the invoice |

> **Say it like this:** "The defining property of ML systems is that they fail silently at 200 OK. Compilers and type systems carry the load in normal software; here the gate chain and the runtime monitors have to carry it. So I design the monitoring around the question *which signal fires first for each failure class*, and I make sure every class has at least one fast signal."

#### Drift statistics: pick deliberately, and know the limits

| Statistic | Applies to | Typical threshold | The caveat you must state |
|---|---|---|---|
| **PSI** (population stability index) | Binned numeric or categorical | <0.1 stable, 0.1–0.25 watch, >0.25 investigate | **PSI is bin-dependent.** Bin edges must be frozen from the baseline, not recomputed per window, or you are measuring your binner |
| **KS** (two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov) | Continuous, unbinned | KS statistic (D), typically 0.1–0.2 depending on the feature's measured baseline volatility | **Sample-size trap:** at 10M rows every trivial difference is significant. Gate on the KS *statistic* (effect size), never on the p-value |
| **JS divergence** | Categorical distributions | ~0.1 watch, ~0.2 investigate (base-2 log) | Bounded in [0,1] **with log base 2** — natural log caps it at ln 2 ≈ 0.693, so state your base. Symmetric, and its square root is a true metric; that is what makes it comparable across features, unlike KL. Note `scipy.spatial.distance.jensenshannon` returns the *distance* (the square root), not the divergence |
| **Chi-squared** | Categorical | statistic + p | Same sample-size trap as KS |
| **Wasserstein / earth-mover** | Numeric | scale-dependent | Sensitive to units; normalise or it is uninterpretable across features |
| **Null / missing rate delta** | Everything | absolute | The cheapest and most often the first to fire. Underrated |

**Threshold setting is empirical, not theoretical.** Backfill the statistic over the last 6–12 months of production data per feature, look at the historical distribution of the metric itself, and set the alarm at a percentile of *that*, not at a textbook 0.25. Features have wildly different natural volatility, and a global threshold guarantees both false pages on the noisy ones and silence on the stable ones. Then review the thresholds quarterly.

**Slice-level monitoring is where the value is.** Aggregate drift is a lagging, diluted signal. Monitor per tenant tier, per region, per model version, and per the two or three business segments that matter, and alert on *slice* movement. The cost is combinatorial explosion, so cap it: define slices explicitly in a versioned config (this is exactly the design of the ResMed utility — data scientists author thresholds and slice definitions, and the tool provisions the dashboards and alerts from them), and reserve automated slice discovery for a weekly report rather than a paging path.

**Label latency drives the whole policy.** Write it down per model: *"labels arrive at a median of 21 days; therefore we page on proxies (L2, L3, L4-prediction-drift), we review L4-accuracy weekly, and we never page on accuracy."* Where labels are partially early (a subset resolves in 24 h), monitor that subset separately and treat it as an early-warning slice with the caveat that it is biased. Where ground truth arrives via human review, feed reviewer decisions back as labels and **measure reviewer agreement** — if two reviewers disagree, the rubric is broken, not the model.

#### Alert routing that survives on-call

| Signal | Route | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| L1 SLO burn (fast burn, 2% budget in 1 h) | **Page** the service owner | Actionable now |
| L2 freshness/volume anomaly on a table feeding a live model | **Page** the data owner; auto-degrade the model to stale-feature mode | Actionable, and the model should already have degraded |
| L3 train/serve skew or a required feature missing | **Page** — this is a correctness break | Silent 200s otherwise |
| L4 prediction drift beyond threshold on a slice | **Ticket** with a 1-business-day SLA, plus a Slack digest | Not a 3 a.m. problem, and 3 a.m. cannot fix it |
| L4 accuracy regression on delayed labels | **Weekly review**, can trigger rollback | By definition not urgent |
| L5 business metric | Weekly business review | Confounded by everything |

Two rules that make it survivable: **multi-window multi-burn-rate alerts** rather than static thresholds (fast burn pages, slow burn tickets), and **every alert links to a runbook whose first line is the degradation ladder**. If an alert has no action, it is a dashboard, and it belongs on a dashboard.

**The degradation ladder must be designed before the incident**, and the caller must be told which rung it got:

```text
 1. full model, fresh features                      <- normal
 2. full model, cached/stale features               <- feature store degraded
 3. last-known-good model version                   <- new model misbehaving
 4. smaller/cheaper model                           <- capacity lost
 5. precomputed batch score for this entity         <- hours old, but real
 6. rules / population baseline                     <- 10-line rule table
 7. static safe default + explicit downstream flag  <- e.g. route to manual review
```

Return `model_version` and `degraded: true` in the response envelope. Silently returning a rules-based score as if it were the model is how you get a regulatory problem.

#### Where a Monte Carlo-class tool fits, versus what you build

> **Say it like this:** "A data-observability product like Monte Carlo owns **L2** — table freshness, volume anomalies, schema change, and lineage-aware blast-radius across the warehouse — and it's genuinely good at the thing that's tedious to build: automatic monitors across thousands of tables with learned baselines. What it does **not** own is L3 and L4: per-feature train/serve skew, prediction-distribution drift keyed to a model version, calibration, or slice-level model quality against delayed labels. So my split is buy L2, build L3–L4, and — this is the part people skip — **join them on lineage**, so when a table alert fires I can immediately answer 'which models consume this, and should they degrade?' Without that join you have two disconnected alerting systems and an on-call engineer doing the join by hand at 3 a.m."
>
> **Cut to these two if you are short:** "Monte Carlo owns L2 — freshness, volume, schema, lineage — and it's good at the tedious part, automatic monitors across thousands of tables." / "It doesn't own L3 and L4, so my split is buy L2, build L3–L4, and join them on lineage."

Be explicit about the build side: L3/L4 metrics are emitted by the scorer itself (per-feature missing rate, prediction histogram, latency, model version) into the normal metrics pipeline, plus a windowed job computing PSI/JS against a pinned **baseline that is the training or validation set** — that is the only baseline that answers "has the world moved away from what this model learned." Consecutive-window drift and baseline drift are different questions; compute both.

#### Named tradeoffs

| Decision | Chosen | Rejected | Because |
|---|---|---|---|
| Buy vs build the data layer | **Buy L2** (freshness, volume, schema, warehouse lineage); **build L3–L4** and join them on lineage | Build L2 too, "we already have Airflow sensors" | Automatic monitors with learned baselines across thousands of tables is exactly the tedious, low-differentiation work worth paying for. Model-aware skew, calibration and slice quality is not a thing you can buy that knows your model versions |
| Paging signal | **Page on proxies** (L2 freshness, L3 skew and missing-feature, L1 SLO burn) | Page on model accuracy | With a 7–60 day label lag, an accuracy page is a page about a decision made six weeks ago. Nobody can act on it at 3 a.m., so it must be a review item with a rollback path |
| Slice definitions | **Explicit, versioned config** authored by data scientists, provisioned as code | Automated slice discovery in the paging path | This is the ResMed design and the reason is on-call trust: discovered slices produce statistically-real, operationally-meaningless alerts. Discovery stays, as a weekly report |
| Drift baseline | **Pinned training/validation set**, versioned, *plus* a rolling window as a second series | Rolling window alone | A rolling baseline silently absorbs the drift you are trying to detect — the frog-boiling failure. But rolling answers "did something change *this week*", which pinned cannot, so compute both and route them differently |
| Metric cardinality | **Capped deliberately**: top-N tenants explicit, the rest bucketed; per-feature stats on the model's declared important features only | Per-feature × per-slice × per-tenant for everything | Cardinality is the bill, and an unbounded cardinality design fails by getting switched off after the first invoice review — which is a worse outcome than never having built it |
| Alert thresholds | **Empirical**, backfilled per feature from 6–12 months of history and set at a percentile of the metric's own distribution | Textbook constants (PSI > 0.25 everywhere) | Features have wildly different natural volatility; a global constant guarantees false pages on the noisy ones and silence on the stable ones |

> **Say it like this on the buy/build line:** "I'd buy L2 and build L3 and L4, and the part people skip is that the two have to be joined on lineage. Otherwise you own two alerting systems and an on-call engineer doing the join by hand at 3 a.m."

#### Cost, failure modes, and the senior thing

Cost: cardinality is the bill. Per-feature, per-slice, per-model-version, per-tenant time series multiply fast; cap cardinality deliberately (top-N tenants explicitly, the rest bucketed), sample raw prediction logs rather than storing everything hot, and tier the log store. Trace/prediction-log storage is also a compliance liability, not just a cost line.

Failure modes: a monitor whose baseline silently became the drifted data (freeze and version baselines); alerts on metrics nobody owns; slice definitions rotting away from the business's definitions; a drift alarm firing on a *fixed* upstream bug and triggering a retrain on the broken window; and the classic, monitoring that is green because the pipeline that computes it also died.

**The senior thing:** the detection-order table. Anyone can list PSI, KS and JS. Very few can say, per failure class, which layer fires first and why the others do not — and then route alerts accordingly so on-call survives. Second senior thing: refusing to page on model accuracy when labels lag, and having a written label-latency policy instead.

#### Follow-ups

- *"How do you monitor an LLM feature where there is no label at all?"* — Trace everything (OpenTelemetry-shaped spans for the run, retrieval, tool calls and generation), then run the *same scorers you used in offline eval* against a sampled slice of live traces, attaching results as feedback on the trace. Plus the free signals: refusal rate, citation-validation failures, and user edits.
- *"What's your first week on an unmonitored platform?"* — Instrument before changing anything: cost and latency per tenant, an inventory of what is in the index and who can see it, and a golden set with a measured baseline. Then the two things that are almost always missing — an eval gate in CI and a tenant-isolation probe.
- *"How do you avoid alert fatigue?"* — Every page must have a runbook and a documented action. I would audit the last 90 days of pages, count how many resulted in an action, and delete the rest. A monitoring system nobody trusts is worse than none, because it consumes the attention you need for the real one.

### D5. Foundation-model serving and cost control at SaaS scale

> *"We're shipping AI across the product. Design the model-serving layer and tell me how we control cost."*

#### If you only have eight minutes

**Crux sentence:** "Everything goes through one gateway, because budgets, model allow-lists, redaction and audit are only enforceable at a choke point — and then the metric on the dashboard is cost per successful outcome per tenant, not cost per token."

**Draw:** the gateway box with its seven jobs, and the provider fan-out underneath with the circuit breaker. Nothing else.

**The one senior thing:** raise the gateway's own single-point-of-failure risk before the interviewer does, and insist on **metering before pricing** — showback for a quarter, then budgets.

**The Bedrock disclaimer is mandatory** and it costs you fifteen seconds. Say it in the first thirty.

Guardrail first, and say it early and without drama.

> **Say it like this:** "One thing to state plainly: I haven't run AWS Bedrock in production. My managed-serving experience is SageMaker — including multi-container endpoints on ResMed's internal MLOps platform, where several models shared infrastructure to cut inference cost while holding per-model SLAs — plus self-hosted serving on Kubernetes and OpenShift. So I'll design the gateway on first principles and map to Bedrock where the analogy is exact, and I'll flag where I'd be reading docs rather than recalling scars."

#### Clarifying questions

1. **How many distinct AI features, and what are their latency classes?** Inline suggestion, modal, async digest, batch enrichment.
2. **What is the pricing model** — bundled into the seat, a credit pack, an enterprise add-on? This determines whether cost is a margin problem or a metering problem.
3. **Which SKUs must this serve** — commercial, EU-resident, FedRAMP? The gov SKU has a materially different model menu.
4. **Is there an existing gateway**, or does every service call the provider directly?
5. **What is the current per-tenant cost attribution**, if any?

#### Assumed numbers (state them, invite correction)

| Assumption | Value | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Distinct AI features | 8–15 shipped, growing | Below ~5 a gateway is over-engineering; above ~10 it is the only way to keep policy consistent |
| QPS by latency class | Inline suggestion ~100–500 QPS, p95 < 1 s; modal ~10–50 QPS, p95 < 5 s; async/batch unbounded, minutes | The split is what makes provisioned-versus-on-demand a real decision instead of a preference |
| Tokens per call | Inline ~2–4k in / ~100 out; modal ~8–20k in / ~500 out; agentic tasks 50k–500k in aggregate across turns | Input-heavy traffic is what makes prefix caching the dominant lever |
| Cache-hit rate target | 40–70% on prefix cache for structured features; <10% on exact | Determines whether the caching design pays for itself at all |
| Tenants | ~10k, with the top 50 driving a disproportionate share of AI usage | Cost attribution has to be per-tenant or the tail hides the outliers |
| Monthly LLM spend | Order of $100k–$1M, growing faster than seats | Sets whether self-hosting arithmetic is even worth doing |
| Escalation rate (small → large model) | Target under 20% | Above ~35% the router costs more than always using the large model, because you pay twice |
| Gross-margin target | 70%+ on the AI surface, versus 80–90% classic SaaS | This is the number the PM conversation is really about |

> **Say it like this:** "The two numbers I'd want corrected first are the latency-class split and the escalation rate. The first decides the capacity strategy and the second decides whether routing is a saving or a tax — a router that escalates 60% of the time is more expensive than no router at all, because you pay for both calls."

#### The diagram

```text
  feature code (never holds a provider key)
        |
        v
  +============================================================+
  |                    LLM GATEWAY                             |
  |  1 unified API      -> model swap is config, not a deploy  |
  |  2 routing          -> by feature, cost, latency, REGION   |
  |  3 caching          -> exact / prefix-prompt / semantic    |
  |  4 budgets          -> per request / session / tenant / day|
  |  5 rate limits      -> ON TOKENS, not request count        |
  |  6 observability    -> cost attributed at call time        |
  |  7 policy           -> model allow-list per SKU/region,    |
  |                        redaction, guardrail, audit log     |
  +============================================================+
        |            |             |              |
     provider A   provider B    self-hosted    gov-SKU pool
     (primary)    (fallback)    OSS weights    (restricted menu)
        \____________|_____________|______________/
                     |
        circuit breaker on TTFT / error rate / p90
        -> designated backup model per feature
        -> if all fail: DEGRADE the feature, don't 500
```

#### The core design

**One gateway, seven jobs, and it is the highest-leverage piece of platform work available.** Unified provider API so a model swap is a config change. Routing by feature, cost, latency and *region*. Caching. Budgets. Rate limits. Per-request observability with cost attribution. Policy — model allow-list per SKU, redaction, guardrail invocation, audit logging. Raise the obvious objection yourself before they do: **the gateway is now a single point of failure in every request path**, so it needs its own SLO, multi-region deployment, and a documented bypass.

**Routing pays for itself.** Teams that have published routing results report double-digit latency wins on short, high-volume calls and quality wins on the hard tail, simply from matching model to feature — and within a single vendor the price spread across tiers is 5x or more, which is the part you can verify yourself off the price list. So: each feature declares a **capability class** and a latency class; the router maps class to model; the mapping is data, reviewed like code, and changeable without a deploy. Treat the mapping as something you own empirically rather than something you inherit from a blog post — the right model for *your* feature is an eval result, not a citation. Small-model-first with escalation on low confidence handles 70–90% of traffic — but gate it on a measured escalation rate, because a router that escalates 60% of the time costs *more* than the big model alone, since you pay twice.

**Caching, three kinds, and one of them is a security control.**

| Kind | Mechanism | Where it wins | The catch |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Exact** | Hash of the full request | Retries, idempotent duplicates, shared system prompts | Low hit rate on real traffic |
| **Prefix / prompt caching** | Provider-side reuse of a stable prefix (system prompt, schema digest, few-shots) | Structured features where 80% of the prompt is fixed | On Anthropic's 5-minute cache the write is 1.25x input and the read is 0.1x, so **you are ahead from the first cache hit** — 1.25 + 0.1 = 1.35 against 2.0 uncached. The thing to watch is hit rate and TTL, not break-even: a prefix rewritten before it is ever read is pure overhead, and the 1-hour TTL costs 2x to write. Other providers price this differently, so it is a per-provider calculation |
| **Semantic** | Embedding-similarity match on the query | FAQ-shaped traffic | Dangerous on personalised or temporal queries. **The cache key must include tenant plus the caller's effective principal set**, or the cache becomes a cross-tenant leak. Measure the false-hit rate |

**Rate limiting must meter tokens, not requests.** One request can burn 100k tokens; request-count limits are theatre. Budgets at four levels — per request, per session, per tenant, per day — enforced **at the gateway so an over-budget request never reaches the provider**. Anomaly alerts on 3x the daily baseline, on a single tenant exceeding some share of platform spend, and on estimate-versus-actual drift beyond ~20%. A hard spend ceiling per window is the circuit breaker. Name the cost-abuse classes: infinite reasoning loops, recursive reflection, tool-chain amplification, and the classic agent case, where a retry loop makes hundreds of calls to a broken tool in minutes because nothing in the graph counts.

**Provisioned versus on-demand capacity.** Split by latency class: reserved or provisioned capacity for the latency-sensitive interactive features, on-demand for async, and the discounted batch/async path (typically around 50% off) for anything genuinely offline — evaluation runs, nightly enrichment, backfills. And name the reason multi-provider setups keep appearing, because it is the real one and it is not primarily about price: **multi-month capacity commitments block model upgrades.** Committing to capacity is committing to a model version, and the model you committed to in March is not the one you want in September.

> **Say it like this:** "Half the 'we need more capacity' requests I've seen are solved by moving a workload from online to async. That's not a latency downgrade — it's a change of contract from a latency SLO to a completion SLO, which then lets you use batch pricing, higher batch sizes and spot capacity. It's the cheapest win available."

#### Resource optimisation: the serving-infrastructure half

The JD makes this its own responsibility line — "manage GPU/CPU utilization to minimize cloud costs while maintaining low-latency inference" — so do not let it collapse into one row of a tradeoff table. This is also the section where your genuine ops scars are, so slow down here.

**Start from the honest framing: GPU cost is a utilisation problem, and utilisation is a batching problem.**

| Lever | What it does | The knee to name |
|---|---|---|
| **Continuous (in-flight) batching** | Instead of waiting for a static batch, the scheduler admits new sequences as others finish, so the GPU never idles behind the longest generation in the batch | Throughput rises with batch size until the KV cache saturates; past that you get queueing and **TTFT degrades while tokens/sec still looks great**. Watch TTFT and inter-token latency separately, because a throughput dashboard hides the latency you actually sell |
| **KV-cache sizing** | Per-sequence memory is roughly `2 × layers × kv_heads × head_dim × dtype_bytes × context_len`; total concurrency is (GPU memory − weights) ÷ that | This is the real concurrency limit, not vCPU or QPS. Long-context features are memory-expensive per *request*, which is why a 100k-token feature and a 2k-token feature should not share a pool |
| **Quantisation** | Smaller weights → more room for KV cache → higher concurrency, plus faster memory-bound decode | It is an accuracy change, so it goes through the eval gate like any model swap. Never quantise as an ops decision behind the team's back |
| **Chunked prefill / prefill-decode split** | Prefill is compute-bound, decode is memory-bandwidth-bound; mixing them lets one starve the other | Separating them is what keeps a long-prompt request from spiking everyone's inter-token latency |
| **MIG / time-slicing** | Partition one GPU across several small models | MIG gives hard isolation with fixed partition sizes; time-slicing gives flexibility with no isolation and noisy-neighbour latency. For anything with a per-model SLA, MIG or a dedicated pool |
| **Scale-to-zero** | Kills the idle bill on low-traffic features | Cold start is weights-load-bound and can be tens of seconds. Viable for async and internal features, usually not for interactive. Mitigate with a warm pool of one, or accept it and say so |
| **Spot with checkpointing** | 60–90% off for training and batch inference | Only for interruptible work, and only if checkpointing is frequent enough that the restart cost is under the saving. Never for interactive serving |
| **Right-sizing the instance family** | Matching accelerator memory and bandwidth to the model, rather than defaulting to the biggest available | The commonest waste in the estate: a model that fits comfortably in a smaller accelerator, served on the largest one because that is what the example notebook used |

**Then the point that ties it to your record:**

> **Say it like this:** "The multi-container SageMaker endpoints I built on ResMed's internal MLOps platform were this exact idea one abstraction up. Several models shared endpoint infrastructure instead of each owning idle capacity, and the constraint was that per-model SLAs still had to hold — so the interesting work wasn't the packing, it was proving the packing didn't cost anyone their latency budget. That's the same argument as MIG versus time-slicing, and the same argument as multi-tenant batching: consolidation saves real money and the entire risk is that it silently transfers latency from the platform's budget to somebody's feature."
>
> **Cut to these two if you are short:** "At ResMed I built multi-container SageMaker endpoints so models shared infrastructure instead of each holding idle capacity." / "The hard part wasn't the packing, it was proving it didn't cost anyone their per-model SLA."

**Utilisation metrics that are not lies.** GPU utilisation percentage is close to useless on its own — it reports whether a kernel was resident, not whether it was doing useful work, so a badly-batched server can show 90% and be mostly moving memory. Track instead: tokens per GPU-second, memory-bandwidth utilisation, KV-cache occupancy, batch size at admission, queue depth and time-in-queue, and **cost per 1k output tokens per model per tenant**. The last one is the only one a finance conversation can use.

**The CPU side is not a footnote.** Feature transforms, tokenisation, embedding of short strings, reranking, classical models like the XGBoost propensity pipeline — these are CPU workloads where the wins are ARM64 instance families (the TrueBalance serving path is ARM64 Docker images in ECR for exactly this reason), batching at the queue rather than per-request invocation, and not paying for a GPU to do a job an autoscaled CPU fleet does more cheaply. Naming a workload that should *not* be on a GPU is a credibility marker in this conversation.

#### Fine-tuning workflows: when, and what it costs you to own

The JD names fine-tuning explicitly alongside foundation-model deployment and RAG, so hedging it out of existence reads as ignorance rather than judgement. The position to hold is: **it is the last lever, not the absent one**, and the platform has to support it properly whenever it does get pulled.

| Reach for it when | Do not reach for it when |
|---|---|
| **Format and behaviour** need to be reliable — a strict output schema, a house tone, a fixed refusal style. This is where the lift is most consistent | The problem is **knowledge**. Fine-tuning is a poor way to teach facts; RAG is the right tool and it stays current |
| **Latency and cost** matter and a small tuned model can replace a large prompted one — often the strongest business case, because you are buying a tier downgrade | You have not yet exhausted prompt structure, few-shots and context quality. Those are reversible in an afternoon; a tuned model is a standing commitment |
| You have **thousands of high-quality in-domain examples** with clean labels, and a golden set with a measured baseline | Your examples are model outputs, or your eval set does not exist yet. You will bake in your current bugs and be unable to see it |
| The task is **narrow and stable** | The task or the schema is still moving weekly |

**What the platform must provide, and this is the part that makes it an MLOps answer rather than an ML answer:**

- **Adapters, not full weights.** LoRA/QLoRA adapters are small, so the registry stores an adapter version pinned to a **base model version** — and that pin is the whole governance story. When the base moves, every adapter is invalidated until re-evaluated. Record it as a hard dependency edge, not a note.
- **Adapters are registry objects with the same manifest discipline as D3**: base model + version, training data snapshot, hyperparameters, seeds, eval results on the golden set, and the alias that makes one of them live.
- **Eval before and after on the same golden set, including the regression direction.** The question is never "did the tuned model get better at the target task" — it is "what did it get worse at". Tune for tone, lose refusal correctness. That is why the golden set needs its adversarial and unanswerable buckets before you tune, not after.
- **Adapter-per-tenant serving and its isolation implications.** Multi-adapter serving lets one base model serve many adapters from shared weights, which is what makes per-tenant tuning economically possible at all. The costs to state honestly: each adapter is per-tenant customer-derived artefact, so it inherits deletion, residency and retention obligations exactly like an index does; a mis-routed adapter is a cross-tenant leak with no error message; and adapter count is now an operational scaling dimension with its own memory ceiling. **Route the adapter from the token, never from the request body** — the same rule as `tenant_id` in D1.
- **The maintenance commitment.** A tuned model is a thing you now own forever against a base that keeps improving. Budget the re-tune, or write down the date you will retire it.

> **Say it like this:** "I'd sequence it as prompt, then context and retrieval, then routing, then fine-tuning — and I'd only cross into fine-tuning with a golden set that already has a measured baseline, because otherwise you can't tell improvement from regression, you can only tell change. When I do cross it, I'd want LoRA adapters in the registry pinned to a base model version, so that a base upgrade visibly invalidates every adapter until it's re-evaluated rather than silently changing behaviour underneath us."

#### Agent orchestration: LangChain, LangGraph, and what breaks

This is genuinely yours — you built core parts of the team's internal Claude developer assistant on MCP, including the first Slack integration, a Google Docs skill with 34/34 tests, and a PR skill that writes titles and descriptions from the diff, tying Jira, GitHub, Jenkins, AWS, Grafana and Slack into one plain-English interface with each task running in an isolated Git workspace. The JD asks for LangChain and LangGraph "for AI/ML Ops pipeline integration", and the round is titled Design *and Domain*, so expect to be probed on graph mechanics rather than on the marketing.

| Concern | The design position |
|---|---|
| **State** | The graph state is a typed, reducer-merged object, not a free-form dict. Reducers matter because parallel branches write concurrently; an append reducer on the message list and last-write-wins on scalars is the usual shape, and getting it wrong produces nondeterminism that looks like a model problem |
| **Checkpointing** | Persist state after every node. This is what makes a long task resumable after a crash, and it is also what makes human-in-the-loop possible at all. Checkpoints are customer data — they carry retrieved content — so they inherit retention and deletion obligations, and they are a covert copy in exactly the D1 sense |
| **Human-in-the-loop** | An interrupt before a consequential node — anything that writes, sends, spends or deletes — with the thread resumable from the checkpoint. The important design property is that approval is a *graph node*, so it is recorded, auditable and testable, rather than a UI convention someone can route around |
| **Retries and loops** | Every cycle needs a bounded counter in state and a budget check at the node boundary. This is the concrete defence against the tool-retry blowout named in the cost-abuse list: the loop terminates because the graph counts, not because the model gets bored |
| **Tool-call observability** | Trace the run, and every node, tool call and generation as spans with token counts and cost attached. The metric that matters is **cost and success per completed task**, not per call — a task that took 40 calls and failed is the expensive one, and per-call dashboards hide it entirely |
| **Determinism and testing** | Pin the graph topology in code and version it like any artefact. Test nodes in isolation with recorded tool responses; test the graph with a golden set of tasks scored end-to-end. Trajectory evaluation is its own problem — final-answer-only scoring passes agents that got there by luck through six wrong turns |
| **Failure isolation** | Each task in its own workspace, which is exactly the isolated-Git-workspace pattern from the developer assistant. It bounds blast radius and makes concurrent tasks safe by construction rather than by convention |

> **Say it like this:** "The thing I'd carry over from building our internal MCP-based developer assistant is that the interesting engineering in agents isn't the prompting — it's the boundaries. Each task in its own isolated workspace, tool calls counted and budgeted at the node boundary, approval as an actual graph node so it's auditable, and checkpoints treated as customer data with retention obligations. Most agent incidents I've seen are a missing bound, not a bad model."
>
> ⚠ **Guardrail on the vendor question.** If asked about Mosaic AI Agent Framework: *"I haven't used the Mosaic AI Agent Framework — my agent work is LangChain and LangGraph, plus building on the Model Context Protocol for our internal developer assistant. I'd want to look at how it handles state, checkpointing and evaluation before claiming the concepts map one-to-one, but those are the axes I'd compare on."* Same calm register as the Bedrock and Monte Carlo disclaimers. Do not improvise past it.

**Model deprecation handling — this is where most gateways are naive.** Pin model IDs in config, never in code, and never point production at a floating alias. Run a scheduled job that lists available models and alerts on any pinned ID whose lifecycle status is no longer active. Keep an eval suite that can re-qualify a replacement in CI, and treat a model upgrade as a shipped change: shadow the candidate on live traffic, compare on the golden set and on the shadow diff, canary, cut over, keep rollback warm for two weeks. And keep the two swaps separate — **a generation-model swap is reversible; an embedding-model swap requires a full re-index**, so never bundle them in one release.

**Per-tenant cost attribution and showback.** Attribute at call time, not by reconciling invoices later: every gateway call carries `tenant_id`, `feature`, `prompt_version`, `model_version`, and writes tokens in, tokens out, cached tokens and computed cost. Tag propagation is the perennial failure — enforce it (an untagged call is rejected), because retroactive attribution never happens. Then **showback before chargeback**: publish per-team and per-tenant cost with no financial consequence for a quarter, fix the attribution bugs while they are free, and only then attach budgets. Going straight to chargeback with wrong numbers destroys trust in the platform permanently.

**The unit metric on the dashboard is not cost per token.**

> **Say it like this:** "Cost per 1M tokens is an input price, not a business metric. The number I'd put on the dashboard is **cost per successful outcome, split by tenant** — cost per accepted formula, cost per answered question, cost per completed agent task. It's the honest one because retries and failed trajectories are pure waste, and a per-request metric hides them. And if it isn't attributable per tenant, you can't tell a growing customer from a runaway loop."

#### The gross-margin conversation with the product manager

Have the numbers ready and have the framing ready, because this is a real senior-engineer conversation and it is very likely to be asked in some form.

- Classic SaaS gross margins sit around 80–90%. AI-native products run closer to 50–60%, and early-stage ones lower. AI is COGS and it scales with usage, not with seats.
- **A per-seat product with an unlimited AI entitlement has unbounded per-seat cost against bounded per-seat revenue**, and power users are 10–100x the median. That is the whole problem in one sentence.
- The industry answer has shifted: hybrid base-plus-usage pricing has become the majority pattern among AI vendors, and among established SaaS companies adding AI, "seats plus usage" is the common choice.
- Credits with a **hard stop** are the honest design — Notion's implementation pauses agents immediately when credits run out and *skips* scheduled runs rather than retroactively running them. That hard edge is exactly what most teams avoid designing and exactly what makes the model predictable.

> **Say it like this to a PM:** "I can give you three levers and their cost of exercise. Routing and caching are free — they change cost without changing what the user sees, and I'd expect the largest single win there. Tiering and gating are a product decision, not an engineering one. Metering is the one that has to come first: we cannot price what we cannot attribute, so I'd want per-tenant, per-feature cost instrumented and trusted for a quarter before anyone commits to a price. And I'd push back on one thing — an unlimited AI entitlement on a per-seat plan is a promise engineering can't keep at the tail."
>
> **Cut to these two if you are short:** "Routing and caching are free levers; tiering is a product decision; metering has to come first because we can't price what we can't attribute." / "An unlimited AI entitlement on a per-seat plan is a promise engineering can't keep at the tail."

#### Named tradeoffs

| Decision | Chosen | Rejected | Because |
|---|---|---|---|
| Gateway | Single proxy all traffic must pass | Per-service SDK calls | Budgets, allow-lists, redaction and audit are only enforceable at a choke point; a config flag is not enforcement |
| Multi-provider | Yes, for deprecation risk and residency | Single vendor for simplicity | Capacity commitments pin you to old models; residency constrains vendor before it constrains model |
| Semantic cache | Yes, but tenant + principal-scoped, with a measured false-hit rate | Query-text keys | Otherwise it is a cross-tenant leak with a cost saving attached |
| Self-host OSS weights | Only for high-volume, low-complexity, latency-sensitive tasks | Self-host everything to save money | Break-even is a duty-cycle question: a 4xH100 rig at ~$10/hr against a ~$5/1M blended API needs roughly 555 tok/s sustained just to match the hardware bill — about 16% of peak, and closer to 35–40% once you load the ops FTE |
| Fine-tuning | Last lever, LoRA adapters in the registry pinned to a base version | Fine-tune early to "make it ours" | Prompt and context changes are reversible in an afternoon; a tuned model is a standing maintenance commitment against a base that keeps improving |
| GPU sharing | MIG or dedicated pools where a per-model SLA exists; time-slicing only for internal and async | Time-slice everything for utilisation | Time-slicing has no isolation, so consolidation silently transfers latency from the platform's budget into somebody's feature |
| Agent loop control | Bounded counters and budget checks at the node boundary, in graph state | Rely on the model to stop | The loop has to terminate because the graph counts, not because the model gets bored |

#### Monitoring, failure modes, and the senior thing

Monitor per feature and per tenant: TTFT, total latency, tokens in/out/cached, cost, error and refusal rate, cache hit rate, escalation rate, fallback rate, and circuit-breaker state. Alarm on fallback rate, because a silently-degraded model is the failure nobody notices.

Failure modes: the gateway itself (multi-region it, and document the bypass); a cache poisoned across tenants; a fallback chain that silently downgrades quality with no telemetry; token budgets enforced in application code rather than the gateway, so one code path bypasses them; a model deprecated with no replacement qualified; and cost attribution that looks right but double-counts cached tokens.

**The senior thing:** shifting the conversation from cost-per-token to **cost per successful outcome per tenant**, insisting on metering before pricing, and naming the gateway's own single-point-of-failure risk before the interviewer does.

#### Follow-ups

- *"Would you self-host?"* — For a narrow, high-volume, latency-sensitive task where I can keep a GPU above roughly a third of the clock, yes; otherwise the API is cheaper and I also do not pay for the on-call. The non-cost reasons that legitimately override the arithmetic are residency, a latency floor, and rate-limit independence.
- *"How do you handle the gov SKU?"* — Every feature declares a minimum capability class; every SKU declares an allowed model set; where nothing qualifies, the feature is *visibly disabled* in the admin console, never silently degraded. That is a product decision, not an infrastructure accident.
- *"Where does redaction go?"* — Three points with different rules: at ingest before embedding, at request before egress to a provider, and at log/trace before storage. And be honest that masking is not free — masking identity fields usually preserves task performance, masking substantive domain fields destroys it, so measure task accuracy under masking rather than assuming.
- *"What's the first thing you'd instrument?"* — Cost and latency per tenant per feature. Everything else is an argument until that exists.
