### D10. "Show me CI/CD and IaC for the whole ML estate"

**JD lines this answers:** *CI/CD Pipeline Development*; *modern software engineering practices — Kubernetes, CI/CD, IaC (preferably Terraform)*; *Version Control & Governance*.

**What is actually being scored:** blast radius, and whether a promotion gate can say no without a human's permission.

> **Say it like this:** "Software CI asks whether it compiled and the tests passed. ML CI asks whether this model, on this data snapshot, is better than the incumbent by more than noise, on every slice we care about — and the answer is a distribution, so the gate has to encode a margin. And the defining property of ML systems is that they fail silently at 200 OK, which is why the gate chain and runtime monitoring have to carry the load compilers and type systems carry in software."

#### Terraform layering — by rate of change and blast radius, never by cloud service

```text
live/                      one state per (env × region × layer)
  prod/ap-south-1/
    00-network/            VPC, subnets, TGW            — yearly
    10-platform/           EKS control plane, IRSA, KMS — quarterly
    20-nodepools/          GPU nodepools, AMIs          — monthly
    30-data/               buckets, catalog, FSx        — monthly
    40-mlplatform/         registry, Argo, quotas       — weekly
    50-workloads/          namespaces, IRSA per team    — daily
modules/  eks-cluster/  gpu-nodepool/  dataset-bucket/  team-namespace/
```

**State boundary = blast radius boundary.** A `terraform apply` for a team's namespace must be structurally incapable of touching the VPC. If one state file can destroy the cluster, the design is wrong regardless of how good the review process is. Dependencies flow downward only, via remote state or SSM parameters. Modules expose intent, not resources: `module "gpu_nodepool" { accelerator = "a100", capacity = "spot", max_gpus = 32, team = "search" }`.

**Workspaces are the wrong tool for prod versus staging** — same code path, same backend, one `workspace select` typo from applying staging's plan to prod, and environments always diverge, which pollutes modules with `count = terraform.workspace == "prod" ? 1 : 0`. Separate directories, separate state, separate tfvars, with Terragrunt or a thin CI wrapper removing the duplication.

**Drift** on an ML platform has specific sources: someone scaling a node group in the console during an incident, autoscalers mutating desired counts (`lifecycle { ignore_changes = [desired_size] }` is mandatory), GPU AMI and driver updates, and IAM policies edited by security. A nightly scheduled `plan` that fails loudly and files a ticket.

**Policy as code — two tools doing different jobs.** Checkov/tfsec/Trivy statically over the HCL, pre-commit and in the PR, catching the generic ("public bucket", "unencrypted volume"). OPA via Conftest over the **plan JSON**, expressing organisational rules that need the resolved plan: no instance type outside the approved GPU list; every resource carries `team`, `cost-center` and `data-classification`; GPU nodepools must be spot unless tagged `training-critical`. And the highest-value guardrail on an ML platform, because the expensive resources are stateful:

```rego
package terraform.protect
import rego.v1                       # OPA 1.x: partial set rules need `contains ... if`

deny contains msg if {
  rc := input.resource_changes[_]
  rc.change.actions[_] == "delete"   # also fires inside a replace, which is the point
  rc.change.before.tags.stateful == "true"
  msg := sprintf("refusing to destroy stateful resource %s", [rc.address])
}
```

Worth knowing why that first line is there: since OPA 1.0 the `if` and `contains` keywords are on by default, so the old `deny[msg] { ... }` form is a compile error rather than a deprecation warning unless you run with `--v0-compat`. Conftest has been on OPA 1.x for a while. If you inherit a policy repo written before that, the migration is mechanical (`opa fmt --v1-compatible`) but it is a migration, and it will fail your pipeline the day someone bumps the image.

Sentinel is worth naming only to note it's HCP-Terraform-only and does not work with OpenTofu — a genuine portability constraint.

**Modules are libraries, so test and release them like libraries.** Tag and version them, have consumers pin (`version = "~> 3.2"`) rather than track `main`, and pin provider versions in the lockfile and commit it — an unpinned provider minor is the most common cause of a plan that differs between a laptop and CI. Terraform's native `terraform test` (1.6+) is the right default for module contract tests: plan-only assertions run in seconds, so you can assert in CI that `gpu_nodepool` with `capacity = "spot"` never produces an on-demand ASG and always attaches the taint. Keep Terratest for the few cases that genuinely need a real apply against real cloud, because those cost minutes and money and will be the flaky part of your suite.

**Secrets.** Never in state-visible variables; state stores them in plaintext. OIDC federation from GitHub Actions to AWS so CI holds no long-lived keys, IRSA/Pod Identity for workloads, External Secrets Operator to project into Kubernetes. Terraform manages the secret container and its IAM, not the secret value.

#### The promotion gate chain, as the artifact it should be

The full G0–G8 chain — the non-inferiority margin, the slice gate, the behavioural suites, the shadow/canary ladder — is laid out in **D3**, and I won't re-derive it here. What is worth writing out in a pad is the shape of the artifact, plus the three gates that are most often got *wrong*:

```yaml
# promotion/churn-scorer.yaml — gates are code; each emits signed evidence
model: churn-scorer
champion_alias: champion               # MLflow alias, not a deprecated stage
non_inferiority_margin_auc: 0.004      # pre-registered, reviewed, not tuned per run

gates:
  - id: G0_build
    auto: true
    checks: [lockfile_resolved, image_digest_pinned, git_tree_clean, seeds_recorded]
    blocks_on: any_unpinned_dependency

  # G1 is the gate teams get backwards. Drift is the TRIGGER for a retrain,
  # so a retraining pipeline must not refuse to promote because the data moved.
  - id: G1_data_contract
    auto: true
    checks:
      - schema_equality: {train: features_v7, serve: features_v7}
      - null_rate_max: {default: 0.02, overrides: {last_login_days: 0.15}}
      - label_leakage_scan: true
      - population_shift_vs_last_training_snapshot:
          contract_stable_features:                 # declared stable in the contract
            psi_max: 0.2
            action: block               # shift here means WE changed, not the world
          all_other_features:
            psi_max: 0.2
            action: review              # expected shift → review, do not block
    blocks_on: any_blocking_violation

  # ... G2 offline-vs-champion, G3 slices, G4 behaviour: see D3 ...

  - id: G5_serving_parity
    auto: true
    description: score 5,000 rows THROUGH THE REAL CONTAINER, diff vs offline
    blocks_on: "max_abs_delta > 1e-6"

  # ... G6 performance, G7 shadow (24–72 h): see D3 ...

  - id: G8_canary
    auto: true
    steps: [1, 5, 25, 100]              # same ladder as D3; keep identical
    analysis: prometheus/model-guardrails
    on_failure: abort_and_rollback

approver: { required: true, role: ml-platform-oncall, on_gates: [G3, G7] }
```

Two properties make this a gate rather than a checklist: it can say **no** without a human's permission, and every gate emits a signed evidence artifact whose union is the promotion record.

> **Say it like this on G1, because it is the one they'll poke:** "A naive data-contract gate hard-blocks on population shift, and that's backwards for a retraining pipeline — a genuine shift is precisely the condition that should have *triggered* this retrain, so blocking on it means the pipeline refuses to do its job exactly when it's needed. The split I'd make is: shift in a feature the contract declares stable is a hard block, because that means our pipeline changed rather than the world; shift anywhere else routes to review with the PSI attached. Schema breaks and leakage always hard-block."

#### GitOps for the rollout

```text
train ──▶ MLFLOW: log run (params, metrics, dataset hash, signature)
             │      register model version, link lineage to the run
             ▼
          alias @champion moves to that version   (models:/churn-scorer@champion)
                                                          │ webhook / Argo Events
                                                          ▼
                      bot commits model URI + image DIGEST to the CONFIG repo
                                                          │
                                            Argo CD reconciles ──▶ Argo Rollouts
                                            AnalysisTemplate reads Prometheus
                                                          │
                                 rollback = git revert of that one commit
```

**Naming the registry, because "the registry" is doing real work in that diagram.** MLflow, which I've used. Two specifics worth having ready:

*Aliases, not stages.* `models:/churn-scorer@champion` is an **alias** — a named, movable pointer to an immutable version. The old `Staging`/`Production` **stage** transitions were deprecated in MLflow 2.9 and are gone in 3.x (verify against whichever version you actually run), and the reason matters more than the syntax: a stage was a mutable global enum with exactly one slot per name, so you could not express two champions, a per-region champion, or champion-and-challenger without abusing it. An alias you can have many of, move atomically, and point at from config. Champion/challenger becomes two aliases over the same registry, and the GitOps commit above carries the resolved *version*, not the alias, so a rollback is a revert rather than a race with whoever moves the alias next.

*What the registry stores that the artifact store does not.* S3 holds bytes. The registry holds the answer to "what is this, where did it come from, and is it allowed in prod": the source run with its parameters, metrics and dataset hash; the model **signature** — input/output schema and types, which is what makes the G5 parity check mechanisable rather than bespoke per model; the lineage back to the training snapshot; the aliases, tags and description trail; and the approval record. That is also why D11 insists registry metadata is backed up *with* the artifacts — weights you cannot identify are weights you cannot deploy, and the artifact bucket alone gives you the former without the latter.

Details that show you've run it: config repo separate from the app repo, or Argo CD's sync loop and CI fight each other; ApplicationSets to fan one template across environments and regions rather than hand-maintaining forty Applications; Kargo (or Image Updater plus PR automation) so you **build once and promote the digest** rather than rebuilding per environment; Argo Workflows for the training DAG itself, with GitHub Actions handling code-side CI and handing off anything needing an accelerator — do not run six-hour GPU training in a hosted Action runner.

| Stage | Runs | Budget |
|---|---|---|
| pre-commit | lint, type check, secret scan, notebook strip | seconds |
| PR | unit tests, transformation tests on a fixture, Checkov + Conftest on `plan.json`, `dvc repro` on a 1% sample, container build + SBOM + artifact scan | < 10 min |
| merge to main | full training on the pinned snapshot, G0–G4 | hours, GPU |
| pre-deploy | G5 parity through the container, G6 load test | ~20 min |
| deploy | G7 shadow, G8 canary with auto-abort | 24–72 h |
| nightly | drift/lineage reconciliation, IaC drift plan, cross-tenant probe, red-team suite | — |

#### Self-service without the console

The reason data scientists break IaC discipline is not indiscipline: the feedback loop is 45 minutes and the experiment is 5, notebooks are inherently imperative, most experiments genuinely are ephemeral, and the console never says "this is $28k a month". More process makes it worse. A paved road fixes it: a CLI or Backstage template (`mlp env create --gpu a100 --hours 8`) that opens a PR against the IaC repo or writes a custom resource a controller reconciles; Crossplane compositions so a six-line claim in their namespace produces the bucket, IAM role, nodepool and quota; Kueue quotas plus `ResourceQuota` and `LimitRange` so the blast radius is bounded by construction; hard TTLs on everything self-served; and the price shown in the same UI where they request it.

**Where I stop:** what I've actually run is fork-based CI/CD with a feature-contract subset assertion as a promotion gate at TrueBalance, and an end-to-end SageMaker MLOps platform at Tiger Analytics for an FCA-regulated bank with training, inference, drift detection and automated retraining. Argo CD, Argo Rollouts, Kargo, Crossplane, Kueue and Backstage are what I'd choose for this shape of estate — they are design, not operations, for me. My CI/CD, IaC and registry tooling in production has been GitHub Actions, Jenkins, Terraform, CloudFormation and MLflow.

> **Say it like this:** "I'd rather be precise about which half of that I've run. The gate chain, the parity assertion and the SageMaker platform are mine. The Argo CD and Kargo layer is the design I'd argue for, and I'd want you to weight it as design."

### D11. "Multi-region, HA and DR for AI services in enterprise SaaS"

**JD lines this answers:** *Enterprise SaaS with high availability and scalability*; *Security & Compliance*; *Infrastructure Management*.

**What is actually being scored:** whether you notice this is three questions bundled together — where the data may live, which model endpoints are legally callable per region, and what happens when either is unavailable — and whether you know a RAG index is stateful.

> **Say it like this:** "The failover most teams design is for the stateless half. The parts that actually decide your RTO are the vector index, the online feature store and the model registry — and if the standby region can't identify or pull the weights, the failover is theatre."

```text
   EU tenants                GLOBAL tenants               GOV tenants
       │                          │                            │
 ┌─────▼──────┐            ┌──────▼──────┐              ┌──────▼───────┐
 │ eu-central │  active-   │ ap-south-1  │              │ gov region   │
 │  full stack│◀─active───▶│  full stack │              │ isolated,    │
 └─────┬──────┘            └──────┬──────┘              │ no 3P API    │
       │                          │                     └──────┬───────┘
       │      gateway: region-aware routing + model allow-list │
       │      FAIL CLOSED on disallowed model (never spill)    │
       ▼                          ▼                            ▼
  index + traces + cache + evals + checkpoints stay in-region, per class
       │
  S3 CRR of CHUNK TEXT + MANIFEST (source of truth), not just vectors
```

**Residency covers more surfaces than people list.** Index, trace store, semantic cache, eval datasets, agent checkpoint tables and the inference endpoint. The trace store is the one that gets forgotten, and it holds full retrieved chunks — which is why the D7 tracing design redacts in a collector processor before export and stores document IDs and content hashes rather than bodies wherever the product allows. The agent checkpoint tables are the same problem wearing a different hat: they hold the full message state, so they are in scope for residency, retention and deletion requests exactly like the database.

**Which endpoints are legal where.** This is a policy artifact, not tribal knowledge: a versioned routing policy keyed on `(tenant_class, region, model, deployment_mode, subprocessor_status)`, reviewed by legal, enforced at the LLM gateway, with a CI test asserting no tenant class can reach a disallowed model.

```yaml
model_policy_version: 2026-09-01
tenant_classes:
  eu_standard:
    allowed_regions: [eu-central-1]
    allowed_models: [regional-hosted-a@2026-06-11, self-hosted-8b@v4]
    on_unavailable: fail_closed_then_degrade_in_region   # never spill cross-region
  gov:
    allowed_regions: [gov-1]
    allowed_models: [self-hosted-8b@v4]                  # no third-party API at all
    byok: required
  global_standard:
    allowed_regions: [ap-south-1, us-east-1]
    allowed_models: [vendor-large@2026-07-02, self-hosted-8b@v4]
```

The rule that matters: **a cross-region fallback during a provider outage is itself the residency breach.** Fail closed on authorization and residency; degrade gracefully on enrichment. Skip the reranker; never skip the filter or the region pin.

**Failing over a stateful RAG index.** Three options, and you must have measured the third:

| Approach | RPO | RTO | Cost | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Independent per-region index built from a replicated source of truth | ingest lag (minutes) | alias swap (seconds) | 2× index storage/compute | The default. Replicate **chunk text + manifest + tombstones**, not just vectors |
| Engine-native cross-region replica | seconds | seconds | high | Only if your engine genuinely supports it; verify per index type |
| Cold rebuild from source | 0 | **hours to days** | low | If your DR plan is "re-embed everything", your RTO is measured in days. Say the number out loud |

Two traps, and the first has a specific, checkable default behind it:

**Tombstone replication.** If deletes don't fail over, you resurrect documents someone exercised a deletion right over, which converts an availability event into a privacy incident. The concrete version on AWS: **S3 Cross-Region Replication does not replicate delete markers by default** — it is a per-rule opt-in (`DeleteMarkerReplication`), and a `DELETE` that specifies a version ID is *never* replicated at all. So a team that believes it "replicates the bucket" genuinely does resurrect deleted source documents on failover, and will rebuild the standby index from them. Turn the flag on, and add a reconciliation job that counts source objects against index vectors per region, because the flag only covers deletes made after you set it.

**Delete semantics inside the index.** Most ANN implementations soft-delete: the vector stays in the graph and is filtered at query time until compaction, so "deleted" and "unreachable" are not the same thing until the merge runs. For a deletion right you need the compaction to be a scheduled, evidenced job, not an emergent property of write volume — otherwise your proof of erasure is "probably, eventually".

**RTO/RPO per tier, with numbers — because a tier without a number cannot be tested.** These are the targets I'd propose on day one and then negotiate down against the cost of each, rather than inherit as folklore `[proposed targets, not measured on a real estate]`:

| Tier | Example workload | RTO | RPO | What has to be true to hit it |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|
| **1** | Customer-facing synchronous inference | **15 min** | **0** | Warm standby, digest-pinned images pre-cached in region, model artifacts cross-region replicated with Object Lock, registry metadata replicated with them, reserved GPU capacity or a declared degraded rung |
| **1** | RAG retrieval path behind that inference | **15 min** | **≤ 15 min** (ingest lag) | Only the independent per-region index meets this; a cold rebuild cannot |
| **2** | Agent runs in flight | **1 h** | **5 min** | Checkpoint tables replicated — *or* explicitly declare in-flight runs abandoned and re-driven from the idempotency key, which is cheaper and is usually the right answer |
| **2** | Batch / offline scoring | **4 h** | **24 h** | Re-run from the last snapshot; the snapshot's retention has to outlive the model |
| **3** | Experiment tracking, eval history, trace store | **72 h** | **24 h** | Nightly backup is enough. Say so, so nobody gold-plates it |

The one line in that table that must never be a target is the **online feature store rebuild**: it is a *measured* number, re-measured quarterly at production cardinality, and whatever it measures becomes the tier's RTO. An aspirational rebuild time is how you discover during an incident that your Tier-1 RTO is actually six hours.

**RTO/RPO per asset:**

| Asset | Requirement |
|---|---|
| Model artifacts | Versioned, immutable (Object Lock), cross-region replicated; RPO ≈ 0 |
| Registry metadata | Backed up **with** the artifacts — otherwise you have weights you cannot identify |
| Online feature store | Replicated, but the offline store is the source of truth; the online store must be rebuildable from it and you must have **measured** how long that takes (usually hours) |
| Offline store / training snapshots | Retention must outlive any model referencing them — a short `VACUUM`/retention policy silently deletes the snapshot your "reproducible" pipeline depends on |
| Container images | Replicated registry, digest-pinned, pre-cached in the standby region |
| Terraform state | Versioned and replicated; you cannot rebuild a region without it |
| Agent checkpoints / traces | Region-pinned, retention-bounded, in scope for deletion requests |

**Health checks must test inference**, not `/healthz` — a region whose model failed to load will pass a TCP check all day. And in 2026 the binding constraint on active-active is that **GPU capacity is regionally scarce**: either reserve capacity in the secondary or explicitly accept degraded capability there, which is a product decision, not an infrastructure one.

**Degradation ladder when the provider is down.** Design it before the incident and make each rung independently testable:

```text
1 full model, fresh features        ← normal
2 full model, cached features       ← feature store degraded (mark staleness)
3 last-known-good model version     ← new model misbehaving
4 smaller / CPU / self-hosted model ← provider or GPU capacity lost
5 precomputed batch score for this entity   ← hours old, but real
6 rules / population baseline
7 static safe default + explicit downstream flag ("route to manual review")
```

The non-negotiable: **the caller is told which rung it got** — `model_version` and `degraded: true` in the response envelope — so downstream systems and the audit log can make their own risk decision. Silently returning a rules-based score as if it were the model is how you get a regulatory problem rather than an availability one. Precompute is the underrated rung: a nightly batch scoring job into a KV store turns a total GPU outage into "yesterday's scores."

Around all of it: timeouts derived from the SLO, with **each downstream hop given a shorter timeout than its caller, so the deepest call cannot outlive the request that started it** — the budget shrinks as you go inward, and any hop that can exceed its caller's deadline is doing work nobody will read; retries only on idempotent retryable failures with exponential backoff and full jitter and a retry budget capped at roughly 10% of requests, because three retries at three layers is 27× load on a struggling backend; circuit breakers to give the failing service room to recover; bulkheads so one slow provider can't exhaust the shared pool; and load shedding by priority before you queue, because an unbounded inference queue converts a capacity problem into a total outage.

**Game day, quarterly:** delete the model registry entry and the primary-region artifact bucket in staging and try to serve traffic. A documented failover that has never been executed is a document, not a capability.

**Where I stop:** my regulated-data experience is real — HIPAA-class medical-report pipelines at ResMed and an FCA-regulated bank platform at Tiger Analytics — but that was single-region. Multi-region active-active, formal RTO/RPO ownership and a run game day are design for me, not operations. I have not owned an RTO target or executed a region failover.

> **Say it like this:** "I want to be clear about the boundary, because it's what makes the rest of it credible. The regulated-data work is mine — HIPAA-class pipelines at ResMed, an FCA-regulated bank platform at Tiger. But that was single-region, and I haven't owned formal RTO or RPO targets or run a failover. So treat the residency model and the degradation ladder as design, and push me on the parts I've actually operated: shared multi-container endpoints, drift monitoring, and the promotion gates."

### D12. "500 models, $2M a year of inference. Cut it 40% without breaking SLOs."

**JD lines this answers:** *Resource Optimization: manage GPU/CPU utilisation to minimise cloud costs while maintaining low-latency inference*; *Solution cost optimisations and design to cost*.

**What is actually being scored:** whether you start with arithmetic and attribution, or with a list of tricks. And whether you understand the political half, because the technical half is easy.

> **Say it like this:** "I wouldn't commit to 40% in the room, and I'd say so. What I'd commit to is that in two weeks you'd have the bill attributed per model, per team and per tenant, with allocated-versus-utilised GPU-hours next to it. I won't put a number on the saving before I've seen that breakdown — but the shape I'd expect is that most of the headroom is in idle and long-tail capacity rather than in the models anyone is defending, and that is usually the cheapest 40% to find. Cost is `price per accelerator-hour × accelerator-hours consumed ÷ useful predictions produced`. Three independent levers: buy cheaper, use less, produce more per unit. Most teams only ever pull the first, and buying a committed-use discount on waste is the classic wrong first move."

#### Questions before any answer

Is that spend GPU or CPU, and what fraction is training versus serving? Of the 500 models, what's the QPS distribution — I'd expect a handful of head models and a long tail of near-idle ones. What are the actual SLOs, per tier, and are they written down or folklore? Is the bill attributable per model today? Is any of it LLM token spend through a provider API? And what's the utilisation floor we've committed to?

#### Where the money is — a worked model

`[illustrative]` figures: an order-of-magnitude shape to do arithmetic on in the room, not a claim about any real estate.

| Line item | Annual | % | Driver | Primary lever | Realistic saving | Effort | Risk |
|---|---:|---:|---|---|---:|---|---|
| Long-tail model serving (≈380 models, always-on dedicated capacity, <1 QPS) | $760k | 38% | ≈380 models pinned across ~110 always-on small accelerators at ~$0.79/hr, ~4% duty cycle | Consolidate onto multi-model / multi-LoRA shared pools | $530k | M | cold-start p99 on LRU miss |
| Head model serving (12 models, real traffic) | $420k | 21% | under-batched, no prefix cache, FP16 | Batching knobs at the knee, prefix caching, FP8 + FP8 KV | $130k | M | needs an eval gate on quantisation |
| Idle / orphaned (dev endpoints, notebooks, zombie clusters) | $300k | 15% | nobody owns them | TTLs, scale-to-zero, decommission policy | $260k | **L** | political, not technical |
| Batch / offline scoring | $220k | 11% | on-demand instances, online-shaped code | Spot + checkpointing, async contract, ARM64 | $120k | M | needs idempotent jobs |
| Provider API tokens | $180k | 9% | uncached, verbose outputs | Prefix caching, output caps, batch tier, small-first routing | $80k | L–M | routing must be measured |
| Storage, egress, cross-AZ | $120k | 6% | checkpoints, cross-AZ all-reduce and fetches | Tiering, co-locate data + compute + registry | $30k | L | — |
| **Total** | **$2.00M** | | | | **~$1.15M identified** | | |

You do not need every lever. Identifying $1.15M of headroom to deliver $800k means you can drop the two riskiest and still land it — and being able to say *that* is what makes the number credible.

#### The arithmetic behind the three biggest lines

**Long-tail consolidation.** 380 models pinned to always-on capacity at roughly 4% duty cycle is the definition of paying for idle silicon — you are renting the accelerator for 8,760 hours a year and using about 350 of them. A shared pool loads and evicts models like a cache; LoRA multiplexing is the modern version, one base in HBM with many adapters swapped per request at about 1% of the memory cost of separate replicas, at a 5–20% throughput penalty versus a single-adapter batch. The trade you must state: **cold start moves from per-deploy to per-model on first request**, which is a tail-latency landmine — so tier it. Keep the top ~20 models on dedicated capacity with their own SLO, put the rest on the shared pool with a documented, *lower* p99 commitment and a pinned-resident set for anything customer-facing.

**Batching and cache on the head models.** Same caveat as the table: assume ~$9.80/GPU-hr on-demand for an H100 and substitute your actual rate — reserved, committed-use and neocloud pricing all land well below that, sometimes by 3–4× — because the shape of the argument is what matters here, not the rate card.

```text
Decode is memory-bandwidth bound, not FLOP bound:
  steps/s ≈ HBM bandwidth / model bytes
  70B @ FP8 = 70 GB on H100 SXM (≈3.35 TB/s) → ~48 steps/s theoretical at batch 1

So batching is the master lever: batch=64 reads the same 70 GB once and emits 64 tokens.

KV cache sets the concurrency ceiling:
  KV bytes/token = 2 × n_kv_heads × head_dim × n_layers × bytes_per_elem
  4×H100 = 320 GB; weights 70 GB; overhead 20 GB → 230 GB free
  FP16 KV @ 4k context: 1.31 GB/req → ~175 concurrent
  FP8  KV @ 4k context: 0.66 GB/req → ~350 concurrent    ← doubles capacity, no new hardware

$ per 1M output tokens = GPU $/hr ÷ (tok/s × 3600) × 1e6
  4×H100 @ $9.80/hr = $39.20/hr; ~3,400 tok/s aggregate → 12.24M tok/hr → $3.20/1M
  At 30% duty cycle, multiply by 3.3 → $10.56/1M   ← duty cycle, not price, is the story
```

Little's Law makes the SLO conversation concrete, and the thing to say out loud is that **the aggregate is not a constant**. At batch 256 the pool does ~3,400 tok/s aggregate, so each user sees ~13 tok/s — fine for async, poor for chat. Drop to batch 32 and aggregate falls to roughly 1,200 tok/s because you are no longer amortising the weight read, but each user now sees ~37 tok/s. You are trading total throughput for per-user interactivity. Throughput and interactivity are the same dial pointed in opposite directions, so **pick the SLO first, derive max concurrency, then derive replica count** — and run separate pools for chat and batch rather than one compromise pool.

**Prefix caching arithmetic on the API line:** on Anthropic-shaped pricing a cached-input read is roughly 0.1× and the cache write costs 1.25×, so you are ahead from the **second request onward** — `1.25 + 0.1 < 2.0` is a write plus one read beating two uncached requests. Other providers discount cached input differently and some newer models read cache far cheaper still, so check the rate card before modelling it rather than carrying these multipliers around. On RAG and agent traffic with a stable system prompt that's 50–90% of input token cost. The asynchronous batch tier at 50% of standard price covers everything not latency-bound, and is the single laziest saving on the list.

**Small-first routing, with the caveat that stops it being a disaster:** a cheap model handling 70–90% of traffic with escalation on low confidence blends the cost toward the cheap model's price — but it must be gated on a *measured* escalation rate, because a router that escalates 45% of the time costs more than the big model alone, since you pay twice.

#### What you measure, before and after

Instrument first, and pre-register the guardrails so "we saved money" cannot quietly mean "we broke p99."

| Metric | Why |
|---|---|
| **Allocated vs utilised GPU-hours (the ratio)** | The platform team's north star. Absolute GPU-hours tell you nothing |
| $ per 1k predictions; $ per 1M tokens split input / output / **cached** | The unit economics that go on the dashboard, per model, per tenant |
| $ per **successful** task (agents) | Retries and failed trajectories are pure waste that a per-request metric hides |
| p99, and for LLMs TTFT and TPOT separately | They have different causes and different fixes; one "latency" number hides which moved |
| SLO error-budget burn per service | The veto. Any optimisation that burns budget is reverted, no debate |
| Cold-start rate and LRU miss latency on shared pools | The specific harm the consolidation lever causes |

⚠ Two measurement traps. `nvidia-smi` utilisation is a *residency* metric — it reports the fraction of time at least one kernel was resident, so a tiny kernel looping forever reports 100%. Use DCGM `SM_ACTIVE`, occupancy, and achieved HBM bandwidth. And low SM utilisation on LLM decode is *expected*, because decode is bandwidth-bound; the meaningful number there is tokens/sec per GPU-dollar. Neither OpenCost nor Kubecost derives per-pod GPU utilisation on its own — you need DCGM joined to pod labels to separate allocated from used. OpenCost 1.121 (July 2026) added AI inference cost metering — notable not because token costing is new but because it is the first time per-token spend sits in the *same allocation model* as pod cost, so one dashboard covers both halves and per-team attribution stops being two joins. Token-level costing on its own has been in LiteLLM, Langfuse, OpenLLMetry and Helicone for a while.

#### The political reality — this is the half that fails

1. **Showback before chargeback.** Publish per-team cost with no financial consequence for a quarter and fix the attribution bugs while they're free. Going straight to chargeback with wrong numbers destroys trust in the platform permanently, and you only get one attempt.
2. **Never take capacity without giving back data.** "You are allocated 8 GPUs and used 0.7 GPU-equivalents last month" is an argument. "We're cutting you to 4" is a war.
3. **Let teams keep the saving.** Budget carry-forward, or first call on the freed capacity. If cost reduction is confiscation, everyone hides their usage in a shared untagged cluster and your attribution dies.
4. **Make the paved road cheaper than the console.** Enforcement is a tax; a self-service path with TTLs, quotas and the price shown at request time is a product.
5. **Untagged is unschedulable.** An admission webhook rejecting pods without `team`, `model`, `cost-center` and `env` sounds harsh and is the only thing that works — retroactive tagging never happens.
6. **Get exec cover for exactly one unpopular policy.** Mine would be: any endpoint with no traffic for 30 days is scaled to zero after a two-week notice and an owner sign-off, and deleted after 90. That single policy is usually the largest line in the table, and it is the only one that needs air cover.
7. **Sequence it so the first win is uncontroversial.** Idle and orphans first — nobody defends a zombie endpoint — which buys you the credibility to touch the head models later.

> **Say it like this, and don't inflate it:** "The closest thing I've done to this is at ResMed, where I ran multi-container SageMaker endpoints on our internal MLOps platform so several models shared infrastructure instead of each holding its own, which cut inference cost while holding the per-model SLAs. That's this exact lever — the long-tail consolidation row — but at team scale, not 500 models, and I don't have a percentage I can quote for it publicly. What I'd bring is the method: attribute first, rank by effort-to-saving, pre-register the SLO guardrail, and never buy a discount on waste."

**Where I stop:** I have not owned a multi-million-dollar inference budget, and I haven't used Monte Carlo or any commercial data-observability product — the monitoring I've built is Datadog dashboards auto-provisioned from Snowflake feature statistics, Prometheus/Grafana, and CloudWatch.

## 5. Domain primer — the Databricks Lakehouse AI stack

### The rule that governs every sentence in this section

You have ~1.5 years of **Azure** Databricks — Spark, Deequ data-quality checks, Azure Data Factory orchestration of drift jobs. That is real and it is ETL/DQ work, not Lakehouse-platform ownership. The recruiter already has in writing that you have **not** used Unity Catalog, Mosaic AI Agent Framework, Databricks Vector Search, Monte Carlo, or AWS Bedrock in production. Round 2 is where an interviewer will probe exactly those five.

The winning move is not to dodge and not to bluff. It is to be **fluent in the vocabulary, precise about the mechanics, and explicit about the boundary**. A candidate who can say "here is how UC's three-level namespace and governed tags work, here is the governance layer I have actually operated, and here is the specific thing I'd expect to bite me in week one" reads as *senior*. A candidate who says "yes I've used Unity Catalog" and then fumbles the model-signature requirement reads as *finished*.

> **Say it like this (the frame, deploy it once, early, unprompted):**
> "Before we go deep — let me set the boundary honestly so you can calibrate, and I'd rather over-disclose than have you find it later. My Databricks time is about a year and a half on Azure Databricks: Spark, Deequ-based data-quality checks, drift jobs orchestrated from Data Factory. Five things in your JD I have not operated, and I told the recruiter this in writing: Unity Catalog, the Mosaic AI Agent Framework, Databricks Vector Search, Monte Carlo, and Bedrock in production. What I have operated is the same set of problems on AWS and open source — SageMaker MLOps end to end for a regulated bank, MLflow, feature stores, drift monitoring, pgvector and FAISS retrieval, Terraform and Airflow, and a knowledge graph in production that I'm going to want to tell you about because it's in your JD too. So when you ask about a Databricks component I'll tell you what it does, what I'd do with it, and which system I've actually run that's the closest analogue. If I haven't run it, I'll say so."

That paragraph, said once, buys you permission to talk confidently about everything below.

**Lead your platform credibility with the parity failure, not with a tool list.** The single most persuasive thing in your record for this role is the TrueBalance train/serve feature-parity collapse — 4,001 offline features against 28 keys actually present in the real-time payload, silently imputed to defaults, nothing raising. It is written out in full under *MLflow → Signatures* below. If the interviewer opens with "tell me about a hard platform problem," go there first. It establishes that your platform instincts are earned rather than read, and everything you say afterwards about signatures, contracts and promotion gates lands differently.

### The 2026 naming drift — cheapest depth signal in the room

Most public material is 2024–25 vintage. Databricks renamed nearly everything in 2025–26. Knowing **both** names costs nothing and instantly separates you from someone who read a blog last night. Phrase it as *"X — which I think is now called Y."*

| Old name (what tutorials say) | Current name (2026) |
|---|---|
| Delta Live Tables (DLT) | **Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines** (docs path `/ldp/`) |
| Databricks Workflows | **Lakeflow Jobs** |
| Databricks Asset Bundles (DABs) | **Declarative Automation Bundles** — acronym kept, `databricks.yml` unchanged |
| Lakehouse Monitoring | **Data profiling**, under **Data quality monitoring** (now in the UC docs tree) |
| Mosaic AI Vector Search | **Databricks AI Search** |
| Mosaic AI Gateway | **Databricks AI Gateway → Unity AI Gateway** |
| Mosaic AI Agent Framework | **Custom Agents** — author with `ResponsesAgent`, deploy on Model Serving or Databricks Apps |
| Mosaic AI Model Training | **Databricks Model Training / AI Runtime** |
| Online Tables | **Online Feature Stores**, on **Lakebase** |

Two rows in that table need a caveat rather than an arrow, and volunteering the caveat is worth more than the row:

- ⚠ **Agent Bricks is not a rename of the Agent Framework.** Agent Bricks is a *separate, adjacent family* of managed and declarative agent offerings — **Knowledge Assistant** and **Supervisor Agent** are the two to name. The authoring framework you write code against is **Custom Agents**, using MLflow's `ResponsesAgent`. Custom agents can be *orchestrated by* a Supervisor Agent, which is why people conflate them. Getting this right in one sentence is a better depth signal than the whole rest of the table.
- ⚠ **Delta Sharing → OpenSharing is not a straight rename either.** OpenSharing (announced mid-2026, now a Linux Foundation project) is positioned as the Delta Sharing protocol *extended for the agentic era* — sharing agent skills, models and unstructured data, plus Iceberg REST Catalog client support. Delta Sharing documentation and branding still exist alongside it. Say "the next evolution of the protocol", not "the new name".

⚠ **The trap: "Lakewatch".** If an interviewer says Lakewatch they do *not* mean model monitoring. Lakewatch is Databricks' agentic **SIEM / security lakehouse**, launched early 2026; the **Panther Labs acquisition mid-2026 folded Panther's SOC workflows and detection engine into it**. Note the direction — Lakewatch came first, Panther was folded in, not the other way round. Confusing Lakewatch with Lakehouse Monitoring is an instant tell. Lakehouse Monitoring became **data profiling**. Likewise **Lakebase** is the managed Postgres-compatible OLTP layer (now powering Online Feature Stores and Agent Memory), not a warehouse.
