### (b) The exact scripts

**1. Asked directly: "Have you used Unity Catalog?"**

> **Say it like this:**
> "No — and I told the recruiter that in writing, so let me be exact about what I do have. My Databricks time is Azure Databricks, about a year and a half, and it was Spark plus Deequ data-quality work with Data Factory orchestration. I wasn't doing governance work in that workspace at all — my surface was Spark jobs and quality checks, so I never touched the catalog layer. What I have operated on the governance side is Snowflake's role model and object hierarchy, schema design against it, and IAM and S3 path scoping under Athena and Iceberg catalogs. The concepts transfer: a three-level `catalog.schema.object` namespace, storage credentials and external locations instead of raw bucket grants, tags driving policy instead of per-object grants. But I want to be straight that I have not run Lake Formation or any tag-based policy engine, so I'd be learning Unity Catalog's governance surface as a *product*, not as an idea. The parts I'd treat as genuinely new are ABAC policies with governed tags, volumes replacing DBFS mounts, and UC governing models and functions and now agents rather than only tables. Two things I already know will catch me: a model version won't register to UC without a signature, and row filters or column masks kill time travel and CLONE for anyone not in the policy's EXCEPT list — which is a reproducibility problem you have to design for rather than discover."

**2. Asked to design something that needs Vector Search.**

> **Say it like this:**
> "I'd design it against Databricks AI Search and I'd be upfront that my hands-on retrieval work is pgvector, FAISS and Chroma, plus a hybrid vector-and-metadata retrieval pipeline at ResMed. Concretely: source documents chunked into a Delta table in Unity Catalog, then a **Delta Sync index with Databricks-managed embeddings** so I don't own a reindex job — that is the main thing the managed product buys me over the pgvector setup I have run, where I had to build and monitor the reindexer myself. Two design decisions I'd flag before writing anything. First, the index is HNSW over L2 distance, so if I want cosine behaviour I normalise embeddings at write time. Second, and this is the one I'd raise loudest: **AI Search has endpoint and index ACLs but no row- or column-level permissions**, so a row filter on the source table does not propagate into the index, and the index is queried as a service principal, not as the end user. If this is multi-tenant, tenancy has to be enforced server-side — a `filters` argument on the retrieval call keyed on a tenant column, never post-filtering in application code, because post-filtering can hand you an empty page while the right rows sat just outside `num_results`. And honestly, for tenancy specifically I'd argue for an index per tenant above a certain customer count, because a filter that eliminates ninety-nine per cent of the index fights HNSW — the traversal keeps landing on candidates it has to discard, so you over-fetch and pay in latency or lose recall. Filters are the right tool for facets like doc type and year; partitioning is the right tool for tenancy. If the corpus is large enough to need a storage-optimized endpoint I'd also be trading away continuous sync and accepting roughly 250 milliseconds more latency, so I'd want the freshness SLA before choosing."

**3. Asked about the Mosaic AI Agent Framework.**

> **Say it like this:**
> "I have not used it. I've built the equivalent with LangGraph and MCP — at TrueBalance I built core parts of an internal developer assistant on the Model Context Protocol, tying Jira, GitHub, Jenkins, AWS, Grafana and Slack into one interface, with each task running in an isolated Git workspace. So I know the agent problem; I don't know the Databricks packaging of it. From reading: what used to be the Mosaic AI Agent Framework is now the Custom Agents surface, and the authoring class is `ResponsesAgent` — a pyfunc subclass aligned to the OpenAI Responses API rather than Chat Completions, the practical difference being that it returns intermediate tool-calling steps and annotations, so citations survive. It's framework-agnostic, so a LangGraph graph is still the payload. I'd separate that from Agent Bricks, which is a different family — Knowledge Assistant and Supervisor Agent, declarative rather than something you write code against, though a Supervisor Agent can orchestrate custom agent endpoints and Genie and UC functions. The detail I'd expect to lose a day to is `resources` at log time: you declare the vector index, serving endpoints and UC functions the agent needs, and Databricks mints short-lived scoped credentials for exactly those. If you forget one, it works in the notebook and 403s in production, which is exactly the class of bug I've spent my career trying to make loud instead of silent. And I'd check the deployment target with the team, because the recommended path appears to be moving from `agents.deploy()` on Model Serving toward Databricks Apps with `AgentServer` — although I've seen no published end-of-life for the Model Serving path, so I wouldn't rewrite anything on that basis alone."

**4. Asked about petabyte scale.**

> **Say it like this:**
> "I haven't worked at petabyte scale and I'm not going to claim it. My largest datasets have been hundreds of thousands to low millions of rows in the ML paths — a hundred and nine thousand credit-bureau tradelines, a hundred thousand production SMS through a knowledge-graph parser — plus Spark and Deequ data-quality jobs on Azure Databricks, and I don't have a reliable volume figure for those, so I'd rather not guess at one. What I'd say transfers is the discipline rather than the volume: partitioning and file-size behaviour, why data skipping only indexes the first thirty-two columns so column order matters on wide tables, why small-file explosion is usually the real cost problem rather than compute, and why you push predicates down instead of scaling the cluster up. Where I'd expect to be genuinely out of my depth is shuffle behaviour and skew handling at that size, and cost decisions that only bite at petabyte scale. If that's a hard requirement for this role I'd rather you know now."

**5. Asked what you'd do first with their Databricks estate.**

> **Say it like this:**
> "I wouldn't build anything in the first fortnight. I'd measure. Three things in parallel. One, spend on `system.billing.usage` joined to `list_prices` and grouped by SKU and job — I want to know within a week whether scheduled jobs are running on all-purpose clusters, what fraction of compute is unattributable because it's untagged, and where Photon is on and not earning its multiplier, which since it's on by default now is mostly a question about UDF-heavy pipelines. Two, the promotion path: for every model currently serving traffic, which artifact is live, which alias points at it, whether the training code that produced it is in Git, and whether anyone can actually reproduce it — which also means checking VACUUM retention and whether ABAC policies are quietly blocking time travel on the tables we'd retrain from. In my experience the answer to that question is where the real risk is, not in the modelling. Three, monitoring coverage: which endpoints have inference tables enabled, which models have a data-profiling monitor with a baseline that is actually the training set rather than last month's traffic, whether anyone has turned on the fairness metrics, and how ground-truth labels get joined back given the label lag. Then I'd write down what I found and agree the top three with the team before touching anything, because on a platform team the wrong first change is more expensive than a slow one."

**6. Asked what you'd need to learn, and how fast.**

> **Say it like this:**
> "Concretely: Unity Catalog's operational side — securable hierarchy, external locations, ABAC policies, and the migration story if you're still partly on Hive metastore, which matters because new workspaces go UC-only from the end of this month. Databricks AI Search as a product rather than a concept. The agent stack — `ResponsesAgent`, the resources model, and whether you're on Model Serving or Apps. And the cost model in enough depth to be trusted with a budget conversation. My honest estimate is that I'm useful in weeks two to three on pipelines, CI/CD and monitoring, because DABs is Terraform-shaped, expectations are Deequ-shaped, and MLflow I already use daily — and I'm not the person you ask about Unity Catalog governance design for a couple of months. What makes that credible rather than optimistic is that I've done this migration once already: I came into Tiger Analytics and designed an end-to-end MLOps platform on SageMaker for an FCA-regulated bank — training, inference, drift detection, CI/CD, automated retraining — and AWS showcased it at re:Invent. The components are different here; the shape of the problem is one I've solved."

**7. Asked about AWS Bedrock (the JD says "AWS Bedrock preferable" and "AWS hosted data platform preferable" — expect this one).**

> **Say it like this:**
> "I have not run Bedrock in production, and that's one of the five things I flagged to the recruiter in writing. What I have run is the rest of that stack on AWS. At ResMed I built a production GenAI query-routing assistant and a RAG medical-report pipeline on AWS over HIPAA-class data, with hybrid vector-and-metadata retrieval and evaluation harnesses with human review — I just wasn't calling Bedrock for the model layer. On the serving side I've run SageMaker endpoints across real-time, serverless and async, multi-container endpoints sharing infrastructure across models to cut cost while holding per-model SLAs, and a Lambda-plus-SQS real-time scorer at TrueBalance with ARM64 images in ECR and S3-versioned artifacts.
> On Bedrock specifically I can talk about the mechanics even though I haven't operated them: the on-demand versus provisioned-throughput split, which is the same decision as pay-per-token versus provisioned throughput in Foundation Model APIs — on-demand for exploration, provisioned when you need committed capacity and predictable latency, and provisioned being the path for customised models. Model access has to be requested per model per region before anything works, which is the classic first-day surprise. And the honest Databricks bridge is that on this stack I probably wouldn't call Bedrock directly at all — I'd register it as an **external model** behind the AI Gateway, so rate limits, guardrails, usage and cost tracking and payload logging are uniform across Bedrock, an internal endpoint and anything else. That's a better architecture than scattering SDK calls, and it means the thing I'd have to learn is the gateway configuration rather than a new inference API."

**Bonus A — asked about Monte Carlo (the JD says it's preferable).**

> **Say it like this:**
> "I haven't used Monte Carlo. The problem it solves — automated freshness, volume, schema and distribution monitors over warehouse tables, with lineage-aware incident routing so you get one alert instead of forty downstream ones — is a problem I have solved with Deequ on Azure Databricks and with a drift-monitoring utility I built at ResMed that ingested data-scientist-authored thresholds and slice definitions and auto-provisioned Datadog dashboards and alerts from Snowflake feature statistics. What Monte Carlo adds on top of what I built is the automatic anomaly baselines and the lineage-based deduplication of alerts. If you're already running it I'd be productive on it quickly; I'd just be learning the product, not the discipline."

**Bonus B — the likelier version of that question: "design data observability across our lakehouse."**

This is a *design* prompt, not an honesty prompt, and you can answer it entirely from things you have built plus platform primitives you can name precisely. Draw the layers on the CoderPad.

```text
              ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  ingest      │  Lakeflow pipeline: bronze → silver → gold   │
              │  EXPECTATIONS inline, ON VIOLATION per tier  │
              │    bronze: expect (warn)  — observe only     │
              │    silver: expect_or_drop — quarantine table │
              │    gold:   expect_or_fail — stop the update  │
              └──────────────────┬──────────────────────────┘
                                 │  metrics
                                 ▼
              ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  measure     │  event log (UC table)  +  data profiling     │
              │    profile metrics table   (per col/window)  │
              │    drift metrics table     (PSI, KS, JS...)  │
              │    inference profile       (+ fairness)      │
              └──────────────────┬──────────────────────────┘
                                 │  SQL
                                 ▼
              ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  route       │  one alerting layer, severity by tier        │
              │  dedupe on UC lineage: alert the ROOT table  │
              │  not the 40 downstream ones                  │
              └─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

> **Say it like this:**
> "Four layers, and the ordering matters more than the tooling. **Layer one, constraints at write time** — expectations inline in the Lakeflow pipeline, with the violation policy varying by tier. Bronze warns because I want to see the badness, not hide it; silver drops into a quarantine table because I want the good rows to flow; gold fails the update because nothing downstream should ever read a broken gold table. The thing I'd say loudly to the team is that warn is the default and warn still writes the bad rows, which is not what people assume when they add their first expectation.
> **Layer two, measurement** — expectation metrics land in the event log, which is a UC-backed queryable table, and data profiling gives me the profile metrics table and the drift metrics table on top. So freshness, volume, null rates, distinct counts and distribution drift are all SQL, not a vendor UI. For scored tables I'd use inference profiles so I get model quality with delayed labels and the fairness metrics in the same place.
> **Layer three, routing** — this is the part people skip, and it's the part Monte Carlo actually sells. One broken upstream table produces forty downstream alerts. UC captures lineage automatically from query plans, table-level and column-level, so I'd use `system.access.table_lineage` to collapse an incident to its root and alert once on that. That's the lineage-aware deduplication, built rather than bought.
> **Layer four, ownership** — every monitor has a named owner and a documented action, or it gets deleted. I've watched dashboards nobody opens absorb an entire quality programme.
> And I'd be clear about where this comes from: I built roughly this shape twice, with Deequ on Azure Databricks and with a Python and IaC drift utility at ResMed that read data-scientist-authored thresholds and slice definitions and auto-provisioned Datadog dashboards and alerts from Snowflake feature statistics. What Databricks gives me that I had to hand-build is the inline violation policy and the drift table. What I'd still be building is layer three."

**Bonus C — the Knowledge Graph play.** Full script under *Knowledge Graph on Databricks* above. Do not wait to be asked; if the conversation touches RAG, retrieval, unstructured data or "varied data sources", steer into it. It is the one topic in this round where you are on the front foot.

### What I would verify in week one

Say this list out loud if the conversation stalls. Asking the right questions of an estate you have not seen is worth more than pretending you have seen it — and every item below is a real failure mode, not a generic checklist.

**Governance and catalog**
1. Are all workspaces on Unity Catalog, or is there a Hive metastore still in play — and if so, is the plan UCX or HMS federation? (New workspaces go UC-only from 30 September 2026.)
2. How many metastores, and therefore where can lineage and queries *not* cross?
3. Are we on classic per-table row filters and column masks, or on ABAC with governed tags? If per-table, how many tables and who maintains them?
4. Which tables are managed vs external — because that decides whether predictive optimization is doing our compaction for us or nobody is.
5. Are we federating any external sources — Snowflake, Postgres, SQL Server — and if so, which predicates actually push down and which are quietly network transfers?

**Models and promotion**
6. For every model currently serving traffic: which alias points at which version, and is the producing code in Git?
7. Do we promote code or artifacts across environments, and is that a decision or an accident?
8. Are there registered models without signatures — or, more likely, does anything still assume MLflow stages?
9. What is the rollback procedure for a bad model version, and when was it last exercised?

**Serving and cost**
10. Which endpoints are pay-per-token and which are provisioned throughput, and does the split match production vs experimentation?
11. Which endpoints have scale-to-zero on, and does any of them have a user-facing latency SLA that a cold start would breach?
12. Are any models sitting on GPU `workload_type` that don't need one, and is `workload_size` set from measured p95 concurrency or from a guess?
13. What fraction of DBUs is all-purpose compute running scheduled work?
14. What fraction of usage is unattributable because clusters are untagged or serverless has no budget policy?
15. Photon is on by default now — so where is it on and *not* earning its multiplier, i.e. which pipelines are mostly Python UDFs? (The query profile's percentage-of-task-time-in-Photon answers this.)

**Data quality and monitoring**
16. Which pipelines have expectations, and what fraction are `warn` — i.e. are we writing known-bad rows and calling that monitored?
17. Which models have an inference profile, and is the baseline the training set or just an earlier traffic window?
18. Are we computing fairness metrics — predictive parity, predictive equality, equal opportunity, statistical parity — on any scored population, and who actually reads them?
19. How do ground-truth labels get joined back, and what is the label lag? Given that lag, how far back do we need history — and was the baseline properly backfilled when the profile was created, since a profile only looks back 30 days from creation and the first window can be partial?
20. Do we alert on drift metrics, or only produce a dashboard nobody opens? Is anyone tracking PSI per feature against a threshold, or is it all eyeballed?

**GenAI and retrieval**
21. Which AI Search indexes exist, Delta Sync or direct access, managed or self-managed embeddings — and are self-managed ones stuck that way? (They cannot be converted.)
22. Are embeddings normalised, given the index uses L2?
23. How is multi-tenancy enforced in retrieval, since the index does not inherit row filters — server-side filters, or an index per tenant? And has anyone measured what the tenant filter does to recall?
24. Are agent `resources` declared at log time, or do we find out in production?

**Reproducibility**
25. What is `deletedFileRetentionDuration` on the tables we retrain from, and has anyone run VACUUM in a way that already destroyed the time travel we'd need to reproduce a model?
26. Separately: do those tables carry ABAC row filters or column masks? Because if so, time travel and CLONE fail for anyone not in the `EXCEPT` list — so the reproducibility path needs an exempted ETL service principal by design, not as a discovery.
27. Is anything deployed outside DABs — and if so, what is the manual step nobody has written down?

### 30 rapid-fire Databricks Q&A

| # | Question | Tight answer |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | How do you promote a model to Production? | Trap — in UC there are **no stages**. Set an **alias** (`@champion`). Stages were deprecated in MLflow 2.9 and don't exist in the UC registry. Recommended pattern is promoting **code** through dev/staging/prod and retraining. |
| 2 | Why would a UC model registration fail? | **Missing model signature.** Mandatory in UC. |
| 3 | Is an external location a catalog-level object? | No. Storage credentials, external locations, connections, shares and recipients are **metastore-level**, outside `catalog.schema.object`. |
| 4 | Difference between a storage credential and an external location? | Credential = the identity (IAM role / Azure Access Connector). External location = credential **+** a URI path. You grant on the location, not the bucket. |
| 5 | What replaces DBFS mounts? | **UC volumes**, `/Volumes/cat/sch/vol/...`, with `READ VOLUME` / `WRITE VOLUME`. |
| 6 | Do column tags inherit from the table? | **No.** Column tags must be applied directly; everything else inherits from catalog/schema. |
| 7 | Can a GRANT policy revoke access? | No — **GRANT policies only add**, and their scope is catalog or schema only. Removal is `REVOKE` on the underlying grant plus the policy's `EXCEPT` clause; the ABAC surface also references **DENY policies** as the counterpart — flag that as "I'd check the current status". |
| 8 | Row filters vs ABAC? | Classic row filters/column masks are UDFs attached **per table**. ABAC policies attach at **catalog, schema OR table** scope and apply by tag; Databricks recommends the **highest applicable level**, which is what stops policy count scaling with table count. (Catalog/schema-only is true of **GRANT** policies.) |
| 9 | ABAC quotas? | **10,000** policies per metastore, **100** per catalog or schema, **50** per table, **20** principals per policy (`TO` + `EXCEPT`), **3** conditions per `MATCH COLUMNS`. |
| 10 | Which ABAC attribute functions exist? | `has_identity_attribute_value()` and `has_identity_attribute_tag_match()` — **only** in the `WHEN` clause of column mask policies, not in `MATCH COLUMNS`, not in GRANT or DENY. Catalog Explorer can't author them; SQL only. |
| 11 | Gotcha with ABAC and reproducibility? | **Time travel queries fail** and **deep/shallow CLONE isn't supported** on tables with active row filters or column masks. Workaround is an `EXCEPT`-exempted service principal — design it in. |
| 12 | When is column lineage lost? | When source or target is referenced **by path rather than table name**, and UDFs obscure column mapping. Lineage is also per-metastore, never cross-region. |
| 13 | My agent works in the notebook and 403s in production. | You didn't declare `resources=[DatabricksVectorSearchIndex(...), DatabricksServingEndpoint(...)]` at `log_model`, so no scoped credentials were minted. |
| 14 | Agent Bricks vs the Agent Framework? | Not the same thing. The framework is now **Custom Agents** — write a `ResponsesAgent`, deploy to Model Serving or Databricks Apps. **Agent Bricks** is a separate declarative family: **Knowledge Assistant** and **Supervisor Agent**. |
| 15 | Does an AI Search index inherit the source table's row filter? | **No.** Endpoint/index ACLs only, no row/column-level permissions. Multi-tenant RAG needs server-side query-time filters or per-tenant indexes. |
| 16 | How do you filter a vector query? | A `filters` dict on `similarity_search` (`filters_json` over REST): keys are columns with optional operator suffixes (`NOT`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`, `LIKE`, `OR`), list values mean OR, keys are ANDed. Server-side always — post-filtering in app code can return an empty page while the right rows sat outside `num_results`. |
| 17 | Downside of a very selective filter? | It fights HNSW. The graph is built over the whole index, so a 99%-eliminating filter makes traversal over-fetch — latency or recall, pick one. Filters for facets; **index per tenant** for tenancy above a certain customer count. |
| 18 | Cosine similarity in AI Search? | It's **HNSW with L2**. Normalise embeddings at write time to get cosine behaviour. |
| 19 | Hybrid search fusion? | Vector + BM25 fused with **Reciprocal Rank Fusion, `rrf_param = 60`**. Hybrid results cap at **200** (ANN caps at 10,000). |
| 20 | Storage-optimized vs standard endpoint? | Storage-optimized: >1B vectors, 10–20× faster indexing, but **no continuous sync** and ~250 ms more latency; embedding dim must be divisible by 16. |
| 21 | Default behaviour of a failing expectation? | **warn** — the bad rows are **still written** to the target and merely flagged. Only `ON VIOLATION DROP ROW` / `FAIL UPDATE` change that. |
| 22 | Which Python module for declarative pipelines? | Current: **`from pyspark import pipelines as dp`** — `@dp.table`, `@dp.materialized_view`, `@dp.expect_or_drop`. Legacy `import dlt` has `@dlt.table`/`@dlt.view` and **no** `materialized_view`. |
| 23 | Should Photon be on everywhere? | It already **is** on by default — always for serverless, SQL warehouses and serverless pipelines, and by default (toggleable) for classic all-purpose, jobs and pipelines. It carries a DBU multiplier, around 2× (check current pricing), and doesn't support UDFs, RDD/Dataset APIs or stateful streaming — it **falls back per operation**. So the question is which pipelines are mostly UDFs and aren't earning it; check percentage-of-task-time-in-Photon in the query profile. |
| 24 | Z-order vs liquid clustering? | Liquid clustering is recommended for **all new tables**: incremental, keys changeable without rewrite, `CLUSTER BY AUTO` available. **Mutually exclusive with partitioning and with ZORDER.** |
| 25 | We ran VACUUM — can we roll back a month? | No. Default `deletedFileRetentionDuration` is **7 days**; VACUUM destroys older time travel. `logRetentionDuration` (30 days) is a **separate** property, and log files aren't governed by VACUUM at all. |
| 26 | How many columns get data-skipping stats? | The **first 32** by default (`delta.dataSkippingNumIndexedCols`) — so column order matters on wide tables. |
| 27 | What are deletion vectors? | Merge-on-read: DELETE/UPDATE/MERGE mark rows in a DV file instead of rewriting Parquet. Faster writes, slightly slower reads until `REORG ... APPLY (PURGE)` or OPTIMIZE materialises them. |
| 28 | Should I still schedule OPTIMIZE and VACUUM? | On **UC managed tables**, mostly no — **predictive optimization** runs ANALYZE/OPTIMIZE/VACUUM automatically on serverless jobs compute. |
| 29 | Three profile types in data quality monitoring? | **Snapshot** (whole table, max 4 TB), **time series** (needs a timestamp column), **inference** (model request log, optional ground-truth labels, `model_id_col` for slicing). At creation a time-series or inference profile looks back **30 days**, so the first window may be partial — a cold start, not a rolling cap. |
| 30 | Which drift metrics does it emit? | **Numeric: `population_stability_index` (PSI — bands <0.1 none, <0.2 moderate, ≥0.2 significant), `wasserstein_distance`, `ks_test` (statistic + p-value).** Categorical: `chi_squared_test` (statistic + p-value), `js_distance` (Jensen–Shannon **distance**), `tv_distance`, `l_infinity_distance`. Shared deltas: `count_delta`, `avg_delta`, `percent_null_delta`, `percent_zeros_delta`, `percent_distinct_delta`, `non_null_columns_delta` — **no median or stddev delta.** Consecutive drift vs previous window, baseline drift vs a baseline table — training set for inference profiles. |
| 31 | Fairness metrics on an inference profile? | For classification `problem_type`, on **boolean-valued slices**: `predictive_parity` (precision), `predictive_equality` (false positive rate), `equal_opportunity` (recall), `statistical_parity` (acceptance rate). |
| 32 | Biggest Databricks cost mistake you've seen? | Scheduled jobs pinned to an **all-purpose cluster** (~3–4× the jobs-compute rate), no auto-termination, and untagged shared clusters so nothing is attributable. |
| 33 | What's Lakewatch? | ⚠ The **agentic SIEM / security lakehouse**, launched early 2026 — *not* model monitoring. The **Panther acquisition mid-2026 was folded into it**, not the other way round. Lakehouse Monitoring became **data profiling**. (Same family of trap: **Lakebase** is managed Postgres OLTP powering Online Feature Stores, not a warehouse.) |
| 34 | Status of Foundation Model Fine-tuning? | **End of life** as of August 2026 — `databricks_genai` and the FMFT UI are gone. Fine-tuning goes through **AI Runtime**, serverless GPU-backed training. |
| 35 | How would you query Snowflake from Databricks without copying it? | **Lakehouse Federation** — a connection plus a foreign catalog, governed by UC in place, with predicate pushdown where the source supports it. Same machinery as Hive Metastore Federation. |

**Provenance note.** Everything above is from the Databricks/MLflow documentation and release notes current to early September 2026, and the items an earlier draft of this chapter got wrong have since been checked against the docs rather than hedged: the **drift metric set** (PSI, Wasserstein and KS on numeric; chi-squared, JS distance, TV and L-infinity on categorical; the six shared deltas), the **30-day behaviour** (a backfill cutoff at profile creation affecting the first window, not a rolling cap), the **ABAC scoping and quotas**, the **ABAC/time-travel incompatibility**, the **fairness metrics**, the **Photon fallback semantics and default-on status**, and the **FMFT end-of-life**. Items I would still flag as *verify* if pressed: exact DBU dollar rates, the Photon multiplier, and the precise all-purpose-to-jobs ratio; the exact operator spellings in the AI Search `filters` argument; the formal deprecation status of `ChatAgent`/`ChatModel`, which is "superseded", not "removed"; whether agent Model Serving gets a published EOL, which as of the 25 August 2026 migration doc it does not; the `artifact_path` → `name` deprecation status in `log_model`; the current status of the OSS MLflow deployments/gateway server, which I have deliberately not asserted was removed; the DENY-policy surface in ABAC; and the UC lineage retention window, for which I have no reliable figure. If an interviewer contradicts one of these, take the correction — being corrected on a version detail costs nothing; being caught inventing one costs the loop.
