## 6. Domain primer — AWS Bedrock, the AWS ML plane, and data observability

Two of the JD's named preferences — **AWS Bedrock** and **Monte Carlo** — are things Sachin has not used. The winning move in both cases is identical: disclose in one clean sentence, then demonstrate that you understand the *category* better than most people who have clicked around the console. This section makes that possible. Round 1 (Ch. 54) covered the coding pad and the Smartsheet object model; assume all of that.

---

## PART A — AWS Bedrock and the AWS ML plane

### A0. Say the disclosure once, early, and then be fluent

Do not let this leak out under pressure at minute 40. Volunteer it the first time Bedrock is mentioned, in one breath, and immediately convert to adjacency.

> **Say it like this:** "I should be straight with you — I haven't run Bedrock in production. My generative-AI production work was on ResMed's stack: RAG over a clinical knowledge base with hybrid vector-plus-metadata retrieval, eval harnesses, human review, HIPAA-class data — but the model layer there wasn't Bedrock. What I do have is about five years of the AWS plane underneath it: SageMaker endpoints, Lambda, SQS, ECR, S3, Athena, CloudWatch, CodePipeline, VPC. **The Bedrock-specific surface is new to me; the operational problems it creates are not.** Every one of them has an analogue I have owned on the AWS plane: per-service quotas and backoff, VPC endpoints and endpoint policies, artefact and config versioning promoted through CI, KMS-scoped logging, and cost allocation by tag. Happy to be tested on any of it; I'll flag anything I'm reasoning about rather than recalling."

That last clause is the licence to be fluent without over-claiming. Use it.

### A1. The shape of the service — four endpoints, not one

```text
            ┌──────────────────── CONTROL PLANE ────────────────────┐
            │  bedrock.{region}                                     │
            │  ListFoundationModels · GetFoundationModel            │
            │  CreateGuardrail · CreateEvaluationJob                │
            │  PutModelInvocationLoggingConfiguration               │
            └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌──────────────── DATA PLANE (per-token, latency-critical) ────────────────┐
  │  bedrock-runtime.{region}      InvokeModel · Converse · ConverseStream   │
  │                                + OpenAI Responses / Chat Completions     │
  │                                + Anthropic Messages                      │
  │                                → Guardrails ✔ KB ✔ invocation logging ✔  │
  │                                                                          │
  │  bedrock-mantle.{region}       OpenAI Responses / Chat Completions       │
  │                                + native Anthropic Messages               │
  │                                → NO guardrails, NO KB, NO invocation     │
  │                                  logging, NO batch, NO PT, NO CRIS       │
  │                                → separate quota pool, input/output TPM,  │
  │                                  no RPM, no burndown multiplier          │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌──────────── AGENT / KB PLANE ────────────┐
  │  bedrock-agent.{region}         build    │  ingestion jobs, KB CRUD
  │  bedrock-agent-runtime.{region} invoke   │  Retrieve · RetrieveAndGenerate
  └──────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

The `bedrock-mantle` split is a *governance* fact, not a trivia fact. If you route production through mantle to dodge RPM quotas, you have silently given up guardrails, knowledge bases, and model-invocation logging — i.e. your entire audit story. AWS's own guidance is "for new applications we recommend `bedrock-runtime`."

> **Say it like this:** "There's a newer `bedrock-mantle` endpoint that serves the OpenAI Responses API and the native Anthropic Messages API with its own quota pool and no RPM limit — attractive if you're throughput-bound. But it has no Guardrails, no Knowledge Bases and no model-invocation logging. In a SaaS company with enterprise customers I wouldn't put a regulated workload on it; I'd keep prod on `bedrock-runtime` and use mantle only for internal batch-ish experimentation."

### A2. Which API to call

| API | Shape | When to reach for it |
|---|---|---|
| `InvokeModel` / `InvokeModelWithResponseStream` | Raw provider-native JSON body; you own each model's schema | Provider-only params, beta features. Every model supports it |
| **`Converse` / `ConverseStream`** | Model-agnostic messages API: `inferenceConfig`, `toolConfig`, `system`, `cachePoint`, `guardrailConfig`, `additionalModelRequestFields` for the provider-specific tail | **Default.** You can swap `modelId` without rewriting the payload — that is the whole point, and it is what makes model-lifecycle churn survivable |
| OpenAI **Responses API** (`/openai/v1/responses`) | OpenAI-SDK compatible — change `OPENAI_BASE_URL` and key | Migrating an existing OpenAI codebase with minimal diff |
| Anthropic **Messages API** | Native `anthropic` SDK + `aws-bedrock-token-generator` | Anthropic-native features |

Two caveats that separate reading-the-docs from having-been-burned: the Responses API on `bedrock-runtime` is **always synchronous**, rejects **application inference profiles** with a 400, and **Guardrails do not apply to it** — so if you need a guardrail on a GPT model, you must use `Converse`. And it defaults to `store=true`, which means Bedrock retains input and output for **30 days** to support `previous_response_id`; with a *global* inference profile that stored copy can land in any commercial Region.

Streaming (`ConverseStream`, `InvokeModelWithResponseStream`) is the default for anything a human waits on; its SLOs, its mid-generation failure semantics and the `streamProcessingMode` guardrail trap are in §A13.

Auth is either SigV4 or a long-lived Bedrock **API key** (`AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK`). In an enterprise, prefer SigV4 with role assumption; the bearer key is a static credential with all the lifecycle problems that implies.

### A3. Capacity modes — the cost/latency lever, 2026 edition

| Mode | Billing | Notes worth saying out loud |
|---|---|---|
| **On-demand** | per token, quota-governed (TPM/TPD, plus RPM on runtime) | 429s when you exceed. Default |
| **Batch inference** | **≈50% of on-demand** | JSONL in S3 → async job → JSONL out. Accepts `InvokeModel` *or* `Converse` format. **No tool calling, no structured output, no prompt caching, not on provisioned models.** Drive job-state via EventBridge, not polling |
| **Provisioned Throughput** | hourly per **Model Unit** (fixed in-TPM + out-TPM), no-commit / 1-month / 6-month | **Mandatory for custom / fine-tuned models.** Not compatible with cross-Region inference profiles or batch. Cannot be created on a Legacy model. You invoke it by passing the provisioned model ARN as `modelId` |
| **Service tiers** — `Reserved` \| `Priority` \| `Standard` \| `Flex` | request param `"service_tier"` | The modern replacement for "just buy PT". **Reserved**: min 100k input TPM / 10k output TPM, 1- or 3-month term, targets 99.5% uptime, **overflows to Standard instead of throttling**. **Flex**: discounted, slower — AWS names evals, summarisation and agentic workflows as the fit. `ResolvedServiceTier` is emitted in CloudWatch and CloudTrail so you can *verify you got what you paid for* |

> **Say it like this:** "I'd size it as a portfolio, not a single mode. Interactive customer-facing traffic on Reserved so it can't be throttled by a noisy internal job; internal tooling and agentic background work on Flex; anything offline — backfills, evaluation runs, bulk enrichment — on batch at roughly half price. And I'd assert on `ResolvedServiceTier` in CloudWatch, because paying for Priority and silently getting Standard is exactly the kind of thing nobody notices for a quarter."

### A4. Quotas and throttling — the highest-value operational detail in Bedrock

It is the number-one production surprise in Bedrock, and it is where an interviewer who has operated the service will probe.

**Bedrock reserves `input_tokens + max_tokens` against your TPM at request start**, then settles at completion to `input + cacheWrite + (output × burndown)` and refunds the difference.

| Model family | Output-token burndown multiplier |
|---|---|
| Claude Opus 4.8 (AWS writes it "Anthropic Claude models version 4.8") | **15×** |
| Claude Sonnet 5 / Opus 5 / Fable 5.1 | **10×** |
| Claude 4.7 and below | **5×** |
| OpenAI GPT-5.6 Sol/Terra/Luna on `bedrock-runtime` | **10×** |
| Everything else | 1× |

`CacheReadInputTokens` **never** count against quota.

Two consequences, and they are the answer to "why am I getting 429s at 10% of my quota":

1. A lazily-set `max_tokens=32000` on a call that actually returns 900 tokens reserves 36,000 up front. Ten concurrent requests and you have burned 360k TPM to produce 9k tokens.
2. On a 15× burndown model, 1,000 real output tokens cost you 15,000 tokens of quota. Your capacity plan built on "average response length" is off by an order of magnitude.

> **Say it like this:** "The first thing I'd audit is `max_tokens` hygiene, because Bedrock reserves input plus max_tokens up front and refunds the difference at settlement — so an over-generous max_tokens throttles you for tokens you never generate and are never billed for. Second, the output burndown multipliers: on the newest Claude models an output token can cost five to fifteen tokens of quota. Third, prompt caching, because cache reads don't count against the quota at all — it's a throughput lever, not just a cost lever. After that: exponential backoff with jitter, per-tenant token buckets in a gateway, and spreading across a geographic and a global inference profile for headroom."

```text
      client ──► LLM GATEWAY ──────────────────────────────────► bedrock-runtime
                 │  per-tenant token bucket (TPM, not RPM)
                 │  max_tokens clamp by route
                 │  model-id pin from config (never hardcoded)
                 │  retry: exp backoff + full jitter on 429/5xx
                 │  failover: us.<model> → global.<model> → smaller model
                 │  emit: requestMetadata{team,env,tenant}, ResolvedServiceTier
                 └─ ApplyGuardrail on INPUT before it ever reaches a model
```

### A5. Cross-Region inference profiles and residency

| | **Geographic** (`us.` `eu.` `apac.` `au.`) | **Global** (`global.`) |
|---|---|---|
| Residency | stays within the geography | any commercial Region |
| Cost | standard | **≈10% cheaper** |
| SCP requirement | allow the destination Regions | must allow `"aws:RequestedRegion": "unspecified"` |

No routing surcharge; priced by the Region you *call from*; up to roughly 2× the in-Region default quota; routes to Regions not even enabled in your account, over the AWS backbone. **CloudTrail logs in the source Region and `additionalEventData.inferenceRegion` tells you where it actually executed** — that is your audit answer when a customer asks where their prompt was processed. Inference profiles do **not** support Provisioned Throughput.

**Application inference profiles** wrap a system profile with cost-allocation tags — this is how you do per-team or per-tenant chargeback in a multi-tenant SaaS. (Not supported on the Responses API on `bedrock-runtime`.)

A real 2026 constraint worth naming: for several frontier Claude models some Regions are **Global-only** — no geographic, no in-Region option. If you have an India or UAE data-residency commitment, that is a hard architectural constraint on model choice, not a config toggle. ⚠️ Verify per model card on the day; this moves.

### A6. Model lifecycle — the thing nobody builds until it bites

States are **Active → Legacy → EOL**, exposed as `modelLifecycle` on `GetFoundationModel` / `ListFoundationModels`. Guarantees: at least **12 months** on Bedrock before EOL, at least **6 months** in Legacy. New for 2026: models with EOL after 1 Feb 2026 get a **"public extended access"** window of ≥3 further months, during which **the provider may raise the price**. In Legacy: no new customers, no new fine-tuning jobs, no new Provisioned Throughput, and existing customers can lose access after **15 days of inactivity**. There is **no automatic migration** — post-EOL requests just fail.

Concrete near-term EOLs to name if pushed, read off the Bedrock model-lifecycle table on 2026-09-04: **six models EOL this month** — Claude 3 Haiku on the 10th, Nova Premier and Nova Sonic on the 14th, Nova Canvas and both Nova Reel versions (`v1:0` and `v1:1`) on the 30th — then **Claude Sonnet 4 on 14 Oct 2026**, with Claude Opus 4.1 entering public extended access on 8 Oct 2026 ahead of an 8 Jan 2027 EOL.

> **Say it like this:** "Model IDs belong in config, never in code, and I'd run a weekly `ListFoundationModels` job that alerts on any pinned ID whose `modelLifecycle` isn't ACTIVE. That alert has to be paired with an eval suite that can re-qualify a replacement in CI, otherwise the alert just creates anxiety. Six models EOL this month alone and another next month — that's a standing quarterly chore, not an occasional event, and it's the strongest argument for using `Converse` rather than `InvokeModel`, because swapping the model ID shouldn't mean rewriting the payload."

### A7. Prompt caching — the biggest single cost lever

Implicit (best-effort prefix reuse) or explicit (`cachePoint` in Converse, `cache_control` in InvokeModel). Minimum tokens per checkpoint: **Opus 5 = 512; Opus 4.8 / Sonnet 5 / Sonnet 4.6 / Sonnet 4.5 = 1,024; Opus 4.7 = 2,048; Opus 4.6 / Opus 4.5 / Haiku 4.5 = 4,096**. **The minimum is not monotonic across generations — that is the point worth making**, because a 3K-token system prompt caches on Opus 5 and Opus 4.8 and silently does not on Opus 4.6, with no error, just `cacheWriteInputTokens: 0`. These minimums are model properties and apply on Bedrock exactly as on the first-party API; there is no per-platform override left. Max 4 checkpoints per request for Claude. TTL **5 min default, 1 h opt-in**; ordering is **`tools` → `system` → `messages`**, the minimum is evaluated on the *cumulative* total, and changing `tools` invalidates the cached `system` and `messages` behind it. Cache writes can cost *more* than normal input (≈1.25×); reads run ≈90% off. Not supported with batch.

Monitor `cacheReadInputTokens`, `cacheWriteInputTokens`, `cacheDetails` — and note `inputTokens` **excludes** cached tokens, so `total = inputTokens + cacheRead + cacheWrite`. A cache-hit-rate regression after an innocent prompt edit will multiply your bill overnight with zero quality signal. That belongs on a dashboard.

```python
# Converse with a cache point, a guardrail, and disciplined max_tokens.
# Scratch-pad grade; the shape is the point.
resp = brt.converse(
    modelId=CFG["model_id"],                    # pinned in config, not code
    system=[{"text": SYSTEM_PROMPT},            # ~3k tokens, stable
            {"cachePoint": {"type": "default"}}],
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": [{"text": user_turn}]}],
    inferenceConfig={"maxTokens": 700,          # sized to p99 of observed output
                     "temperature": 0.0},
    guardrailConfig={"guardrailIdentifier": CFG["guardrail_id"],
                     "guardrailVersion": CFG["guardrail_version"],  # never DRAFT
                     "trace": "enabled"},
    requestMetadata={"team": "ml-platform", "env": "prod", "tenant": tenant_id},
)
u = resp["usage"]
emit("bedrock.tokens.input",  u["inputTokens"])
emit("bedrock.tokens.output", u["outputTokens"])
emit("bedrock.cache.read",    u.get("cacheReadInputTokens", 0))
emit("bedrock.cache.write",   u.get("cacheWriteInputTokens", 0))
```

### A8. Knowledge Bases, and the honest build-versus-buy

The 2026 split: **Managed KB** (AWS owns ingestion, indexing, storage, retrieval, autoscaling) versus **customer-managed KB** (you bring the vector store). Managed-only features are the ones that matter for enterprise SaaS: third-party connectors (SharePoint, Confluence, Google Drive, OneDrive, Web Crawler alongside S3), **document-level ACL permission filtering at retrieval time**, Smart Parsing, Agentic Retrieval (query decomposition, multi-hop, sufficiency evaluation), and AgentCore Gateway integration so any MCP agent can call the KB as a tool.

| Vector store | The thing that bites you |
|---|---|
| **OpenSearch Serverless** | Quick-create path; engine must be **faiss** (nmslib breaks metadata filtering); best operator support (`in`, `notIn`, `stringContains`, `startsWith`); supports binary vectors; can be VPC-private |
| **OpenSearch Managed Cluster** | **Must be publicly accessible — VPC-fronted domains are not supported.** Custom metadata fields must be `keyword` (or `text` with a `keyword` subfield) or filters fail with "Rewrite first" |
| **Aurora PostgreSQL / pgvector** | Same AWS account as the KB; needs a **GIN index on the jsonb metadata column**; hybrid search wants `to_tsvector('english', chunks)`; **enable HNSW iterative scans** (`hnsw.iterative_scan='relaxed_order'`) or selective metadata filters silently return too few rows, because the filter is applied *after* the HNSW scan |
| **Neptune Analytics (GraphRAG)** | Vector index **can only be created at graph-creation time**; sized in m-NCUs |
| **S3 Vectors** | Cheapest; sub-second cold, ~100 ms warm; float32 only; **total metadata ≤40 KB per vector across ≤50 keys, of which filterable metadata is capped at 2 KB and non-filterable keys at 10 per index**. Hierarchical chunking pushes parent text into metadata and can breach the 40 KB ceiling, which is why it is **discouraged** here |
| Pinecone / MongoDB Atlas / Redis Enterprise | Credentials via Secrets Manager. Atlas metadata filtering **does not work by default** — you must configure filters in the Atlas index |

Chunking: default ~300 tokens; fixed-size with overlap **percentage**; hierarchical (overlap as an absolute token count — and retrieval fetches children then *substitutes parents*, which is why "`numberOfResults` seems to be ignored"); semantic (buffer size + breakpoint percentile, and it **calls an FM so it costs extra**); or none.

Retrieval: `Retrieve` returns chunks with scores and metadata (you own the prompt); `RetrieveAndGenerate` returns a grounded answer with `citations[]`. `numberOfResults` defaults to **5**. `overrideSearchType` is `HYBRID | SEMANTIC` or omitted — but **hybrid only actually works on Aurora/RDS, OpenSearch Serverless and MongoDB**; elsewhere it silently degrades to semantic. Metadata filters: eleven operators, `andAll`/`orAll`, **max 5 filters per group, max 5 groups, one level of nesting**, with uneven per-store support. Reranking is configured via `rerankingConfiguration`, and managed reranking is currently **included at no charge**.

The gotcha to volunteer, because it is genuinely surprising:

> **Say it like this:** "Guardrails are applied to the model input and the generated output — they are **not** applied to the references retrieved from a Knowledge Base at runtime. So if your corpus contains PII or an indirect prompt injection, the guardrail won't see it on the retrieval path. That's exactly what the standalone `ApplyGuardrail` API is for: I'd run it over retrieved context as a separate call before it enters the prompt."

Now the build-versus-buy, which is where his actual experience lives:

| | Bedrock Knowledge Bases | Roll your own (his ResMed shape: hybrid vector + metadata retrieval, pgvector/FAISS/Chroma) |
|---|---|---|
| Time to first working RAG | hours | weeks |
| Ingestion, incremental sync, parsing | managed, incremental, metadata-only fast path | you build and operate it |
| Chunking control | five strategies + a transformation Lambda | total |
| Retrieval control | `numberOfResults`, filters, hybrid where supported, managed rerank | total — custom fusion, query rewriting, per-tenant index routing |
| Doc-level ACLs | **native on Managed KB** | you build it, and it is the hardest part in a multi-tenant SaaS |
| Cost | **Managed KB**: $5/GB/month index + $1 per 1,000 `Retrieve` + embedding and generation tokens + the underlying store. (Customer-managed KB is priced by the store you brought, not by these rates) | infra + your team's time |
| Debuggability | good but bounded by the surface AWS exposes | complete |

> **Say it like this:** "At ResMed I built the hand-rolled version — hybrid vector plus metadata retrieval over a clinical knowledge base, with an evaluation harness and human review in the loop because it was HIPAA-class data. Having done that, my honest read is that Bedrock Knowledge Bases would have removed maybe 70% of the work and none of the interesting 30%. The interesting 30% is chunking policy for the actual document shapes, the eval set, and per-tenant access control. So my default now would be: managed KB for ingestion and storage, `Retrieve` rather than `RetrieveAndGenerate` so I keep the prompt and the fusion logic, and my own eval harness in CI regardless."

### A9. Guardrails — and `ApplyGuardrail` as a standalone control

**Six policy types** — get the count right, because "eight" invites a correction from anyone who has built one. They are: **content filters** (Hate, Insults, Sexual, Violence, Misconduct and **Prompt Attack**, each `NONE|LOW|MEDIUM|HIGH` separately for input and output; AWS documents prompt attacks as *"offered as a category within content filters"*, not as its own policy, and the Standard tier adds **prompt-leakage** detection and extends coverage into code elements — comments, variable and function names, string literals); **denied topics** in natural language (1,000 chars per definition on Standard, 200 on Classic); **word filters** plus a managed profanity list; **sensitive-information filters** (ML-based PII plus custom regex, action `BLOCK` or `ANONYMIZE`); **contextual grounding checks** with separate `GROUNDING` and `RELEVANCE` thresholds that return the actual score; and **Automated Reasoning checks**.

Tiers: **Standard** gets extensive language coverage, cross-Region inference, prompt-leakage detection and code-domain support; **Classic** is English/French/Spanish only and no CRIS.

The piece to lead with is `ApplyGuardrail`: `POST /guardrail/{id}/version/{version}/apply` with `source: INPUT|OUTPUT`. It is **decoupled from any foundation model**, which means you can put Bedrock Guardrails in front of a self-hosted vLLM model on EKS, a SageMaker endpoint, or a third-party API. The response carries `action`, per-policy `assessments[]`, a `usage` block that is literally your bill, and `guardrailCoverage.textCharacters.{guarded,total}`, which is how you *prove* the guardrail saw the whole payload rather than assuming it did.

**Automated Reasoning checks** are GA in six Regions, English (US) only. You upload a source document, Bedrock extracts formal logic rules and a variable schema, gives you a **fidelity report** grounding each rule back to source text, and you save an immutable policy version. It is **detect-only — it does not block**; it returns `VALID` / `INVALID` / `TRANSLATION_AMBIGUOUS` / `TOO_COMPLEX` with the rules and variable assignments that justify the verdict, and your application decides. Limits: no streaming, no prompt-injection protection, source docs ≤5 MB / 50,000 chars. AWS's own example of the ceiling is good: *"I can submit my homework late because I have a fake doctor's note"* returns VALID if no variable captures "fake".

The compliance landmine to raise unprompted:

> **Say it like this:** "One thing I'd check on day one: all blocked content from guardrail policies appears **as plain text in Bedrock model-invocation logs**. If you're using the guardrail to catch PII, your log bucket now contains the PII you just blocked. So invocation logging has to be a deliberate decision — scoped, KMS-encrypted, with a retention policy — not something you turn on because it seemed like good hygiene."

Version them like code: guardrails have a `DRAFT` plus numbered immutable versions. Pin versions in production, promote through CI, and never ship from DRAFT.

### A10. Agents: Classic is in maintenance, AgentCore is the platform

**Bedrock Agents is now "Agents Classic", closed to new customers and in maintenance mode.** Saying "I'd build it with action groups" dates you by two years. Still know it, because you will be asked to migrate one: action groups are an OpenAPI 3 spec or function-detail schema plus an optional Lambda; without a Lambda you use **RETURN_CONTROL**, where the agent hands parameters back and your application executes the call (the right pattern when the tool sits behind your own auth). Orchestration is **ReAct** over four editable prompt templates — pre-processing, orchestration, KB response generation, post-processing. Versions and **aliases** give you blue/green and rollback; `enableTrace` is the only real debugging surface.

**Classic multi-agent collaboration, since "why would you migrate off it" is only answerable if you can describe it.** You designate one agent as the **supervisor** and associate one or more **collaborator** agents with it — a hierarchical, not peer-to-peer, topology. The supervisor must be saved *before* collaboration can be enabled, then updated to attach collaborators. Each association carries a **`collaborationInstruction`** (required, natural language, max 4,000 characters) describing that collaborator's role and responsibilities — this is the entire routing signal, which is why AWS's guidance is to make roles crisp and non-overlapping. **`relayConversationHistory`** is `TO_COLLABORATOR | DISABLED` per collaborator, and it is the interesting knob: relaying gives the sub-agent context and costs tokens on every hop; disabling it keeps the sub-agent cheap and stateless but means the supervisor must restate everything it needs. Two collaboration modes: **`SUPERVISOR`**, where the supervisor plans, decomposes, may fan out to several collaborators and synthesises their answers; and **`SUPERVISOR_ROUTER`**, where it classifies the request and hands it to exactly one collaborator, falling back to full supervision when classification is ambiguous — router mode is markedly cheaper because it skips a planning round-trip. **Payload referencing** passes large intermediate results between agents by reference rather than inlining them into the next prompt, which is the difference between a three-agent chain that fits in context and one that does not. Every agent on the team, supervisor included, keeps the full Bedrock Agents surface: action groups, knowledge bases, and its own guardrail. ⚠️ The mode enum names are worth a re-check on the day if you plan to say them verbatim; the mechanism is not in doubt.

> **Say it like this (asked to walk through it and justify migrating):** "The mechanism is a supervisor agent with associated collaborators, where each association carries a natural-language collaboration instruction and a relay-conversation-history flag, and you pick supervisor mode or supervisor-router mode depending on whether you need real planning or just classification. It works, and for a three-or-four-specialist assistant it works well. I'd migrate off it for three reasons, none of them 'it's old': the routing logic is a prompt rather than code, so it isn't unit-testable; the debugging surface is `enableTrace` and nothing else, so you cannot get an OpenTelemetry span tree out of it; and it's Classic, closed to new customers, so it's a dead end you'd have to leave eventually anyway. The migration target is a framework-native supervisor — LangGraph or Strands — where routing is code you can test, running on AgentCore Runtime, with the tools behind AgentCore Gateway and the traces in AgentCore Observability."

**AgentCore** is the 2026 answer, and it is framework-agnostic (LangGraph, Strands, CrewAI, LlamaIndex, OpenAI Agents SDK) and model-agnostic. The modules worth naming: **Runtime** (serverless, true session isolation, MCP and A2A protocols), **Gateway** (turns APIs/Lambdas/OpenAPI specs into MCP tools with inbound and outbound authZ), **Memory**, **Identity**, **Observability** (OTEL-native, CloudWatch-backed), **Code Interpreter**, **Browser**, **Evaluations** (over sessions/traces/spans instrumented with OpenTelemetry or OpenInference), **Optimization** (versioned config bundles, A/B via Gateway traffic splitting), **Policy** (deterministic guardrails in natural language or **Cedar**, intercepting every tool call *before* execution), **Registry**, **Payments** (microtransactions so an agent can pay for paid APIs and MCP servers over the **x402** protocol and the **Machine Payments Protocol**, with wallet integration, configurable spending limits and end-to-end observability — the one everybody forgets, and the one with the most obvious governance question attached), and the newest, **Harness** (`CreateHarness`/`InvokeHarness`, each session in an isolated microVM).

This is where his MCP work is a direct, honest bridge:

> **Say it like this:** "Multi-agent in 2026 doesn't live in the Classic supervisor feature any more — it lives at the Gateway and Registry layer plus a framework-native supervisor in LangGraph or Strands. That maps directly onto what I built at TrueBalance: our internal Claude developer assistant is an MCP server surface over Jira, GitHub, Jenkins, AWS Athena and EC2, Grafana and Slack, with each task running in an isolated Git workspace. AgentCore Gateway is the managed version of the thing I hand-built — turning existing APIs into MCP tools with authorisation on both sides — and AgentCore Policy with Cedar is the deterministic tool-call gate I'd want in front of it in a SaaS product."

### A11. Evaluation, and how it becomes a CI gate

Four job types: **programmatic/automatic** model evaluation, **human** evaluation (+$0.21 per completed human task), **LLM-as-a-judge**, and **RAG evaluation** in `retrieve-only` or `retrieve-and-generate` mode. The important one for this JD: RAG evaluation accepts **bring-your-own inference response data from an external RAG system**, so you can benchmark a non-AWS RAG stack with Bedrock evals. Metrics on the generate side include correctness, completeness, helpfulness, **citation precision and citation coverage**, plus the responsible-AI set; ground truth is required. ⚠️ Verify the exact metric list per job type before quoting it as definitive.

AWS does not hand you a turnkey CI story, so describe one:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/rag-regression.yml
name: rag-regression
on: [pull_request]
permissions:
  id-token: write          # OIDC role assumption; no static keys in CI
  contents: read
jobs:
  rag-eval:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    env:
      BUCKET: my-eval-bucket
      EVAL_ROLE_ARN: arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/BedrockEvalJobRole
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/GitHubActionsCI
          aws-region: us-east-1
      - name: Publish the versioned golden set
        run: |
          echo "GIT_SHA=${GITHUB_SHA}" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"
          aws s3 cp golden/ "s3://${BUCKET}/eval/${GITHUB_SHA}/" --recursive
      - name: Start the RAG evaluation job
        run: |
          aws bedrock create-evaluation-job \
            --job-name "rag-${GIT_SHA}" \
            --role-arn "${EVAL_ROLE_ARN}" \
            --application-type RagEvaluation \
            --evaluation-config "file://rag_eval_config.json" \
            --inference-config "file://kb_target.json" \
            --output-data-config "s3Uri=s3://${BUCKET}/eval-out/${GIT_SHA}/"
      - name: Wait for the job, then gate on regression
        run: |
          python ci/wait_and_gate.py \
            --sha "${GIT_SHA}" \
            --baseline "s3://${BUCKET}/baselines/main.json" \
            --fail-on "citation_coverage:-0.03,correctness:-0.02"
      - name: Red-team the guardrail
        run: python ci/redteam_guardrail.py
        # ApplyGuardrail over a red-team corpus; asserts action == GUARDRAIL_INTERVENED
        # and guardrailCoverage.textCharacters.guarded / .total ~= 1.0
```

Three details that make this the version a platform engineer wrote rather than the version an LLM wrote, and they are worth saying if the pad is on screen: `runs-on` is mandatory and a workflow without it is rejected outright; every multi-line `run` is a **block scalar** (`run: |`), because a backslash continuation inside a single-line `run:` folds into one physical line and `\ ` then escapes the space, silently gluing `$GIT_SHA --baseline` into one argv entry; and `create-evaluation-job` **requires `--role-arn`** — the role Bedrock itself assumes to read your golden set and write results, which is a different principal from the one CI authenticates as.

Run eval jobs on the **Flex** service tier and generate candidate responses via **batch** at ~50% off. Gate model-version bumps on the same suite — that is what makes the Legacy/EOL churn in §A6 a routine chore instead of an incident.

### A12. Security posture — the answer an enterprise SaaS wants

- **PrivateLink**: interface endpoints for `bedrock`, `bedrock-runtime`, `bedrock-mantle`, `bedrock-agent`, `bedrock-agent-runtime`, plus FIPS variants in six Regions. Enable private DNS and there is zero code change. **Endpoint policies are the enforcement point** — e.g. allow only `bedrock:InvokeModel` and `InvokeModelWithResponseStream`. VPC config also covers model-customisation and batch-inference jobs. Constraint to remember: an OpenSearch **Managed Cluster** backing a KB must be publicly accessible.
- **Training-data guarantee**: Bedrock runs each provider's inference software in a per-provider, per-Region **Model Deployment Account** owned by the Bedrock service team. **Providers have no access to those accounts, and therefore no access to your prompts, completions or logs.** The nuance to volunteer rather than be caught by: AWS separately runs automated **abuse detection** over inputs and outputs — different mechanism, same conversation. And **AgentCore is explicitly different**: it may use and store your content to improve *your* service experience.
- **Model-invocation logging**: off by default, per account and Region, S3 and/or CloudWatch (same account and Region only), **100 KB inline cap** on bodies — anything larger or binary goes to S3 with a pointer, so **CloudWatch-only logging silently drops large payloads**. The `requestMetadata` field is the one caller-supplied key-value bag: use it for team/env/tenant chargeback. Not available on `bedrock-mantle`.
- **CloudTrail** records all API activity in the source Region, with `additionalEventData.inferenceRegion` for cross-Region routing, and surfaces service tier and latency config. ⚠️ Don't claim dedicated CloudTrail *data* events for `InvokeModel` — the payload-capture mechanism is model-invocation logging, and CloudTrail is the management-event record.
- **KMS** CMKs cover customisation jobs and artefacts, KB resources including third-party vector-store secrets, S3 Vectors buckets (immutable choice at bucket creation), agent sessions and `RetrieveAndGenerate` session state.
- **Residency**: geographic inference profiles, never `global.`; verify with `inferenceRegion`; `store=false` on the Responses API or an account retention mode of `none`.

### A13. The decision matrix — Bedrock vs SageMaker vs self-hosted vLLM on EKS

AWS's own decision guide compresses to one sentence, and quoting it is a strong move: *"Choose SageMaker AI when you need to access the container or orchestration layer to directly manage cost-latency-throughput and other tradeoffs."*

| Axis | **Bedrock** | **SageMaker AI** | **vLLM / KServe / Ray on EKS (or HyperPod)** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Unit of cost | per token; never idles | per instance-hour (serverless customisation is per-token) | per GPU-hour; **idles brutally** |
| **Latency floor and its shape** | TTFT set by AWS, not by you; no cold start on on-demand; a throttle costs you a full retry, so p99 is set by your backoff policy, not by the model. Levers: prompt caching, `maxTokens`, Priority/Reserved tier, a smaller model | Real-time endpoint is warm and predictable; **Serverless Inference cold-starts** (tens of seconds for a large container); Async adds queue time by design. You own instance type, model server and batching | Lowest achievable TTFT and the only place you can *engineer* it — continuous batching, FP8/AWQ quantisation, speculative decoding, disaggregated prefill/decode. A warm pod has no cold start; an autoscaled-to-zero one has the worst of all worlds |
| Scaling | invisible | you size it; **inference components scale to zero** | you own HPA, queue-depth signals, node groups |
| Models | Claude, Nova, Llama, Mistral, Qwen, GPT-OSS + 100s via Marketplace. **Claude is not in JumpStart** | ~1,000 JumpStart models, classical ML, custom containers | anything with weights |
| Control | prompt, RAG, fine-tune, distillation, custom model import | container + orchestration; SFT/DPO/RLVR/RLAIF; HyperPod | engine config: FP8/AWQ quantisation, tensor/pipeline parallelism, continuous batching, PagedAttention, speculative decoding, disaggregated prefill/decode |
| Governance you get free | Guardrails, invocation logging, managed evals | Model Registry, Pipelines, Model Monitor, Clarify, Feature Store | **none — you rebuild it**, though `ApplyGuardrail` still works in front |
| Discounts | batch −50%, global profile −10%, cache read −90%, Flex tier | Savings Plans up to −64%; Inferentia/Trainium | your existing EC2/Savings Plan commitments |

**The arithmetic, and say it out loud — this is the differentiator.** All figures ⚠️ approximate, us-east-1, read on 2026-09-04; verify on the pricing page before quoting.

*Per-request, per-token.* Anchor read directly from the page: Claude 3.5 Sonnet in public extended access is **$6.00 in / $30.00 out per 1M tokens**, batch $3.00/$15.00, cache write $7.50, cache read $0.60. A RAG turn with 4,000 input and 500 output tokens:

```
uncached:  4000/1e6 × $6  = $0.0240
         +  500/1e6 × $30 = $0.0150   →  $0.0390 / request
                                          × 100k req/day = $3,900/day

with a 3,600-token cached prefix:
  cache read 3600/1e6 × $0.60 = $0.00216
  fresh in    400/1e6 × $6.00 = $0.00240
  output      500/1e6 × $30   = $0.01500   → $0.0196 / request  (≈ −50%)
```

Add the KB layer — and label it precisely, because these are **Managed-KB** prices and do not apply to a customer-managed KB, where you pay the underlying vector store instead: `Retrieve` at **$1.00 per 1,000 calls** = $0.001/query; index storage **$5.00/GB of raw data/month**; agentic retrieval **$4.00 per 1,000** on top of the underlying retrieves.

Guardrails are priced per **text unit**, and a text unit is **up to 1,000 characters** — an input longer than that is processed as multiple units, so a 5,600-character payload bills as 6. That makes the arithmetic concrete rather than hand-wavy: content filters and denied topics **$0.15 per 1,000 text units**, sensitive-information filters and contextual grounding **$0.10**, Automated Reasoning **$0.17 per 1,000 per policy** — charged regardless of verdict. Word filters and regex-based sensitive-information detection are **free**. Image content filters are billed separately per image, and the `InvokeGuardrailChecks` API has its own cheaper rates (content filters $0.07, prompt attack $0.08 per 1,000).

```
The 4,000-token RAG turn above is roughly 16,000 characters of prompt = 16 text units.
Guard the input with content filters + denied topics + contextual grounding:
   16 units x ($0.15 + $0.15 + $0.10)/1000  =  $0.0064 / request
Guard the ~2,000-character output as well (2 units):        +$0.0008
                                                             ────────
                                            guardrail cost ≈ $0.0072 / request
```

That is **~37% on top of a $0.0196 cached inference turn** — not a rounding error, and the reason `ApplyGuardrail` over retrieved context is a deliberate cost decision rather than a free safety net. If you guard 4,000 tokens of retrieved chunks too, you roughly double it again.

*Provisioned Throughput break-even.* The worked example still on the pricing page: Claude Instant, 1-month commitment, **$39.60/hour → $29,462.40/month** for one Model Unit. At a ~$5/1M blended token rate that is roughly **5.9 billion tokens/month** of on-demand equivalent. Unless you are genuinely saturating that MU nearly all the time, on-demand or the Reserved service tier wins.

*Self-hosting break-even.* Take `ml.g5.12xlarge` (4×A10G) for SageMaker real-time inference in us-east-1 at **~$7.09/hour** — about **$5,180/month** at 24×7. Assume, and you must *measure* rather than assume, a sustained 700 output tokens/second for a mid-size open-weight model on that box:

```
700 tok/s × 3600 × 730 h ≈ 1.84B output tokens/month
$5,180 / 1,840 (millions) ≈ $2.82 per 1M output tokens  @ 100% utilisation
                            $28.20 per 1M output tokens  @ 10%  utilisation
```

> **Say it like this:** "Self-hosting has a marginal cost per GPU-hour and Bedrock has a marginal cost per token, so the whole decision is a utilisation question with a governance surcharge. On the numbers I'd sketch, a 4×A10G box amortises to roughly three dollars per million output tokens at full utilisation and nearly thirty at ten percent — and that's an open-weight model, not a frontier one, so it isn't even the same product. Below the break-even, self-hosting is strictly worse, and you also give up Guardrails, invocation logging and managed evals unless you rebuild them. Above it, and if you need a specific p99 or a model nobody hosts, EKS with vLLM is right — and I'd still keep `ApplyGuardrail` in front of it, because that API is model-independent by design."

The progressive path AWS recommends is a good closing line: Bedrock with prompt and RAG → SageMaker serverless customisation (SFT/DPO) → RLVR/RLAIF → full training jobs or HyperPod → deploy back to *either* SageMaker endpoints for control *or* Bedrock via **Custom Model Import** for serverless.

#### Latency: the budget, and how you hold it

In a design round, the question straight after "what would you build" is "what's your latency budget and how do you hold it". Have the answer in this shape, because a single p99 number for "the LLM call" is the wrong unit.

**Split the SLO in two.** For anything streamed, **TTFT** (time to first token) and **TPOT** (time per output token) are different SLOs with different causes, and total latency is a derived quantity, not a target:

```
total ≈ TTFT + (output_tokens × TPOT)

TTFT  is driven by: prompt length (prefill is compute-bound and roughly linear
      in input tokens), cache hit or miss, retrieval hops before the call,
      queueing, cold start, and guardrail input processing.
TPOT  is driven by: model size, decode batch occupancy, output token count.
```

The practical consequence: **prompt caching is a latency lever, not only a cost lever** — a cached 3,600-token prefix removes that prefill work from TTFT on every hit. And **`maxTokens` discipline is a p99 lever**, because the tail of your latency distribution is just the tail of your output-length distribution multiplied by TPOT.

**A budget worth quoting for a Smartsheet-style in-product assistant** (⚠️ these are targets I would set and then measure against, not measurements I have):

| Stage | Target | What blows it |
|---|---|---|
| Gateway + authZ + tenant resolution | < 20 ms | a synchronous per-request DB lookup instead of a cached tenant config |
| `ApplyGuardrail` on input | 50–150 ms | guarding a huge payload; it is billed and timed per 1,000-character text unit |
| Retrieve (vector + metadata filter) | p95 < 150 ms | HNSW iterative scan disabled on pgvector with a selective filter |
| Rerank | p95 < 100 ms | reranking 100 candidates when 25 would do |
| **TTFT at the client** | **p95 < 1.2 s, p99 < 2.5 s** | cache miss, over-long prompt, a 429 forcing a full retry |
| TPOT | < 30 ms/token | model too large for the job |
| Full answer, ~400 tokens | p95 < 13 s streamed | measuring "total" instead of TTFT and optimising the wrong thing |

**Cold start is the axis the matrix hides.** Bedrock on-demand has none — that is genuinely its strongest latency argument. SageMaker **Serverless Inference** cold-starts in the tens of seconds for a large model container, which disqualifies it for interactive use unless you keep it warm. A warm EKS pod running vLLM has no cold start and the best achievable TTFT, but only because something is paying for the GPU while it idles — which is the same utilisation argument as the cost section, arriving from the other direction. **Continuous batching** is the reason self-hosting can win both: vLLM admits new sequences into the batch at every decode step rather than waiting for the slowest member, so throughput rises steeply with concurrency while per-request TPOT degrades only gradually — until the batch saturates, at which point queueing dominates and TTFT collapses. That knee is the number to load-test for; it is where your autoscaling signal should sit, and it is why **queue depth is a better HPA metric than GPU utilisation**, which sits near 100% both when you are healthy and when you are melting.

> **Say it like this:** "I'd hold two SLOs, not one: time-to-first-token and time-per-output-token, because they have different causes and different fixes. TTFT is prefill plus retrieval plus guardrail, so it's attacked with prompt caching, a shorter retrieved context and a rerank that isn't rescoring a hundred candidates. TPOT is model size and batch occupancy. Total latency I'd report but never target, because it's just TTFT plus tokens times TPOT, and it moves whenever the answers get longer for reasons that have nothing to do with the system being slower. And I'd instrument p95 per stage — embed, retrieve, rerank, generate, post-process — because a single end-to-end number tells you that you're slow and nothing about where."

#### Streaming, and the guardrail gotcha inside it

`ConverseStream` / `InvokeModelWithResponseStream` are the default for anything a human is watching, and the operational details are where this gets interesting.

**A throttle mid-generation is not the same failure as a throttle at the start.** Bedrock reserves `input + maxTokens` at request start, so most 429s land before any token is emitted and a clean retry is safe. But a stream can also fail *after* partial output — a `modelStreamErrorException` or a dropped connection — and at that point you have shown the user half an answer. Decide the semantics deliberately, and say which you chose:

| Strategy | Behaviour | When |
|---|---|---|
| Discard and retry silently | Buffer client-side; only render on completion | Short answers; loses the entire point of streaming |
| Render, then retry and **replace** | Show partial, restart, swap the block | Best UX for prose; jarring if the retry diverges |
| Render, then **continue** from the partial | Feed the partial back as an assistant turn and ask for continuation | Cheapest, but the seam is visible and it is not deterministic |
| Render, then fail closed | Show partial with an explicit "interrupted" marker and a retry affordance | The honest default for anything regulated |

Whichever you choose, the retry is **not idempotent and not free** — you are billed for the partial output already generated, and on a 15× burndown model that partial also already consumed quota. Cap retries at one for streamed requests and fail visibly.

**The gotcha worth volunteering: `streamProcessingMode`.** Guardrails on a streaming response run in one of two modes, set in the `amazon-bedrock-guardrailConfig` object:

- **`SYNCHRONOUS`** (default) — Bedrock buffers one or more chunks, applies the policies, *then* releases them. Adds latency to every chunk; every chunk is scanned before the user sees it.
- **`ASYNCHRONOUS`** — chunks go to the user immediately while policies are applied in the background. No latency penalty, but **response chunks may contain inappropriate content until the scan completes**; once a violation is detected, subsequent chunks are blocked. And a hard constraint that decides it for many teams: **Guardrails does not support masking of sensitive information in asynchronous mode at all.**

> **Say it like this:** "Asynchronous stream processing is a real trap in a product with enterprise customers. It buys you TTFT by letting tokens reach the user before the guardrail verdict lands — so the blocked content is blocked *after* it has already been rendered, and PII masking doesn't work in that mode at all. For an internal developer tool I'd take it. For anything customer-facing under a data-protection commitment I'd stay synchronous and buy the latency back somewhere honest — prompt caching, a smaller retrieved context, a faster model — rather than by narrowing the guardrail."

### A14. Model customisation — the fine-tuning workflow the JD actually names

"Fine-tuning workflows" is a named bullet in the JD, so one cell in a matrix is not enough. Know the mechanics and, more importantly, know when the answer is "don't".

**The workflow, end to end.** Training data is **JSONL in S3**, one example per line, in the schema the target model expects (`{"prompt": ..., "completion": ...}` for text-to-text on several families; the Converse-style `{"system": ..., "messages": [...]}` shape for the chat-tuned ones — check the model card, the schemas are not interchangeable). You supply a **train** set and, separately, an optional **validation** set; supplying validation is what gets you per-epoch validation loss in the output metrics rather than a single number at the end. You call **`CreateModelCustomizationJob`** with `customizationType` of `FINE_TUNING` or `CONTINUED_PRE_TRAINING`, a `roleArn` Bedrock assumes to read S3 and write artefacts, `hyperParameters` (epochs, batch size, learning-rate multiplier), an output S3 URI, and optionally a VPC config and a KMS CMK. The job emits a **custom model** plus `step_wise_training_metrics` and `validation_metrics` files you should be plotting, not eyeballing.

**Then the part that surprises people, and the part that decides the architecture.** A custom model is not directly invocable on-demand the way a base model is. You have two deployment routes:

| Route | What it costs | The constraint |
|---|---|---|
| **Provisioned Throughput** | hourly per Model Unit, no-commit / 1-month / 6-month | The classic path. **Cannot be created on a Legacy-state base model**, and PT is **incompatible with cross-Region inference profiles and with batch inference** — so the moment you fine-tune, you have given up CRIS failover, the ~10% global-profile discount, and the ~50% batch discount |
| **Custom Model Import** | serverless, per-token | Bring compatible open-weight architectures; you get on-demand economics back, at the price of being limited to supported architectures |

That incompatibility is the sentence to say out loud, because it reframes fine-tuning as an *availability and cost* decision rather than a modelling one: a fine-tune deployed on PT is a single-Region, fixed-capacity, always-paid-for asset sitting inside an architecture whose entire resilience story was cross-Region inference profiles.

**Distillation** is the cheaper cousin worth naming: you provide prompts (optionally with production invocation logs as the source), Bedrock generates responses from a large teacher model and fine-tunes a small student on them. It targets the common real case — "Sonnet-quality answers on our narrow task at Haiku prices and Haiku latency" — without a labelled dataset.

**The cost comparison that matters, and the honest recommendation:**

| Lever | Rough cost shape | Buys you |
|---|---|---|
| Better retrieval (chunking policy, hybrid search, reranking) | days of engineering; managed reranking currently free | Factual grounding, freshness, citations. **Fixes "it doesn't know our data"** |
| Prompt engineering + few-shot + caching | hours; caching *reduces* run cost | Format, tone, task adherence |
| Fine-tune + PT | training job, then **a Model Unit running 24×7 whether or not you use it** — the pricing page's own worked example is $39.60/hour, i.e. **$29,462/month** | Format and behaviour learned rather than instructed; lower per-request token count |
| Distillation | training job + serving the smaller student | Latency and unit cost on a narrow task |

> **Say it like this:** "My default is that fine-tuning is the third thing you try, not the first. If the complaint is 'it doesn't know our data', that's retrieval and a fine-tune won't fix it — you'll get a model that's fluent about the wrong facts. If the complaint is 'it won't follow our output format', try the prompt and few-shot first, because that's hours instead of a training job. Fine-tuning earns its place when you need behaviour that instructions can't reach, or when you're distilling to cut latency and unit cost on a narrow task at volume. And I'd want the deployment consequence on the table before anyone approves the training job: a custom model needs Provisioned Throughput or Custom Model Import, and Provisioned Throughput doesn't compose with cross-Region inference profiles or batch — so you're trading your failover story and your batch discount for it. On the pricing page's own example that's about twenty-nine thousand dollars a month for one Model Unit. That's not a modelling decision, it's a capacity commitment."

### A16. The reference architecture to draw in the pad

If the round is "AI/ML Ops **Design** and Domain" and there is a CoderPad open, at some point you should be *drawing*, not describing. This is the artefact. It fits in a text editor, it takes about ninety seconds to reproduce, and every box is defensible.

```text
 TENANT REQUEST
      │
      ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ EDGE / API                 authN, tenant resolution from JWT    │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
      │  tenant_id, tier, residency_class
      ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ LLM GATEWAY  (the only thing that talks to Bedrock)             │
│   · per-tenant token bucket — TPM, not RPM                      │
│   · maxTokens clamp per route  (p99 of observed output)         │
│   · model id + guardrail version from CONFIG, never code        │
│   · picks app inference profile  → per-tenant cost allocation   │
│   · picks geographic profile     → residency commitment         │
│   · retry: exp backoff + full jitter; 1 retry max if streaming  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
      │
      ├──► ApplyGuardrail (source=INPUT) ── BLOCK ──► refusal + metric
      │
      ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ RETRIEVE          Retrieve (not RetrieveAndGenerate)            │
│   · metadata filter pinned to tenant_id  ← isolation lives HERE │
│   · hybrid where the store supports it; rerank top-k            │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
      │  chunks + scores + doc ids
      ├──► ApplyGuardrail over RETRIEVED CONTEXT   ⚠ guardrails do
      │      (indirect injection, PII in corpus)     NOT see KB refs
      ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ GENERATE     ConverseStream                                     │
│   system + cachePoint  │  guardrailConfig pinned to a VERSION   │
│   streamProcessingMode = SYNCHRONOUS for customer-facing        │
│   requestMetadata{tenant, team, env}  → chargeback in the logs  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
      │
      ▼  stream to client (TTFT SLO)          ┌──────────────────┐
      └───────────────────────────────────────► OBSERVE          │
                                              │ OTel spans/stage │
                                              │ tokens + cache   │
                                              │ ResolvedSvcTier  │
                                              │ inferenceRegion  │
                                              │ sampled judge    │
                                              └────────┬─────────┘
                                                       │
   CI GATE: golden set → create-evaluation-job → block deploy on
            citation-coverage / correctness regression  ◄─────────┘
```

Three things to say while you draw it, in this order:

1. **"Tenant isolation lives in the retrieval filter, not in the prompt."** Point at the metadata filter. Prompt-level instructions to "only use tenant X's documents" are not a security control; a metadata filter pinned server-side from a validated JWT claim is. On a Managed KB this is document-level ACL permission filtering; on a self-managed store it is a filter the gateway sets and the caller cannot override.
2. **"There are two guardrail invocations, and the second one is the interesting one."** Point at the retrieved-context call. Guardrails apply to model input and model output; they do **not** inspect KB references. Indirect prompt injection arrives inside retrieved documents.
3. **"Everything expensive or regulated is a config value, not a literal."** Point at the gateway box. Model ID, guardrail version, inference profile, `maxTokens` — all config, all promoted through the same pipeline as code, all gated by the eval job at the bottom. That is what makes the six-EOLs-a-month problem in §A6 a chore rather than an incident.

### A17. Scripts for the direct Bedrock question

> **Say it like this (if asked "how much Bedrock have you done?"):** "None in production, and I'd rather say that than dress it up. The nearest thing I've shipped is a RAG assistant on AWS at ResMed with hybrid retrieval and an eval harness, and a GenAI query-routing assistant over a clinical knowledge base. What I've read carefully is the operational surface — quota burndown, inference profiles and residency, guardrail versioning, invocation logging for chargeback — because that's where a platform engineer earns their keep, and none of it is unfamiliar territory after five years of AWS."

> **Say it like this (if asked "design a Bedrock-backed feature for Smartsheet"):** — draw §A16 while you say this, don't just narrate it — "First question is what leaves the customer's tenancy. Enterprise SaaS means per-tenant isolation, so I'd want `bedrock-runtime` behind a PrivateLink endpoint with an endpoint policy limited to InvokeModel and ConverseStream; an application inference profile per tenant tier so cost allocation falls out of the tags rather than a spreadsheet; `requestMetadata` carrying tenant and environment into invocation logs; a geographic inference profile if any customer has residency terms, and I'd verify it with `inferenceRegion` in CloudTrail rather than trusting the config. Then a gateway in front for per-tenant token buckets, a `max_tokens` clamp per route, and backoff with jitter. Guardrails pinned to a numbered version, promoted through the same pipeline as code, with `ApplyGuardrail` also running over retrieved context — because guardrails don't inspect KB references. And a golden-set eval job that blocks the deploy on a citation-coverage regression."
