## PART B — Data and model observability

### B0. What Monte Carlo is, said accurately

It is **not** Monte Carlo *simulation*. It is a data-and-AI observability SaaS (montecarlo**data**.com → **montecarlo.ai**), Barr Moses's company, which coined "data observability" in 2019 and repositioned in 2026 as an **"Agent Trust Platform"**. It sits beside your warehouse, reads **metadata and query logs** rather than row-level data by default, builds ML baselines of "normal" per table, and raises **incidents**.

The intellectual claim, which is the thing to repeat back: **testing catches known unknowns; observability catches unknown unknowns.** Nobody writes a dbt test for every failure mode across 5,000 tables.

**The five pillars — know the failure mode, not just the name:**

| Pillar | Question | Canonical failure |
|---|---|---|
| Freshness | Did the data arrive when expected? | Dashboard silently stale for weeks; an exec finds it |
| Volume | Did we get the expected row count? | 200M rows → 5M after an upstream partition drop |
| Schema | Did the structure change? | Column dropped, renamed or retyped; a JSON schema change fans out row counts |
| Distribution / quality | Is the data itself sane? | Null rate 0.1% → 40%; currency flips cents↔dollars; a new enum value |
| Lineage | What is upstream and downstream? | Blast radius — which 40 dashboards and which feature table just broke |

⚠️ Monte Carlo's own pages sometimes label the fourth pillar "quality" rather than "distribution". Say "distribution or data quality" and you are correct either way.

**Monitor taxonomy (current — five categories):** *Table monitors* (automated, ML-baselined, zero-config on connection — cadence, size, growth); *Metric monitors* (automated or manual, dozens of field-level metrics plus custom SQL, **ML thresholds** backfilled from history or manual thresholds, segmentation up to 5 fields and up to 10,000 metric×field×segment combinations per monitor); *Validation monitors* (row-level business logic in SQL); *Job monitors* (query runtime/pipeline outliers); *Agent monitors*. ⚠️ Do **not** say `field_health` or `dimension_tracking` — those monitor types are deprecated and naming them dates you to a 2022 blog post.

**Monitors as Code**: YAML plus CLI, version-controlled — `compile` → `apply --dry-run` (which previews changes *and estimates credits*) → `apply --namespace $NS --auto-yes`, with `MCD_DEFAULT_API_ID`/`_TOKEN`. dbt integration works two ways: monitors embedded under a model's `meta:` block, or auto-generated from existing dbt tests. Quotable gotcha: refs use `[[ ref('model') ]]` with double square brackets to avoid colliding with dbt's Jinja.

**What it actually connects to** — the first question a buyer asks, and the doc's weakest area if you only know "it does dbt". Five categories, and the shape of the answer matters more than an exhaustive list:

| Layer | Connects to | Why it needs this one |
|---|---|---|
| **Warehouse / lakehouse** (the primary integration — this is where the metadata and query logs come from) | Snowflake, Databricks, BigQuery, Redshift, Athena/Glue, Postgres, plus object storage | Without the **query log** there is no field-level lineage; this is the integration the product is built on |
| **Transformation** | dbt Core and dbt Cloud, Airflow, Dagster, Spark | dbt gives model-level lineage from the manifest and can auto-generate monitors from existing tests; the orchestrators give **Job monitors** — runtime and failure outliers on the pipeline itself, not just the table |
| **BI** | Looker, Tableau, Power BI, Mode, Sigma | Extends lineage *downstream* past the warehouse, which is what turns "this table broke" into "these 40 dashboards and this exec report are wrong" — the actual blast radius |
| **Catalog / governance** | Atlan, Alation, Collibra | Pushes incident and health status back where owners already look, instead of asking them to open a second tool |
| **Alerting / workflow** | Slack, Teams, PagerDuty, Opsgenie, email, webhooks, Jira, ServiceNow | The Audience model below |

The honest read: warehouse and BI are the ones that matter, because they bound the lineage graph at both ends. Everything else is convenience.

**Lineage and triage**: automatic **field-level** lineage derived from warehouse query logs plus dbt manifests plus BI tools. **Incident IQ** groups related alerts into one incident with status, severity, owner and blast radius; **RCA Insights** adds correlation findings ("the nulls are all `region=APAC`"). 2026 adds **Observability Agents** — monitoring, troubleshooting and operations agents with a claimed >80% reduction in time-to-resolve (⚠️ vendor claim).

**Alerting**: the unit is an **Audience** — a named recipient group mixing Slack channels, emails, Teams, PagerDuty routing keys. Routing rules key off audience, domain, table importance/tag, monitor and incident type. Severity and owner are editable **from the Slack message**. Grouping happens at the *incident* level, so N related table alerts collapse into one page.

**Data Products and SLAs**: a Data Product groups tables plus reports serving one business outcome, and its dashboard reports coverage, incidents by status and severity, where upstream incidents originated, and **response time and time-to-fix**. That is the artefact you take to a stakeholder to commit to an SLA. SLIs: freshness, volume, incident count, TTD, TTR.

**Deployment**: SaaS with a lightweight collector reading metadata, query logs and `information_schema`, with optional and disable-able row sampling — that is the "no row-level data leaves our VPC" conversation every security review has. There is an agent/hybrid mode where the collector runs in your cloud. The 2026 agent-observability stack is explicitly in your account: agents emit **OTLP** traces → OpenTelemetry Collector → **ClickHouse** in your account; an LLM worker runs evals using your cloud's native LLM service (**Bedrock** on AWS); deployed to EKS/AKS/GKE via a single Terraform module.

**Pricing shape**: not public. **Consumption credits**, four tiers (Start, Scale, Enterprise, Business Critical); a public order form shows **$0.25/credit** as a reference (⚠️ 2025 document, not a current price list — everything real is negotiated). Cost drivers: number and size of tables observed, connected sources, and monitor depth. **Segmented metric monitors multiply as fields × segments × schedule and are the classic budget blowout.**

The differentiator worth raising, because it is the one genuinely interesting idea in their 2026 positioning:

> **Say it like this:** "Monte Carlo's real moat isn't the anomaly detection — everyone has ML thresholds now. It's query-log-derived **field-level lineage**, because that's what turns forty alerts into one incident with a blast radius. And their 2026 argument is a good one: an agent hallucinating because its RAG index is six days stale is a *data* incident, not a model incident, and you can only see that if data lineage and agent traces live in the same system."

### B1. The honest positioning — he has built this loop twice, with different tools

This is the most important paragraph in Part B. Do not claim the product; claim the control loop.

| Monte Carlo concept | What Sachin actually built | Where his version was weaker |
|---|---|---|
| Automated metric monitors with ML thresholds | **ResMed**: a Python/IaC drift-monitoring utility that ingests data-scientist-authored thresholds and slice definitions and **auto-provisions Datadog dashboards and alerts from Snowflake feature statistics** | Thresholds were human-authored, not ML-baselined from history. No unknown-unknown coverage — it monitored what someone thought to declare |
| Volume / distribution / schema checks at scale | **Tiger Analytics**: large-scale data-quality checks with **Deequ on Azure Databricks (Spark)**, drift-detection jobs orchestrated via Azure Data Factory | Deequ is a library, not a product: he built the scheduler, the metrics store, the alerting. Deequ *does* have constraint suggestion and anomaly detection over a metrics repository — that is the closest analogue to the ML-baselined layer |
| Monitors as code | The ResMed utility was declarative-config-driven and IaC-provisioned — the same idea, before it had a vendor name | No credit estimation, no dry-run diff, no dbt integration |
| Field-level lineage and blast radius | **Not built.** This is the honest gap | Impact analysis was manual: read the DAG, ask the owner |
| Incident grouping and audience routing | Datadog monitors and Grafana alerts, grouped by hand | No incident-level dedupe. N tables broken = N alerts |

> **Say it like this:** "I haven't operated Monte Carlo. I've built the same control loop twice with different tools. At ResMed I wrote a drift-monitoring utility that read data-scientist-authored thresholds and slice definitions out of config and auto-provisioned the Datadog dashboards and alerts from Snowflake feature statistics — declarative, IaC-managed, which is 'monitors as code' with the serial numbers filed off. At Tiger Analytics I ran Deequ data-quality checks on Spark on **Azure** Databricks, with drift jobs orchestrated from Azure Data Factory — about a year and a half, and to be precise about what that was: data-quality and ETL work, not Lakehouse-platform ownership. What I *didn't* have, and what Monte Carlo actually sells, is query-log-derived field-level lineage — so my impact analysis was manual and my alerts didn't group into incidents. Where I'd expect a learning curve is their monitor taxonomy and the credit-consumption model, not the concepts."

Then pivot immediately to the failure that proves the point:

> **Say it like this:** "The reason I take this category seriously is a bug I found at TrueBalance. Our offline feature pipeline built four thousand and one features; the real-time payload actually carried twenty-eight keys. The transform silently imputed defaults for the rest, so the served vector was near-constant and the model was, functionally, not running. No drift statistic would ever have caught that — the *distribution* of what we served was perfectly stable. What caught it was reading the served vectors. So I fixed it structurally: a serialised feature contract shipped next to the artefact, a hard failure on any missing required feature, a CI subset assertion as a promotion gate, and a per-feature missing-rate metric emitted by the scorer itself. That's the lesson — most 'the model broke' incidents are upstream data incidents, and the fix is contracts plus lineage, not a better test statistic."

### B2. The data-quality landscape

Frame it as three layers, not a list: **assertion frameworks** you run in-pipeline, **ML-baselined observability platforms** that watch everything without rules, and **diff/CI tools** that stop bad data before merge. They are complements. The mature line: *assertions in CI, observability in prod, diffs at PR time.*

| Tool | Good at | Honest catch |
|---|---|---|
| **Great Expectations (GX Core)** | Expressive Python assertions, huge expectation library, Spark/pandas/SQL backends, Apache-2.0 | Heavy boilerplate; known-unknowns only, no ML baselining, no lineage. Currency signal, and only say the part that is checkable: **the OSS project now lives under the Fivetran GitHub organisation** (`github.com/great-expectations/great_expectations` redirects to `fivetran/great_expectations`) **and GX Core is still Apache-2.0 and actively maintained** |
| **Soda (Core / Cloud)** | SodaCL is the most readable check DSL in the category; 2026 pivot to data contracts | **Soda Core v3 is Elastic License 2.0 — source-available, not open source.** Do not call it OSS in the room |
| **dbt tests** | Zero marginal cost if you already run dbt | Only covers dbt models — blind to raw ingestion. Pass/fail with no history, no baseline, no lineage to BI. Gets `severity: warn`-ed into meaninglessness |
| **Elementary** | dbt-native observability as a dbt package — anomaly detection plus a report, no extra infra. Best cost/benefit for a dbt shop | dbt-bounded; lineage is manifest lineage, not query-log lineage |
| **Deequ / PyDeequ** | Amazon's Spark-native library; **constraint suggestion** and **anomaly detection over a metrics repository**; scales on EMR/Glue; free | Scala-first, Spark-only, library not product — you build scheduler, storage, UI, alerting. *(His.)* |
| **AWS Glue Data Quality** | Managed Deequ with **DQDL**, rule recommendation, anomaly detection, native to Glue/Catalog/Lake Formation | AWS-only, weak outside Glue orchestration, no BI lineage |
| **Databricks Lakehouse Monitoring** | Schema-wide anomaly detection with intelligent scanning; assesses freshness and completeness from history; **uniquely, monitors inference tables** so data and model drift live together | Databricks-only, **Unity Catalog required** — which he has told the recruiter he has not used |
| **Anomalo** | Strongest unsupervised ML story; human-readable root-cause explanations of what changed | Black box; still needs rules for business logic; thinner lineage than Monte Carlo |
| **Bigeye** | Autometrics — auto-deployed ML-thresholded metrics; 2026 "AI Trust Platform" pivot with cost anomaly detection | Smaller lineage footprint; the AI-trust pivot is recent and unproven |
| **Metaplane** | Fast, cheap ML monitoring plus column-level lineage | **Acquired by Datadog (April 2025).** Right answer if you're already all-in on Datadog; re-platforming risk otherwise |
| **Datafold** | A different axis: **data-diff** wired into CI on dbt PRs, so data impact appears next to the code diff. Column-level lineage from query logs, catching ad-hoc tables and CTEs dbt can't | Prevention, not detection — no production incident management. OSS `data-diff` is far thinner than the cloud product |

### B3. Model observability is a different problem

> **Say it like this:** "Data observability answers 'is the table right?' — the unit is a table and the owner is data engineering. Model observability answers 'is the model still right?' — the unit is a prediction, the owner is ML engineering, and the hard part is that **ground truth arrives late or never**. A Monte Carlo-class tool will never tell you your AUC dropped."

| Tool | What it gives you |
|---|---|
| **Evidently** (OSS, Apache-2.0) | The reference library: 100+ metrics — per-column data drift with automatic test selection, target/prediction drift, data quality, classification/regression performance, text and embedding drift, LLM evals. Its auto-selection heuristic is worth memorising (§B4) |
| **Arize Phoenix** (OSS) / **Arize AX** | **OTel-native** tracing plus evals; strongest RAG/agent eval library. Best OSS pick if OpenTelemetry is your substrate |
| **WhyLabs / whylogs** | Profile-based: lightweight statistical *sketches*, so no raw data leaves. Privacy-friendly and cheap at volume; limited to what the sketch captured |
| **Fiddler** | Explainability (SHAP/IG) plus fairness, drift and performance; 2026 agentic observability with hierarchical traces and bring-your-own-judge. The pick when a regulator is in the room |
| **NannyML** (OSS) | The differentiated one: **estimates performance without labels** (CBPE, DLE), plus multivariate drift via PCA reconstruction error and a LightGBM **domain classifier** |
| **SageMaker Model Monitor** | Four monitors — data quality (Deequ-derived baseline constraints), model quality (needs ground truth merged back), bias drift, and **feature attribution drift** (SHAP-based, and genuinely under-known: it catches "the model started relying on a different feature" when marginals look fine). Writes violation reports to S3 → CloudWatch. **Billed as processing-job instance hours at standard SageMaker rates** — you pick the instance (AWS's own pricing example uses an `ml.m5.4xlarge`-class box) — with the **first 30 hours of built-in-rule monitoring free**, aggregated across endpoints; custom rules are charged separately. Cost scales with schedule frequency × instance size × number of monitored endpoints, **not** a flat per-endpoint fee |
| **Vertex AI Model Monitoring v2** | Training-serving skew and prediction drift with TFDV/L∞ and JS-style distances; monitors BQ/GCS batch sources too |

> **Say it like this:** "A model-monitoring stack that doesn't watch its feature pipelines is monitoring the symptom. Feature-attribution drift on SageMaker will tell you the model changed its mind; only lineage tells you it changed its mind because a dbt PR redefined `days_since_last_txn` last Tuesday."

### B4. The statistics a senior must own cold

**PSI (Population Stability Index).**

```
PSI = Σ_i (a_i − e_i) · ln(a_i / e_i)
```

where `e_i` is the reference/expected proportion in bin *i* and `a_i` the actual/production proportion. It is **symmetric KL** — `KL(A‖E) + KL(E‖A)` — known in the literature as **Jeffreys' J-divergence**, a close cousin of Jensen–Shannon.

Where people get it wrong: bins are defined on the **reference** distribution and then **frozen** (usually 10 quantile bins); categoricals need one bin per level plus an `__other__` bucket, or an unseen level gives `e_i = 0` and `PSI = ∞`; zero-cell handling (ε ≈ 1e-4, or a floor) materially changes the number so two teams "computing PSI" routinely disagree by 2×; and **PSI grows with bin count**, so thresholds are not comparable across binning schemes. If you cannot say "10 quantile bins fitted on the training set", your PSI is meaningless.

The 0.1 / 0.25 constants are **folklore**. They trace to Lewis (1994) and Siddiqi (2005) on credit scorecards, where the cadence was a monthly report on a few thousand applications, and later authors acknowledge them as arbitrary.

The killer quantitative point: from the χ² asymptotics of the KL estimator, under **no drift**, with `B` bins, `n_ref` reference rows and `n_prod` production rows,

```
E[PSI] ≈ (B−1) · (1/n_ref + 1/n_prod)
```

Both sample sizes enter, and forgetting that is the usual mistake. The formula collapses two ways, and you should be able to say both:

| Regime | Collapses to | Worked number (B = 10) |
|---|---|---|
| Large frozen reference, small daily window (**the everyday case**) | `(B−1)/n_prod` | `n_prod=100` → **0.09**; `n_prod=200` → **0.045** |
| Both sides the same size `n` | `2(B−1)/n` | `n=1,000` → **0.018**; `n=5,000` → **0.0036** |

I simulated all four of those cells against a standard normal: the empirical null means came out 0.094, 0.047, 0.018 and 0.0036 respectively — the formula holds to two significant figures. The consequence is the point: at `n_prod=100` against a large reference you sit **on** the 0.1 alarm line with zero real drift, and at `n_ref = n_prod = 100,000` the null expectation is 0.00018, so 0.1 is a five-hundred-fold effect you will never fire on. ⚠️ Present this as asymptotic scaling, not an exact identity.

And there is empirical backup. *"When Drift Detectors Cry Wolf: False Alarm Rates in Continuous ML Monitoring"* (arXiv 2607.17336, Raj Shekhar Singh, ICLR 2026 CAO workshop) compares five detectors — PSI, KS, MMD, LSDD and adversarial validation — under **no injected drift**. Quote the abstract's findings, which are what you can actually defend:

- **PSI "exhibits strong sensitivity to batch size, producing frequent false alarms at small sample sizes"**, improving markedly once batches exceed roughly **200 samples** — the same threshold the formula above predicts.
- **KS, MMD and LSDD "display persistent fluctuations across batch sizes, while remaining comparatively more reliable than PSI in low-data regimes."** They are steadier, not clean.
- **Bonferroni correction "reduces false positive rates, but often at the cost of reduced true positive sensitivity"** — the stability/sensitivity trade-off, stated by the authors rather than by you.

⚠️ Quote it at that granularity. The per-batch-size false-alarm counts are in the PDF, not the abstract; do not recite ± figures you cannot source in the room, and do not claim the paper crowns a single winner — it does not.

**KS test.** `D = sup_x |F_ref(x) − F_prod(x)|`, critical value at α=0.05 ≈ `1.36·√((n+m)/nm)`. At `n = m = 10⁶` that is `D_crit ≈ 0.0019` — a 0.2% maximum CDF gap is "statistically significant". The null (*the distributions are exactly identical*) is never true in production, so with enough rows you reject everything, always. Four fixes, say all four: alert on **effect size** not p-value; **fix the comparison sample size** by subsampling to a constant n so sensitivity doesn't wander with traffic; remember KS is univariate, continuous-only and **insensitive in the tails** — exactly where credit and fraud risk live; and gate on **materiality** ("significant AND the mean moved >0.25σ AND the feature is top-10 by importance").

**Chi-square** has the same large-n pathology; threshold **Cramér's V** = `√(χ²/(n(k−1)))` instead, and pool rare categories (expected cell counts ≳5).

**JS divergence.** `JS(P,Q) = ½KL(P‖M) + ½KL(Q‖M)`, `M = (P+Q)/2` — symmetric, always finite, bounded, and `√JS` is a true metric. The sane default for categorical drift. Plain **KL** is asymmetric, unbounded and undefined when `q_i = 0`; use it only when you have a genuine reference *model*, not two samples.

**Wasserstein (W₁)** = `∫|F(x) − G(x)|dx`, the mean absolute difference between quantile functions. Two properties make it the best default for numeric drift: it is **in the units of the feature** (a W₁ of 4,200 on `monthly_income` is instantly interpretable; divide by reference σ to compare across features), and it **respects ordering** — KL/JS/PSI treat bins as unordered, so moving mass from bin 3 to bin 4 and from bin 3 to bin 10 look identical, and Wasserstein knows the second is ten times worse.

**Evidently's default selection heuristic** — a clean, quotable rule:

| Reference size | Numeric (`n_unique` > 5) | Categorical / numeric `n_unique` ≤ 5 | Binary |
|---|---|---|---|
| ≤ 1,000 | two-sample **KS**, conf 0.95 | **chi-square**, conf 0.95 | Z-test on proportions |
| > 1,000 | **Wasserstein**, threshold 0.1 | **Jensen–Shannon**, threshold 0.1 | JS |

The logic is exactly the large-n argument: hypothesis tests for small samples where you need the noise model, distance metrics for large samples where p-values are useless and you want effect size.

**Multivariate drift.** Univariate tests miss correlation-structure breaks — income and loan-amount marginals identical, the *ratio* distribution flipped. Two methods: a **domain classifier / adversarial validation** (label reference 0, production 1, train LightGBM, report cross-validated AUROC — 0.5 means indistinguishable; the gift is that its feature importances tell you *which* features carry the drift and its per-row scores give you reweighting importance weights; the cost is compute and over-sensitivity at scale, so threshold on magnitude, e.g. >0.65, not on "above 0.5"); and **PCA reconstruction error** (fit on reference capturing ~65% of variance, project production in and back out, monitor error — cheaper and less sensitive). Also name **MMD** (kernel two-sample, O(n²) naively, fiddly bandwidth) and **LSDD**.

**Get the drift taxonomy's causal direction right:**

| Type | Formally | Does the model become wrong? | How you catch it |
|---|---|---|---|
| Data / covariate drift | `P(X)` moves, `P(Y|X)` stable | **Not necessarily** — only if mass moves where the model was always weak | Univariate + multivariate drift; CBPE estimates the impact |
| Concept drift | `P(Y|X)` moves | **Always** | **Requires labels.** Invisible to input-drift monitors, and CBPE will confidently say "fine" |
| Label / prior drift | `P(Y)` moves | Ranking survives; **calibration and thresholds break** | Score distribution + ECE. **AUC flat + ECE degraded ⇒ prior shift ⇒ recalibrate, don't retrain** |
| Upstream schema drift | The pipeline changed, not the world | **Yes, catastrophically and silently** | **Not statistics.** Schema monitors, lineage, CI diffs, feature contracts |
| Training-serving skew | Feature computed differently offline vs online | Yes, from day one | Log serving features, replay against the training pipeline, diff |

> **Say it like this:** "Drift statistics are the *least* common root cause of production model failure. The ranking, roughly, is upstream pipeline and schema breakage, then training-serving skew, then concept drift, then smooth covariate drift. Which is exactly why an MLOps job description asks about *data* observability tooling rather than about drift tests."

**Prediction drift** — monitoring `P(ŷ)` — is your cheapest label-free early alarm: immediate, no labels, and the last signal before business impact. Honest limits: it is ambiguous by construction (it moves under covariate drift, under a legitimate population change like a marketing campaign, and under a broken feature), it is **not sensitive to concept drift at all**, and if the model's output determines who you observe next, part of it is self-inflicted. Treat it as a page-worthy *symptom* that triggers a drill-down, never a diagnosis.

**Performance estimation without labels.** **CBPE** (classification): calibrate scores on reference; for each production row with calibrated probability p, a positive prediction contributes p to expected TP and 1−p to expected FP, a negative contributes 1−p to TN and p to FN; sum into an expected confusion matrix and derive accuracy, precision, recall, F1, ROC-AUC — no labels at all. **DLE** (regression): train a "nanny" model on reference to predict the child model's absolute or squared error from the features plus the child's prediction, then apply it to production. State the assumptions unprompted: **no concept drift** (these are covariate-shift estimators), well-calibrated or calibratable probabilities, enough rows per chunk, no extrapolation into unseen feature space.

> **Say it like this:** "CBPE tells you what performance *would* be if only the inputs changed. It is silent on the one failure mode you most fear. So I run it *with* a multivariate drift detector: if CBPE says estimated AUC is fine but the domain classifier's AUROC spikes to 0.9, the inputs have moved into territory the estimator can't vouch for, and that's my trigger to pull a manual label sample."

**Calibration drift.** ECE = `Σ_m (|B_m|/n)·|acc(B_m) − conf(B_m)|` — binning-dependent and biased downward with few bins, so use equal-mass (adaptive) bins and report MCE alongside. Brier score decomposes (Murphy) into **reliability − resolution + uncertainty**: reliability is calibration, resolution is discrimination, and reporting the decomposition tells you which half broke. Calibration silently breaks whenever someone changes the decision threshold, the class weights, or the population mix — and monitor **per segment**, because a globally calibrated model is routinely badly miscalibrated on the small segment that matters.

**Delayed labels** — credit, churn, chargebacks land 30–180 days late, and never for the population you declined. Five moves: validated **proxy labels** (30-day first-payment default as a read on 90-day default — validate the correlation first, and re-validate, because the proxy relationship drifts too); **performance estimation**; explicit awareness of **reject inference / selective labels** (your realised labels are censored by the model's own decisions, so naive backtests are optimistic and every retrain narrows the observed region further); the move that separates senior from mid — **hold out a small randomised control slice** approved irrespective of score, so you retain an unbiased label sample; and **vintage/cohort analysis**, comparing each origination cohort at the same maturity rather than raw monthly bad-rates that mix maturities.

**Slice-level monitoring and multiple comparisons.** 200 features × 20 segments × daily = **4,000 tests/day**; at α=0.05 that is **200 false alarms a day** before anything is wrong. Use **Benjamini–Hochberg FDR** rather than Bonferroni for monitoring (you care that the on-call alert list is mostly real, not that you never had a single false positive); use **hierarchical gating** — test the multivariate signal or estimated performance first and only drill into per-feature and per-segment tests when the top-level gate fires, turning 4,000 daily tests into ~1; alert only on top-k features by SHAP or permutation importance; **pre-register segments** with minimum-size floors instead of scanning all slices; and always check for Simpson's paradox — aggregate drift can be flat while every segment drifts.

**Thresholds that survive an on-call rotation.** Paging philosophy: **page on symptoms, ticket on causes.** Page on served-metric SLO burn — p95 latency, error rate, null rate on a required feature, estimated-performance drop, approval-rate anomaly. File a *ticket* for drift; drift is a diagnosis aid, not an incident. Every page needs a runbook and a named owner or it gets deleted. Tier severity by blast radius **derived from lineage**, not hand-set. Mechanics: baseline from **60–90 days of known-good production**, take p99 of the metric's own variation and set the threshold above it; require **persistence** (3 consecutive windows, or 3 of 5); fix the sample size per window; keep **two references deliberately** — a static training reference that catches slow decay, and a rolling reference (same weekday, previous 4 weeks) that absorbs seasonality and catches step changes, because rolling-only is a boiling frog; treat seasonality as not-drift; suppress during deploys, backfills and migrations; group by cause not symptom.

> **Say it like this:** "I treat monitors as a product with their own metrics. I track alert precision — the percentage of alerts that led to an action — plus MTTA, MTTR and coverage, and I review the alert log monthly. Any monitor below about 50% precision gets retuned or deleted. Target is single-digit actionable alerts per on-call day. A monitoring system you have to mute is worse than none, because it manufactures false confidence."

### B5. PSI, implemented with the edge cases handled

Good CoderPad artefact if the design round asks for "a monitor".

```python
"""PSI with frozen reference bins, an honest noise floor, and unseen-category handling."""
from __future__ import annotations
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

OTHER = "__other__"


@dataclass
class PSIBinner:
    """Fit bin edges ONCE on the reference sample, then freeze them."""
    n_bins: int = 10
    eps: float = 1e-4            # empty-bin floor; reported, because it moves the number
    other_floor: float = 0.01    # min reference mass deliberately pooled into __other__
    edges: np.ndarray | None = None          # numeric
    levels: list | None = None               # categorical
    expected: np.ndarray | None = None
    kind: str = "numeric"
    n_ref: int = 0
    warnings_: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)

    def fit(self, ref: pd.Series) -> "PSIBinner":
        ref = ref.dropna()
        self.n_ref = len(ref)
        if ref.empty:
            raise ValueError("empty reference sample")

        p = None
        if pd.api.types.is_numeric_dtype(ref) and ref.nunique() > 5:
            qs = np.linspace(0, 1, self.n_bins + 1)
            e = np.unique(np.quantile(ref, qs))       # dedupe on spiky/zero-inflated data
            if len(e) >= 3:
                self.kind = "numeric"
                e[0], e[-1] = -np.inf, np.inf         # open tails: prod can exceed ref range
                self.edges = e
                p = np.histogram(ref, bins=self.edges)[0].astype(float)
            else:
                # Zero-inflated or near-constant: a single bin makes PSI structurally 0.0
                # forever. Fall through to the categorical path instead of pretending.
                self.warnings_.append(
                    "quantiles collapsed (zero-inflated or near-constant); "
                    "falling back to the categorical path so PSI is not structurally 0")

        if p is None:
            self.kind = "categorical"
            s = ref.astype("string")
            counts = s.value_counts()
            if len(counts) == 1:
                self.warnings_.append("reference has a single level; PSI cannot move on it")
            # Pool from the rarest level upward until __other__ carries REAL reference mass,
            # so an unseen production level lands in a bucket with a non-epsilon expectation.
            asc = counts.sort_values()
            pooled, cum = [], 0.0
            for lvl, c in asc.items():
                frac = c / self.n_ref
                if (frac < 0.01 or cum < self.other_floor) and len(asc) - len(pooled) > 1:
                    pooled.append(lvl); cum += frac
                    if cum >= self.other_floor and frac >= 0.01:
                        break
                else:
                    break
            keep = [lv for lv in counts.index.tolist() if lv not in set(pooled)]
            self.levels = keep + [OTHER]
            mapped = s.where(s.isin(keep), OTHER)
            p = mapped.value_counts().reindex(self.levels).fillna(0).to_numpy(float)
            if cum < self.other_floor:
                self.warnings_.append(
                    f"__other__ holds only {cum:.4f} of reference mass; an unseen level's "
                    "PSI contribution is epsilon-determined, so read unseen_rate instead")

        self.expected = np.maximum(p / p.sum(), self.eps)
        return self

    def _actual(self, prod: pd.Series):
        prod = prod.dropna()
        if prod.empty:
            raise ValueError("empty production sample")
        unseen = 0.0
        if self.kind == "categorical":
            s = prod.astype("string")
            known = set(self.levels[:-1])
            unseen = float((~s.isin(known)).mean())   # its own metric, not a PSI magnitude
            mapped = s.where(s.isin(known), OTHER)
            a = mapped.value_counts().reindex(self.levels).fillna(0).to_numpy(float)
        else:
            a = np.histogram(prod, bins=self.edges)[0].astype(float)
        return np.maximum(a / a.sum(), self.eps), unseen

    def score(self, prod: pd.Series) -> dict:
        a, unseen = self._actual(prod)
        e = self.expected
        contrib = (a - e) * np.log(a / e)
        n_prod = int(prod.dropna().shape[0])
        b = len(e)
        # Null expectation uses BOTH sample sizes. Using n_ref alone reports a floor of
        # 0.00009 at n_ref=100k / n_prod=200, where the true null mean is ~0.045.
        floor = (b - 1) * (1.0 / self.n_ref + 1.0 / n_prod)
        notes = list(self.warnings_)
        if floor > 0.02:
            notes.append(
                f"null-expectation PSI ~= {floor:.3f} (B={b}, n_ref={self.n_ref}, "
                f"n_prod={n_prod}); the 0.1 threshold is not meaningful here")
        if n_prod < 200:
            notes.append(f"n_prod={n_prod} < 200: PSI false-alarms frequently at this "
                         "batch size (arXiv 2607.17336)")
        if unseen > 0.01:
            notes.append(f"unseen-level rate {unseen:.3f}: treat as its own alarm, "
                         "not as a PSI magnitude")
        top = int(np.argmax(np.abs(contrib)))
        return {"psi": float(contrib.sum()), "null_psi": float(floor),
                "psi_excess": float(contrib.sum() - floor),   # the number worth alerting on
                "unseen_rate": unseen,
                "n_ref": self.n_ref, "n_prod": n_prod, "bins": b, "eps": self.eps,
                "per_bin": contrib.tolist(),
                "worst_bin": {"index": top, "contribution": float(contrib[top]),
                              "expected": float(e[top]), "actual": float(a[top])},
                "notes": notes}


if __name__ == "__main__":
    rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
    ref = pd.Series(rng.normal(0, 1, 50_000))
    b = PSIBinner().fit(ref)
    print(b.score(pd.Series(rng.normal(0.0, 1.0, 5_000)))["psi"])   # 0.0021, no drift
    print(b.score(pd.Series(rng.normal(0.4, 1.2, 5_000)))["psi"])   # 0.1627, drifted

    big = PSIBinner().fit(pd.Series(rng.normal(0, 1, 100_000)))     # the everyday shape:
    r = big.score(pd.Series(rng.normal(0, 1, 200)))                 # frozen ref, tiny window
    print(r["psi"], r["null_psi"], r["notes"])   # 0.097 vs a 0.045 null -> not drift
```

Verified behaviour, because the edge cases are the entire reason to show this rather than the four-line version:

| Case | The naive implementation | This one |
|---|---|---|
| No drift, 50k ref / 5k window | 0.002 | 0.002 |
| Real shift (μ 0→0.4, σ 1→1.2) | 0.163 | 0.163 |
| **100k ref / 200-row window, no drift** | noise floor computed from `n_ref` alone reports **0.00009** and stays silent | `null_psi` **0.045** against a measured null mean of 0.044 — and it says so out loud |
| **Unseen category at 50% of the window** | `__other__` expectation is ε, so PSI = **12.8**, a number determined entirely by your epsilon | `__other__` deliberately seeded with 20.5% real reference mass → PSI **0.68**, plus `unseen_rate` **0.595** reported as its own signal |
| **95% zero-inflated column** | quantiles collapse to a single bin; PSI = **0.0 forever** | falls back to the categorical path; PSI **0.89** when the zero mass moves |
| **Constant column** | `nunique() <= 5` routes it to the categorical path, so the "near-degenerate" warning never fires for the most obvious degenerate case | warns "single level", and still moves when a new value appears |

Four things to point at while the interviewer reads it: bins are fitted once and frozen; the tails are open so production values outside the reference range don't silently vanish; `eps` is a declared field and echoed in the output, because epsilon choice moves the number and that is exactly why two teams "computing PSI" routinely disagree by 2×; and the object refuses to be quiet about its own noise floor — it returns `psi_excess`, the drift *above* what the sample sizes alone would manufacture, which is the number you should actually threshold.

### B6. LLM and agent observability in 2026

**OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions — and the honest state of them.** Nothing in the GenAI conventions is marked **Stable**; everything is Development. They were **deprecated in the main `semantic-conventions` repo at v1.42.0 (12 June 2026)** and moved to a dedicated `open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai` repo which **has no releases or tags yet** — so there is currently no finalised schema URL to pin against. Breaking renames to know: `prompt_tokens`/`completion_tokens` → `gen_ai.usage.input_tokens`/`output_tokens` (v1.27.0); **`gen_ai.system` → `gen_ai.provider.name`** with events replaced by message attributes (v1.37.0); `gen_ai.evaluation.result` (v1.38.0); agent spans refined and reasoning tokens added (v1.41.0). **`OTEL_SEMCONV_STABILITY_OPT_IN` lets you dual-emit old and new attribute names** — that is the practical answer to "how do you survive an unstable spec".

**The span tree to be able to draw:**

```text
invoke_agent  (root — gen_ai.conversation.id, gen_ai.agent.name)
├── chat <model>            gen_ai.request.model, temperature, max_tokens
│                           gen_ai.usage.input_tokens / output_tokens
│                           gen_ai.response.finish_reasons
├── retrieval               index name, k, top-1 similarity, chunk ids
├── execute_tool <name>     gen_ai.tool.name, gen_ai.tool.call.id, error.type
├── chat <model>            (observation → next step)
└── execute_tool <name>
```

Metrics: `gen_ai.client.token.usage` and `gen_ai.client.operation.duration` as histograms, plus server-side TTFT and time-per-output-token. **Message content capture is opt-in and env-gated** — prompts and completions are PII and secrets by default. Say that; it is the first thing a security review asks.

**What to actually measure.** *Retrieval*: recall@k / precision@k / nDCG against a golden set; **empty-retrieval rate** and **low-similarity rate** (the best cheap out-of-domain detector you have); retrieved-chunk distribution, i.e. index collapse; **index staleness** — the age of the embedding index versus source of truth, which is the bridge back to data observability, because a "hallucination" is very often a six-day-stale index; reranker score drift. *Generation*: **groundedness/faithfulness** (is every claim entailed by retrieved context), **answer relevance** (orthogonal — a perfectly grounded non-answer scores well on faithfulness), **citation validity**, and **refusal rate in both directions** — over-refusal after a prompt or model change is a real, common, invisible regression. *Operations*: **p95/p99 latency by stage** (embed → retrieve → rerank → generate → tool → post-process; never a single number, never the mean), TTFT versus total, token cost split input/output/**cache-read** with **prompt-cache hit rate**, **cost per successful task rather than per call** (a cheap model that loops forty times is not cheap), tool-call error and **tool-argument schema-validation failure rate** (the leading indicator of a degrading model or a drifted tool spec), steps-per-session at the p99 tail for runaway-loop detection, and provider error/rate-limit rates by model. *Quality over time*: a golden-set regression gate blocking deploy, sampled LLM-as-judge scoring on live traffic with a human review queue — and **pin the judge model version**, because judge drift silently moves your quality metric. *Security*: prompt-injection attempt rate as a first-class metric (OWASP **LLM01**, #1 since 2023), and the RAG-specific one people miss — **indirect injection arriving inside retrieved documents**, so scan retrieved context, not just user input. Honest framing: detection is not solved; reported attack success rates in the literature run wide, so the answer is defence in depth plus monitoring, never "we added a classifier".

| Tool | Position |
|---|---|
| **Langfuse** | The open-source default in 2026. Self-hostable (Postgres + ClickHouse), framework-agnostic, ingests OTel. The pick when you need residency or want to avoid lock-in |
| **LangSmith** | Fastest path if you're on LangChain/LangGraph — and the highest lock-in risk |
| **Arize Phoenix / AX** | OTel-native by design, strongest open eval-metric library, best RAG evaluation |
| **MLflow Tracing** | Right answer **if MLflow is already your registry** — extends the workflow you have rather than adding a tool. Relevant here: the JD names MLflow explicitly |
| **W&B Weave** | Natural if you're already on W&B; rarely the standalone winner |
| **RAGAS / DeepEval / Braintrust** | Eval-first rather than observability-first; RAGAS and DeepEval are the OSS metric libraries you'd import |

The architectural distinction worth stating: *proxy/gateway* tools (Helicone, Portkey) log every call with zero instrumentation but only see individual HTTP calls and **cannot reconstruct the orchestration graph**; *SDK/OTel* tools require instrumentation but give you the real span tree. For agents you need the tree; for a cost audit the proxy is enough.

### B7. The three sentences to have loaded

> **Say it like this (on Monte Carlo):** "I haven't run Monte Carlo. I've built the same loop by hand — Deequ on Spark on Azure Databricks at Tiger, about eighteen months of it and all data-quality and ETL rather than platform ownership, and a config-driven drift utility that auto-provisioned Datadog monitors from Snowflake feature statistics at ResMed. The reason the category exists is that most production model incidents are upstream *data* incidents — a schema change or a silent null-rate jump — which no drift statistic will ever catch. Five pillars: freshness, volume, schema, distribution and lineage. Lineage is the one that actually saves your on-call."

> **Say it like this (on statistics):** "I'd rather monitor effect sizes than p-values. At a million rows a KS test rejects a 0.2% CDF gap. And PSI has a null expectation of roughly bins-minus-one times one-over-n-reference plus one-over-n-production — so against a big frozen reference with ten bins it's about 0.09 on a hundred-row window and 0.0002 at a hundred thousand a side. The 0.1 line is hair-trigger at one end and deaf at the other, and it's the *same* threshold. There's a 2026 ICLR workshop paper on this — PSI false-alarms frequently at small batch sizes and only settles above about two hundred samples. So I set thresholds from ninety days of the metric's own historical variation, require persistence across windows, and apply FDR control across features and segments."

> **Say it like this (on what you'd do first here):** "Instrument before I optimise. Feature pipelines get freshness, volume and schema monitors plus a contract asserted in CI — I've been burned by exactly that failure. Models get prediction drift plus label-free performance estimation, because in lending the labels arrive months late. The LLM surface gets OTel spans with per-stage p95, cost per successful task, groundedness on sampled traffic, and a golden-set regression gate in CI. Then I page on symptoms, ticket on causes, and audit alert precision monthly."


---

## 7. Domain primer — Kubernetes, serving, CI/CD, Terraform, design-to-cost

### The three sentences that carry this round

Almost every infrastructure question in this JD collapses into one of three claims. Learn them as sentences, not bullet points, because the interviewer is listening for a frame, not a tool list.

1. **ML workloads break the assumptions the platform was built on.** Kubernetes assumes small, stateless, fast-starting, fungible pods. ML gives you 20 GB images, weights measured in tens of gigabytes, indivisible accelerators, gang-scheduled jobs, and per-replica cache state that makes replicas *non*-interchangeable.
2. **The unit of cost is not the instance, it is the duty cycle.** Nobody pays for GPUs; they pay for predictions. Every cost lever either raises the numerator (throughput per accelerator) or lowers the denominator (idle time, over-provisioning).
3. **The promotion decision for a model is evidential, not binary.** Software CI asks *did it compile and pass*. ML CI asks *is this model, on this data snapshot, better than the incumbent by more than noise, on every slice we care about* — which is a distribution, so the gate must encode a margin.

> **Say it like this:** "Before the specific question, the frame I use is that ML breaks three Kubernetes assumptions — pods are cheap, resources are divisible, replicas are interchangeable. None of those hold once there is an accelerator and a KV cache involved, and most of the platform design work is compensating for that."

**A note on the scripts in this chapter.** Five are marked **[verbatim]** — those are the ones where exact wording earns or loses credibility, and they are worth delivering as written. Every other script is a two-sentence spine plus bullets you expand only if the interviewer pulls on it. A sixty-minute round with a rubric to cover punishes monologue; the signal lives in the follow-ups, and you only get follow-ups if you stop talking.

#### The calibration that has to come first

Sachin's two most recent production serving surfaces are **AWS Lambda + SQS with ARM64 containers at TrueBalance** and **multi-container SageMaker endpoints at ResMed**, plus a **SageMaker-based MLOps platform for NatWest at Tiger Analytics**. He has used Kubernetes and OpenShift, but he has not run a large GPU fleet. Present the Kubernetes and GPU-fleet material as design knowledge and the serverless/SageMaker material as operated experience, and say which is which. Interviewers reward the distinction and punish its absence.

> **Say it like this [verbatim]:** "I should be precise about what I have run versus what I have designed. The production serving I own end to end is the Lambda-plus-SQS scorer at TrueBalance; before that, multi-container SageMaker endpoints at ResMed and a SageMaker MLOps platform for NatWest. Kubernetes and OpenShift I have used, but the GPU-scheduling and vLLM-on-Kubernetes material is design knowledge from evaluating it, not years of operating an accelerator fleet. I would rather say that up front than have you discover it in a follow-up."

The same discipline applies to the Databricks line in the JD, and it is worth pre-empting once rather than being caught by it:

> **Say it like this [verbatim]:** "On the Databricks stack I want to be exact, because the JD names things I have not touched. What I have is about eighteen months of Azure Databricks — Spark jobs, Deequ data-quality checks, drift jobs orchestrated from Data Factory. That is data-quality and ETL work, not Lakehouse platform ownership, and it was not at petabyte scale. Unity Catalog, Mosaic AI Agent Framework and Databricks Vector Search I have not used — my vector work is pgvector, FAISS, Chroma and Pinecone. MLflow I have used. I would rather tell you the shape of the gap than have you find it in week three."

---

### How to run the hour

This round is titled "AI/ML Ops Design and Domain" and there is a CoderPad open. The overwhelmingly likely task is *design a platform or a serving stack*, with the pad used for a diagram, a schema, a manifest or a small stub. The method below is worth more than any single fact in this chapter, because a design round is graded on whether you drove it.

| Minute | Phase | What you are doing | What the interviewer is scoring |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0-5 | **Clarify** | Ask the six questions below. Write the answers in the pad as a requirements block | Do you design against constraints or against a fashion? |
| 5-8 | **Assumptions and non-goals** | State what you are assuming and what you are explicitly not solving | Do you know where the risk is? |
| 8-20 | **Spine** | Draw the nine-box reference architecture. Narrate the data flow once, end to end, including the feedback loop | Coverage and coherence |
| 20-40 | **Deep dive** | Offer two or three candidate dives and let them pick. Go to code/YAML in the pad | Depth in at least one place |
| 40-50 | **Failure modes** | Walk the degradation ladder and the rollback story for the thing you just designed | Operational maturity |
| 50-57 | **Cost** | Unit economics, the crossover, the one lever you would pull first | The JD names cost twice |
| 57-60 | **Their questions** | Two prepared, specific to their stack | Interest |

**The six clarifying questions.** Ask them in this order; each one changes the architecture.

1. **Latency contract** — is this synchronous with a user waiting, or can it be asynchronous with a completion SLO? This single answer decides serverless-vs-endpoint, spot-vs-on-demand, and batch size.
2. **Volume and shape** — peak QPS, sustained QPS, and the ratio between them. Duty cycle is the cost driver, not peak.
3. **Model kind** — tree ensemble, small encoder, or a generative model with a KV cache? The third one is a different platform.
4. **Tenancy** — one model for everyone, per-tenant models, or per-tenant fine-tunes? Smartsheet is multi-tenant SaaS, so assume this matters and ask it early.
5. **Label latency and retraining cadence** — when do you learn you were wrong? This decides whether monitoring can gate on quality or only on proxies.
6. **Regulatory surface** — data residency, PII, audit, who has to be able to explain a decision.

> **Say it like this [verbatim]:** "Before I draw anything, six questions, because each one moves the design. Is there a user waiting on the response, or is a completion SLO acceptable? What is peak versus sustained QPS — I care about the ratio more than the peak. Is the model a tree ensemble, an encoder, or generative with a KV cache? Is it one model for all tenants, or per-tenant? How long until labels arrive? And what is the compliance surface — residency, PII, audit? I will state my assumptions for anything you would rather I not pin down, and I will keep them visible in the pad so we can change one and see what breaks."

**Time-boxing rules that keep you out of trouble.** Draw the whole spine before you go deep on any box — a design round is lost by spending twenty-five minutes on the feature store and never reaching monitoring. Say "I am going to keep this shallow and come back if you want it" out loud. When you do not know something, name the shape of the answer and say you would check: "I do not know Bedrock's per-region model-unit quota from memory; the design question is whether quota or GPU capacity is the scaling limit, and for Bedrock it is quota." And when the interviewer pushes on a specific technology, answer for the technology, then immediately restate the property that made you pick it — that is how you show the choice was reasoned rather than recited.

### The reference architecture

This is the artefact to reproduce in the pad in under three minutes. Memorise the nine boxes and the direction of the arrows; everything else in this chapter hangs off one of them.

```text
 [1 ingest] -> [2 feature] -> [3 train] -> [4 registry] -> [5 gates] -> [6 serve]
      ^                                                                     |
      |                                                                     v
 [9 retrain trigger] <- [8 monitor: drift/quality/cost] <- [7 log preds+features]
```

Two things about that picture carry the whole design. First, **the loop is the architecture** — boxes 1 to 6 are a deployment pipeline that any competent engineer draws; boxes 7, 8 and 9 are what makes it an ML platform, and they are the ones candidates leave out. Second, **box 2 is drawn once but exists twice** — the same transformation code has to serve an offline, point-in-time-correct store for training and a low-latency online store for serving. Every train/serve skew bug in the industry lives in the gap between those two, including the one described later in this chapter.

### Why ML is awkward on Kubernetes

| Kubernetes assumption | ML reality | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| Pods are cheap and fungible | A pod holds an accelerator worth tens of thousands of dollars plus tens of GB of loaded state | Eviction is expensive; the scheduler's cost model is wrong |
| Containers start in seconds | 15-40 GB CUDA/framework images, then weights load after | Scale-up latency of 3-15 min; HPA reacts far too late |
| Resources are divisible (`cpu: 500m`) | `nvidia.com/gpu: 1` is an integer; there is no 0.4 GPU | Bin-packing fails; fragmentation is the steady state |
| Workloads are stateless | KV caches, feature caches, shard-local state | Round-robin balancing destroys the most valuable state in the cluster |
| Jobs are short or infinitely restartable | A multi-day training run with gang semantics | Node upgrades and spot reclamation become correctness events |
| One pod is one unit of work | Multi-node tensor/pipeline-parallel serving, all-or-nothing | Partial scheduling deadlocks the cluster |
| The control plane can move things around | NVLink/InfiniBand topology matters; cross-rack placement halves throughput | Scheduling must be topology-aware, not just resource-aware |

#### The four GPU sharing mechanisms

This is used as a filter question. Be able to produce the table on demand.

| Mechanism | Isolation | Memory | Fault domain | Use it for |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Whole GPU via device plugin** | Full | Full | Per-pod | Training, large-model inference |
| **MIG** (A100/H100 class, up to 7 slices) | Hardware — dedicated SMs, L2 slice, memory path | Hard-partitioned | Isolated | Multi-tenant inference where a noisy neighbour is unacceptable; predictable p99 |
| **Time-slicing** (device plugin `replicas: N`) | None — context switch between processes | Shared, **unenforced** | Shared: one OOM kills the neighbours | Dev, notebooks, CI pools. Never for SLO traffic |
| **MPS** | No *performance* isolation; kernels run concurrently rather than time-sliced | Shared, but a per-client cap is available (`CUDA_MPS_PINNED_DEVICE_MEM_LIMIT`) | Volta and later contain a client's fatal fault to that client | Many small cooperating kernels from one team |

The MPS row is where people are out of date, so it is worth getting right out loud: the folklore that one MPS client crashing takes down every other client is **pre-Volta**. On Volta and later, a client's fatal fault is contained to that client, and you can cap per-client device memory. That makes MPS strictly better than time-slicing — but it still gives you no performance isolation, so it is for cooperating small kernels, never for something carrying an SLO.

> **Say it like this:** "Time-slicing oversubscribes with no memory enforcement, so it converts a capacity problem into an OOMKilled problem. MPS is better than its reputation on Volta and later — fault containment and a per-client memory cap — but it still has no performance isolation. MIG is the only one of the four that gives you a real p99, because the partition is in hardware."

**Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA)** is the current answer to *expressing* the request. The core of DRA went GA in Kubernetes v1.34. The device-plugin API can only say `gpu: 1` — an integer with no attributes. DRA lets a pod express intent through a `ResourceClaim`/`DeviceClass` — "a device with at least 80 GB HBM, NVLink-connected to its peers, MIG profile 3g.40gb" — and lets the scheduler and driver negotiate. Be honest about the limit: **DRA does not create fractional GPUs and does not make sharing safe.** It is a better allocation and expression layer, not a new isolation primitive.

#### Gang admission, quota, and the scheduling primitives

Vanilla Kubernetes will schedule six of your eight worker pods and leave two Pending forever, holding six GPUs hostage. That failure mode is why these exist:

- **Kueue** — the mainstream answer. `ClusterQueue`/`LocalQueue`, cohorts with borrowing, all-or-nothing gang admission; natively admits `Job`, `JobSet`, `RayCluster`/`RayJob`, and `LeaderWorkerSet`.
- **LeaderWorkerSet** — one leader plus N workers replicated as a single unit; the right primitive when one model does not fit on one node.
- **Volcano** or the coscheduling plugin as the older alternative.

The quota shape worth proposing unprompted: per-team `ClusterQueue` with a guaranteed nominal quota **plus borrowing from a cohort**. Research gets burst capacity when production is not using it, and gets preempted first. That one design answers "how do you stop the research team eating production's GPUs" without buying a single extra GPU.

**Taints, affinity, spread, PDBs** — the details that separate someone who has run a cluster from someone who has read about one:

- Taint every GPU node (`nvidia.com/gpu=present:NoSchedule`) so a CPU-only sidecar cannot land on an expensive node. A **toleration only permits, it does not attract** — you need toleration *plus* node affinity or a `nodeSelector` on the accelerator label. That triple is the complete answer.
- `PodDisruptionBudget` with `minAvailable` on inference deployments so a node drain cannot take the last replica. The classic bug: `minAvailable: 1` with `replicas: 1` blocks all voluntary disruption forever and node upgrades silently stop. Fix is `replicas >= 2` with `maxUnavailable: 1`. And say the part people miss: **PDBs do not protect against node failure, preemption, or spot reclaim** — only voluntary disruption.
- Topology spread: `topologySpreadConstraints` on zone with `maxSkew: 1` for inference, because you want availability. Training wants the *opposite* — pack into one zone or placement group, because cross-AZ all-reduce is both slow and billed. **Inference wants spread, training wants packing.**

#### Autoscaling: Karpenter vs Cluster Autoscaler, and KEDA

| | Cluster Autoscaler | Karpenter |
|---|---|---|
| Model | Scales pre-defined ASGs / node groups | Provisions nodes just-in-time from a `NodePool` constraint set |
| GPU fleets | One ASG per instance type × AZ × capacity type — combinatorial explosion | Two or three NodePools cover the same fleet |
| Instance choice | You pre-decided | Cheapest instance that fits the actual pending pods; can fall back across GPU families |
| Scale-down | Timeout-based, conservative, leaves idle capacity | Active consolidation — replace three under-used nodes with one; respects PDBs |
| Disruption control | Cluster-wide flags | Per-NodePool `spec.disruption`: `consolidationPolicy` (`WhenEmpty`, `Balanced`, `WhenEmptyOrUnderutilized`), `consolidateAfter`, `budgets` |

The three consolidation policies are worth naming precisely, because it is the exact field you are claiming fluency in. `WhenEmpty` only removes nodes with nothing but daemonsets on them — the safe setting for training. `WhenEmptyOrUnderutilized` will also replace or remove a node whose pods fit elsewhere more cheaply — the aggressive setting, correct for stateless inference. `Balanced` sits between them: it consolidates where the cost saving outweighs the disruption to running pods, which is the reasonable default for a mixed fleet where you want savings without a policy that treats every long-running pod as movable. Node expiry is a *separate* field and lives elsewhere in the API — see the Terraform section.

Karpenter is the default for GPU fleets, but the senior answer is the ML-specific traps:

- **Consolidation will kill your training jobs.** A five-day run on a node Karpenter decides to consolidate is gone. Mitigate with `karpenter.sh/do-not-disrupt: "true"` on the pod, a dedicated training NodePool with `consolidationPolicy: WhenEmpty` and a long `consolidateAfter`, and disruption budgets that freeze consolidation during a training window.
- **A cold GPU node is not a 90-second node.** Provision, then DaemonSets (device plugin, DCGM exporter, CNI), then a 20 GB image pull, then weights. Budget 5-15 minutes and design the stabilisation window around that, or keep warm headroom with low-priority balloon pods that real work preempts.
- Set node expiry so AMI and driver updates actually roll, and disruption budgets so they roll slowly.

**HPA or KEDA for inference?** KEDA — and the reason matters: KEDA *is* HPA underneath, plus external triggers and scale-to-zero. CPU is a lie for a GPU pod; a vLLM replica at 95% GPU utilisation sits at single-digit CPU. Scale on queue depth (`num_requests_waiting`), SQS `ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible`, or time-to-first-token. Size the stabilisation window to the measured node-plus-weights start time or the autoscaler flaps: scale up on a spike, scale down before the node is warm, repeat.

> **Say it like this:** "At TrueBalance the scaling signal is SQS depth, because the scorer is Lambda behind a queue — the queue is the autoscaler and Lambda handles concurrency. On Kubernetes I would use KEDA against an equivalent signal rather than CPU, because CPU is uncorrelated with GPU work, and I would set the stabilisation window from the measured node-plus-weights start time rather than the default."

#### Cold start: image pull and weight loading

The most concrete "have you operated this" topic on the infrastructure surface. The chain is: pull image, start container, download weights, load to device memory, warm kernels, pass readiness.

1. **Split the image from the weights.** Weights do not belong in the container image — a thin runtime image plus a startup fetch is versionable and pullable; a baked 140 GB image is neither.
2. **Lazy or streamed pulls.** SOCI (Seekable OCI) on EKS, nydus/eStargz elsewhere, GKE Image Streaming on Google — the container starts before the whole image is down. All three vendors report large reductions on multi-GB images; those are vendor-reported figures rather than anything measured here, so quote the *mechanism* — the runtime lazily fetches blocks on demand instead of waiting for the full layer — and offer to benchmark rather than citing a number.
3. **Pre-pull with a DaemonSet** so the image is on the node before the pod lands. Crude, effective, works everywhere.
4. **Parallel weight loading.** Multipart concurrent download from object storage beats a single-threaded `from_pretrained`. The pattern that wins: **object store as truth, node-local NVMe as cache, an init container or DaemonSet populating it.** EFS is simple and shared but its per-operation latency punishes many-small-file loads; FSx for Lustre is fast, expensive, and belongs on training data.
5. **Readiness must include a real inference on a canary input; liveness must not.** A twelve-minute weight load gets liveness-killed into a restart loop. Use `startupProbe` with a generous `failureThreshold`, then hand over to liveness.
6. In-region registry pull-through cache, `imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent`, immutable **digest** tags rather than `:latest`.

> **Say it like this:** "The first thing I would check on a slow-starting GPU deployment is whether liveness is killing it. If weights take twelve minutes and liveness has a sixty-second threshold, the pod restarts forever and the symptom presents as a crash loop rather than a probe misconfiguration. `startupProbe` exists for exactly that."
