### Serving patterns — the decision table

| Mode | Latency budget | Trigger | Typical infra | Failure semantics |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Real-time / online** | 10-500 ms p99 | Synchronous request | Deployment + HPA/KEDA behind a gateway; SageMaker real-time | Fail fast, degrade, never queue indefinitely |
| **Async / near-real-time** | Seconds to minutes | Enqueue plus callback or poll | SQS/Kafka into KEDA-scaled workers; SageMaker Asynchronous Inference | At-least-once plus idempotency key; DLQ |
| **Batch / offline** | Minutes to hours | Schedule or data arrival | Argo Workflows, Ray Data, Spark, SageMaker Batch Transform; spot | Retry the partition; checkpoint |
| **Streaming** | 100 ms to seconds, continuous | Event per record | Flink or Spark Structured Streaming with embedded/sidecar model | Exactly-once *effects*, watermarks, state backend |
| **Serverless** | 50 ms-15 min, spiky | Synchronous or event | Lambda container image, ARM64, SQS; SageMaker Serverless Inference | Cold start is the tail; no GPU |

The senior distinction: **async is not "slow real-time."** It changes the contract from a latency SLO to a completion SLO, which unlocks spot, aggressive batching, and scale-to-zero. A large share of "we need more GPUs" requests are solved by moving a workload from online to async.

#### SageMaker in depth — the platform he has actually operated

The JD prefers AWS, and this is the surface where Sachin has the most defensible depth. Know the four inference options cold, because "which SageMaker inference option and why" is the highest-probability AWS question in this round.

| Option | Scales to zero | GPU | Payload / duration ceiling | Cost model | Right when |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Real-time endpoint** | No — a classic endpoint has a minimum of one instance | Yes | Small payload, sub-minute | Instance-hours, 24×7 | Steady synchronous traffic with a latency SLO |
| **Serverless Inference** | Yes | No | Modest payload, limited memory | Per-invocation duration | Spiky, low-duty-cycle, CPU-sized models |
| **Asynchronous Inference** | Yes (min instance count 0) | Yes | Large payloads, long processing | Instance-hours while draining the queue | Big inputs, generous latency, cost-sensitive |
| **Batch Transform** | N/A — job, not endpoint | Yes | Whole dataset | Instance-hours for the job | Offline scoring; no endpoint to keep alive |

Three details that separate operators from readers:

- **The always-on trap.** A classic real-time endpoint does not scale to zero, so forty low-QPS models on forty endpoints is forty instances of idle spend, ×2 if you are running two for availability. That is the single most common line item on a SageMaker bill and it is what drove the ResMed consolidation.
- **Inference components** are the modern fix. They let you place multiple models — or multiple copies of one model — onto the instances behind a single endpoint, with their own CPU/memory/accelerator allocation and their own autoscaling, and copy count can go to zero. That is the AWS-native answer to the long tail, and it is what you would reach for today rather than hand-rolling consolidation. *(Capability and regional availability move; check the current docs before asserting scale-to-zero in a specific region.)*
- **Autoscaling signal.** Application Auto Scaling on `SageMakerVariantInvocationsPerInstance` is the default target-tracking metric, and it is a *proxy*. For a model where per-request cost varies (variable-length inputs, generative), a custom CloudWatch metric on concurrency or queue depth is the correct signal — same argument as CPU-versus-queue-depth on Kubernetes.

**SageMaker Pipelines and the Model Registry.** The AWS-native equivalent of the alias-move-triggers-deploy pattern: a training pipeline registers a **model package** into a **model package group**; the package carries an approval status (`PendingManualApproval`, `Approved`, `Rejected`); an **EventBridge rule on the status change** fires the deployment. The registry event is the trigger and the approver's identity is recorded — which is exactly the audit artefact a regulated review will ask for.

**The NatWest platform layout.** At Tiger Analytics, the platform Sachin designed on SageMaker for NatWest — FCA-regulated banking, later showcased by AWS at re:Invent — had five components: training, inference, drift detection, CI/CD, and automated retraining. Draw it as the nine-box spine with the AWS names filled in, and be careful to describe only those five as delivered; anything else is how you would extend it.

```text
  feature build (Glue/Spark)  -->  SageMaker Training  -->  Model Registry
        ^                                                        |
        |                                                        v
        |                                          CI/CD: approval -> deploy
        |                                                        |
        |                                                        v
  retraining trigger  <--  drift detection job  <--  SageMaker inference
  (automated)              (feature + prediction     (endpoints)
                            distributions)
```

> **Say it like this:** "The NatWest platform was five pieces on SageMaker — training, inference, drift detection, CI/CD, and automated retraining — for an FCA-regulated bank, so the constraint that shaped it was auditability rather than latency. Every model had a lineage record and every promotion had a named approver, because a regulator's question is not 'is it accurate', it is 'show me how this decision was produced and who signed it off'."

#### AWS Bedrock — the honest answer, prepared in advance

The JD says "AWS Bedrock preferable" and the recruiter has been told in writing that Sachin has not used it. Silence is worse than a disclaimer; a disclaimer plus a correct structural account of how it differs is close to as good as experience for a platform role.

> **Say it like this [verbatim]:** "I have not run Bedrock in production, and I would rather say that than bluff a service you probably operate. The closest things I have run are Azure OpenAI at ResMed for a production GenAI assistant, and self-hosted RAG on AWS with my own vector store — pgvector, FAISS, Chroma, Pinecone. What I would expect to be structurally different is that there are no weights to host, so the scaling limit stops being GPU capacity and becomes quota: on-demand throughput with per-model, per-region limits, versus provisioned throughput bought in model units on a commitment. That flips the cost calculation from duty-cycle-on-hardware to a straight token price, and it moves the platform work from scheduling to governance — model access enablement per model per region, guardrail policies as separate objects, invocation logging to S3 or CloudWatch for the audit trail, and PrivateLink so inference never leaves the VPC. What ports over unchanged is everything I actually care about: the eval harness, the promotion gates, cost attribution per tenant, and the degradation ladder."

The three follow-ups to be ready for, answered as inference rather than experience:

| They ask | The structural answer |
|---|---|
| On-demand or provisioned throughput? | On-demand for spiky and unpredictable; provisioned when you need a latency floor or a throughput guarantee, because it is a commitment with a capacity reservation. The decision is the same shape as reserved-versus-on-demand instances, sized to the measured *floor* not the peak. |
| How do you handle a throttle? | Quota is the scaling limit, so treat `ThrottlingException` as a capacity signal, not an error: backoff with full jitter, a retry budget, and a degradation rung to a smaller or different model. Cross-region inference profiles are the capacity lever if latency and residency allow. |
| How is this different to hosting vLLM? | You lose control of batching, quantisation and the KV cache — all my throughput levers disappear — and you gain not operating an accelerator fleet. So the break-even question is the same duty-cycle arithmetic, and the answer favours the managed service until you can keep hardware busy. |

#### Lambda for ML — the honest limits, learned first-hand

TrueBalance runs the loan-withdrawal propensity scorer on **Lambda behind SQS, with ARM64 Docker images in ECR and S3-versioned model artefacts**. That makes this the part of the serving surface Sachin owns end to end rather than has read about.

- **Package size**: 250 MB unzipped for a zip deployment; **10 GB for a container image**. Anything with a real ML dependency tree is a container — that is not a preference, it is the limit.
- **Memory up to 10,240 MB, and vCPU scales with memory** (roughly 1 vCPU per 1,769 MB), so raising memory is often the *latency and cost* fix, not only an OOM fix — a function that runs twice as fast at double the memory costs about the same and returns sooner.
- **`/tmp` up to 10 GB**, enough to cache a mid-size model between warm invocations.
- **Fifteen-minute maximum execution.** Training is out; long batch is out.
- **No GPU. Ever.** The decisive constraint, and the reason Lambda is a tree-model and small-encoder platform.
- **Cold starts** dominated by image pull, framework import, and weight load. The mitigations are not a menu — they exclude each other, and knowing that is the senior answer. SnapStart snapshots the initialised execution environment and now covers container images on the managed Python, Java and .NET runtimes; but **SnapStart is mutually exclusive with provisioned concurrency, with EFS, and with ephemeral storage above 512 MB**. So SnapStart is the fix when the model fits inside the snapshot, and provisioned concurrency is the fix when it does not and you need the 10 GB `/tmp` cache. Lazy imports help either way.
- **ARM64/Graviton**: roughly 20% cheaper per GB-second and usually faster for int8/ONNX CPU inference. The thing to check before committing to Graviton is `aarch64` wheel coverage across the whole dependency tree — one source-only package changes your build and can fail at import.

> **Say it like this:** "The scorer at TrueBalance is XGBoost on Lambda with ARM64 images in ECR, fronted by SQS. Serverless is right there because the model is a tree ensemble, traffic is spiky, and the latency budget is generous — I get scale-to-zero and no cluster to run. It becomes wrong the moment we need a GPU, sustained high QPS, or anything over fifteen minutes."

#### Multi-container endpoints, multi-model endpoints, and LoRA multiplexing

These are three different products solving three different versions of "too many models", and conflating them is a visible tell in front of an AWS-preferring interviewer.

| | Model-per-endpoint | **Multi-container endpoint (MCE)** | **Multi-model endpoint (MME)** |
|---|---|---|---|
| What it is | One model, one endpoint | Up to **15 containers**, different models or frameworks, on one endpoint; `Direct` mode invokes one by hostname, `Serial` mode chains them as an inference pipeline | One container, many model artefacts in S3, loaded into memory on demand |
| Residency | Always | **All containers resident and running** on the shared instance | Dynamic — models pulled from S3 on first request, evicted under memory pressure |
| Cold start | Per deploy | Per deploy | **Per model, on a cache miss** — a tail-latency landmine |
| Ceiling | Your budget | 15 containers, one instance family, one shared fleet | Thousands, bounded by instance memory and S3 |
| Isolation | Full | Shared instance and shared blast radius; separate containers, so separate dependency trees | Shared process; one bad model degrades all |
| Versioning | Clean and independent | Coupled — updating the endpoint config re-deploys the set | Per artefact in S3, decoupled from the server |
| Best for | A handful of high-QPS, business-critical models | A **modest number of heterogeneous models** you want on one fleet | **Hundreds of low-QPS homogeneous models** — per-tenant, per-region, per-customer |

The ResMed work was **MCE**: multi-container SageMaker endpoints on the internal IHS MLOps platform, sharing infrastructure across models to cut inference cost while holding per-model SLAs.

> **Say it like this:** "At ResMed the driver was a long tail of models with low individual QPS, and a dedicated endpoint each means paying for an idle instance per model. We consolidated onto multi-container endpoints — several different models and frameworks behind one endpoint, invoked directly by container hostname — so we paid for one fleet instead of N."
>
> Expand only if pulled on:
>
> - The trades: shared blast radius on one instance, a coupled release cycle because updating the endpoint config redeploys the set, and a ceiling of fifteen containers.
> - On the saving: "I don't have the percentage in front of me — it was material enough to be the reason we did it, but I'd rather not quote a figure I can't stand behind."
> - The road not taken: hundreds of *homogeneous* models would have been a multi-model endpoint instead, where artefacts load from S3 on demand and evict under memory pressure — a different product with a different trade, a per-model cold start on a cache miss.
> - Today: inference components first, because they give you the packing without the fifteen-container ceiling.

The modern LLM equivalent of the same idea is **LoRA multiplexing** — one base model resident, many adapters swapped per request — giving per-tenant fine-tunes at roughly one percent of the memory cost of a replica each. Note that the routing layer has to be adapter-aware, or you get the same cache-blindness problem described next.

#### The current LLM-serving stack, and the thing most people get wrong

- **vLLM** as the engine: **PagedAttention** puts the KV cache in non-contiguous pages so fragmentation stops capping concurrency; **continuous batching** lets new requests join at token granularity instead of waiting for the slowest sequence in a static batch.
- **KServe** as the serving contract (`InferenceService` — scale-to-zero, canary traffic split, transformer/predictor graph), or plain `Deployment` plus `LeaderWorkerSet` if you would rather not operate Knative.
- **Kueue** for quota and gang admission, **Argo CD** for rollout.
- On **Seldon Core v2**: it moved off Apache 2.0 to the Business Source License a couple of years back, so commercial use of current versions needs a licence. That is why greenfield picks KServe, and knowing it signals evaluation rather than reading. *(Cite the version and date only if you have checked it that morning; the licence fact is the load-bearing part.)*

**Ray Serve, properly.** It gets named in these JDs and then handled with one clause, which is a missed opportunity because it is genuinely the right answer for a particular shape.

```python
# The three things that define a Ray Serve deployment.
from ray import serve

@serve.deployment(
    autoscaling_config={
        "min_replicas": 0,              # scale to zero between bursts
        "max_replicas": 8,
        "target_ongoing_requests": 4,   # the real signal: in-flight, not CPU
    },
    ray_actor_options={"num_gpus": 0.25},   # bookkeeping, NOT isolation
    max_ongoing_requests=16,
)
class Reranker:
    def __init__(self):
        self.model = load_reranker()     # loaded once per replica

    async def __call__(self, query, docs):
        return self.model.rank(query, docs)


@serve.deployment
class Pipeline:
    def __init__(self, embed, rerank, generate):
        self.embed, self.rerank, self.generate = embed, rerank, generate

    async def __call__(self, req):
        # composition is Python: each stage is its own deployment,
        # its own replica count, its own hardware.
        vecs = await self.embed.remote(req.text)
        docs = await self.rerank.remote(req.text, retrieve(vecs))
        return await self.generate.remote(req.text, docs)
```

Say the three honest things about it. **`num_gpus: 0.25` is a scheduling fiction** — Ray does the accounting, CUDA does not enforce it, so four co-located replicas can still OOM each other; it is for cooperating models you control, not for tenant isolation. **Composition is the reason to choose it**: a preprocess → embed → rerank → generate graph where each stage wants different hardware and scales independently is awkward in KServe (whose transformer/predictor pair really only covers two stages) and natural in Ray. **The head node is the reason not to**: it is a failure domain and a scaling bottleneck, a `RayCluster` upgrade is a cluster-level event, and you now have three autoscalers to reconcile — Ray's, KubeRay's, and Karpenter's. If the shape is one model, HTTP in, HTTP out, KServe or a plain `Deployment` is far less machinery. Running vLLM *under* Ray Serve is common and defensible, but be aware you then have two layers of batching to reason about.

The argument worth making unprompted:

> **Say it like this:** "For LLM serving the load balancer is the performance-critical component, not the pod. A Kubernetes Service is cache-blind — it round-robins. So a multi-turn request lands on replica three when replica one already holds that conversation's eight-thousand-token prefix in HBM, and you re-prefill from scratch. Round-robin is actively destroying the most valuable state in the cluster. The fix is the Gateway API Inference Extension — an inference gateway plus an endpoint picker scoring replicas on prefix-cache hit, queue depth, KV utilisation and LoRA affinity. The vendors publish qualitative claims rather than a benchmark I can cite, so I would not quote you a multiplier; the mechanism is what matters, because routing on prefix-cache hit turns a full re-prefill into a cache hit, and prefill is where the tokens are. It is a routing change, not a hardware purchase."

**Disaggregated prefill/decode** is the companion idea: prefill is compute-bound and bursty, decode is memory-bandwidth-bound and steady, so separate pools let you size and scale each against its own bottleneck.

---

### Progressive delivery — what each pattern proves, and what it does not

| Pattern | Traffic | Proves | Does **not** prove | ML-specific gotcha |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Shadow / mirror** | 100% to old; copy to new, response discarded | Operational fitness — latency, memory, crashes — and prediction-distribution agreement, at zero user risk | Anything causal; the challenger influenced nothing | Doubles inference cost; side effects (writes, downstream calls, billing) must be stubbed or you corrupt state |
| **Canary** | 1 → 5 → 25 → 50 → 100% with automated analysis | Real user impact under real load, with automatic abort | Business effect with statistical power | Business metrics move too slowly to gate on; gate on proxies — error rate, p99, prediction PSI, null-feature rate |
| **Blue/green** | 100% switch, old kept warm | Instant rollback | Gradual risk exposure — you find out at full traffic | Doubles accelerator spend during the overlap; time-box it |
| **A/B** | Split by entity hash, held for a fixed horizon | Causal business effect, powered | Operational safety — it assumes the thing already runs | Pre-registered hypothesis, powered sample size, fixed duration; a different instrument from canary |
| **Interleaving** | Both models score the same request, results interleaved | Relative preference at much higher sensitivity than A/B | Absolute effect size | Ranked-list products only; needs debiasing |

> **Say it like this:** "Shadow is the most under-used pattern in ML and the one I would add first. It proves the challenger runs, resolves its features, and produces a comparable score distribution, at zero user risk — and it proves nothing causal, because the challenger never influenced a decision. So the sequence is shadow, canary, then A/B if the business metric warrants it. Skipping shadow is how you discover in production that the challenger takes four hundred milliseconds."

**Rollback design, volunteered without being asked:**

- Rollback is a **config change, not a rebuild**. Target under sixty seconds, one action, no CI run.
- Keep N-1 **warm** through the bake window, then scale it to a single replica rather than leaving a full fleet running. On accelerators, a week of warm N-1 is a real bill and it contradicts everything in the cost section.
- Every artefact **immutable and content-addressed** (image digest, model SHA) so "roll back to v3" is unambiguous.
- **Automate the trigger** — an Argo Rollouts `AnalysisTemplate` reading Prometheus with a `failureLimit`. Humans are slow and optimistic at 3 a.m.
- **Rehearse it.** An untested rollback is a hypothesis.
- The stateful catch: rolling back a model does not roll back the scores, embeddings, or decisions it already wrote downstream. You need a compensating re-score job or a documented, accepted smear.

---

### CI/CD for ML — how it actually differs

| Software CI/CD | ML CI/CD |
|---|---|
| Input is code | Inputs are **code × data × config × environment × seed** |
| Tests are deterministic pass/fail | Tests are **statistical** — metrics with variance; "better" needs a confidence interval and a margin |
| Artefacts are megabytes | Artefacts are gigabytes; registry plus object store plus checksums |
| Build takes minutes | Training takes hours and costs real money; you cannot re-run it per commit |
| Promotion is "tests green" | Promotion is an **evidence bundle**: offline metrics, slice metrics, drift, load test, shadow results, model card, approver |
| Rollback is the previous image | Rollback is the previous image **plus** weights **plus** feature transformations |
| Failure is loud (500s) | Failure is **silent** — the model returns 200 with a confidently wrong number |

That last row is the money quote, and it is exactly the class of bug Sachin already found in production.

> **Say it like this [verbatim]:** "The defining property of ML systems is that they fail silently at 200 OK. I hit that at TrueBalance: the offline pipeline computed four thousand and one features, and the real-time payload only ever carried twenty-eight keys. The transform imputed defaults for the rest, so the served vector was near-constant and nothing errored — the endpoint was green. The fix was structural rather than a patch: serialise a feature contract next to the artefact, hard-fail on a missing required feature instead of imputing, add a CI subset assertion as a promotion gate, and emit a per-feature missing-rate metric from the scorer so the next occurrence is visible in a dashboard instead of in a business metric three weeks later."

#### The promotion gate chain

Design it as stages with an owner, an evidence artefact, and a verdict. Every gate emits a signed artefact; the union of artefacts is the promotion record.

```text
[commit] -> G0 build -> G1 data -> G2 offline -> G3 slices -> G4 behaviour -+
                                                                            |
   [100%] <- G8 canary <- G7 shadow <- G6 perf <- G5 parity <---------------+
```

| Gate | Checks | Blocks on |
|---|---|---|
| **G0 Reproducible build** | Lockfile resolved, image built and **digest-pinned**, training config hashed, seeds set, data snapshot id recorded | Any unpinned dependency, or a dirty git tree |
| **G1 Data contract** | Schema, null rates, cardinality, ranges, **train/serve schema equality**, leakage check, PSI vs the last training snapshot | Contract violation |
| **G2 Offline vs champion** | Same held-out snapshot, same slicing code; gate on the lower bound of a bootstrap CI on the **delta**, against a pre-registered non-inferiority margin — never a point estimate | `delta_lower_95 < -margin` |
| **G3 Slices and fairness** | Per-segment metrics; no material slice may regress even if the aggregate improves — Simpson's paradox is the classic ML incident | Any material slice regression |
| **G4 Behavioural tests** | Invariance (a typo should not flip the label), directional expectation, minimum functionality on curated edge cases | Any MFT failure |
| **G5 Serving parity** | Score N rows **through the real container** and diff against offline predictions; `max abs delta < eps` | Eps breach — this is the gate that would have caught the TrueBalance bug |
| **G6 Performance and cost** | p50/p99, throughput per replica, peak memory, warm-up time, **cost per 1k predictions** | SLO or cost-budget breach |
| **G7 Shadow** | 24-72 h of mirrored traffic: prediction-distribution divergence, error rate, latency, feature null rate in the wild | Divergence beyond threshold |
| **G8 Canary** | 1 → 5 → 25 → 50 → 100 with automated analysis and auto-abort | Analysis failure |

**Artefact 1 — a promotion pipeline you can paste into the CoderPad.** Written as a generic declarative gate spec rather than a specific CI vendor's dialect, which is what you want in a design round.

```yaml
# promote.yaml — evidence-based model promotion. Every gate emits an artifact.
model: loan_withdrawal_propensity
champion:  models:/loan_withdrawal@champion      # alias, resolved at run time
candidate: models:/loan_withdrawal@challenger

manifest_required:                 # G0: refuse to proceed without full lineage
  - git_commit
  - git_dirty == false
  - image_digest                   # sha256, never a tag
  - lockfile_hash
  - data_snapshot_id               # delta/iceberg version or content hash
  - feature_contract_hash          # the serialized train/serve contract
  - seeds: {python: 42, numpy: 42}

gates:
  - id: G1_data_contract
    run: python -m pipeline.checks.data_contract --snapshot {{ data_snapshot_id }}
    assert:
      - schema_equal_to: feature_contract_hash
      - null_rate_max: 0.02
      - psi_vs_last_training_snapshot_max: 0.20
    on_fail: block

  - id: G2_offline_vs_champion
    run: python -m pipeline.eval.compare --champion {{ champion }} --candidate {{ candidate }}
    assert:
      # gate on the CI of the DELTA, with a pre-registered non-inferiority margin
      - metric: roc_auc
        delta_lower_95: ">= -0.005"
    on_fail: block

  - id: G3_slices
    run: python -m pipeline.eval.slices --by tenant,region,channel,tenure_bucket
    assert:
      - no_slice_regression_gt: 0.02
      - min_slice_support: 500          # do not gate on 12 rows of noise
    on_fail: block

  - id: G5_serving_parity                # the gate that catches train/serve skew
    run: |
      python -m pipeline.parity \
        --image {{ image_digest }} \
        --rows s3://golden/parity_sample_5k.parquet \
        --max-abs-delta 1e-6 \
        --require-all-features-present
    assert:
      - rows_scored: 5000
      - features_defaulted: 0            # zero silent imputation, ever
    on_fail: block

  - id: G6_perf_and_cost
    run: python -m pipeline.loadtest --replay s3://traffic/shape_p99.jsonl
    assert:
      - p99_ms_max: 250
      # set from the CURRENT champion's measured unit cost plus margin,
      # not from a round number. Measured champion here is ~$0.0034/1k.
      - cost_per_1k_predictions_max_usd: 0.005
    on_fail: block

  - id: G7_shadow
    duration: 48h
    traffic: mirror
    assert:
      - prediction_psi_vs_champion_max: 0.10
      - error_rate_max: 0.001
      - feature_null_rate_max: 0.02
    on_fail: block

  - id: G8_canary
    steps: [1, 5, 25, 50, 100]
    analysis:
      provider: prometheus
      queries:
        # a RATIO, not an absolute per-second rate, or the limit is traffic-dependent
        error_rate: |
          sum(rate(http_requests_total{code=~"5..",model="{{ candidate }}"}[5m]))
          /
          sum(rate(http_requests_total{model="{{ candidate }}"}[5m]))
        # histogram_quantile needs a rate over the bucket counter, grouped by le
        p99_latency: |
          histogram_quantile(0.99,
            sum(rate(model_latency_seconds_bucket{model="{{ candidate }}"}[5m])) by (le))
      failure_limit: 1
    on_fail: rollback           # config flip to N-1, no rebuild

promotion:
  registry_alias_transition: challenger -> champion
  approver_required: true                   # a named human, recorded
  triggers: gitops_commit                   # the registry event writes the config repo
rollback:
  mechanism: config_flag                    # NOT a pipeline re-run
  target_seconds: 60
  keep_previous_warm_for: 24h               # bake window only, then scale to 1 replica
```

Two lines in there are worth defending out loud if asked, because both are places where a plausible-looking version is wrong. `error_rate` must be a **ratio** — `sum(rate(5xx))` alone is an absolute errors-per-second figure, so a fixed `failure_limit` on it means the gate is strict at low traffic and useless at high traffic. And `histogram_quantile` must be given a **rate over the bucket counters grouped by `le`** — handed the raw cumulative counter it computes a quantile over everything since process start, which barely moves during a canary and would never trip.

#### MLflow — what it is, what it is not

The JD names MLflow in the governance bullet and it is on the safe-to-claim list, so this needs to be crisp.

| Component | What it stores | The question it answers |
|---|---|---|
| **Tracking** | Runs: params, metrics, tags, artifacts, source commit, dataset reference | "What did I try, and what happened?" |
| **Registry** | Named models, numbered versions, aliases, tags, description; each version points back to its producing run | "Which artefact is production, and where did it come from?" |
| **Artifact store** | The bytes — under the hood it is S3/ADLS/GCS | "Give me the weights" |

**Aliases, not stages.** MLflow deprecated the old registry stages (`None`/`Staging`/`Production`/`Archived`) in version 2.9 in favour of **aliases and tags**, and models registered in Databricks **Unity Catalog do not support stages at all** — the documentation is explicit that "Stages are not supported for models in Unity Catalog", and recommends the three-level namespace to express environment plus aliases to express deployment status. So the modern vocabulary is `models:/loan_withdrawal@champion`, and promotion is *moving the `champion` alias*, which is atomic, reversible, and readable as an event.

This matters for the round because the deploy trigger question has a dated answer and a current one:

> **Say it like this:** "The deploy trigger is a registry event, not a human running a pipeline — an alias move, champion to challenger or back, fires a webhook that commits the model URI and image digest into the config repo. On older MLflow you would see this written as a stage transition; stages were deprecated in 2.9 in favour of aliases, and Unity Catalog models only support aliases, so I would write it as an alias move. On the AWS side the exact analogue is an EventBridge rule on a SageMaker model package's approval status."

**What MLflow does not give you**, which is the part that shows you have used it rather than installed it: it is **not a deployment system** — there is no traffic splitting, no progressive delivery, no rollback primitive beyond pointing an alias somewhere else; it is **not a feature store**, so train/serve skew is entirely your problem; it is **not a data versioner**, so `data_snapshot_id` has to come from Delta/Iceberg/lakeFS and be recorded by you; and the registry is **metadata over an artifact store**, so retention, immutability and access control on the underlying bucket are yours to get right. A registry entry pointing at a deleted S3 object is a very common and very embarrassing outage.

#### Reproducibility, and "which commit produced this model"

This question exposes whether you have run a platform. The answer: **the artefact must carry a manifest, and the manifest must be sufficient to rebuild it.** The manifest below is the *shape*; the only figure carried over from real work is the out-of-time ROC-AUC of 0.84 from the TrueBalance propensity model.

```yaml
model_version:   propensity-v14
git_commit:      a3f9c1e
git_dirty:       false             # refuse to promote a dirty tree
image_digest:    sha256:9b2f...    # environment, never a tag
lockfile_hash:   sha256:41cd...
data_snapshot:   delta:events@version=1182
feature_contract: sha256:7e11...   # the serialized train/serve contract
training_config: sha256:e0aa...
seeds:           {python: 42, numpy: 42}
metrics:         {roc_auc: 0.84}
trained_by:      workflow/train-propensity-8821
approved_by:     <named human, recorded at alias move>
```

> **Say it like this:** "Reproducibility is a spectrum and I would rather be precise about which rung I am claiming. Bit-exact re-training on multi-GPU is usually not achievable — non-deterministic reductions, cuDNN autotuning, dataloader interleaving. The achievable and correct bar is statistical reproducibility plus complete lineage: I can re-run on the pinned snapshot and land inside the noise band, and I can always answer what went in."

The data-versioning options, one line each: **DVC** is Git-centric and file-level, good when the workflow is file-shaped; **lakeFS** gives Git semantics over the whole object-store repository and is the right answer for a zero-copy isolated branch of a large lake; **Delta/Iceberg time travel** is right when the training data already lives in a lakehouse. The caveat to raise unprompted for the last one: **`VACUUM` and retention policy will delete the history your "reproducible" pipeline depends on**, so pin the snapshot id in the manifest and extend retention for anything a production model references. Retention is set by the audit horizon, not by the storage bill.

#### GitOps for models

1. Training registers the model version with metrics and lineage.
2. **The registry event is the deploy trigger** — an alias move (`champion`/`challenger`), or a stage transition on pre-2.9 MLflow, or a SageMaker model-package approval — fires a webhook. Never a human running a pipeline.
3. An automated commit writes the model URI and image digest into the environment's values file in the **config repo** — separate from the app repo, or the sync loop and CI will fight.
4. Argo CD reconciles; Argo Rollouts or KServe's `canaryTrafficPercent` executes the progressive rollout with metric analysis.
5. Rollback is `git revert` of the config commit — auditable and instant.

Details that show experience: **ApplicationSets** to fan one template across environments and regions rather than hand-maintaining forty Applications; **build once, promote the digest** rather than rebuilding per environment; Argo Workflows for the training DAG itself (Kubeflow Pipelines is Argo Workflows underneath); GitHub Actions for code-side CI with a handoff to a GPU-capable executor rather than running a six-hour training job in a hosted runner. On Jenkins — still the enterprise reality — the honest framing is that Jenkins is a fine *executor* and a poor *source of truth*; wrap it so deployment state still lives in Git.

---

### Terraform for an ML platform

#### Module structure — layer by rate of change and blast radius, not by cloud service

```text
live/                          # one state per (env x region x layer)
  prod/ap-south-1/
    00-network/                # VPC, subnets, peering      -- changes yearly
    10-platform/               # EKS control plane, IRSA, KMS -- quarterly
    20-nodepools/              # Karpenter NodePools, GPU AMIs -- monthly
    30-data/                   # S3 buckets, catalog, FSx      -- monthly
    40-mlplatform/             # registry, Argo, Kueue quotas  -- weekly
    50-workloads/              # namespaces, quotas, per-team IRSA -- daily
modules/
  eks-cluster/  gpu-nodepool/  model-endpoint/  team-namespace/  dataset-bucket/
```

**The rule that matters: state boundary equals blast radius boundary.** A `terraform apply` for a team's namespace must be structurally incapable of touching the VPC. If one state file can destroy the cluster, the design is wrong regardless of how good the review process is. Remote state in S3, versioned, encrypted, locked, replicated — state is simultaneously a credential store and a disaster-recovery artefact. Dependencies flow downward only, and modules expose **intent, not resources**.

**Workspaces vs separate state.** Workspaces are fine for ephemeral identical copies — per-PR preview environments, developer sandboxes. They are the wrong tool for prod versus staging: same code path, same backend, one `workspace select` typo from applying staging's plan to production, and environments always diverge, which pollutes the module with `count = terraform.workspace == "prod" ? 1 : 0`. Use separate directories, separate state, separate tfvars, and a thin wrapper to remove the duplication.

**Artefact 2 — a module sketch.** The point of showing this is the interface, not the HCL — but the HCL still has to parse, and two details in it are the ones that separate current knowledge from stale.

```hcl
# modules/gpu-nodepool/variables.tf  -- expose INTENT, not raw resources
variable "team"        { type = string }
variable "accelerator" { type = string }   # "a100" | "l4" | "cpu-graviton"
variable "capacity" {
  type    = string
  default = "spot"
}
variable "max_gpus"      { type = number }
variable "workload_kind" { type = string }   # "training" | "inference"
variable "cost_center"   { type = string }

# modules/gpu-nodepool/main.tf
locals {
  # training must not be consolidated out from under a multi-day run
  consolidation_policy = var.workload_kind == "training" ? "WhenEmpty" : "Balanced"
  consolidate_after    = var.workload_kind == "training" ? "24h" : "2m"
  # node expiry forces AMI + GPU driver rotation
  expire_after         = var.workload_kind == "training" ? "Never" : "720h"

  allowed = {
    a100         = ["p4d.24xlarge"]
    l4           = ["g6.xlarge", "g6.2xlarge", "g6.4xlarge"]
    cpu-graviton = ["c7g.4xlarge", "c7g.8xlarge"]
  }

  # ONE source of truth, projected into two different systems below
  required_tags = {
    team                = var.team
    cost-center         = var.cost_center
    workload            = var.workload_kind
    data-classification = "internal"
    managed-by          = "terraform"
  }
}

resource "kubernetes_manifest" "nodepool" {
  manifest = {
    apiVersion = "karpenter.sh/v1"
    kind       = "NodePool"
    metadata   = { name = "${var.team}-${var.accelerator}-${var.workload_kind}" }
    spec = {
      template = {
        # Kubernetes LABELS: drive scheduling and OpenCost allocation
        metadata = { labels = local.required_tags }
        spec = {
          # in Karpenter v1 expireAfter lives HERE, not under spec.disruption
          expireAfter = local.expire_after
          nodeClassRef = {
            group = "karpenter.k8s.aws", kind = "EC2NodeClass"
            name  = kubernetes_manifest.nodeclass.manifest.metadata.name
          }
          taints = [{ key = "nvidia.com/gpu", value = "present", effect = "NoSchedule" }]
          requirements = [
            { key = "karpenter.sh/capacity-type", operator = "In", values = [var.capacity] },
            { key = "node.kubernetes.io/instance-type", operator = "In",
              values = local.allowed[var.accelerator] },
          ]
        }
      }
      limits = { "nvidia.com/gpu" = var.max_gpus }   # hard ceiling, per team
      disruption = {
        consolidationPolicy = local.consolidation_policy
        consolidateAfter    = local.consolidate_after
        budgets             = [{ nodes = "10%" }]
      }
    }
  }
}

resource "kubernetes_manifest" "nodeclass" {
  manifest = {
    apiVersion = "karpenter.k8s.aws/v1"
    kind       = "EC2NodeClass"
    metadata   = { name = "${var.team}-${var.accelerator}" }
    spec = {
      role = var.node_role
      # AWS TAGS: this is what reaches EC2 and what the billing export keys on.
      # Node labels above do NOT produce AWS tags. You need both.
      tags = local.required_tags
      amiSelectorTerms       = [{ alias = "al2023@latest" }]
      subnetSelectorTerms    = [{ tags = { "karpenter.sh/discovery" = var.cluster } }]
      securityGroupSelectorTerms = [{ tags = { "karpenter.sh/discovery" = var.cluster } }]
      metadataOptions = { httpTokens = "required", httpPutResponseHopLimit = 1 }
    }
  }
}

# Never manage the autoscaler's own mutations; that is guaranteed perpetual drift.
resource "aws_eks_node_group" "system" {
  # ...
  lifecycle { ignore_changes = [scaling_config[0].desired_size] }
}
```

Two sentences to say while that is on screen, both of which are credibility markers:

> **Say it like this:** "Two things in there are easy to get wrong. `expireAfter` moved in Karpenter v1 — it used to sit under `spec.disruption` in the alpha API and it now lives under `spec.template.spec`, so a manifest with it in the old place fails schema validation. And the tags: Kubernetes node labels drive scheduling and OpenCost allocation, but AWS tags on the EC2NodeClass are what actually reach the instance and what the billing export keys on. You need both, projected from one source of truth, or the cost attribution in the next section does not exist."

#### Policy as code, drift, secrets

Layer two tools because they do different jobs:

- **Checkov / tfsec / Trivy** — static analysis over raw HCL. Fast, big built-in library, catches "public bucket", "unencrypted volume". Runs pre-commit and in the PR.
- **OPA/Rego via Conftest over the JSON plan** — expresses organisational rules that need the *resolved plan*: no instance type outside the approved GPU list; every resource carries `team`, `cost-center`, `data-classification`; GPU node pools must be spot unless labelled training-critical.

The single highest-value guardrail on an ML platform is a **plan-assertion gate**: parse the plan JSON and fail if `resource_changes[].change.actions` contains `delete` for anything tagged `stateful=true`. The expensive resources on an ML platform are the stateful ones.

**Drift** on an ML platform has predictable sources: someone scaling a node group in the console during an incident, autoscalers mutating desired counts (`ignore_changes` is mandatory), GPU AMI and driver updates, security editing IAM. Scheduled nightly `plan` that fails loudly and files a ticket, not a silent report nobody reads.

**Secrets**: never in state-visible variables — state stores them in plaintext. Short-lived identities (IRSA / Pod Identity, OIDC federation from CI to the cloud, no long-lived keys), External Secrets Operator to project into Kubernetes. Terraform manages the *secret container and its IAM*, not the *secret value*.

#### Self-service without console access — the honest answer

Ask why ML teams break IaC discipline before proposing more process. The feedback loop is forty-five minutes and the experiment is five; notebooks are inherently imperative; experiments genuinely are ephemeral so codifying them feels like bureaucracy; and the console never says "this is twenty-eight thousand dollars a month."

> **Say it like this:** "The fix for console clicking is not more process, it is a paved road — a CLI or Backstage template that opens a PR against the IaC repo, or a Crossplane claim a controller reconciles, so scientists never see the console and never write HCL and the result is still reconciled infrastructure."
>
> Expand only if pulled on: bound the blast radius by construction with namespace and Kueue quotas; hard TTL on everything self-served so idle resources expire; show the price in the same screen as the request. Terraform for the foundation, Crossplane or a PR bot for self-service — complements, not competitors.

---

### Security and compliance in the infrastructure

The JD names security and compliance, and this is where Sachin's regulated-industry background is a differentiator rather than a caveat: **HIPAA-class data at ResMed** and an **FCA-regulated bank at NatWest**. An enterprise SaaS GCC will probe this, and the wrong answer is a list of AWS service names.

#### The seven layers, in the order you would build them

| Layer | The control | The ML-specific twist |
|---|---|---|
| **Network** | VPC-only inference, no internet egress, PrivateLink endpoints for S3/ECR/SageMaker/Bedrock | SageMaker supports `VpcConfig` plus **network isolation**, where the model container gets no network at all — the strongest statement you can make about a model not exfiltrating data |
| **Identity** | IRSA or EKS Pod Identity, one role per workload, IMDSv2 with hop limit 1 | Scope S3 permissions to the **model's prefix**, not the bucket; a training role that can read every dataset is the default and it is wrong |
| **Data at rest** | KMS CMK on artefacts, feature store, Terraform state, EBS/EFS | Put the key policy under a different owner than the bucket policy, so the data team cannot grant itself decrypt |
| **Supply chain** | Sign images with cosign, verify at admission (Kyverno or the Sigstore policy controller), SBOM and SLSA provenance | Sign the **model artefact** too, not just the image. A model is a deployable with no source review |
| **The artefact is executable** | Prefer safetensors or ONNX; checksum-verify; load only from a signed registry path | A pickle or joblib file is arbitrary code execution on load. `torch.load` on an untrusted artefact is an RCE, and "the model came from the registry" is only safe if the registry write path is authenticated |
| **Tenant isolation** | Tenant id from the auth token, never the request body; server-enforced filter in the vector store; per-tenant quotas | A prefix-cache-aware router **must key on tenant** or you have created a cross-tenant channel; per-tenant collections beat a client-supplied filter |
| **Audit** | Immutable promotion record: registry event, config commit, approver identity, evidence bundle | Retained to the **audit horizon**, which is also what sets your Delta/Iceberg retention |

#### CVEs on a 20 GB CUDA base image — the question with no clean answer

Worth rehearsing, because the naive answer ("we scan and fix criticals") collapses immediately: a CUDA base image routinely carries hundreds of findings, most of them in packages the inference process never reaches.

> **Say it like this:** "A CUDA base image is not going to be CVE-zero, and pretending otherwise just teaches people to click through the scanner. So I would run a triage policy rather than a threshold — and shrink the surface first, because a runtime image with no compiler toolchain and weights fetched at startup removes a large share of the findings before you scan anything."
>
> Expand only if pulled on:
>
> - Scan at build **and continuously in the registry**, so a new CVE against an already-deployed digest raises a ticket.
> - Distinguish **reachable** from **present** — most findings sit in packages the inference path never loads.
> - Fix by **rebasing on a refreshed base image on a cadence**, not patching in place: a rebuild is reproducible, a patch is not.
> - Every exception is a written record with an owner and an expiry date, never a permanently suppressed finding.

#### PII in prompts, logs, and training data

- **Do not log raw prompts or raw feature payloads by default.** Log the model version, the degraded flag, feature *statistics*, and a hashed request id; put raw payloads behind a separate, shorter-retention, access-logged sink that requires a reason to read.
- **Redact before the sink, not after.** Once PII is in the observability pipeline it is in five systems and three retention policies.
- **The hard one, and the one that impresses:** deleting a training record does not delete its influence on trained weights. A right-to-erasure request is satisfied at the data layer immediately and at the model layer only at the next retrain, so you need a documented retraining cadence and a stated position on it. Say that out loud — most candidates have never considered it.
- ResMed context is the credible version of this: HIPAA-class medical reports through a RAG pipeline with hybrid vector-plus-metadata retrieval, evaluation harnesses, and human review in the loop. The human-review step is a compliance control, not a quality nicety.

#### Compliance framings worth naming by their real shape

| Regime | What it actually demands of the platform |
|---|---|
| **Model risk (FCA / SR 11-7 style)** | A model inventory, documented independent validation, ongoing monitoring against a challenger, and someone accountable. This is why the NatWest platform's audit trail mattered more than its latency |
| **HIPAA** | BAA with the provider, encryption in transit and at rest, access logging, minimum-necessary access. De-identification is a control, not a checkbox |
| **DPDP / GDPR** | Purpose limitation, data residency, erasure — and the retraining-cadence answer above |
| **SOC 2 for enterprise SaaS** | Change management is the one that bites an ML team: every production model change needs an approval record. The promotion manifest *is* that record if you designed it that way |

### Reliability: SLOs, error budgets, degradation, shedding, retries

**Three layers of SLO, and the third is the hard one.**

| Layer | SLI | Example SLO *(illustrative)* |
|---|---|---|
| System | Fraction of requests served under 300 ms with a non-5xx | 99.9% over 28 days |
| Pipeline correctness | Fraction of requests scored with the **full, fresh feature vector** — no nulls, no stale reads | 99.5% |
| Model quality | Rolling AUC or calibration on delayed labels; a proxy (prediction PSI) when labels lag | AUC above threshold on a 7-day window; PSI < 0.2 |

The middle row is the one Sachin can speak to directly — it is exactly the SLI his feature-contract fix created. And say the label-delay point: **you cannot page on accuracy when labels arrive in thirty days**, so you page on proxies and review accuracy on a slower cadence.

#### Do the error-budget arithmetic out loud

Asserting "99.9%" without knowing what it buys you is the standard follow-up trap. The arithmetic is trivial and almost nobody does it in the room.

```text
28-day window = 28 x 24 x 60 = 40,320 minutes
  99.9%   -> 0.1%  of 40,320  = 40.3 min of budget    <- about forty minutes
  99.95%  -> 0.05%             = 20.2 min
  99.99%  -> 0.01%             =  4.0 min             <- needs multi-region, be honest
  99%     -> 1%                = 403 min (6.7 hours)
```

Forty minutes a month is the sentence that makes the number real: it means **one bad deploy that takes twelve minutes to notice and eight to roll back has spent half the month's budget**. That is the argument for a sub-sixty-second automated rollback, and it lands far better as arithmetic than as a principle.

**Burn-rate alerting, multi-window and multi-burn-rate.** Alerting on "SLO breached" is useless — by then it is over. Alert on the *rate* at which budget is being consumed, with a long window for signal and a short window to stop alerting after recovery.

| Severity | Burn rate | Long window | Short window | Budget consumed if sustained |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Page** | 14.4× | 1 h | 5 min | ~2% of the 28-day budget in one hour |
| **Page** | 6× | 6 h | 30 min | ~5% in six hours |
| **Ticket** | 3× | 1 day | 2 h | ~10% in a day |
| **Ticket** | 1× | 3 days | 6 h | ~10% in three days |

The short window is what stops the alert firing for an hour after the incident is fixed: both windows must exceed the threshold for the alert to hold.

**The error-budget policy**, stated as a rule rather than a sentiment: when the budget is exhausted, feature work stops and reliability work starts, and **a model promotion counts as a change that consumes budget** — so a team burning budget cannot ship a new model either. That last clause is the one that makes the policy real for an ML team, because otherwise "we only shipped a model, not code" becomes the loophole.

#### The degradation ladder

Design it before the incident and make each rung independently testable.

```text
1. Full model, fresh features                 <- normal
2. Full model, cached / stale features        <- feature store degraded
3. Last-known-good model version              <- new model misbehaving
4. Smaller / cheaper model (CPU or distilled) <- accelerator capacity lost
5. Cached score for this entity               <- precomputed batch scores, hours old
6. Rules / heuristic / population baseline    <- segment average, or a rule table
7. Static safe default + explicit flag        <- e.g. route to manual review
```

> **Say it like this:** "The essential rule is that the caller must be told which rung it got. The response envelope carries `model_version` and `degraded: true`, so downstream systems and the audit log can make their own risk decision. Silently returning a rules-based score as if it were the model is how you turn an availability incident into a regulatory one. In lending that distinction is not academic."

#### Circuit breakers, wired to the ladder

The breaker is not a slogan; it is a three-state machine, and the follow-up question is always "what does it return when it is open?" — which is why it must be designed together with the ladder above.

```text
        failures exceed threshold in the rolling window
CLOSED  ------------------------------------------------->  OPEN
  ^                                                           |
  |  probe succeeds                        cool-down elapses  |
  |                                                           v
  +---------------------  HALF-OPEN  <------------------------+
                            |  probe fails -> back to OPEN
```

| Element | Setting that actually works | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Trip criterion | Failure **ratio** over a rolling window, with a **minimum call volume** (e.g. 20) | Without a volume floor, one failure out of two trips the breaker on a quiet endpoint |
| Count slow calls as failures | Yes — a call over the timeout is a failure | A model server that has stopped returning is the common failure, not one that 500s |
| Open duration | Short and jittered (e.g. 20-60 s ± jitter) | Un-jittered cool-downs make every caller retry in lockstep and re-flatten the service |
| Half-open | A **small fixed number** of probe calls, not a percentage of traffic | Percentage of traffic at peak is not a probe, it is a second outage |
| Placement | **Outside** the retry loop | Otherwise retries feed the breaker's own failure counter and it trips on its own traffic |
| Open behaviour | Return the **next ladder rung immediately** | A breaker whose open state is a 500 has converted a slow dependency into an outage. Breaker open on the model call → rung 3, 4 or 5, with `degraded: true` |

The point of the breaker is not protecting the caller — it is giving the failing service room to recover instead of being pinned at 100% by a retry storm.

**Load shedding, timeouts, retries, idempotency:**

- **Shed before you queue.** An inference queue that grows unbounded converts a capacity problem into a total outage, because every request eventually times out having already consumed compute. Admission control at the gateway: `429` with `Retry-After` when queue depth or estimated wait exceeds the SLO, and **shed by priority** — analytics and shadow traffic first, paid interactive last.
- **Timeouts derive from the SLO** and shrink at each hop outward (caller 300 ms, callee 250 ms), or the caller has already given up while you are still burning compute.
- **Retries** only on idempotent, retryable failures, with **exponential backoff and full jitter**, plus a **retry budget** (say, retries capped at 10% of requests). Without a budget, three retries at three layers is 27× load on a service that is already struggling.
- **Idempotency** is mandatory the moment SQS or Kafka is in the path. Every async request carries a client-supplied `idempotency_key`; the worker writes results keyed by it. At-least-once delivery plus idempotent effects equals effectively-once. This is directly relevant to the TrueBalance SQS architecture and worth naming as such.

### Design to cost

The JD names cost twice, so lead with a framework rather than a list.

> **Say it like this:** "I hold cost as one equation: cost equals price per accelerator-hour, times accelerator-hours consumed, divided by useful predictions produced. That gives three independent levers — buy cheaper, use less, produce more per unit. Most teams only ever pull the first one, which is why they negotiate a discount on waste."

#### First: the arithmetic for the stack he has actually run

Do this one before the GPU material, because it is the version he can be believed on and it is the one that matches a fintech/SaaS scoring workload. All prices below are **illustrative published list rates**; the method is the point, and you would substitute the measured duration and memory.

**(i) Lambda unit cost, per 1,000 predictions.**

```text
Function:  2,048 MB memory, 120 ms billed duration, ARM64
GB-seconds per invocation = 2.0 GB x 0.120 s          = 0.24 GB-s
Per 1,000 invocations                                  = 240 GB-s
Compute  240 x $0.0000133 (arm64 GB-s)                 = $0.0032
Requests 1,000 x $0.20 / 1,000,000                     = $0.0002
                                                   ---------------
Total per 1,000 predictions                            ~ $0.0034
```

Two things fall out of that immediately, and both are worth volunteering. **Memory is a latency lever, not just a capacity lever** — vCPU scales with memory, so doubling memory on a CPU-bound scorer often halves duration and leaves the bill flat while cutting p99. And **the request charge is not negligible at small durations**: at 120 ms it is 6% of the bill, so a function that is mostly overhead is paying a tax you remove by batching several entities per invocation.

**(ii) The crossover: when does Lambda stop being the cheap answer?**

```text
Always-on endpoint: 2 x ml.m5.large @ ~$0.134/hr        = $0.268/hr = $6.43/day
Lambda cost per prediction                              = $0.0000034
Break-even volume  =  $6.43 / $0.0000034                ~ 1.89M predictions/day
                   =  1.89M / 86,400                    ~ 22 requests/sec sustained
```

So: **below roughly twenty requests per second sustained, serverless wins; above it, a provisioned endpoint wins** — and the number moves with duty cycle, because the endpoint pays for the trough and Lambda does not. That single calculation is the most useful thing to be able to do live in this round, because it turns "serverless or endpoint" from a preference into an answer.

**(iii) Endpoint consolidation, the ResMed shape.** Illustrative, and framed as arithmetic rather than as his measured result:

```text
40 low-QPS models, 2 instances each for availability
  40 x 2 x ml.m5.xlarge @ ~$0.269/hr    = $21.5/hr   ~ $15,700/month
Consolidated: 3 multi-container endpoints (<=15 containers each),
  3 x 2 x ml.m5.4xlarge @ ~$1.075/hr    = $6.45/hr   ~ $4,700/month
```

The saving is not magic — it is that you stopped buying idle capacity forty times over. The trades are the ones named earlier: shared blast radius, coupled release cycle, a fifteen-container ceiling. Today the same shape is expressed with **inference components**, which remove the ceiling and let copy count go to zero.

#### The levers, ordered by typical realised saving

**Tier 1 — pure win, no quality cost. Always first.**

| Lever | Mechanism | Typical effect *(illustrative)* |
|---|---|---|
| **Kill idle** | Idle notebooks, zombie dev clusters, forgotten endpoints, un-terminated jobs | 20-40% of the bill in an unmanaged org |
| **Right-sizing** | Requests versus actual usage; over-requested CPU/memory blocks bin-packing and forces extra nodes | 15-30% on the CPU fleet |
| **Scale to zero** | KEDA plus Knative/KServe for dev, batch, and low-QPS endpoints; SageMaker async or serverless on AWS | Up to 100% of off-hours accelerator cost |
| **Continuous / dynamic batching** | vLLM continuous batching, Triton dynamic batcher | 2-20x throughput per accelerator against a naive baseline |
| **Prefix / prompt caching** | Cached input is priced far below fresh input | 50-90% of input token cost on RAG and agent workloads |
| **Batch/async discount** | Asynchronous batch APIs commonly price at half of standard | 50% on anything not latency-bound |
| **Storage tiering and locality** | Lifecycle old datasets and checkpoints; keep data, compute, and registry in one region and, for distributed jobs, one AZ | 5-15%, and egress is the most common bill surprise |

On prompt caching specifically, get the economics right rather than repeating the folklore. A cache **write** is priced at a small premium over fresh input and a **read** at roughly a tenth of it, so **one reuse already pays for the write** on the standard short-TTL cache; a longer-TTL cache carries a larger write premium and needs correspondingly more reuse. The number to watch is therefore not the break-even count, it is the **hit rate** — and a five-minute TTL against bursty, long-tail traffic is exactly where the economics fail, because you keep paying the write premium and never collect the read discount.

**Tier 2 — pricing and hardware arbitrage.** Spot is typically 50-70% off on GPU and occasionally more, but the honest constraint on GPU spot is **availability and interruption rate, not the headline discount** — getting sustained `p4d` spot capacity is a scheduling problem before it is a pricing one, which is why spot is correct for training *with checkpointing*, batch scoring and CI, and wrong for stateful online serving without an on-demand floor. Commitments should be sized to your measured **floor**, never your peak (a shape like 60% committed, 25% on-demand, 15% spot). **Graviton/ARM64** for CPU inference, embeddings, feature engineering, and all the non-GPU platform tax — the constraint is `aarch64` wheel coverage, which is the same constraint that governs the Lambda build. Accelerator alternatives such as Inferentia/Trainium carry their real cost in the compiler toolchain and the recompilation on every model change, so they suit stable high-volume architectures and not a fast-moving research surface.

**Tier 3 — model-level, trades some quality, needs an eval gate.** FP8 is effectively lossless on modern hardware and is the default; INT8 weight-only is close to free; INT4 buys 2.5-3x throughput at a measurable quality cost and, more importantly, halves weight memory so a bigger model fits on fewer devices; speculative decoding gives 1.5-3x on decode at low concurrency and *hurts* at high batch; FP8 KV cache nearly doubles concurrency; distillation is the biggest lever available, at 10-50x when a small student can replace a large teacher; and small-model-first routing with escalation only pays if you *measure* the escalation rate, because a router escalating 60% of traffic costs more than the big model alone since you pay twice.

#### The GPU arithmetic a senior does live

Be ready to do these on the CoderPad or out loud. The numbers below are order-of-magnitude illustrations, not quotes, and this is the material to present as design knowledge rather than operated experience.

**(a) Decode is memory-bandwidth bound.** Each decode step reads the full weight matrix once.

```text
steps/sec ~= aggregate HBM bandwidth / model bytes read per step
70B at FP8 = 70 GB;  H100 SXM HBM ~ 3.35 TB/s per GPU

Single GPU, if it fitted:  3350 / 70          ~=  48 steps/s theoretical
TP4 (weights shard 4 ways, ~17.5 GB per GPU): ~= 191 steps/s theoretical

Real batch-1 is nowhere near the TP4 theoretical: memory efficiency ~65%,
and tensor-parallel scaling at batch 1 is only ~0.35-0.5, because every
layer ends in an all-reduce and the step is latency-bound, not throughput-bound.
191 x 0.65 x 0.35  ~=  ~43 tok/s   <- a realistic batch-1 figure
```

Implication: batch-1 latency is set by bandwidth and you cannot buy your way out with FLOPs. That is *why* batching is the master lever — batch 64 reads the same weights once and emits 64 tokens. And when someone quotes you a batch-1 number above about 60 tok/s for a 70B, ask which quantisation and which parallelism, because the arithmetic does not get there without one of them changing.

**(b) KV cache sets the concurrency ceiling.**

```text
KV bytes/token = 2 (K,V) x n_kv_heads x head_dim x n_layers x bytes_per_elem
N_max ~= (total HBM - weights - overhead) / (KV_per_token x avg_context)
```

Implication: "add GPUs for throughput" is often wrong — you are KV-memory-bound, and FP8 KV or a shorter context doubles concurrency for free. Corollary worth volunteering: **a 32k-context feature request silently cuts max concurrency by 8x**, which is a capacity-planning conversation, not a product one.

**(c) Little's Law ties throughput to interactivity.** `concurrency = arrival rate x latency`. Aggregate throughput divided by concurrency is per-user token rate. Throughput and interactivity are the same dial pointed in opposite directions: pick the SLO first, derive maximum concurrency, then derive replica count — never the reverse. Separate pools for chat (low batch) and async (max batch) is usually cheaper than one compromise pool.

**(d) Self-host versus API is a duty-cycle question.**

```text
Rig: 4 x H100 reserved ~ $2.50/GPU-hr effective = $10/hr
API blended ~ $5 per 1M tokens [illustrative]
Tokens/hr to match the GPU bill: 10 / 5 = 2M tok/hr = ~555 tok/s sustained
Rig peak ~3,400 tok/s -> break-even ~16% sustained utilisation on hardware alone
Add ~0.5 FTE of platform ownership fully loaded (~$12/hr amortised over
wall-clock hours) -> break-even rises to ~36% sustained utilisation
```

> **Say it like this:** "Self-hosting does not win because GPUs are cheap. It wins when you can keep them above roughly a third of the clock. Below that the API is cheaper and you also do not pay for the on-call rota. Then there are non-cost reasons that legitimately override the arithmetic — data residency, a latency floor, owning your fine-tunes, independence from someone else's rate limits — and those are decisions, not calculations."

**Artefact 3 — a calculator to type into the CoderPad.** Small, dependency-free, and it answers six different questions, including the two about his own stack.

```python
"""Back-of-envelope inference cost / capacity calculator.
Everything here is arithmetic a senior should be able to reproduce on a whiteboard.
Note: decimal GB (1e9) throughout, while HBM is specified in GiB. That understates
capacity by ~7%, which is fine for a whiteboard and worth saying out loud.
"""
from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass
class Rig:
    gpus: int
    gpu_hourly_usd: float
    hbm_gb_per_gpu: float
    hbm_tbs_per_gpu: float          # memory bandwidth, TB/s


def kv_bytes_per_token(layers: int, kv_heads: int, head_dim: int, dtype_bytes: int) -> int:
    """Whole-model KV bytes for ONE token: K and V, summed over all layers."""
    return 2 * layers * kv_heads * head_dim * dtype_bytes


def max_concurrency(rig: Rig, weights_gb: float, overhead_gb: float,
                    kv_per_token: int, avg_context: int) -> int:
    free_bytes = (rig.gpus * rig.hbm_gb_per_gpu - weights_gb - overhead_gb) * 1e9
    per_request = kv_per_token * avg_context
    return max(0, int(free_bytes // per_request))


def decode_ceiling_tok_s(rig: Rig, weights_gb: float,
                         mem_efficiency: float = 0.65,
                         tp_scaling: float = 0.35) -> float:
    """Batch-1 decode is bandwidth bound: one full weight read per token.

    tp_scaling is the honest term most napkin maths omits. Sharding weights
    across N GPUs multiplies aggregate bandwidth by N, but at batch 1 every
    layer ends in an all-reduce and the step is latency-bound, so realised
    scaling is ~0.35-0.5 of ideal. Set tp_scaling=1.0 for the single-GPU case.
    """
    ideal = (rig.hbm_tbs_per_gpu * 1e12 * rig.gpus) / (weights_gb * 1e9)
    return ideal * mem_efficiency * tp_scaling


def usd_per_million_tokens(rig: Rig, aggregate_tok_s: float, duty_cycle: float = 1.0) -> float:
    if aggregate_tok_s <= 0 or duty_cycle <= 0:
        return float("inf")
    hourly = rig.gpus * rig.gpu_hourly_usd
    tokens_per_hour = aggregate_tok_s * 3600 * duty_cycle
    return hourly / (tokens_per_hour / 1e6)


def breakeven_utilisation(rig: Rig, api_usd_per_m: float, peak_tok_s: float,
                          ops_usd_per_hour: float = 0.0) -> float:
    """Fraction of peak throughput you must sustain for self-hosting to win."""
    hourly = rig.gpus * rig.gpu_hourly_usd + ops_usd_per_hour
    tok_s_needed = (hourly / api_usd_per_m) * 1e6 / 3600
    return tok_s_needed / peak_tok_s


def cost_per_1k_predictions(hourly_usd: float, predictions_per_second: float) -> float:
    """The classical-ML unit economic for an always-on endpoint."""
    if predictions_per_second <= 0:
        return float("inf")
    return hourly_usd / (predictions_per_second * 3600) * 1000


def lambda_cost_per_1k(memory_mb: float, duration_ms: float, arm64: bool = True,
                       req_usd_per_million: float = 0.20) -> float:
    """Serverless unit economic. List rates are illustrative; substitute your own."""
    gb_sec_usd = 0.0000133 if arm64 else 0.0000167
    gb_seconds = (memory_mb / 1024.0) * (duration_ms / 1000.0)
    return gb_seconds * 1000 * gb_sec_usd + 1000 * req_usd_per_million / 1e6


def serverless_crossover_rps(endpoint_hourly_usd: float, lambda_per_1k_usd: float) -> float:
    """Sustained req/s above which an always-on endpoint beats per-invocation billing."""
    per_prediction = lambda_per_1k_usd / 1000.0
    return (endpoint_hourly_usd / 3600.0) / per_prediction


if __name__ == "__main__":
    rig = Rig(gpus=4, gpu_hourly_usd=2.50, hbm_gb_per_gpu=80, hbm_tbs_per_gpu=3.35)
    kv = kv_bytes_per_token(layers=80, kv_heads=8, head_dim=128, dtype_bytes=2)
    print("KV KiB/token       :", kv / 1024)
    print("max concurrency @4k:", max_concurrency(rig, 70, 20, kv, 4096))
    print("batch-1 tok/s (TP4):", round(decode_ceiling_tok_s(rig, 70), 1))
    print("$/1M @3400 tok/s   :", round(usd_per_million_tokens(rig, 3400), 2))
    print("$/1M @30% duty     :", round(usd_per_million_tokens(rig, 3400, 0.30), 2))
    print("break-even util    :", round(breakeven_utilisation(rig, 5.0, 3400, 12.0), 3))
    print("$/1k preds (endpt) :", round(cost_per_1k_predictions(0.60, 250), 4))

    lam = lambda_cost_per_1k(memory_mb=2048, duration_ms=120)
    print("$/1k preds (lambda):", round(lam, 4))
    print("crossover rps      :", round(serverless_crossover_rps(0.268, lam), 1))
```

> **Say it like this:** "The most useful thing this shows is the difference between the list-price number and the honest number. Published self-hosting figures are usually quoted at full saturation and often mix prefill tokens with decode tokens, and prefill is an order of magnitude cheaper per token. So the question I ask whenever someone quotes a cost per million tokens is: input or output, and at what utilisation."

#### Cost attribution in a multi-tenant SaaS

You cannot optimise what you cannot attribute, and in a product like Smartsheet the attribution question is per-tenant, not just per-team.

1. **Mandatory tags and labels enforced by policy** — OPA on the Terraform plan, plus an admission webhook that rejects pods without `team`, `model`, `cost-center`, `env`. Untagged means unschedulable. Retroactive tagging never happens. Remember the two-projection point from the Terraform module: **Kubernetes labels drive allocation inside the cluster, AWS tags drive the billing export outside it**, and both must come from one source of truth.
2. **Namespace per team or per model, with ResourceQuota**, so the allocation engine has a boundary to sum over.
3. **OpenCost** (the CNCF allocation engine) or **Kubecost** for per-namespace and per-label cost, joined to the cloud billing export for everything outside the cluster.
4. **GPU allocation needs DCGM-exporter.** Neither OpenCost nor Kubecost derives per-pod GPU utilisation on its own — you join `DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_UTIL` to pod labels to separate *allocated* from *used*. That ratio, not the absolute, is the platform team's north star.
5. **Token-level metering** for LLM workloads: per-tenant input, output, and cached tokens from the engine's own metrics, because a per-request average hides the tenant sending 32k contexts.
6. **Showback before chargeback.** Publish per-team and per-tenant cost with no financial consequence for a quarter, fix the attribution bugs while they are free, then attach it to budgets. Going straight to chargeback with wrong numbers destroys trust in the platform permanently.

The unit-economic that goes on the dashboard: `cost per 1,000 predictions` for classical ML; `cost per 1M tokens` split input/output/cached for LLMs; **`cost per successful task`** for agents, which is the honest one because retries and failed trajectories are pure waste that a per-request metric hides; and `allocated versus utilised accelerator-hours` for the platform itself.

#### Anomaly detection on spend

Monthly billing review is too slow — a runaway job costs a month before anyone notices. What you actually build:

- **Daily granularity, not monthly.** Cloud cost exports at daily or hourly grain, loaded into the warehouse alongside the Kubernetes allocation data, keyed by tag.
- **Forecast plus residual, per key.** A simple seasonal baseline per `(team, service, tag)` — day-of-week matters enormously — and alert on residual in *relative* terms and with an absolute floor, so a dev namespace tripling from four dollars to twelve does not page anyone.
- **Leading indicators, not just spend.** Allocated GPU-hours, node count by NodePool, endpoint count, running-job count, and storage growth all move *before* the bill does. A GPU node group that grew overnight is visible hours before the invoice line.
- **Budget guardrails at the source**, not only alerts: per-namespace quotas, per-tenant token budgets with a hard cap, TTLs on self-served resources. An alert tells you the money is gone; a quota prevents it.
- **A weekly top-mover report** with an owner per line. The report has to be short enough to be read.

> **Say it like this:** "The pattern I would build is boring on purpose: daily cost by tag joined to Kubernetes allocation, a seasonal baseline per key, alerts on relative residual with an absolute floor — but the leading indicators matter more than the spend series, because allocated GPU-hours and node count move hours before the invoice does. The closest thing I have built is the drift-monitoring utility at ResMed: the owner declared the threshold and the slice, and the platform auto-provisioned the Datadog dashboard and alert. Same shape for spend — nothing hand-built."

#### How to say no without being the department of no

This is a behavioural question wearing a technical costume, and it is very likely to appear in a round tagged "Design and Domain."

> **Say it like this:** "I try never to answer a capacity request with no — I answer it with a price and two alternatives, because the requirement is usually not what was asked for. 'Eight A100s dedicated is roughly this per month. Same work on spot with checkpointing is about a third of that, and async on the shared pool is near zero marginal cost with a completion SLO instead of a latency SLO. Which does your deadline actually need?'"
>
> Expand only if pulled on: most of the time the honest answer is async, because the requirement was never latency, it was that the job finishes overnight. When I do have to hold a line I hold it on written policy — quotas, tagging, TTLs — not on personal judgement, because a policy is arguable in a forum and a person is just an obstacle.

Three supporting moves worth naming: give every team a **self-service paved road** so the default path is the cheap one; **publish the prices in the request UI** so the trade-off is visible at the moment of decision; and run **showback** so a team's own number is what changes their behaviour, not your email.
