### Forty rapid-fire infrastructure Q&A

| # | Question | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Why is ML hard on Kubernetes? | It assumes small, fungible, fast-starting, stateless pods. ML gives 20 GB images, tens of GB of weights, indivisible accelerators, gang-scheduled jobs, per-replica KV state. Bin-packing, round-robin balancing, liveness probes, and consolidation are all wrong by default. |
| 2 | How do you share a GPU? | MIG for hardware isolation and predictable p99; time-slicing only for dev, since there is no memory enforcement; MPS for many small cooperating kernels — and on Volta and later MPS does contain a client's fatal fault and can cap per-client memory, it just has no performance isolation. DRA improves how you *express* the request; it does not create safe fractional sharing. |
| 3 | Toleration or affinity? | Both. A toleration permits scheduling onto a tainted node; it does not attract. You need taint plus toleration plus node affinity or a nodeSelector. |
| 4 | What does a PDB not protect against? | Node failure, preemption, and spot reclaim. It only governs voluntary disruption. And `minAvailable: 1` with one replica blocks all drains forever. |
| 5 | Karpenter or Cluster Autoscaler for GPUs? | Karpenter — it collapses the ASG explosion into two or three NodePools and picks the cheapest instance that fits pending pods. Pin training pods with `do-not-disrupt` and `WhenEmpty` or consolidation eats a five-day run. |
| 6 | Name the consolidation policies. | `WhenEmpty` (safe, for training), `Balanced` (consolidate where the saving outweighs the disruption — good mixed-fleet default), `WhenEmptyOrUnderutilized` (aggressive, for stateless inference). Node expiry is a separate field under `spec.template.spec`, not under disruption. |
| 7 | HPA or KEDA for inference? | KEDA — it is HPA plus external triggers and scale-to-zero. CPU is uncorrelated with GPU work; scale on queue depth or TTFT, and size the stabilisation window to the real node-plus-weights start time. |
| 8 | Our GPU cold start is 12 minutes. | Split weights from the image; lazy pull (SOCI/nydus) or a pre-pull DaemonSet; parallel object-store to NVMe streaming; `startupProbe` not liveness; keep warm headroom with preemptible balloon pods, because no pull optimisation makes 140 GB instant. |
| 9 | Readiness versus liveness for a model server? | Readiness runs a real inference on a canary input. Liveness must not, or a slow weight load becomes a restart loop. `startupProbe` bridges the gap. |
| 10 | Inference wants spread, training wants what? | Packing. Cross-AZ all-reduce is slow and billed; pack a distributed job into one zone or placement group. Spread inference for availability. |
| 11 | How do you stop research eating production GPUs? | Kueue ClusterQueues with a guaranteed nominal quota per team plus cohort borrowing, and research preempted first. No extra hardware required. |
| 12 | Why gang scheduling? | Vanilla Kubernetes schedules six of eight workers and leaves two Pending forever, holding six GPUs hostage. Kueue admits all-or-nothing. |
| 13 | When is Lambda right for ML? | Spiky, low-duty-cycle, CPU-sized models; pre/post-processing; glue. Wrong for any GPU need, sustained high QPS, sub-cold-start p99, models over 10 GB, or anything over 15 minutes. |
| 14 | Lambda limits, from memory? | 250 MB zip, 10 GB container image, 10,240 MB memory with vCPU scaling with it, 10 GB `/tmp`, 15-minute cap, no GPU. |
| 15 | Would you pair SnapStart with a 10 GB `/tmp` model cache? | No — they are mutually exclusive. SnapStart covers container images on the managed Python/Java/.NET runtimes but does not support provisioned concurrency, EFS, or ephemeral storage above 512 MB. SnapStart when the model fits in the snapshot; provisioned concurrency when it does not. |
| 16 | Why ARM64 on Lambda? | Roughly 20% cheaper per GB-second and often faster for int8/ONNX CPU inference. The gate is `aarch64` wheel availability across the whole dependency tree — audit before committing. |
| 17 | Serverless or an always-on endpoint? | Do the crossover. At ~$0.0034 per 1,000 predictions on Lambda against a ~$0.27/hr two-instance endpoint, the break-even is around 22 req/s sustained — below that serverless wins, above it the endpoint does, and duty cycle moves the line. |
| 18 | Which SageMaker inference option? | Real-time for synchronous traffic with a latency SLO (no scale-to-zero — that is the always-on trap); Serverless for spiky CPU-sized work; Asynchronous for large payloads, long runs and min-instances-zero; Batch Transform for offline scoring with no endpoint at all. Inference components when you want many models packed on one endpoint's fleet. |
| 19 | MCE or MME? | Multi-container: up to 15 containers, all resident, different models or frameworks, invoked directly by hostname or chained as a pipeline — you pay for one fleet instead of N, and accept a shared blast radius and a coupled release. Multi-model: one container, artefacts loaded from S3 on demand and evicted under memory pressure — for hundreds of homogeneous low-QPS models, and the cost is a per-model cold start on a cache miss. |
| 20 | You have not used Bedrock. | Say so, then give the structure: no weights to host, so quota replaces GPU capacity as the scaling limit; on-demand versus provisioned throughput in model units is the reserved-versus-on-demand decision; access enablement, guardrails and invocation logging are the governance surface; PrivateLink keeps it in the VPC. The eval harness, gates, attribution and degradation ladder all port unchanged. |
| 21 | Why is round-robin wrong for LLM serving? | It is cache-blind. Routing a conversation away from the replica holding its prefix turns a cache hit into a full re-prefill. Use an inference gateway with a prefix-cache-aware endpoint picker — and key it on tenant, or you have built a cross-tenant channel. |
| 22 | What does PagedAttention buy? | KV cache in non-contiguous pages, so fragmentation stops capping concurrency — you can actually reach the batch size the memory supports. |
| 23 | Continuous versus static batching? | Static waits for the batch and is held hostage by the longest sequence. Continuous schedules per decode step: finished sequences leave, queued ones join, the GPU stays saturated. |
| 24 | When does Ray Serve beat KServe? | Multi-stage heterogeneous graphs — preprocess, embed, rerank, generate — where each stage wants different hardware and scales independently. Not when the shape is one model, HTTP in, HTTP out: then the head node is a failure domain and a third autoscaler for no benefit. And `num_gpus: 0.25` is bookkeeping, not isolation. |
| 25 | Shadow versus canary versus A/B? | Shadow proves it runs, at zero user risk, and proves nothing causal. Canary is a safety ramp with automated abort. A/B is a powered experiment with a pre-registered hypothesis and a fixed horizon. |
| 26 | What is the rollback target? | Under sixty seconds, a config or flag change, no CI run, with N-1 kept warm through the bake window then scaled down. And rehearse it — an untested rollback is a hypothesis. |
| 27 | How is ML CI different? | Inputs are code times data times config times environment times seed; verdicts are statistical so gates need a margin; artefacts are gigabytes; and failure is silent at 200 OK, which is why train/serve parity and shadow are gates software does not have. |
| 28 | Which gate catches train/serve skew? | Score a sample through the real container and diff against offline predictions, asserting zero silently-defaulted features. That is the gate that would have caught my 4,001-versus-28 feature bug at TrueBalance. |
| 29 | Which commit produced this model? | The manifest answers it: git commit and clean tree, image digest, lockfile hash, data snapshot id, feature-contract hash, config hash, seeds, approver. If the manifest cannot rebuild it, you do not have reproducibility. |
| 30 | Is bit-exact retraining achievable? | Rarely on multi-GPU — non-deterministic reductions, autotuning, dataloader interleaving. The right bar is statistical reproducibility plus complete lineage. |
| 31 | What breaks data-snapshot reproducibility silently? | Retention. `VACUUM` or a short time-travel window deletes the files your pinned snapshot references. Retention is set by the audit horizon, not by storage cost. |
| 32 | MLflow stages or aliases? | Aliases. Stages were deprecated in MLflow 2.9 in favour of aliases and tags, and Unity Catalog models do not support stages at all — Databricks recommends the three-level namespace for environment plus aliases for deployment status. `models:/name@champion`. |
| 33 | What does MLflow *not* give you? | It is not a deployment system, not a feature store, not a data versioner, and not an orchestrator. It is metadata over an artifact store, so bucket retention and immutability are still your problem — a registry entry pointing at a deleted object is a classic outage. |
| 34 | GitOps for models — what triggers deploy? | A registry event: an alias move, or a SageMaker model-package approval, via a webhook or EventBridge rule that commits the model URI and image digest into the config repo. Argo CD reconciles. Rollback is `git revert`. Never a human running a pipeline. |
| 35 | Terraform state layout? | One state per environment, region, and layer, ordered by rate of change. State boundary equals blast radius boundary — a team-namespace apply must be structurally incapable of touching the VPC. |
| 36 | Highest-value Terraform guardrail on an ML platform? | A plan-assertion gate that fails if the plan contains a `delete` for anything tagged stateful. The expensive resources are the stateful ones. |
| 37 | Labels or tags for cost attribution? | Both, from one source of truth. Kubernetes labels drive scheduling and OpenCost allocation inside the cluster; AWS tags on the EC2NodeClass reach the instance and key the billing export outside it. A NodePool label alone gives you no cloud cost attribution. |
| 38 | What does 99.9% actually buy you? | About 40 minutes over a 28-day window. One bad deploy noticed in twelve minutes and rolled back in eight spends half the month. Alert on burn rate — 14.4× over 1 h pages, 6× over 6 h pages, 3× over a day tickets — and make model promotion consume the same budget. |
| 39 | What does an open circuit breaker return? | The next rung of the degradation ladder with `degraded: true` — never a 500, or you have converted a slow dependency into an outage. Trip on a failure ratio with a minimum call volume, count slow calls as failures, jitter the cool-down, half-open on a fixed small probe count, and keep the breaker outside the retry loop. |
| 40 | GPU utilisation is 15% and the bill is huge. | First distrust the metric — `nvidia-smi` utilisation is a residency metric, not a work metric; get SM occupancy or achieved bandwidth. Then split training (usually input-pipeline starvation) from inference (decode is bandwidth-bound, so low SM is expected). Then attack the bill's real shape, which is usually orphaned endpoints and idle dev capacity rather than the busy GPUs. |

## 8. Domain primer — RAG, vector stores, knowledge graphs, agents, LLMOps governance

Open on the failure you personally watched, not on an architecture.

At TrueBalance you shipped an XGBoost loan-withdrawal propensity model whose offline pipeline computed 4,001 features while the real-time payload carried 28 keys. The transform imputed defaults for everything else, so the served vector was near-constant. Out-of-time ROC-AUC 0.84 offline; garbage online; **nothing errored**. The fix was four cheap invariants: a serialized feature contract shipped next to the artifact, a hard fail on a missing required feature, a CI subset assertion as a promotion gate, and a per-feature missing-rate metric emitted by the scorer.

That story is the spine of this whole chapter, because **RAG fails the same way**. Post-filtering returns four rows for a top-10 request and does not error. A query embedded with last quarter's model returns plausible neighbours and does not error. A stale ACL projection returns a document the caller may not see and does not error. Same disease, same medicine: name the invariant, assert it cheaply, gate promotion on it, emit a metric. Say the TrueBalance story once, in the first ten minutes, and then let every later answer point back at it.

> **Say it like this:** "The bug I care most about in retrieval systems is the one that reports success. I have shipped one — offline the model computed four thousand features, in production the payload had twenty-eight, and the imputer filled the rest silently. Everything downstream of that is why I now put a contract next to the artifact and gate promotion on it."

### Triage — what to read if you have ninety minutes

| Section | Odds it comes up | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **8.5 — the five "no" answers** | Near certain | The JD names Bedrock, Unity Catalog, Mosaic AI Agent Framework, Databricks Vector Search and Monte Carlo. You have used none of them, and the recruiter has that in writing |
| **8.3 — permission-aware / multi-tenant retrieval** | Near certain | Their product is shared work, and they ship an MCP server that exposes live sheet data to agents |
| **8.0 — the sixty-minute plan** | Certain (it *is* the round) | Design rounds are graded on shape as much as content |
| **8.1 + 8.2 — pipeline and evaluation** | High | "Design RAG over our data" is the obvious opening prompt |
| **8.6 — retrieval drift monitoring** | High | JD line, in terms: "post-deployment monitoring for model performance, data drift, and latency" |
| **8.7 — serving economics** | High | JD line: "Manage GPU/CPU utilization to minimize cloud costs while maintaining low-latency inference" |
| **8.9 — agents in production** | Medium-high | Your MCP assistant is on the CV; they will pull that thread |
| **8.11 — the first ninety days** | Medium-high | Platform-owner rounds usually close on it |
| **8.8 — knowledge graphs** | Medium | The JD names KG, and you have a real one |
| **8.10 — governance** | Medium | India GCC, enterprise SaaS buyers, EU customers |

### The six sentences

Have these in your mouth before you join the Zoom. They are the spine of everything below. Three are safe to assert flat; three are marked because they need a hedge or a source.

1. **Retrieval quality is a config problem before it is a model problem.** Chunking, hybrid and reranking move retrieval quality as much as the embedding model does. Tune those three before you shop for embeddings.
2. **Recall@k is not the metric that pays.** ⚠ Say the *direction*, not a number you cannot source: published chunking evaluations repeatedly find semantic chunking wins on retrieval recall and loses on end-to-end answer accuracy against plain recursive splitting — right fragment, not enough surrounding context. Always report retrieval and end-to-end separately.
3. **Post-filtering is a silent recall bug and a latent breach.** The pgvector arithmetic that proves it is in §8.3. Know it cold and deploy it *once*, in the permissions answer, where it does the most work.
4. **An embedding model upgrade is a data migration, not a config change.** Vectors from two models are not comparable. Blue/green the index; never mix.
5. **Permission-aware retrieval is a pre-filter or it is a breach.** Post-filtering means the model already read the document.
6. **Agents fail on economics before they fail on reasoning.** An unbounded retry against a tool that fails without signalling failure will make hundreds of identical calls before a human notices, and the bill is the first symptom. That is why the caps go at the gateway, not in the agent loop.

### 8.0 Running the sixty minutes, and what to put in the pad

The invite says *COMPETENCY ASSIGNMENT: AI/ML Ops Design and Domain*, and round 1 already took the coding competency. So CoderPad here is a **shared whiteboard that happens to have a monospace font**. Treat it as one.

#### The shape of the hour

| Minutes | What is happening | What you do |
|---|---|---|
| 0–5 | Intro, warm-up | The 90-second intro from Ch.54. "8 years engineering, about 4.5 of them in ML engineer titles." Do not extend it |
| 5–12 | The prompt lands | **Do not draw yet.** Ask the four scoping questions below. Write the answers in the pad as a requirements block |
| 12–22 | The sketch | The eight-minute drawing order below. Talk while you draw; narrate the constraint each box exists to satisfy |
| 22–40 | They pick an axis and go deep | Whatever they pick, answer with a failure you have watched, then the invariant, then the metric |
| 40–50 | Trade-offs and the honest "no" | §8.5 lives here. Get the nos out early enough that they are calibration, not a late reveal |
| 50–57 | Your questions | Three, listed below. Ask them as a platform owner would |
| 57–60 | Close | Notice period 60 days, buyout discussable. Do not volunteer compensation unless asked |

#### The four scoping questions, asked before you draw anything

Type them into the pad as you ask. Typing them is itself signal — it says you build from requirements, not from a diagram you memorised.

1. **Who is the caller and what may they see?** One tenant per query, or cross-tenant? Document-level permissions, or row-level? *(This one question decides the chunking strategy, the isolation model and the index layout. Ask it first.)*
2. **What is the freshness requirement, and separately, the revocation requirement?** Seconds, minutes or a day for new content; and how long may a revoked document stay retrievable? They are different numbers and only one of them is a security control.
3. **What is the query mix?** Lookup, exploratory, aggregate, multi-hop. Roughly what share is each? A corpus of lookups does not need a vector database at all.
4. **What is the scale that matters?** Not documents — tenants, and the distribution across them. 200 tenants at 1 GB is a completely different system from 200,000 tenants where 2,000 are active this week.

> **Say it like this:** "Before I draw anything — the answer changes shape depending on whether permissions are document-level or row-level, so let me ask that first. Everything else I sketch is downstream of it."

#### The eight-minute drawing order

Draw in this sequence, one band at a time, saying the constraint out loud as each box appears. Do not draw the finished picture; draw the reasoning.

| Minute | Draw | Say while drawing |
|---|---|---|
| 0:00–1:30 | The serve lane, left to right: retriever → fuse → rerank → re-check → pack → generate | "Right to left is how it fails; left to right is how it runs" |
| 1:30–3:00 | Put **PRE-filter** inside the retriever box and draw the JWT arrow into it | "The caller's tenant and principal set come from the token and enter here. This is the whole security design in one arrow" |
| 3:00–4:30 | The ingest lane above it: sources → change queue → chunk/enrich/embed → index | "Content hash to skip unchanged is where the cost savings live" |
| 4:30–5:30 | The **ACL projection priority lane** feeding the index, drawn separately from content | "Permission events on their own lane, ahead of content events, because the revocation SLA is tighter" |
| 5:30–6:30 | The blue/green box beside the index with the alias arrow | "The app resolves an alias, never an index name" |
| 6:30–8:00 | Audit log hanging off generate; then the two dashed monitors: `returned < requested` and `query_model == index_model` | "These two alarms are the cheapest things on the diagram and they catch the two failures that do not error" |

Then stop and say: *"That is the skeleton. Which part do you want me to open up?"* Handing them the axis is a stronger move than picking one yourself.

#### The three things you might actually be asked to type

Keep each under five minutes. All three are in this chapter and all three are things a platform owner has written before.

1. **The permission-filtered retrieval query** — §8.3. Pre-filter, bounded iterative scan, the model assertion, the under-return alarm. This is the single highest-signal thing you can type in this round.
2. **One retrieval eval assertion** — §8.2. Ten lines of Python that load a golden set, run retrieval, compute recall@20 against labelled doc ids, and fail on a regression relative to the recorded baseline.
3. **One monitor** — §8.6. The `returned < requested` counter, or the no-good-chunk rate, expressed as a metric emission plus the alert rule and, crucially, whether it pages or only dashboards.

#### Your three questions for them

- "You ship an MCP server that exposes live sheet data to agents. Does retrieval for that run inside the caller's existing sharing model — same Owner/Admin/Editor/Commenter/Viewer grants, Dynamic View row scoping applied *before* retrieval — or is it filtered after?"
- "Is the ML platform team building for Smartsheet product teams, or for customers directly? That changes whether my job is a paved road or a feature."
- "Where does the GCC sit relative to the platform's decision-making? I have worked in both models and the async one only works if the platform's contract is written down."

### 8.1 The production RAG pipeline, stage by stage

Draw this in CoderPad. It reads well in a plain text pane and it gives you a map to walk while you talk. Note where the two lanes enter: the **ACL projection feeds the index** (that is where `allowed_principals` is written), and the **caller's identity feeds the retriever** (that is where the pre-filter happens). Those are different arrows and confusing them is the whole bug class.

```text
INGEST  /  INDEX
 ┌─────────┐  CDC /  ┌──────────┐  chunk +  ┌─────────────┐  alias  ┌─────────────┐
 │ sources │─webhook▶│  change  │──enrich──▶│   index     │◀─swap──▶│ index vNEW  │
 │ SaaS DB │         │  queue   │   embed   │  vector +   │         │ built off   │
 │ files   │         │ (SQS /   │           │  lexical +  │         │ the serving │
 │ APIs    │         │  Kafka)  │           │  metadata   │         │ path        │
 └─────────┘         └────┬─────┘           └──────┬──────┘         └─────────────┘
                          │ content hash           ▲
                          │ skip-if-unchanged      │ tenant_id + allowed_principals
                          ▼                        │ written onto every chunk
                  ┌────────────────┐               │
                  │ ACL projection │───────────────┘
                  │ (priority lane)│
                  └────────────────┘

SERVE     caller's tenant_id + principal set come from the JWT and enter HERE
                  │
                  ▼
 ┌──────────────┐    ┌────────────┐    ┌────────────┐    ┌───────────────────────┐
 │  retriever   │───▶│ hybrid     │───▶│  rerank    │───▶│ authoritative re-check│
 │  PRE-filter  │    │ fuse (RRF) │    │ timeout +  │    │ of top-N doc ids vs   │
 │              │    └────────────┘    │ fallback   │    │ the system of record  │
 │  reads index │                      └────────────┘    └──────────┬────────────┘
 └──────▲───────┘                                                   │
        └── index (above)                                           ▼
                     ┌───────────────┐      ┌──────────────┐   ┌──────────────┐
                     │  audit log    │◀─────│  generate    │◀──│ context pack │
                     │ who / tenant /│      │ (gateway,    │   │ dedup, head+ │
                     │ doc ids / ver │      │ pinned p+m)  │   │ tail order   │
                     └───────────────┘      └──────────────┘   └──────────────┘
```

Every stage has one operational concern that matters more than the rest of them combined.

| Stage | The thing that actually breaks | The metric that catches it |
|---|---|---|
| Ingestion | Orphan chunks from a re-chunked document; missed deletes | Nightly reconciliation: source doc set vs index doc set |
| Freshness | You published no SLA, so every complaint is unfalsifiable | p95 lag source-change → retrievable |
| Chunking | Chunk spans two ACL domains, or is too small to answer with | End-to-end accuracy, not recall |
| Embedding | Someone bumps the model string and quality silently collapses | Assert `query_model == index_model` at query time |
| Hybrid | Dense-only misses IDs, error codes, SKUs, rare acronyms | BM25-only baseline in the eval suite |
| Rerank | An API call in your request path with no timeout | p99 latency, rerank-skip rate |
| Filtering | Post-filter returns fewer rows than asked, silently | Alert on `returned < requested` |
| Context packing | Duplicate chunks eat the window; middle of context ignored | Distinct-doc count in the packed context |
| Citation | The model invents citation markers | Post-validate every emitted marker against the retriever's list |
| Rebuild | Writes landing during the rebuild are lost | Change-log replay onto vNEW before alias swap |

Two rows in that table are the RAG version of the TrueBalance parity collapse, and it is worth naming the link out loud once:

> **Say it like this:** "Rows five and seven are the same bug I have already shipped once. `query_model == index_model` is a serialized contract asserted at serving time; `returned < requested` is a per-request completeness metric. At TrueBalance the equivalent pair was a feature contract next to the artifact and a per-feature missing-rate metric from the scorer. In both systems the failure is silent success, and in both systems the fix is a cheap invariant enforced as a promotion gate rather than a smarter model."

#### Ingestion and the two SLAs

Keep two clocks, publish both, and never conflate them.

- **Freshness SLA** — source change to retrievable. Typical enterprise targets: under a minute for user-authored content, 15 minutes to an hour for connectors, 24 hours for bulk archives.
- **Correctness/revocation SLA** — permission change to no longer retrievable. This must be *much tighter*. A document appearing late is an inconvenience. A document disappearing late is an incident.

Pipeline shape: CDC/webhook/delta-crawl into a change queue; content-hash comparison to skip unchanged (this is where most cost savings live); **delete-then-insert by `doc_id`**, never upsert-by-chunk-id, because chunk boundaries shift and you leave orphans; tombstones for deletes propagated to index *and* cache; a per-document `index_version`; and a nightly reconciliation job that diffs the source doc set against the index doc set.

> **Say it like this:** "The reconciliation job is the boring part nobody builds. Without it, an orphaned chunk from an old chunking of a since-edited document is how the AI ends up quoting a policy you deleted last quarter."

#### Chunking

| Strategy | Wins when | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| Fixed-size + overlap | Cheap baseline, homogeneous text | Cuts mid-sentence, mid-table |
| **Recursive split — the default** | 256–512 tokens, 10–25% overlap, ~200-token floor with merge | Loses cross-chunk context |
| Structure-aware (headings, code AST) | Wikis, API docs, help centres | Parser per format |
| Semantic (embedding-distance boundaries) | Long unstructured narrative | Higher retrieval recall, *worse* end-to-end accuracy in the published evaluations; expensive to compute |
| Parent-document / small-to-big | Retrieve small, generate from the parent | Two stores to keep consistent |
| Contextual Retrieval (one cheap LLM call prepending a 50–100 token situating blurb) | Corpora you can afford to enrich | Anthropic reports up to a **67% reduction in top-20 retrieval failures** when combined with reranking; indexing cost scales with corpus |

On semantic chunking, say the direction and refuse the digits:

> **Say it like this:** "Published chunking evaluations keep finding the same thing — semantic chunking wins on retrieval recall and loses on end-to-end answer accuracy against plain recursive splitting. You retrieve the right fragment without enough surrounding context to answer from. I would not adopt it without measuring end-to-end on our own corpus, and I would not quote you a number I cannot source."

The rule that binds chunking to §8.3: **chunk boundaries must never cross ACL boundaries. If a chunk has two owners, it has no safe filter.**

#### Embedding choice and the re-embedding tax

The operational answer to "which embedding model" is not the MTEB leaderboard. It is: dimensions × corpus size × index type determines your RAM bill more than the model's score does. 1536-dim float32 is ~6 KB per vector before index overhead, and HNSW adds roughly 1.5–2×. Matryoshka truncation and int8/binary quantisation with full-precision rescoring on the top candidates are how you keep it in memory.

Hard rules to state:

- Store `embedding_model`, `model_version` and `chunk_strategy_version` in every chunk's metadata.
- **Assert at query time that the query model matches the index model.** One assertion prevents the most common self-inflicted RAG outage. This is the same class of control as the feature contract you shipped at TrueBalance.
- Budget **two to three full re-index events in year one**.
- Never bundle a generation-model swap and an embedding-model swap in one release. The first is reversible in minutes; the second is a full re-index.

On re-index cost, give the shape rather than a price you cannot defend:

> **Say it like this:** "The embedding API bill is usually the small half. The pipeline dominates — re-parse, re-chunk, re-enrich, build, validate — and the index build is CPU-hours that scale super-linearly with `ef_construction`. There is no single number for it because it moves by two orders of magnitude with index type, dimensionality, build parameters and instance class. I would price it on our own corpus before committing to a re-index cadence, and I would price it *before* the first embedding upgrade rather than during it."

#### Hybrid retrieval and RRF

Dense retrieval fails on exact IDs, error codes, SKUs, proper nouns, rare acronyms and negation. BM25 fails on paraphrase and synonymy. Run both, fuse with Reciprocal Rank Fusion:

`score(d) = Σ_lists 1 / (k + rank_i(d))`, with **k = 60** as the near-universal default.

Two separate properties get conflated here, and the interviewer may pull the thread, so keep them apart:

- **Why RRF works at all:** it consumes *ranks*, not scores, which sidesteps the BM25-vs-cosine score-scale incompatibility entirely. It is a consensus vote, not a confidence blend.
- **Why k = 60 needs no tuning:** because `1/(k+r)` is a flat curve over the plausible range of k, so changing k rescales every contribution almost uniformly and the induced *ordering* barely moves. At k=60, rank 1 contributes 1/61 ≈ 0.0164 and rank 100 contributes 1/160 ≈ 0.00625 — a 2.6× spread across a hundred positions.

What k actually controls is how sharply the top of each list dominates. **Small k sharpens** — rank 1 dwarfs rank 5, so use it when you trust the head of each list and the lists are short. **Large k flattens** toward a plain appearance count, which is what you want when the lists are long and individually noisy and you are fusing for breadth. That is the reasoning; the 60 is a default, not a law.

RRF is the *wrong* choice when one retriever reliably dominates a query class, or when you have calibrated scores worth preserving. And query routing — classify the query as lookup / exploratory / aggregate, then pick the retriever — is usually cheaper and better than fusing blindly.

#### Reranking

Reranking is the highest-ROI single addition after hybrid retrieval, and it is close to standard in production stacks now.

| Reranker | Latency | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Cohere Rerank 3.5 | ~80–150 ms p50 under 2k-token chunks; **>200 ms p99 past 3k tokens** | Strong API default |
| Voyage rerank-2.5 | comparable | |
| BGE-reranker-v2-m3 | 50–100 ms on GPU; ~1.2 s for a 100-pair batch | Most-deployed open weight |
| Qwen3-Reranker 4B | >1 s/query | Top open quality, wrong latency for interactive |

Rerank top-50 down to top-5..8, not top-200 — cross-encoder cost is linear in candidates and your p99 is where the pain is. Chunk length drives reranker latency more than candidate count past ~2k tokens, so truncate what you send. The self-host-versus-API arithmetic is in §8.7.

> **Say it like this:** "An API reranker is a hard external dependency inside the request path, so it gets a timeout and a documented fallback: skip the rerank, return fusion order, and emit a `rerank_skipped` counter. Degrade the enrichment, never degrade the filter."

#### Query rewriting — gate it, don't always-on it

Query rewriting, HyDE and multi-query buy roughly 10–20% answer-quality lift on *ambiguous* queries, and cost one extra LLM call — 200–500 ms and about $0.001–0.005 per query at current API prices — plus N× retrieval for multi-query. HyDE is measurably *worse than the raw query* in narrow, high-jargon corpora, because a hallucinated hypothetical document drags retrieval toward plausible-but-absent content.

The operator answer: run vanilla retrieval first; if top-1 reranker score is below threshold, *then* fire the rewrite and re-retrieve. You pay latency on 10–20% of traffic instead of all of it. And in any chat product, **conversational query rewriting matters more than HyDE** — "what about the second one?" has no standalone embedding.

#### Metadata, dedup, context packing, citations

Every chunk carries: `tenant_id`, ACL keys, `source_system`, `doc_id`, `version`, `created_at/updated_at`, type, language, `embedding_model`, `chunk_strategy_version`.

- **Recency:** never sort by date, that destroys relevance. Use a decay multiplier on the fused score, a hard `updated_at >` pre-filter for volatile domains, or a "current version only" flag maintained by the pipeline.
- **Dedup:** exact hash on normalised text at ingest, MinHash/SimHash for near-dupes, and a cosine-similarity cap (or MMR) between selected results at retrieval time. Enterprise corpora are full of forwarded threads and copy-pasted templates; without dedup, top-10 becomes top-3-distinct.
- **Packing:** models attend to head and tail — put the highest-ranked chunk first and the second-highest last. Give every chunk an explicit header `[doc_id | title | updated_at | url]`, because that is what makes citation possible. Budget the window: system prompt, history and output reserved first, then fill.
- **Citations must be verifiable identifiers emitted by the retriever**, not free text the model invents. Pass chunks with stable `[1]..[n]` markers, require the model to cite markers, then post-validate that every cited marker exists and overlaps the chunk lexically or semantically. Drop or flag unsupported claims. That post-validation is the difference between "grounded" and "claims to be grounded".

#### Incremental updates, and when incremental stops being enough

Most of the day-to-day is incremental: content-hash skip, delete-then-insert by `doc_id`, tombstones propagated to index and cache. That is correct and it is what you run 99% of the time. What people miss is that **the ANN structure itself degrades under sustained incremental churn**, in two different ways depending on index family.

| Index family | What degrades | Symptom you will actually see |
|---|---|---|
| **HNSW** | Deleted nodes are tombstoned but stay in the graph as waypoints; new inserts attach to a graph whose entry points and layer assignment were chosen for the old distribution | Recall at a fixed `ef_search` slides down; memory does not fall after deletes; you find yourself raising `ef_search` to hold quality |
| **IVF / IVF-PQ** | Centroids were fit once on a sample. As the corpus shifts, clusters go unbalanced and the nearest cluster stops containing the nearest neighbours | You have to raise `nprobe` to hold recall, which raises latency; a few fat partitions dominate the scan |
| **Lexical (BM25) segments** | Deleted docs live in segments until merge; term statistics (df, avgdl) skew toward deleted content | Scores drift; deleted-doc ratio climbs; merge pressure shows up as periodic latency spikes |

**The clean trigger condition for a rebuild is not a doc count — it is that you had to raise a search parameter to hold recall.** That is one number and it is measurable weekly.

Ship a weekly job that samples ~1,000 real queries, computes exact-kNN ground truth by brute force, and plots recall against latency at the current parameters. Rebuild when any of these fire:

1. Recall@k at the *frozen* `ef_search`/`nprobe` drops below your floor.
2. You had to raise `ef_search`/`nprobe` to stay above the floor — the cleanest single signal, because it converts a quality problem into a latency bill.
3. Tombstoned or deleted fraction passes roughly 10–20% of the index.
4. The corpus has roughly doubled since the last build, so build-time parameters chosen for the old size are no longer right.

> **Say it like this:** "Incremental update is the steady state; the rebuild is the release valve, and the thing to get right is the *trigger*, not the mechanics. I would rebuild when I notice I have been raising `ef_search` to hold recall, because at that point I am paying latency to hide graph degradation. That is a weekly job producing one recall-versus-latency curve against exact-kNN ground truth on a thousand sampled queries — a thirty-minute build that almost nobody does, and it is what turns 'the index feels slow' into a scheduled blue/green."

#### Blue/green index rebuilds

The standard answer, and you should give it in this order:

1. Build `v_new` alongside live `v_old`; the app resolves an **alias**, never a hard index name.
2. Validate `v_new` against the golden query set before any traffic: recall@k, nDCG@10, side-by-side answer diff.
3. Shadow / dual-read a percentage of live queries to both, compare offline, zero user impact.
4. Canary 5% → 25% → 100% with automatic rollback on metric regression.
5. Keep `v_old` hot for 24–72 hours.
6. **The delta problem:** writes that land during the rebuild. Either freeze writes, which is rarely acceptable, or replay the change log onto `v_new` before the swap.

Mechanics differ. Elasticsearch/OpenSearch alias swap is atomic. Pinecone is a new index plus a traffic switch. On pgvector, build the new table and index it with **plain `CREATE INDEX`** plus a large `maintenance_work_mem` and raised `max_parallel_maintenance_workers` — nothing is reading the blue table yet, so `CONCURRENTLY` buys you nothing and costs a second table scan. `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` is the right tool for the *other* job: adding an index to a table that is already serving live traffic without taking an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock. The swap itself is the part that goes inside a transaction.

> **Say it like this:** "Mentioning the change-log replay is the tell that someone has actually run one of these. Everything up to step five is in every blog post; step six is what bites you at 2am."

### 8.2 Evaluating RAG properly

Layer the evals and never report one number.

| Layer | Metrics | LLM needed? | Where it runs |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Retrieval** | recall@k (the ceiling on everything downstream), nDCG@10, MRR, context precision | No — deterministic and cheap | **Every PR, as a merge gate** |
| **Permission** | precision@k on the filter — fraction of returned docs the caller may see | No | A *test*, not a metric. Must be 1.0 |
| **Generation** | faithfulness/groundedness, answer relevance, context recall, **refusal correctness** | Yes | Nightly + on prompt change |
| **End-to-end task** | did the user's job get done | Human or judge | Weekly sample + online proxies |

Most teams never measure **refusal correctness** — does the system say "I don't know" when the context genuinely lacks the answer — and then ship a confident hallucinator.

#### RAGAS, in one sentence each

RAGAS is the common vocabulary; DeepEval, Langfuse, Braintrust and Phoenix are the alternatives. Naming the metrics is table stakes; being able to say what each one measures and which one you would gate on is the actual probe.

| Metric | What it measures | Needs a reference answer? | Gate on it? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **`context_recall`** | Of the claims in the ground-truth answer, what fraction is supported by the retrieved context — *did you retrieve everything needed* | Yes | **Yes — this is the ceiling.** If the context lacks the answer, no generator can recover it |
| **`context_precision`** | Of the retrieved contexts, what fraction is actually relevant, weighted by rank — the signal-to-noise of what you handed the model | Usually | Track, don't gate. It is the dial you tune to cut tokens and reduce distraction |
| **`faithfulness`** | Of the claims in the *generated* answer, what fraction is inferable from the retrieved context — the hallucination measure | No | **Yes, on prompt and model changes.** It is the one that regresses when someone "improves" a prompt |
| **`answer_relevancy`** | Does the answer address the question asked — not whether it is *correct* | No | Track. A confidently wrong answer scores well here, which is exactly why it is not a gate |

> **Say it like this:** "`context_recall` and `faithfulness` are the two I gate on, and they gate different pull requests. A retrieval change has to hold `context_recall`, because that is the ceiling on everything downstream. A prompt or model change has to hold `faithfulness`, because that is where grounding regresses. `context_precision` I watch rather than gate — it is how I decide whether to send five chunks or fifteen. And `answer_relevancy` is the weakest of the four, because a fluent wrong answer scores well on it."

**Golden sets are the part that matters.** 100–300 real queries, human-labelled, versioned in git, owned by a named person. Stratified into head queries, long tail, multi-hop, aggregations, unanswerable, adversarial/injection, and one bucket per tenant shape.

> **Say it like this:** "Our eval set is a graveyard of every bug we have shipped. Every production incident becomes a permanent regression case, and that is the only asset in the system that compounds."

#### LLM-as-judge, and the four biases you must name unprompted

| Bias | What to say | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| Position | "Large and model-dependent — published measurements run well past a 2:1 preference for whichever answer is shown first on some benchmarks" | Run both orderings, average |
| Verbosity | "**15–30 points** of inflated preference for longer answers" | Length-normalise; rubric that penalises padding |
| Self-preference | "The original MT-Bench work measured roughly **+10 to +25 points** of self-preference depending on the judge" — quote the range, not a 2023 model by name | Judge from a different model family than the generator |
| Calibration drift | "Judge behaviour changes with judge model version" | **Pin the judge version. A judge upgrade is an eval migration.** |

⚠ Quote *ranges and mechanisms*, not per-model constants. The self-preference numbers are real but they are three years old, and naming a 2023-vintage model in a September 2026 interview signals stale reading. The mitigation has not changed and that is the part they are grading.

Calibration protocol: sample 100–300 production traces → two or three human annotators label them → compute inter-annotator agreement (Cohen's κ > 0.6 acceptable, > 0.8 strong) → score the same traces with the judge → compare judge↔human agreement on the same scale. **If the judge cannot beat your humans' agreement with each other, the judge is noise.** Prefer binary rubrics over 1–5 Likert, because models cluster at 3 and 4. Report the judge's own cost and latency as a line item — serious eval can be 10–30% of your LLM spend.

**Online proxies**, because offline evals do not tell you whether it worked:

- Acceptance rate is a vanity metric that rewards short, safe, obvious suggestions. The proxy that actually correlates with value is whether the accepted output **survives** — retained after N days, still in the file, still in the document.
- Better proxies: did the generated artefact survive N days; was the answer copied or shared; escalation-to-human rate; thumbs-down as a *triage queue*, not a metric.
- Guardrail metrics that must not regress even when the primary metric improves: p95 latency, refusal rate, cost per accepted output, and **permission-violation rate, which is alarmed rather than dashboarded because the only acceptable value is zero.**

#### A CI gate you can sketch in the pad

```yaml
# .github/workflows/rag-eval.yml   (shape, not a copy-paste)
on:
  pull_request:
    paths:                        # path filter belongs on the TRIGGER
      - 'retrieval/**'            # (pull_request.changed_files in the webhook
      - 'prompts/**'              #  payload is an integer count, not a path list,
      - 'evals/**'                #  so contains() on it never matches)

jobs:
  retrieval-gate:                 # no LLM, runs in ~90s, blocks the merge
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: retrieval metrics vs the production baseline
        run: |
          python -m evals.retrieval \
            --set golden/v7 \
            --baseline main \
            --max-regression 0.02 \
            --floor "recall@20>=0.85" \
            --floor "ndcg@10>=0.65"
      - name: permission filter must be exact
        run: |
          python -m evals.permissions \
            --tenants golden/tenants.yaml \
            --assert filter_precision==1.0

  generation-gate:                # judge pinned to an immutable dated model id
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    needs: retrieval-gate
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: judged generation eval
        run: |
          python -m evals.generation \
            --judge "<pinned-dated-model-id>" \
            --both-orderings \
            --baseline main \
            --max-regression 0.02 \
            --report-cost
```

Two design decisions in that file are worth defending out loud, because an interviewer who reads config will notice them.

**First, relative-to-baseline is primary and the absolute floor is a backstop, not the other way round.** An absolute assert like `recall@20 >= 0.92` breaks the moment the golden set grows or gets harder — the honest response to a harder eval set is a lower absolute number, and a gate that punishes you for improving your test suite gets disabled within a month. So the gate that blocks is "no more than ~2% below the recorded production baseline", and the floor sits well underneath as a catastrophe stop. Two different jobs: one catches regressions, one catches disasters.

**Second, the path filter is on the trigger.** `pull_request.changed_files` in the webhook payload is an integer count of files, not a list of paths, so `contains()` on it silently never matches and the job never runs — a gate that never fires is worse than no gate, because you believe you have one. If you need per-job path granularity, that is `dorny/paths-filter` or separate workflow files.

> **Say it like this:** "The gate blocks on a regression relative to the baseline, not on an absolute number, because an absolute number punishes you for making the eval set harder — and I want people adding their incidents to the golden set, not avoiding it. The absolute floor stays as a backstop. And I report cost alongside quality: a change that improves quality three percent and doubles cost is a rejection, not a win."

### 8.3 Permission-aware and multi-tenant retrieval

This is the section to win the interview on. What is verifiable about Smartsheet is that they ship an MCP server that lets agents query live project data and take action on it. Do not attribute a trust posture to them from memory — **ask**, which is a stronger platform-owner move anyway.

> **Say it like this:** "You ship an MCP server that exposes live sheet data to agents, so I assume the hard constraint is that retrieval runs inside the customer's existing sharing model rather than beside it. Is that how it is scoped today — the agent resolves as the calling user, with the same Owner-through-Viewer grants and any Dynamic View row scoping applied *before* retrieval rather than after? Because that one answer decides most of the architecture I would draw."

#### The failure everyone in the room already fears

A user asks "summarise Q3 headcount plans." Retrieval pulls a chunk from a document in a folder someone shared with "everyone except external users" three years ago. The model summarises it. That summary now lives in the user's chat history, the trace store, possibly the eval dataset, and possibly the semantic cache.

Three properties make this worse than classic search leakage: the summary is a **new artefact with no ACL of its own**; it is **undetectable by the user**, who does not know they were not supposed to see it; and it is **amplified** — search made you find one document, RAG reads ten and extracts the sensitive line into a sentence.

Microsoft's framing is the honest one and worth borrowing: Copilot grounds answers in content the user already has access to and adds no access. **AI does not create oversharing; it makes existing oversharing legible at scale.** Every large tenant that has published anything about Copilot readiness finds the same long tail of sites and folders shared with "everyone" that nobody remembers creating. ⚠ Do not attach a number to that unless you can name the source it came from.

> **Say it like this:** "My first question on any permission-aware RAG project is not 'how do we filter?' It is 'what does the permission graph actually look like today?' Because in most tenants, the AI's real first job is to prove the ACLs were already wrong. I would ship a sharing assessment before I ship workspace-wide AI search."

#### Pre-filter vs post-filter — the highest-signal technical point here

Four options, and the distinction between the last two is the one people get wrong.

| Approach | What happens | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| **Post-filter** | ANN returns top-k, then you drop what the caller may not see | Two failures: the pipeline already touched forbidden data, and recall collapses silently |
| **Pre-filter, brute force** | Filter first, exact-search the survivors | Correct; degrades to a full scan when the predicate is unselective |
| **Filter-aware index** | The predicate is respected **during** graph traversal | The right answer at scale. Qdrant filterable HNSW builds per-tenant subgraphs; Elasticsearch/OpenSearch filtered kNN |
| **Iterative over-fetch** | The filter is still applied **after** the index scan; the planner just keeps pulling more candidates until `LIMIT` is satisfied | pgvector 0.8 `iterative_scan`. Correct results, unbounded cost unless you bound it. **Not** a filter-aware graph |

Be precise about that last distinction, because it is the one an expert will correct you on. pgvector's own README states it flatly: *with approximate indexes, filtering is applied after the index is scanned.* Iterative scan does not teach HNSW about your predicate — it re-scans more of the index and re-applies the filter until enough rows survive. It is repeated over-fetch. Qdrant's filterable HNSW, with `payload_m` building per-tenant subgraphs, genuinely is filter-aware. Same outcome, completely different cost model, and conflating them makes the rest of your permission argument sound memorised.

**The number to quote.** pgvector's default is `hnsw.ef_search = 40`. A predicate matching 10% of rows on a top-10 query therefore returns roughly **4 rows on average, silently**. pgvector 0.8.0 introduced iterative index scans to fix it — `strict_order` for exact distance ordering, `relaxed_order` for lower latency and better recall at the cost of slightly out-of-order results — and **they are off by default**. Bound them with `hnsw.max_scan_tuples` (default 20,000) or an unselective filter turns into an unbounded scan.

```sql
-- pre-filter, bounded, with the model assertion and the under-return alarm.
-- SET LOCAL only takes effect inside an explicit transaction block; outside one
-- Postgres warns and IGNORES it, so you would silently run at ef_search=40 with
-- iterative scans off -- i.e. exactly the bug this query exists to avoid.
BEGIN;

SET LOCAL hnsw.ef_search       = 200;           -- default 40
SET LOCAL hnsw.iterative_scan  = strict_order;  -- default: off
SET LOCAL hnsw.max_scan_tuples = 40000;         -- default 20000; bound the over-fetch

SELECT c.doc_id, c.chunk_id, c.body,
       c.embedding <=> :qvec AS dist
FROM chunks c
WHERE c.tenant_id       = :tenant_from_token      -- from the JWT, never the request body
  AND c.embedding_model = :query_embedding_model  -- fail loud on a model mismatch
  AND c.allowed_principals && :caller_principals  -- array overlap = pre-filter
  AND c.deleted_at IS NULL
ORDER BY dist
LIMIT 20;

COMMIT;
-- caller asserts: len(rows) == 20, else emit under_return{tenant} and log
```

#### The isolation design space

| Model | Isolation | Query cost | Ops burden | Fits |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Index per tenant** | Strongest, physical | Poor at high tenant count | High — N indexes to build, migrate, monitor | Gov, BYOK, residency, under ~1k tenants |
| **Namespace / partition per tenant** | Strong logical, often separate physical storage | **Best — you scan only that tenant's slice** | Medium | **The SaaS default** |
| **Shared index + metadata filter** | Weakest; one bad filter is a breach | Worst — you pay to consider everything | Lowest | Small tenants, internal tools, long tail |
| **Tiered hybrid** | Big tenants get dedicated shards, long tail shares | Best overall | Highest design cost, worth it | The mature answer |

The number that ends the argument: on Pinecone serverless, read cost is metered at roughly **1 RU per GB of namespace scanned**, and `top_k` does not change it. With 100 tenants at 1 GB each, querying one tenant's namespace costs **1 RU**; the same query as a metadata filter over a single 100 GB namespace costs **100 RU**, because a filter does not stop the scan being billed. **Namespaces are not only a security choice, they are a 100× cost choice.**

Vendor specifics worth naming because they signal hands-on:

- **Qdrant** wants a payload index on the tenant field with `is_tenant: true`, `hnsw_config.payload_m = 16` and `hnsw_config.m = 0` — `m = 0` disables the global graph so Qdrant builds per-tenant subgraphs. Create that payload index **before ingest**; adding it later forces a reindex, which on a large collection is the same multi-hour job blue/green exists to avoid.
- **Weaviate** has native per-tenant shards plus offloading of inactive tenants to cold storage, which is the answer to "200k tenants, 2k active this week".
- **Milvus** gives you database → collection → partition-key.

#### ACL denormalisation and the staleness you must publish

The standard pattern is to denormalise effective readers onto each chunk as `allowed_principals: [user:123, group:eng, group:pm-leads]` and pre-filter on set overlap. Three real implementations to name:

- **Azure AI Search** query-time ACL/RBAC enforcement — the caller's Entra token goes in an `x-ms-query-source-authorization` header and the service trims results against permission metadata already in the index. ⚠ This is **preview** (2026-08-01-preview REST API), not GA — say so, because claiming GA on a preview feature is a checkable error. Documented hard limits: at most **1000 values** in a `userIds`/`groupIds` permission-filter field, and at most **5 unique `rbacScope` values** per index. Microsoft gives no rationale for those caps, but they tell you index-time expansion of a deeply nested directory is not what the design assumes.
- **Google Vertex AI Search** `acl_info` with `user_id`/`group_id`/`external_entity_id` matched through Workforce Identity Federation.
- **Glean**, whose connectors run a separate permissions crawl into the enterprise graph kept current by delta sync.

Microsoft's own documentation makes the key point for you, and it is the point that separates seniority: permission changes in the source system are reflected in search results *only after that metadata is synchronised to the index*. The projection is a cache.

> **Say it like this:** "A denormalised ACL is a cache of the source system's authorisation state, and like every cache it is wrong for a window. Azure's docs say this outright about their own feature — enforcement runs against the permission metadata that the sync already wrote. So I treat it as an eventually-consistent projection with a published revocation SLA, separate from and much tighter than the content freshness SLA. Permission events go on a priority lane ahead of content events. And because a projection can be wrong, I keep a second authoritative check: after retrieval, before generation, re-verify the top-N document IDs against the source of truth. It is N cheap ID checks, not a re-crawl, and it converts a silent leak into a caught one."

Two published numbers let you put a figure on the lag rather than hand-waving. AWS's API Gateway Lambda authorizer result cache **defaults to a 300-second TTL**, which means revoked access can continue to permit for up to five minutes unless you set it to zero and pay latency on every request — that one is a documented AWS default and safe to quote. There is also a published AWS multi-tenant RAG reference architecture with a **30-second batching window** between document upload and metadata sidecar creation, mitigated by excluding documents that have no sidecar yet — fail closed. ⚠ Before Friday, open that architecture, confirm the number and note its exact title. If you have not, say "a published AWS reference architecture" and do not name it, and do not conflate it with Verified Permissions, which is a different artefact.

#### Group expansion

Groups nest — `alice ∈ eng-india ∈ eng ∈ all-staff` — so you need the transitive closure per user, with cycle detection. Expand at **index time** and every group-membership change fans out to millions of rows. Expand at **query time** and the filter clause gets huge for a user in hundreds of groups. The pragmatic answer: expand at query time, cache the caller's expanded principal set with a 30–120 second TTL keyed on a membership version, and invalidate on membership-change events.

Explicit **deny** rules break the model entirely — a `principal ∈ list` filter cannot express deny-overrides-allow — so either normalise denies away at projection time or keep them in the authoritative post-check. This is the failure mode to raise unprompted in a product with sharing exceptions.

#### Row-level is the hard case

Document-level is easy: one ACL, one filter. Row-level is the case a work-management product actually has, and it dictates chunking. A user may see 40 of 5,000 rows via row-level sharing, an ownership column, a Dynamic View filter, or a report joining sheets. **If you embed the whole sheet as one chunk, there is no filter that can make that chunk safe.** Chunk granularity must be less than or equal to permission granularity.

Aggregations are the trap. "What is the total budget across my projects?" must aggregate **only over rows the caller can see**, which means the aggregate is computed after the filter, in the data layer — not summarised by the model from a pre-computed total. This is the strongest argument for routing analytical questions to SQL rather than to vector retrieval.

#### Everything downstream of retrieval is a covert copy

| Surface | Control |
|---|---|
| Semantic / prompt cache | **Cache key = tenant_id + hash of the caller's effective principal set (or an entitlements version).** Never key on query text alone |
| Conversation history | Store citations, not content; re-check grounding docs on continuation |
| Trace / observability store | Store doc IDs and hashes, redact or tokenise chunk bodies, scope trace access per tenant |
| Eval / golden datasets | Explicit consent, de-identification, tenant allow-list — otherwise customer data is now in a git repo |
| Fine-tuning corpora | Don't. If you must, per-tenant adapters only. It is permanent and unremovable |
| Downstream exports (digest, Slack summary) | Re-authorise at send time against the **recipient**, not the requester |

Invalidation design: event-driven on any change to document, permission, group membership, policy, prompt version, model version or tool version; a bounded max-age for volatile facts because you will miss events; and **versioned namespaces — bump a `cache_epoch` per tenant** so a bad deploy or a bulk permission change moves everyone to a clean logical cache instead of surgically deleting keys.

#### The cross-tenant probe test

This is the artefact you show a customer's security team. Describe it as a nightly CI job, not a one-off pen test.

```python
# tests/isolation/test_cross_tenant.py — runs nightly, fails the build
import pytest

ATTACK_PATHS = [
    "direct_filter_tamper",     # pass tenant_id in the request body
    "jwt_claim_absent",         # omit the tenant claim entirely -> must DENY, not search-all
    "cache_key_collision",      # identical query text, two tenants, one cached answer
    "group_expansion_abuse",    # membership in a group that transitively spans tenants
    "revoked_then_queried",     # revoke, then query inside the published revocation SLA
    "prompt_injection_exfil",   # doc in tenant A instructs the agent to fetch tenant B
    "citation_leak",            # answer withheld but a citation reveals a forbidden doc id
    "trace_store_read",         # tenant A's principal reading tenant B's trace rows
    "deny_rule_ignored",        # explicit deny that the allow-list projection cannot express
]


@pytest.mark.parametrize("path", ATTACK_PATHS)
def test_tenant_b_is_unreachable_from_tenant_a(path):
    result = probe(as_tenant="A", target_tenant="B", path=path)
    assert result.documents == [], f"{path}: leaked {result.documents}"
    assert result.failure_mode in ("denied", "empty"), "must fail closed"
```

Two positions to hold and say clearly: **tenant_id is derived from the authenticated token, never from a request parameter** — that is the number-one real-world bug — and **fail closed on authorisation, degrade gracefully on enrichment**. If the authorisation service is down, deny. If the reranker is down, return fusion order.

> **Say it like this — "tell me how you would build RAG over customer data with permissions":**
>
> "Five things, in this order.
>
> **One, before I build anything, I audit the permission graph.** RAG does not create oversharing, it makes it legible, so I want to know how many documents are effectively world-readable inside the tenant before I let a model read them. That is usually the first finding and it is a product proposal, not an infra one.
>
> **Two, permissions are mirrored, never reimplemented.** I ingest the source's ACLs through the same authorisation libraries the product already uses — Slack made exactly that choice and said so publicly, and it is the right one, because a second implementation of your permission model drifts within a quarter. What lands in the index is a denormalised `allowed_principals` list plus `tenant_id`.
>
> **Three, pre-filter, always.** Post-filtering means the model already read it, and it silently under-returns: on pgvector with default `ef_search` of 40 and a ten-percent-selective predicate, a top-10 query gives you about four rows and does not error. So: namespace or partition per tenant as the boundary, a filter-aware index where the engine supports one, iterative scans turned on and bounded where it does not, and an alarm on `returned < requested`, because that condition should never be invisible.
>
> **Four, the projection is a cache, so I publish a revocation SLA separate from the freshness SLA, and I add an authoritative second check.** After retrieval, before generation, I re-verify the top-N document IDs against the system of record. That is N cheap ID checks and it turns a silent leak into a caught one. Group expansion happens at query time against the caller, cached for thirty to a hundred and twenty seconds keyed on a membership version.
>
> **Five, I assume the derived artefacts leak.** Cache keys include the caller's effective principal set, not just the query text. Traces store document IDs and hashes rather than chunk bodies. Eval datasets are opt-in and de-identified. Exports re-authorise against the recipient at send time. And a nightly cross-tenant probe test tries every path I know of to reach tenant B as tenant A — filter tampering, cache collision, injected instructions in a shared document — and fails the build if any of them returns a row.
>
> The one I would flag unprompted for a product like yours is **row-level permissions**. A sheet is not a document. If a user can see forty of five thousand rows, and I embed the sheet as one chunk, there is no filter that makes that chunk safe. Chunk boundaries have to be at or below permission granularity, and any aggregate has to be computed after the filter in the data layer, not summarised by the model from a total it was handed.
>
> Where I have actually done this: at ResMed the RAG pipeline was over HIPAA-class clinical data with hybrid vector-plus-metadata retrieval, evaluation harnesses and human review in the loop. That was document-level permissioning over clinical data, not multi-tenant row-level retrieval, so the cross-tenant and row-level parts are design experience plus what I have read, not something I have shipped at your tenant count. I would want the first month to be measurement before I touched the retrieval stack."

⚠ **That last paragraph is the honesty gate. Say it. It costs you nothing and it is exactly the calibration a platform interviewer is grading.** Note what it does *not* claim: it does not describe ResMed's deployment topology, because that is not something the brief establishes and an interviewer's follow-up ("so each customer got their own stack?") would catch you inventing an architectural fact inside the sentence meant to prove you do not invent things. Say what you know — document-level, clinical, HIPAA-class — and stop.

### 8.4 Vector stores on operational criteria

| System | Filtered search | Deletes | Multi-tenancy | Ops burden | Real talk |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **pgvector 0.8+** | HNSW + opt-in iterative over-fetch (filter still applied after the scan) | Transactional — DELETE is a delete | `tenant_id` + partial/partitioned indexes; **Postgres RLS gives DB-level enforcement** | Lowest if you already run Postgres | **The right default for most teams.** One system, one backup, one transaction, joins to your real data. Index build is CPU-heavy; raise `maintenance_work_mem` and `max_parallel_maintenance_workers` |
| **Elasticsearch / OpenSearch** | Mature filtered kNN; BBQ quantisation with oversample+rescore | Tombstones until segment merge — **deleted vectors still hold memory** | Index-per-tenant, alias routing, native document-level security | Medium-high | Pick it if you already run it or need serious BM25 + vectors + aggregations in one query |
| **Pinecone serverless** | Metadata filter + namespaces | Live | **Namespace-per-tenant is the canonical pattern** | Lowest managed | Understand the RU model — read cost tracks namespace GB scanned, and `top_k` does not change it |
| **Qdrant** | Best-in-class filter-aware HNSW; per-tenant subgraphs via `payload_m` with `m = 0` | Real | **Best-designed multi-tenancy of the OSS set**; tiered in 1.16 | Medium self-host | Name it if the interviewer cares about multi-tenant filtered search |
| **Weaviate** | Good built-in hybrid | Fine | Native tenants, per-tenant shards, **offload idle tenants to cold storage** | Medium | Best fit for many mostly-idle tenants |
| **Milvus / Zilliz** | Strong, many index types | With compaction | database → collection → partition-key | Highest self-hosted | The answer at genuine billions |
| **FAISS** | You implement it | **No update. `remove_ids()` exists on flat / IVF / IDMap indexes but not on HNSW, needs a pass over the database, and does not reclaim graph structure** — deletion in practice means rebuild | You build it | You are the database | Great offline and as an engine inside something else. Choosing it as your production store means you signed up to write a database |
| **Redis / Vector Sets** | Yes | Instant | Per index/db | Low | The hot cache tier, not the system of record |

Cross-cutting truths to state:

- **Recall is a tuning parameter you must measure, not a property you get.** `ef_construction`/`M` at build, `ef_search` at query. Producing a recall-vs-latency curve against exact-kNN ground truth on 1,000 sampled queries is a thirty-minute job and almost nobody does it — and per §8.1 it is also your rebuild trigger.
- **Index build is the operational cliff.** HNSW build is O(n log n) with a large constant. At 50M+ vectors "just rebuild it" is a multi-hour job that must run off the serving path — which is exactly why blue/green exists.
- **Deletes are usually soft.** Tombstones inflate memory and degrade recall until compaction. In a permission-aware system this is a *security* concern: "deleted" and "unreachable" are not the same thing until the merge runs.
- **DR:** if restoring a 100M-vector index means re-embedding everything, your RTO is days. Snapshot the index and keep the source text.

**When a vector DB is the wrong answer** — have this list ready, it is a maturity signal:

1. Under ~100k chunks. Postgres, or a brute-force numpy scan behind an in-process cache, is faster to build and operate.
2. The query is a lookup, not a similarity. "Show me task #4821" is SQL. Semantic search over structured data is a category error.
3. The query is an aggregation or a constraint. **Vectors cannot count.**
4. The query is multi-hop or relational — that is a graph.
5. The corpus is small, stable and jargon-heavy. BM25 alone often beats naive dense retrieval at 1% of the cost. **Always run BM25 as the baseline in your eval; if it wins you just saved the company a vector database.**
6. Permissions are row-level and change faster than you can re-project them. Query the system of record and use retrieval only for ranking.
7. You need exact, auditable answers. Retrieval plus a model gives a plausible answer; a query gives the answer.

> **Say it like this:** "The most valuable thing I have done on RAG projects is delete the vector database from about a third of the use cases and replace it with a well-typed query."

In a DOMAIN round you will be asked about at least two of them, and a written honesty commitment that breaks under live questioning is far worse than never having made it.

So do not improvise. Use one template, five times.

> **Say it like this (the template):** "No — I have not run <tool> in production. What I have built is <the primitive it wraps>, which means I know what it is doing for me and, more usefully, what it is *not* doing for me: <one specific thing it does not solve>. How much of your stack is on it today?"

Three properties make this work: the "no" comes first and unhedged; the mapping proves you understand the tool rather than the marketing; and the closing question turns a gap into a scoping conversation. **Get these out in the 40–50 minute window, not in the last two minutes**, so they land as calibration rather than as a late confession.
