### 8.6 Retrieval and embedding drift in production

The JD asks in terms for "post-deployment monitoring for model performance, data drift, and latency." For a RAG system, **drift is three different failures wearing one word**, they have different lead times, and only one of them is visible in a classic feature-drift dashboard.

| Kind | What moved | Lead time | Cheapest detector |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Query drift** | Users started asking things the corpus does not cover — a new product, an incident, a season | Days | Nearest-centroid distance of the query embedding against a frozen baseline of corpus clusters; share of queries beyond the p95 baseline distance |
| **Corpus drift** | The content changed underneath the index — bulk import, migration, a big deletion, a re-chunk | Hours | Chunk-count delta per source per day; reconciliation diff size; distribution of `updated_at` |
| **Representation drift** | The embedding or reranker changed, or the *provider* changed it under a floating alias | Instant, and silent | `query_model == index_model` assertion; pinned dated model IDs; embedding-checksum of a fixed probe set |

Representation drift is the one that maps directly to your TrueBalance story. The provider silently updating a model behind an alias is the same shape as the imputer silently filling 3,973 missing features: the contract was implicit, so the violation was invisible.

#### The monitors, and what each one actually tells you

You cannot compute recall@k in production, because production has no labels. So you run cheap proxies continuously and a labelled sample weekly.

| Signal | How to compute it | What it means when it moves |
|---|---|---|
| **`no_good_chunk_rate`** | Fraction of queries where top-1 reranker score is below the answerable threshold | **The best single leading indicator.** Rises before user complaints do. Up = corpus gap or query drift, not a model problem |
| **Retrieval score distribution** | p10 / p50 / p90 of top-1 and top-5 fused score, daily, per tenant | A shifted p50 with stable volume usually means the corpus changed. A shifted tail means a new query population arrived |
| **`returned < requested` rate** | Per query: rows returned vs `LIMIT` | Filter or ANN exhaustion. Should be near zero. Any sustained non-zero is a silent recall bug |
| **Abstention / refusal rate** | Share of answers that decline | Stable is healthy. A jump means corpus, prompt or model changed. A *fall* is more worrying — that is a confident hallucinator |
| **`citation_validation_failure_rate`** | Emitted markers that fail post-validation | Prompt or model regression, usually within hours of a deploy |
| **Distinct-doc count in packed context** | Count after dedup | Falling = near-duplicate corpus growth eating the window |
| **Query OOV rate** | Share of query embeddings beyond the baseline p95 distance to any corpus centroid | Users asking about things you do not have. This is a **product** signal, route it to product |
| **Index freshness p95** | source-change → retrievable | Your published SLA. Breach = incident |
| **Permission-violation count** | From the nightly probe test and from the authoritative re-check disagreeing with the projection | Only acceptable value is zero |

#### What pages and what does not

This distinction is the platform-owner tell. Alert fatigue kills monitoring faster than missing monitors do.

| Pages on-call | Dashboard only, reviewed weekly |
|---|---|
| Permission-violation count > 0 | Retrieval score distribution shift |
| `query_model == index_model` assertion firing | `no_good_chunk_rate` trending up |
| `returned < requested` rate above a floor | Query OOV rate |
| Freshness or revocation SLA breach | Cost per query, cache hit rate |
| Gateway error rate / provider outage | Distinct-doc count in context |
| p99 latency past the SLO | Weekly labelled-sample recall@k |

> **Say it like this:** "Three of those page and the rest do not, and the split is deliberate. What pages is a broken invariant — a permission violation, a model mismatch, an under-return, an SLA breach. What does not page is anything shaped like a trend, because a trend at 3am is not actionable and a pager that fires on trends gets muted within a fortnight. The trends go to a weekly review with a named owner, and that review is where the rebuild trigger and the golden-set refresh get decided."

The weekly labelled sample is the piece people skip: fifty to a hundred real queries a week, human-labelled for whether the retrieved context contained the answer, appended to the golden set. It is a couple of hours of someone's time and it is the only thing that keeps the offline eval connected to what production actually looks like.

> **Say it like this:** "I have built the plumbing for this before. At ResMed I wrote a drift-monitoring utility that took thresholds and slice definitions authored by the data scientists and auto-provisioned Datadog dashboards and alerts off Snowflake feature statistics — the design principle being that the person who understands the slice owns the threshold, and the platform owns the provisioning. I would do exactly the same for retrieval: the retrieval owner declares the metric and the threshold in a config file, and the platform turns that into a dashboard, an alert and a routing rule."

### 8.7 Serving economics — GPU, CPU, latency and where the bill actually lands

The JD line is "Manage GPU/CPU utilization to minimize cloud costs while maintaining low-latency inference." You have a real story here, so lead with it.

> **Say it like this:** "The cost work I am proudest of is packing. On ResMed's internal MLOps platform I ran **multi-container SageMaker endpoints that shared infrastructure across several models while holding per-model SLAs** — the alternative was one endpoint per model, each sitting at low utilisation. That is the whole game in inference cost: you are paying for provisioned capacity, not for tokens, so the question is always how many workloads you can put on one machine before the SLA breaks. At the other end of the range, the propensity scorer at TrueBalance is an ARM64 image on Lambda behind SQS, where you pay per invocation and the design problem is cold start rather than utilisation."

#### Where the money is in one RAG request

Do this arithmetic **live, in the pad, with their numbers**. Bringing a memorised price is a mistake; bringing the decomposition is the point.

```text
one RAG request
  ├─ embed the query          ~1 call,  tens of tokens        → negligible
  ├─ vector search            CPU-seconds or metered RUs      → small, but scales
  │                             with namespace GB scanned
  ├─ rerank 50 candidates     50 cross-encoder pairs          → the latency spike
  │                             (linear in candidates AND
  │                              in chunk length past ~2k tok)
  ├─ generation INPUT         8 chunks x ~400 tok = ~3.2k     → the volume
  │   + system prompt + history                                  (cacheable!)
  └─ generation OUTPUT        ~200-500 tok                    → priced highest
                                                                 per token
```

Two consequences fall straight out of that shape:

1. **Input tokens are the volume; output tokens are the unit price.** Retrieved context is roughly an order of magnitude more tokens than the answer, but output is priced several times higher per token, so the two are usually comparable in dollars. That means *both* levers matter: cutting from twelve chunks to six is a real saving, and so is not asking for a verbose answer.
2. **The system prompt, the tool schemas and the few-shot examples are identical on every request.** Prompt caching on that prefix is the single highest-leverage cost change in most RAG stacks and it requires no quality trade-off at all. Do it before you touch the model.

#### The cache is the dominant lever, and it is an ACL problem

If 40% of queries repeat within the TTL, you have removed 40% of retrieval *and* 40% of generation cost. No model swap gets you that. But per §8.3, the cache key must be `tenant_id + hash(caller's effective principal set) + query`, never query text alone — which mechanically lowers your hit rate, because two users with different group memberships cannot share an entry.

> **Say it like this:** "The uncomfortable bit is that the correct cache key is the expensive one. Keying on query text alone gives you a great hit rate and a cross-tenant leak. So I would key on tenant plus the caller's effective principal set, accept the lower hit rate, and recover some of it by caching the *retrieval* layer separately from the generation layer — the embedding of a query is safe to cache globally, the retrieved document set is not."

#### GPU or CPU, and when to self-host

| Component | Default | When it flips |
|---|---|---|
| **Embedding, batch/backfill** | GPU, large batches | Almost never flips. Backfill is throughput-bound and batching is what GPUs are for. Size the batch to saturate memory, not to a round number |
| **Embedding, single query at serve time** | CPU or a hosted API | One query is a batch of one; a GPU is idle between requests. Only self-host on GPU if you can batch across concurrent requests with a queue |
| **Reranking, interactive** | Hosted API to start | Flips to self-hosted GPU once volume clears the break-even below |
| **Generation** | API | Flips only at very high sustained volume with a small model and tolerance for running an inference server |

The break-even for a self-hosted reranker is one line of arithmetic, and presenting the *formula* rather than a number is the stronger move:

```text
monthly GPU cost      = instance $/hr x 730 x (instances needed for peak QPS)
monthly API cost      = (queries/month / 1000) x $ per 1k rerank calls
break-even queries/mo = (instance $/hr x 730 x instances) / ($ per 1k / 1000)

# and the three costs the formula hides:
#   - you must provision for PEAK, the API bills you for MEAN
#   - an idle GPU at 3am costs the same as a busy one
#   - someone now owns model updates, drivers, and the on-call
```

> **Say it like this:** "I would not quote you a break-even number without your QPS curve, because the answer is dominated by peak-to-mean ratio rather than by the price per call. If traffic is spiky, the API wins far past where the raw arithmetic says it should, because you provision for peak and get billed for mean. If traffic is flat and high, self-hosting wins early. The first thing I would ask for is the QPS histogram, not the invoice."

#### Latency budget and the serverless trade

Write the budget down, per stage, and defend it as a budget rather than as a total:

| Stage | Typical share of a 2-second p95 | Where it goes wrong |
|---|---|---|
| Query embed | 20–50 ms | An API call with no timeout |
| Vector + lexical search | 20–100 ms | `ef_search` raised to hide index degradation |
| Rerank | 80–200 ms | Chunk length, not candidate count, past ~2k tokens |
| Authoritative re-check | 10–40 ms | N ID lookups; batch them, do not loop |
| Generation | Everything else | Output length; streaming hides it from the user but not from the bill |

On serverless: cold start is a **p99 problem, not a p50 problem**, and it is where a large container image hurts most — which is why the TrueBalance scorer is a lean ARM64 image rather than a general-purpose one. Provisioned concurrency converts a latency problem into a fixed cost; it is the right trade for a user-facing path and the wrong trade for a batch scorer behind a queue. Say which one you are optimising before you pick.

> **Say it like this:** "Every cost conversation I have been in went wrong the same way — someone optimised the model when the bill was in utilisation. Fifteen percent GPU utilisation with a huge invoice is not a model problem, it is a packing problem, and the fix is multiplexing workloads onto shared endpoints or moving the bursty ones to serverless. I have done the multiplexing version, on SageMaker, holding per-model SLAs while sharing infrastructure. That is the first place I would look."

### 8.8 Knowledge graphs and GraphRAG

You have a real KG story, so lead with it and keep the numbers exact: seven entity types, 29 predicates, 85+ canonical field mappings, replacing a brittle regex SMS parser, 100% field coverage on 100K production SMS — 169,879 of 169,879 fields — 107 passing tests, migrated into a standalone CI-guarded ML repo.

> **Say it like this:** "The graph I built was not extracted from prose by an LLM. It was an ontology over semi-structured financial SMS, with deterministic canonical field mappings and a test suite. That distinction is the whole ballgame: LLM-extracted graphs with no entity resolution give you forty spellings of the same lender and a graph that is confidently wrong. Noisy graph plus valid Cypher equals a wrong answer with no error."

**Why the JD pairs vector DBs and knowledge graphs:** embeddings encode similarity, graphs encode structure, and enterprise questions need both. In a work-management product most of the graph already exists as foreign keys — **workspace → folder → sheet → row (a forest, via `parentId`) → cell**, plus typed columns, cross-sheet references, cell links, predecessors and dependencies, and share grants. You do not have to extract it. Use their nouns; "task" and "project" are conventions expressed as rows and columns, not first-class objects, and "portfolio" belongs to Control Center rather than the core object model. Getting that right in their vocabulary is worth more than any GraphRAG detail below.

**GraphRAG cost, honestly.** Microsoft GraphRAG does LLM entity/relation extraction per chunk, Leiden community detection, then LLM-written hierarchical community summaries; global queries map-reduce over the summaries. It is genuinely the only thing that answers "what are the main themes across this corpus", because no chunk contains a theme.

> **Say it like this:** "Full GraphRAG indexing is dominated by one LLM extraction call per chunk plus the community summarisation pass, so cost scales with corpus tokens — six figures is reachable on a real enterprise corpus. The numbers I would actually quote are Microsoft's own on **LazyGraphRAG**: indexing cost about **0.1% of full GraphRAG**, effectively the same as vector RAG, with comparable answer quality to Global Search at **over 700× lower query cost**, because it defers all summarisation to query time. LightRAG and KET-RAG are the other pragmatic cost-cut variants, and they have incremental update built in. My first question is what fraction of real questions are global sense-making questions. If it is under five percent, we are paying an enormous indexing bill to serve five percent of traffic, and LazyGraphRAG or a plain router serves them at vector-RAG cost."

**Where a KG genuinely wins:** multi-hop composition ("which projects are blocked by a task owned by someone who left"); aggregation and counting; constraints and negation ("vendors without a signed DPA"); provenance, because the traversal path *is* the citation; temporal reasoning over bitemporal edges; permissions modelled as an explicit access graph; and sparse entities mentioned twice in a corpus, which are invisible to embeddings and perfectly visible in a graph.

**Where it is theatre:** single-hop lookups over prose, where a reranker costs 1%; LLM-extracted graphs with no entity resolution; and any graph with no ontology owner, which after six months has 300 relationship types, half unused, that nobody can change safely.

**Text-to-Cypher, and why you should not ship it free-form.** CypherBench reports GPT-4o at **60.18% execution accuracy**, with no open-weights model under 10B exceeding 20%. Failure taxonomy: schema hallucination (invented labels and relationship types); direction errors; **valid Cypher with the wrong answer, which is the dangerous class because nothing errors**; and cardinality explosions from unbounded variable-length paths.

Production guardrails: **parameterised query templates over free generation** — classify the question into one of about twenty known shapes and fill slots, which takes you from 60% to the mid-90s and gives you caching, cost predictability and auditability; read-only credentials, always; schema injection into the prompt with allowed labels enumerated; validate → EXPLAIN → cost gate → execute with a timeout → self-repair capped at two attempts; mandatory `LIMIT` and bounded hops `[*1..3]`. And the ACL point: a traversal can leak the *existence* of a node the caller cannot see even without its properties, so either filter nodes at traversal time against the caller's principal set or maintain per-tenant subgraphs.

For engine choice: property graph over RDF for a product feature, every time — RDF earns its keep only when multiple organisations must agree on identifiers. Neo4j is the default with the best tooling and a native vector index. Amazon Neptune is really two products and people get this wrong: **Neptune Database** is the OLTP graph, **Neptune Analytics** is the in-memory analytics engine with vector search. A currency check worth having ready, kept to the verified half: **Kuzu was archived on 10 October 2025 with v0.11.3 as the final release** — the maintainers moved on. *"I would not start a new production dependency on Kuzu today."* ⚠ Do not name a cause or the community forks; the repo states neither, and this is a detail you would be volunteering unprompted, which is the worst kind to get wrong.

Also note Dropbox's finding — they kept their knowledge graph but **demoted it from a query-time dependency to an offline enrichment step producing "knowledge bundles"** fed into the index, because graph queries at request time were too slow.

### 8.9 Agents in production

| Option | What it actually gives you | When it is right | The tax |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Raw provider SDK + your own loop** | Full control, nothing to debug through, trivial cost reasoning | **Most single-purpose agents. Start here.** | You write persistence, retries, observability, streaming |
| **LangGraph** | Explicit state graph, checkpointer, `interrupt()` for human-in-the-loop, subgraphs, streaming, replay | Multi-step branching workflows, approvals, resumable state | Concepts to learn; ecosystem churn |
| **LangChain 1.x** | Integrations, `create_agent`, standard message types | Glue and prototyping | Historically heavy abstraction; 1.0 is much leaner |
| **LlamaIndex** | Best-in-class ingestion and indexing, property-graph index | The data side of RAG | Agent layer less mature |
| **MCP** | **A protocol, not a framework** — one way to expose tools to any client | Tool *distribution* across teams; kills the N×M integration problem | Auth, versioning and supply-chain risk are yours |
| **Temporal (+ LangGraph plugin)** | Real durable execution: retries, timeouts, compensation, exactly-once | Long-running, money-touching, SLA-bound work | Another system to run |

> **Say it like this:** "LangGraph is a state machine with persistence and good ergonomics for interrupts. That is genuinely useful and it is the twenty percent of the framework I would use. Most of the reliability we needed came from things frameworks do not give you — budgets, idempotency and replayable traces — so I would rather own the loop and borrow the checkpointer."

#### LangGraph details that signal you have run it

1.0 went GA in October 2025. `StateGraph` with typed state and reducers — the reducer is where the subtle bugs live. The checkpointer goes `InMemorySaver` → `SqliteSaver` → **`PostgresSaver` in production**, and `checkpointer.setup()` belongs in a **CI/CD migration step, not application startup**, or every replica races to create tables on deploy. **Checkpoint tables grow without bound** and need a TTL job. Checkpoints contain full message state — customer data in your Postgres, subject to the same retention, residency and deletion obligations as everything else, which in a multi-tenant product means tenant-scoped rows and RLS. Durability modes trade write frequency against latency; pick `sync` anywhere a lost step means a duplicated side effect.

**How human-in-the-loop actually works**, since the word `interrupt` on its own is not an answer:

```python
# inside a node
def approve_spend(state):
    decision = interrupt({"amount": state["amount"], "vendor": state["vendor"]})
    return {"approved": decision["approved"]}

# 1. graph.invoke(...) suspends; the checkpointer persists state at the thread_id
# 2. the caller sees an __interrupt__ payload in the stream / result
# 3. a human decides, possibly hours later, possibly on another replica
# 4. resume by re-invoking the SAME thread_id with a Command:
graph.invoke(Command(resume={"approved": True}),
             config={"configurable": {"thread_id": tid}})
```

**The gotcha worth naming unprompted: on resume, the node re-runs from the top.** `interrupt()` is not a coroutine suspension point that preserves local execution — the node function is called again and everything before the `interrupt()` executes a second time. So put the interrupt as early in the node as possible, and make anything before it idempotent, or you will send the notification email twice. That single fact is the difference between having read the docs and having run it.

**Streaming modes**, because the table above names streaming and it is a fair follow-up: `values` emits the full state after each step, `updates` emits only the per-node delta (what you usually want for a UI), `messages` emits LLM tokens as they arrive for typewriter output, `custom` emits whatever you write from inside a node, and `debug` emits everything. Streaming `messages` for the user and `updates` for the progress indicator is the normal production pairing.

#### MCP as of the 2026-07-28 spec

This matters for your TrueBalance story and it is a genuine currency signal, so keep it precise.

**Multi Round-Trip Requests (MRTR) replaced server-initiated requests entirely.** Instead of a server pushing `roots/list`, `sampling/createMessage` or `elicitation/create` at the client, the server returns an `InputRequiredResult` — every result now carries a required `resultType`, either `"complete"` or `"input_required"` — whose `inputRequests` field carries what it needs, and the client retries the original request with `inputResponses`. The spec's stated motivation is **statelessness**, and that is the part to lead with: the same revision removed protocol-level sessions and the `Mcp-Session-Id` header, and removed the `initialize` handshake entirely, so every request now carries its own protocol version and client capabilities in `_meta`. That is what makes an MCP server horizontally scalable behind a load balancer with no sticky routing and no shared session store.

> **Say it like this:** "The July 2026 revision made MCP genuinely stateless — sessions gone, the initialize handshake gone, and server-initiated requests replaced by the multi-round-trip pattern where the server returns an `input_required` result and the client retries with the answers. The stated driver is statelessness, and that is the operationally important part: it means a server is just an HTTP handler and I can scale it like one. The side effect I happen to like is that a server can no longer spontaneously prompt a user out of band, but I would not claim the spec sells it as a security control — it does not."

Two more, both verified and both worth having: **client credentials are bound to the issuing authorization server** — clients MUST key persisted credentials by issuer identifier, MUST NOT reuse them across authorization servers, and MUST re-register when the authorization server changes. And **Roots, Sampling and Logging are now deprecated** under a new twelve-month deprecation policy, with Dynamic Client Registration deprecated in favour of Client ID Metadata Documents. If you built against Sampling, that is a migration on your roadmap.

#### Why agents fail in production

The eight, and you should be able to name the fix for each:

| Failure | Fix |
|---|---|
| Non-determinism breaks caching, testing, reproduction | Record the full trajectory so you can replay it offline |
| Retries re-execute non-idempotent tools | **Idempotency keys generated once per logical intent** |
| Cost blowups from unbounded retries against a tool that fails without signalling failure | Hard token/dollar caps per run, user, tenant and day, enforced at the gateway |
| Tools that fail silently (`{"results": []}` on error) | **Structured errors**: `{"error": {"code", "message", "retryable"}}`. Never empty success |
| Infinite or oscillating loops | No-progress detection: hash `(tool, args)`; three repeats breaks the loop |
| Context rot as history grows | Explicit summarisation/pruning policy with a token budget |
| Error propagation through five confident steps | Per-step validation, not just final-answer validation |
| Prompt/model drift when a provider updates a checkpoint | Pin dated model IDs; never point production at a floating alias |

> **Say it like this:** "The agent failures I would design against first are economic, not cognitive. An unbounded retry against a tool that fails without signalling failure will make hundreds of identical calls before a human notices, and the bill is the first symptom — not a wrong answer, an invoice. Which is exactly why the caps go at the gateway rather than in the agent loop: a cap the agent enforces is a cap the agent can be talked out of."

**The controls checklist**, which is the answer to almost any "how do you make it reliable" question: `max_steps` per run and `max_tool_calls` per tool; `max_retries` with exponential backoff and jitter; hard cost cap at four scopes; wall-clock timeout per tool and per run; a repeated-failure rule that terminates rather than retries; and when the budget is exhausted, **fall back or escalate to a human, never silently return a partial answer**. Tools get least privilege, read/write separation, versioned schemas treated as an API contract, and a dry-run mode used in evals. Observability is OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions with token counts and cost as span attributes, plus replayable traces capturing prompt version, model version, tool versions and retrieved doc IDs at every step.

**Agent evaluation, three levels, all of them needed:** final task success (what the business cares about, least diagnostic); trajectory, either matched against a reference in-order/any-order/superset or judged by an LLM with all the biases from §8.2; and single-step tool-call accuracy **decomposed into tool selection, schema validity, argument correctness and side-effect correctness**, because the fixes differ. Plus the operational metrics people forget: step count versus the minimum, loop rate, recovery rate after a tool error, cost per successful task, p95 wall-clock, and human-escalation rate.

> **Say it like this — "you built an MCP assistant; how would you make that production-grade for 500 engineers?":**
>
> "What I built at TrueBalance was an internal Claude developer assistant on MCP — I wrote the first Slack integration, a Google Docs skill with 34 passing tests, and a PR skill that writes titles and descriptions from the diff. It ties Jira, GitHub, Jenkins, AWS Athena and EC2, Grafana and Slack into one plain-English interface, and every task runs in an isolated git workspace. That last bit is the only reason it was safe to let a team use it. It is team-scale, not 500-engineer scale, so let me be explicit about what changes.
>
> **First, the tool surface becomes a governed registry, not a folder.** Today a tool is code someone wrote. At 500 engineers it needs versioned schemas with deprecation windows, an owner per tool, and — this is the one people miss — **tool descriptions reviewed as code, because a tool description is untrusted text that goes into the model's context.** Tool poisoning and rug-pulls are a real supply-chain class. Pin server versions. Scope OAuth per server, and under the July 2026 MCP spec, key persisted credentials by issuing authorization server.
>
> **Second, permissions become per-user, not per-service.** Right now the assistant acts with a service identity. At scale every tool call must run as the requesting engineer, so an assistant cannot become a privilege-escalation path to a repo or an AWS account they cannot reach directly. Asana's published framing is the right one: the agent runs at the **intersection** of its own permissions and the user's, and permission-elevating or destructive actions require human approval regardless of model confidence.
>
> **Third, budgets and idempotency, because the failure mode is economic.** Hard step and dollar caps per run, per engineer and per team, enforced at a gateway so no code path can bypass them. Idempotency keys on every mutating tool — creating a Jira ticket twice because a retry fired is the cheapest possible version of this bug and it is also the one that erodes trust fastest. Structured error returns from every tool, because an agent that reads an empty list as 'no results' will retry forever. And a no-progress rule on repeated tool-and-args hashes.
>
> **Fourth, replayable traces and an eval suite.** Every run records prompt version, model version, tool versions, inputs, outputs and the isolated-workspace commit. Any production run can be re-executed offline, which means a failure becomes a regression test in one click. I would seed with thirty to fifty hand-written scenarios and then grow the suite exclusively from real failures, gate merges on it, and report pass rate alongside cost — a change that improves quality three percent and doubles cost is a rejection.
>
> **Fifth, blast radius.** The agent's blast radius is the union of its tool permissions, so read-only by default, write tools behind approval, no open-ended outbound HTTP, and an egress allow-list from the execution environment — that is the control that actually stops exfiltration when prompt-injection defences fail. The isolated git workspace already gives me that for code; I would extend the same posture to network and cloud calls.
>
> **Sixth, rollout.** Per-team feature flags, shadow mode for new tools where the call is logged but not executed, then canary. And a kill switch per tool and per team that an on-call can hit without a deploy.
>
> The honest gap: I have run this for a team, with mentoring on prompt and tool-calling patterns, not for 500 engineers. The parts I would want to measure before designing further are the tool-call distribution and the cost per successful task, because those two numbers decide whether you need routing, caching or just better tool descriptions."

⚠ **That closing paragraph is the second honesty gate and it is mandatory, exactly like the one at the end of §8.3.** Do not let the six-point answer run long and then drop the calibration for time. If you are running out of clock, cut point six and keep the gap.

### 8.10 LLMOps governance

#### The gateway is the highest-leverage platform work

One proxy between every application and every provider, with six load-bearing features: unified provider API so a model swap is config; routing by task, cost, latency, region and quality tier; retries and cross-provider fallback, which is your availability story; caching — exact-match, prefix, and semantic with **tenant-and-ACL-scoped keys**; per-request observability with cost attribution by tenant, feature, user and prompt version; and rate limits with virtual keys so no raw provider key ever sits in application code.

> **Say it like this:** "The gateway is not a cost tool, it is a compliance control. It is where I enforce redaction, budget caps, per-region model allow-lists and audit logging — and it is the only place a data-residency rule can be enforced rather than documented. The caveat I would raise unprompted is that it is now a single point of failure in every request path, so it needs its own SLO, multi-region deployment and a documented bypass."

Rate limiting on request count **fails** for LLMs, because one request can burn 100K tokens. Meter tokens, with budgets at per-request, per-session, per-tenant and global levels, and anomaly alerts at 3× daily baseline, single-tenant-over-X%-of-spend, and estimate-versus-actual drift over 20%.

#### Prompt registry and model pinning

Prompts are artefacts, not strings in code: semantic versioning, diff, peer review, and environment aliases pointing at immutable versions. Every trace records the exact prompt version so any output is reproducible and any regression is bisectable. CI gate on the golden set, block on regression, canary at 5% before rollout — **a prompt change is a code change and goes through the same pipeline**. The underrated point: a prompt is tuned to a model, so **version the pair**.

Model registry holds which model version, which prompt, which eval results, which cost profile, which regions, and the announced deprecation date. You will run the migration runbook two to four times a year: shadow-run the candidate on live traffic logging both while serving the incumbent, compare on the golden set and the shadow diff, canary, cut over, keep rollback for two weeks.

#### PII redaction

Redact at three points with different rules at each: **ingest** (before embedding, so PII never enters the index), **request** (before the provider), and **log/trace** (before storage). Techniques: NER detection plus regex for structured identifiers, and **reversible tokenisation** where the model needs referential consistency — `PERSON_1` throughout, de-tokenised on the way out.

The trade-off to be honest about, stated as an engineering position rather than a citation:

> **Say it like this:** "Redaction is not free, and the cost is not uniform. Masking identity fields tends to preserve task performance; masking domain-substantive fields destroys it — you have taken away the thing the model needed to reason with. So the design rule is to tokenise identifiers reversibly and leave the substance intact, and to measure task accuracy under masking rather than assume it is free. And because detection is probabilistic, redaction is never the only control: retention limits, encryption and access control over the trace store carry the rest."

⚠ If pressed for evidence, the honest line is "that is my read of the literature plus a benchmark I ran on my own time." **Do not name the outside project.** Volunteering a side venture to a prospective employer while employed elsewhere is a hiring negative, and a private benchmark with no publishable artefact invites "show me" with nothing to show.

#### Prompt injection — containment, not prevention

⚠ The 2026 edition of the OWASP GenAI Top 10 landed in August 2026, but `genai.owasp.org/llm-top-10/` still renders the **2025** list at the time of writing. Do not quote 2026 ordinals from memory; they are the single easiest thing for a security-minded interviewer to check live.

> **Say it like this:** "The 2026 OWASP GenAI Top 10 landed in August. Prompt injection is still number one and the agent-era risks — excessive agency, unbounded consumption — moved up. I would want to re-read it against our own threat model rather than quote positions from memory."

The 2025 list is the one you can state cold if you need the full ordering: LLM01 Prompt Injection, LLM02 Sensitive Information Disclosure, LLM03 Supply Chain, LLM04 Data and Model Poisoning, LLM05 Improper Output Handling, LLM06 Excessive Agency, LLM07 System Prompt Leakage, LLM08 Vector and Embedding Weaknesses, LLM09 Misinformation, LLM10 Unbounded Consumption. **LLM08 is worth naming aloud in this interview** — vector and embedding weaknesses is where cross-tenant retrieval leakage lives in OWASP's own taxonomy, and it connects §8.3 to a framework a security reviewer already uses.

The project's own framing is the best line to quote:

> "Stop trying to build a model that cannot be fooled; build the system around it so that when the model is fooled, nothing important breaks."

No complete fix exists — frontier models remain vulnerable after their best defences, and **neither RAG nor fine-tuning mitigates it.** The layers: structural trust boundaries so retrieved content and tool output are never concatenated into the instruction region; least-privilege tools; human approval for consequential actions; output validation with allow-lists for URLs, commands and recipients, and **never rendering model output as HTML or markdown-with-links without sanitisation**, because a markdown image whose URL carries the secret is the exfiltration vector; injection classifiers on retrieved content, which help and are not sufficient; **egress allow-listing, which is the control that actually works**; anomaly monitoring on tool sequences; and an adversarial suite in CI on every prompt and model change.

The multi-tenant version, which is the one to raise here: **a document is an injection vector.** Any user who can put text into a shared sheet or a comment can attempt to steer another user's agent — and it executes with the victim's permissions. The Notion 3.0 agent exfiltration finding (a PDF with white-on-white hidden text steering the agent to concatenate private data into a URL) is the concrete case to name.

#### Structured outputs and the constraint tax

Constrained decoding compiles a JSON Schema into an FSM that masks invalid tokens. But structured mode is not free.

> **Say it like this:** "Constrained decoding is not a free lunch. There is published evidence — 'Let Me Speak Freely?' is the paper people cite — that forcing the model to maintain grammar state degrades quality on reasoning-heavy tasks relative to prompting for the format and validating afterwards. The hypothesis is that grammar state competes with attending to the document. So my stance is: use structured output for *shape* and validate semantics separately. Schema-valid is not correct."

Layer it: constrained decoding → Pydantic/JSON-Schema validation → business-rule validation (enum membership, referential integrity, ranges) → repair loop capped at two attempts → fail closed to a human. Cache compiled grammars; schema compilation is the throughput bottleneck. There is also a reported tool-calling suppression effect under structured constraints on some open-weight models — worth flagging as a thing to test rather than a thing to assert.

#### Red-teaming and audit trails

The red-team suite runs in CI on every model, prompt or tool change, not once before launch — a model upgrade can silently reopen a closed vector. Cover jailbreaks, direct and indirect injection, PII extraction, **cross-tenant access attempts**, tool misuse and cost exhaustion. Garak, PyRIT, promptfoo and Giskard, plus your own probes.

The audit trail is one artefact and it answers most security-review questions: per AI interaction, record who, which tenant, the query, **which document IDs were retrieved**, which policy version authorised them, which model and prompt versions ran, what was returned, what actions were taken, and whether a human approved. Immutable, exportable, retained per contract. Note the second-order obligation nobody mentions: **the audit log now contains customer data and inherits every retention, residency and erasure obligation of the source.**

#### Regulation for an India GCC shipping AI features

| Regime | Dates that matter | What it means for the platform |
|---|---|---|
| **India DPDP** | DPDP Rules 2025 notified in **mid-November 2025** (⚠ sources differ between 13 and 14 November for the Gazette date — do not quote a precise day unless you have re-checked it). Phased commencement: Board and definitional provisions on notification; **Consent Manager obligations at 12 months, i.e. around November 2026**; **the substantive compliance regime at 18 months, i.e. around May 2027**. MeitY proposed in Jan 2026 compressing the Significant Data Fiduciary window from 18 to 12 months — **verify current status** | Notice/consent, security safeguards, breach reporting, data-principal rights including erasure, retention limits, SDF duties |
| **EU AI Act** | Prohibited practices in force Feb 2025; GPAI Aug 2025; **Article 50 transparency live from 2 Aug 2026**; Annex III stand-alone high-risk **deferred from 2 Aug 2026 to 2 Dec 2027** by the Digital Omnibus (final Council approval 29 June 2026); embedded-in-product high-risk to 2 Aug 2028 | A work-management AI feature is likely not Annex III high-risk, but Article 50 disclosure, GPAI downstream duties and documentation/logging expectations apply **now**. Deferred is not cancelled |
| **GDPR** | In force | Lawful basis, DSAR, right to erasure, cross-border transfer mechanics for an India-based processor |
| **SOC 2 / ISO 42001** | ISO 42001 is the AI-specific certification enterprise buyers now ask for alongside SOC 2 | Auditors ask for: access control over RAG data and trace stores, change management for prompts and models, vendor management per model provider, and retention/deletion including traces, checkpoints, caches and eval datasets |

Say the DPDP milestones as **months, not dates** — "twelve months for Consent Manager, eighteen for the substantive regime, so roughly November 2026 and May 2027" — which is precise enough to be credible and does not stake you on a Gazette day. You are interviewing at an India GCC where somebody in the room may know this cold.

**Right to erasure versus the vector index and the trained model** — this is the question that separates people who have read the regulation from people who have implemented it.

The fan-out is the engineering. A deletion request must reach: the source system, the vector index (delete-then-verify, remembering that a tombstone is not an unreachable row until compaction runs), the lexical index, the semantic cache, the conversation history, the trace store, LangGraph or equivalent checkpoint tables, the eval and golden datasets, any derived summaries or digests, and backups within their retention window. **Build the fan-out before the first request arrives, and make erasure a tested path with an SLA, not a runbook.**

The genuinely hard case is a model whose weights saw the data.

> **Say it like this:** "For the index, erasure is a delete plus a verification that the row is unreachable through search, cache and history — and I would test that, because a tombstone is not an unreachable row until the segment merge runs. For a fine-tuned model, erasure is effectively impossible: you cannot subtract a training example from weights, and machine-unlearning research is not something I would put in front of an auditor. So the architectural answer is upstream of the legal one: **do not train on customer content.** RAG keeps the data in a store you can delete from and the request stateless, which is exactly the reason Slack said publicly they chose RAG over fine-tuning on trust grounds. If a business case ever forces fine-tuning, it is per-tenant adapters you can destroy wholesale, on explicitly opted-in and de-identified data, and the retraining-without-the-subject cost is a line in the budget. The tension I would flag unprompted is that the highest-quality training data any product like this will ever have is accepted-and-edited user output — and harvesting it collides head-on with 'we never train on your data'. The honest resolution is aggregate, de-identify, and make it an opt-in data-contribution setting, which is the narrow carve-out Atlassian publishes."

Also note the moving contractual target:

> **Say it like this:** "Zero data retention is not the default. Inputs and outputs are typically retained around thirty days for abuse monitoring unless you have a contractual ZDR arrangement, and the terms move. So I would verify ZDR per model, per endpoint, per quarter — it is not a one-time procurement checkbox, and it is the kind of thing that changes underneath a contract you signed a year ago."

### 8.11 The first ninety days

Platform rounds close on some version of "what would you do first here?" Have the answer assembled rather than reassembling it live. The through-line: **measure before you touch retrieval, and make the first two deliverables things that keep paying after you have moved on.**

| Window | What ships | Why this and not something flashier |
|---|---|---|
| **Days 0–30 — measure** | (1) A **golden set of 100–300 real queries** from the actual query log, human-labelled, in git, owned by a named person. (2) A **permission-graph audit**: how many documents in a representative tenant are effectively world-readable. (3) The **two published SLAs** — freshness, and revocation — written down with current measured values, not targets | You cannot improve retrieval you have not measured, and the permission audit is usually the first finding. Neither requires me to change any code, so neither can break anything while I am still learning the system |
| **Days 30–60 — the cheap invariants** | (1) `query_model == index_model` assertion at query time. (2) `returned < requested` alarm. (3) The **nightly cross-tenant probe test** in CI. (4) The retrieval eval as a **merge gate**, relative-to-baseline with an absolute floor | Four small changes that convert the three silent failures into loud ones. This is the same move as the feature contract at TrueBalance, and it is the highest ratio of risk removed to code written that I know of |
| **Days 60–90 — the platform** | (1) The **rebuild trigger**: a weekly recall-vs-latency curve against exact-kNN ground truth. (2) Retrieval **drift monitors** with the pages/dashboard split from §8.6. (3) One **cost decomposition** per request, so the next optimisation argument is arithmetic instead of opinion | By now I have earned the right to change retrieval. These three are what let the *next* person change it safely |

> **Say it like this:** "First month I would not touch the retrieval stack. I would build the golden set from the real query log, audit the permission graph, and publish the two SLAs with measured values rather than targets. Second month is the cheap invariants — the model-mismatch assertion, the under-return alarm, the cross-tenant probe in CI, and the retrieval eval as a merge gate. Those four are small, they are boring, and they turn the three failures that report success into failures that page. Only in the third month would I start changing retrieval, because by then a regression is visible within ninety seconds of a pull request instead of within a quarter of a customer escalation."

**The GCC-specific part, which you should volunteer** because it is the thing a Bangalore-based platform hire is actually being assessed on:

> **Say it like this:** "One thing I would do differently because this is a GCC. If the platform's consumers are partly in another timezone, then every artefact I just described has to work asynchronously — the golden set, the eval gate, the SLA document, the runbook. A platform whose contract only exists in someone's head, or only gets explained in a call at 9pm my time, is not a platform, it is a dependency on me. So my bias is to over-invest early in the written contract: what the platform guarantees, what it does not, what breaks the build and why. That is slower in month one and it is the only thing that makes month six scale."

### 8.12 Thirty-five rapid-fire GenAI-ops questions

| # | Question | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Default chunking? | Recursive split, 256–512 tokens, 10–25% overlap, ~200-token floor with merge. Retrieve small, generate from the parent. |
| 2 | Why is semantic chunking not the default? | Published evaluations keep finding it wins on retrieval recall and loses on end-to-end accuracy against recursive splitting — right fragment, not enough surrounding context. I would measure end-to-end on our corpus before adopting it. |
| 3 | RRF constant? | k = 60. Rank 1 gives 1/61, rank 100 gives 1/160 — a 2.6× spread. It works on *ranks*, which sidesteps score-scale incompatibility; k is insensitive because 1/(k+r) is a flat curve, and it controls how sharply the head of each list dominates. |
| 4 | When is RRF wrong? | When one retriever reliably dominates a query class, or you have calibrated scores worth preserving. Then weight, or route by query type. |
| 5 | Why is BM25 still in the stack? | Exact IDs, error codes, SKUs, proper nouns, rare acronyms, negation. And it is the baseline that sometimes wins outright. |
| 6 | Rerank how many candidates? | Top-50 into top-5..8. Cross-encoder cost is linear in candidates and chunk length drives latency past ~2k tokens. |
| 7 | Reranker API goes down? | Timeout, skip the rerank, return fusion order, emit a counter. Degrade enrichment, never degrade the filter. |
| 8 | Changing the embedding model? | Full re-index. Vectors from two models are not comparable. Blue/green with an alias, validate on the golden set, canary, keep the old index hot 24–72h. |
| 9 | Cheapest way to prevent a silent quality collapse? | Store `embedding_model` on every chunk and assert query model equals index model at query time. Same class of control as a serialized feature contract next to a model artifact. |
| 10 | Fewer results returned than requested? | Post-filtering or an exhausted ANN scan. pgvector default `ef_search=40` with a 10% filter returns ~4 of 10. Enable bounded iterative scans and alarm on `returned < requested`. |
| 11 | Pre-filter or post-filter for ACLs? | Pre-filter, always. Post-filter means the model already read it. |
| 12 | Is pgvector's iterative scan a filter-aware index? | No — and be precise, because people conflate them. pgvector applies the filter *after* the index scan and iterative scan just re-scans more of the index until `LIMIT` is satisfied. Qdrant's filterable HNSW, with per-tenant subgraphs, is the genuinely filter-aware one. |
| 13 | Per-tenant index or shared with filters? | Namespace-per-tenant as the default — safer and, on a per-GB-scanned cost model, roughly 100× cheaper at 100 tenants. Dedicated indexes for top tenants, residency and BYOK. Tiered, not binary. |
| 14 | Where does tenant_id come from? | The authenticated token. Never a request parameter. That is the number-one real-world bug. |
| 15 | Revocation SLA vs freshness SLA? | Different clocks. Revocation must be much tighter and permission events go on a priority lane. Publish both numbers. |
| 16 | How do you catch a stale ACL projection? | An authoritative second check: re-verify the top-N doc IDs against the source of truth after retrieval, before generation. |
| 17 | Group expansion — index time or query time? | Query time, cached 30–120s against a membership version, invalidated on membership events. Index-time expansion fans one change out to millions of rows. And explicit denies do not fit an allow-list filter at all — normalise them away or keep them in the post-check. |
| 18 | Semantic cache key? | tenant_id plus a hash of the caller's effective principal set, or an entitlements version. Never query text alone — and yes, that lowers the hit rate, which is the correct trade. |
| 19 | Bulk permission change — how do you invalidate? | Bump a per-tenant `cache_epoch` rather than surgically deleting keys. |
| 20 | Chunking rule for row-level permissions? | Chunk granularity ≤ permission granularity. A chunk spanning two ACL domains has no safe filter. |
| 21 | Permission-filtered aggregates? | Compute after the filter, in the data layer. Never let the model summarise a pre-computed total. Route aggregates to SQL. |
| 22 | When is a vector DB the wrong answer? | Under 100k chunks; lookups; aggregations; multi-hop; small jargon-heavy corpora where BM25 wins; row-level ACLs changing faster than you can project; anything needing exact auditable numbers. |
| 23 | Deletes in Elasticsearch/OpenSearch? | Tombstones until segment merge — deleted vectors still consume memory, and "deleted" is not "unreachable" until compaction. Schedule it and alert on deleted-doc ratio. |
| 24 | Deletes in FAISS? | No update at all. `remove_ids()` exists on flat, IVF and IDMap indexes but not on HNSW, it needs a pass over the database, and it does not reclaim graph structure. In practice deletion means rebuild — which is why FAISS is an engine, not a system of record. |
| 25 | When do you stop doing incremental updates and rebuild? | When you had to raise `ef_search` or `nprobe` to hold recall — that is the cleanest signal, because it converts graph degradation into a latency bill. Also at ~10–20% tombstoned, or a doubling of corpus size. Measure it weekly with a recall-vs-latency curve against exact kNN on 1,000 sampled queries. |
| 26 | Which RAGAS metric would you gate on? | `context_recall` for retrieval changes, because it is the ceiling — if the context lacks the answer, no generator recovers it. `faithfulness` for prompt and model changes. `context_precision` I tune, `answer_relevancy` I do not trust as a gate because a fluent wrong answer scores well. |
| 27 | Absolute eval thresholds or relative-to-baseline? | Relative primary, absolute floor as a backstop. Absolute thresholds punish you for making the golden set harder, and a gate that punishes improvement gets disabled. |
| 28 | Do we need a knowledge graph? | Show me the query log. If a meaningful share of questions are multi-hop, aggregate or constraint-shaped, yes — and much of the graph is already foreign keys: workspace → folder → sheet → row-forest → cell, plus cross-sheet references and share grants. Otherwise a reranker gets you there for 1%. |
| 29 | GraphRAG cost? | Full GraphRAG indexing is one LLM extraction call per chunk plus community summarisation, so it scales with corpus tokens — six figures is reachable on a real corpus. Microsoft's LazyGraphRAG numbers are the ones I would quote: ~0.1% of the indexing cost and >700× lower global query cost. |
| 30 | Text-to-Cypher accuracy? | GPT-4o at 60.18% execution accuracy on CypherBench. Ship parameterised templates over ~20 known query shapes, read-only credentials, mandatory LIMIT and bounded hops, free generation only as a fallback. |
| 31 | LangGraph in production — the three gotchas? | `checkpointer.setup()` belongs in a CI migration step, not app startup; checkpoint tables grow unbounded and contain customer message state, so TTL them and scope them per tenant; and on resume from `interrupt()` the node **re-runs from the top**, so put the interrupt first or make the prefix idempotent. |
| 32 | Why did the agent cost 40× estimate? | Almost always an unbounded retry against a tool that failed without signalling failure. Fix structurally: gateway-enforced caps, structured tool errors, repeated-failure termination, no-progress detection on `(tool, args)` hashes. |
| 33 | Why must every mutating tool be idempotent? | Because retries are how a bounded loop becomes an unbounded one, and the visible symptom is duplicate tickets, duplicate emails, duplicate charges. |
| 34 | LLM-as-judge — what will you tell me unprompted? | Position bias is large and model-dependent, well past 2:1 on some benchmarks; verbosity 15–30 points; self-preference roughly +10 to +25 points in the original MT-Bench work. Pin the judge version, run both orderings, judge from a different family, calibrate against humans at Cohen's κ > 0.6. |
| 35 | Right to erasure against a fine-tuned model? | You cannot subtract an example from weights. So do not train on customer content; keep it in RAG where deletion is a delete plus a verified-unreachable test across index, cache, history, traces, checkpoints and eval sets. If fine-tuning is forced: per-tenant adapters, opted-in and de-identified, destroyable wholesale. |

### 8.13 The hour-of card

Read only this if you are short of time.

**The three sentences that must leave your mouth in the first fifteen minutes**

1. "The bug I care most about in retrieval systems is the one that reports success" → the TrueBalance 4,001-vs-28 parity collapse → contract, hard fail, CI gate, missing-rate metric.
2. "Pre-filter, always. Post-filtering means the model already read it." → pgvector `ef_search=40`, ~4 rows of 10, silent.
3. "A denormalised ACL is a cache, so it has a published revocation SLA and an authoritative second check."

**The five nos, in the order you would rather give them** — Monte Carlo (you built it twice by hand: Deequ at Tiger, the Datadog/Snowflake drift utility at ResMed), Bedrock (SageMaker multi-container endpoints and ARM64 Lambda instead), Databricks Vector Search (pgvector/FAISS/Chroma/Pinecone, and you built what Delta Sync replaces), Unity Catalog (MLflow + S3 versioning + the feature contract + Postgres RLS, and you know lineage is the gap), Mosaic AI Agent Framework (LangGraph + MCP + your own eval harness).

**Consistency numbers, unchanged** — 8 years engineering, ~4.5 in ML engineer titles, AI/ML ~6, MLOps ~4.5, Python 8, cloud ~5 (AWS primary, Azure ~1.5), Databricks ~1.5 (Azure Databricks, Spark, Deequ, data-quality and ETL — *not* Lakehouse ownership, *not* petabyte scale). Current [current CTC — private] fixed, expected [expected CTC — private] fixed, notice 60 days with buyout discussable, no offer in hand.

**The two mandatory honesty gates** — the ResMed calibration at the end of §8.3 ("document-level permissioning over clinical data, not multi-tenant row-level retrieval"), and the 500-engineer gap at the end of §8.9 ("I have run this for a team, not for 500 engineers"). Neither is optional and neither costs you anything.

**Five things never to say** — a chunking benchmark with digits; an OWASP 2026 ordinal; a GraphRAG dollar figure; a named study you cannot cite; anything about what Smartsheet's trust posture says. On that last one, ask instead: *"Is retrieval for your MCP server scoped inside the caller's existing sharing model?"*

**If they ask what you would do first** — measure for thirty days (golden set, permission audit, two published SLAs), then four cheap invariants, then the platform. Do not touch retrieval in month one.

### 0. The opening five minutes — your architectural narrative

Almost every design round opens with a variant of "walk me through the most complex system you've designed". Ch.54's STAR stories are behavioural; this is the architectural one, and it is the only thing in this document you should have memorised as a *shape* rather than as sentences. Five beats, five minutes, and you stop talking. Problem → constraints → architecture → the trade-off you rejected → what you'd change. If you improvise this you will ramble, and rambling in the first five minutes sets the register for the whole hour.

**0.1 [OPENER — as likely as anything in the TOP-25] — "Walk me through the most complex system you've designed, end to end."**

Use the NatWest MLOps platform at Tiger Analytics. It is the strongest choice for *this* round because it is a platform, not a model; it is regulated, which maps to the JD's governance and compliance lines; it is AWS-native, which is the JD's preferred cloud; and it was showcased by AWS at re:Invent, which is external validation you can state in one clause without sounding like you're selling.

> **Say it like this — beat 1, problem, 45 seconds:** "NatWest is an FCA-regulated retail bank. They had data scientists producing models in notebooks and no repeatable way to get one into production — every deployment was a bespoke project, and because it was regulated, every deployment also had to be explainable to an auditor two years later. So the problem wasn't 'deploy a model', it was 'make deployment a repeatable, evidenced process that a regulator will accept'."

> **Say it like this — beat 2, constraints, 45 seconds:** "Three hard constraints shaped everything. Regulatory: every production decision had to be reconstructable — which model, which data, which approver. Organisational: the data scientists were not going to write Kubernetes manifests, and if the paved road was slower than what they already did, they'd route around it. And operational: the bank's change process meant a deployment couldn't be a person running a script at 2am."

> **Say it like this — beat 3, architecture, 90 seconds:** "SageMaker as the substrate, with five planes. Training as containerised jobs against a pinned data snapshot, so a run is reproducible from its manifest. A registry holding model plus signature plus manifest, content-addressed. Inference as managed endpoints with the deployment driven off a registry stage transition rather than a human. Drift detection running on a schedule against the training baseline, feeding the retraining trigger. And CI/CD wiring the whole thing so promotion was a gate chain, not a meeting. The contract between the planes was the artefact and its manifest — that's what let the data scientists own everything inside the boundary and me own everything between the boundaries."

> **Say it like this — beat 4, the rejected trade-off, 60 seconds:** "The trade-off I'd defend hardest is that we did *not* build a feature store. The pull was strong — everyone wanted one — but there was one primary consumer, the scoring was batch, and the features were computed in the training job. A feature store would have been a second distributed system, a materialisation bill and a new page in the on-call rotation, in exchange for reuse that didn't yet exist. We got reproducibility from versioned snapshots and a shared transformation library instead. The condition I said would change my mind was a second team consuming the same features online — that's when the skew risk becomes real and the store starts paying for itself."

> **Say it like this — beat 5, what you'd change, 45 seconds:** "Two things. The drift detection was distribution-only, which I now think is the least useful third of monitoring — I'd add train/serve parity checks and a per-feature missing-rate metric from the scorer, because upstream data breakage is a more common cause of a bad model than covariate drift. And the promotion gate was a checklist a human executed. I'd make it code that emits a signed artefact per gate, so 'who waved this through' stops being a question."

**0.2 — "What would you have done differently with more time?"**
The honest answer rather than a rehearsed regret: I'd have instrumented cost per prediction from day one. We could tell you the model was healthy and we could not tell you what it cost to run, and every conversation about consolidating or right-sizing was therefore an argument from intuition. That's the single artefact I now build first, because it's the one that makes every later optimisation measurable.

**0.3 — "Which part of that would you keep, and which was specific to a bank?"**
The artefact-and-manifest contract keeps everywhere — it's what makes a platform a platform. The gate chain keeps, with the thresholds re-tuned; a work-management SaaS doesn't need FCA-grade evidence on every decision, but it does need per-segment non-inferiority and a rollback that's a config change. What was bank-specific was the weight of the audit layer: decision-level lineage on every individual prediction is expensive, and outside a regulated decision it's usually the wrong trade against sampling plus reconstruction from versioned sources.

### 1. Platform and pipeline design

**1.1 [TOP-25] — "Design an ML platform for us. What are the components?"**
Six planes, with immutable artefacts as the contract between them. Data plane: lakehouse with bronze/silver/gold and a conformed feature layer. Training plane: containerised jobs against a pinned data snapshot, with an experiment tracker. Artefact plane: a registry holding model, signature and manifest, content-addressed. Serving plane: online, async and batch treated as three distinct SLA classes rather than one endpoint type. Observability plane: data monitors, model monitors and traces in one place, so a "model incident" can be traced back to a table. Governance plane: lineage, access control, audit log. What makes it a platform rather than a collection of scripts is that promotion between planes is a gate that can say no without a human's permission.

**1.2 — "What would you build first in your first 90 days?"**
Instrument before optimising, because everything else is unmeasurable otherwise. Three artefacts: a lineage manifest stamped on every model (commit, container digest, data snapshot id, feature-spec hash); a promotion gate in CI that includes an offline metric with a confidence interval and a train/serve parity check; and cost per 1,000 predictions per model per team on a dashboard with a named owner. Then an inventory of what is actually deployed — the first finding in most orgs is three models nobody owns and one that has been serving a default for months.

**1.3 — "How do you decide build vs buy for a platform component?"**
I ask whether it is differentiating or merely necessary. Necessary-and-solved — object storage, a registry, a tracker, an orchestrator — I adopt, because operating it earns nothing. Differentiating — the promotion gate, the feature contract, the tenant-isolation rules — I build, because those encode our specific risk model and no vendor knows it. The tiebreaker is on-call: every self-hosted distributed system is a new page in the rotation, and I count that as a recurring cost, not a one-off.

**1.4 — "What's the interface between a data scientist and your platform?"**
Declarative. They write the transformation and the model code plus a config naming the data snapshot, the eval set and the metric thresholds. They do not write Dockerfiles, IAM policies or Kubernetes manifests. On my side that means a paved road: a project template, a base image, a CI workflow, and a self-service way to get compute with a hard TTL.

> **Say it like this:** "If the paved road is slower than clicking in the console, people will click in the console. So I treat developer ergonomics as a governance control, not a nicety — the discipline argument is won on speed, not on policy."

**1.5 — "How do you version a pipeline, not just a model?"**
The pipeline definition is code with a commit, but that isn't sufficient because the same code produces different outputs against different inputs. So I version the tuple: pipeline commit, container digest, input snapshot ids, config hash and feature-definition hashes. Every run records it and every output artefact carries it. The test is: given a run id from six months ago, can someone else rebuild the artefact and explain why it was chosen? If the lineage terminates at "someone's laptop", the pipeline isn't versioned regardless of what Git says.

**1.6 [TOP-25] — "How do you prevent train/serve skew at the platform level?"**
I've been burned by this directly. At TrueBalance the offline feature set had 4,001 features and the real-time payload actually carried 28 keys; the transform silently imputed defaults, so the served vector was near-constant and every schema check passed. The platform fix was four things: serialise a feature contract next to the model artefact; hard-fail at serve time on a missing required feature instead of defaulting; a CI assertion that the serving payload is a superset of the required subset, wired as a promotion gate; and a per-feature missing-rate metric emitted by the scorer so the condition is visible in production, not only in tests. The strongest version, where you can afford it, is log-and-wait — log the exact feature vector at serving time and train on those logs, which makes parity true by construction.

**1.7 — "Do we need a feature store?"**
Only if you can name at least two of four conditions: online low-latency serving where skew is a live risk; genuine reuse of the same feature across teams; point-in-time correctness across entities with different label timelines; or a governance requirement for feature lineage. With one model, batch scoring, and features computed in the training job, a versioned Delta table plus a shared transformation library gives reproducibility and reuse at a fraction of the operational cost. A feature store is another distributed system, another materialisation bill and another source of on-call — and it doesn't make your pipelines correct by itself.

**1.8 — "Batch or streaming for features?"**
Decide from the decision latency, not the technology. If the action can wait an hour, batch is cheaper, trivially backfillable and testable, and micro-batch at 5–15 minutes covers a surprising amount of what people call real-time. Streaming earns its complexity when value decays in seconds — fraud, in-session personalisation, operational alerting. Its honest cost is a second correctness surface: at serving time the aggregate has a watermark and a lateness policy; at training time you rebuild it from the event log with none of those semantics, and the two disagree precisely on the bursty, late, out-of-order events that matter. The usual right answer is hybrid — streaming for the handful of features that need freshness, batch for the other two hundred.

**1.9 — "How do you support forty models from six teams without forty bespoke pipelines?"**
Standardise the contract, not the code. Every model must produce a signature, a manifest, a container implementing one predict interface, and an eval report in a fixed schema. Everything inside that boundary belongs to the team. The platform then provides orchestration, registry, serving substrate and monitoring wiring generated from the manifest. The failure mode to avoid is a framework that tries to own the modelling code — it always ends with teams forking it and you maintaining six versions.

**1.10 — "What does 'reliable pipeline' actually mean operationally?"**
Idempotent tasks parameterised by an explicit interval; atomic writes via build-and-swap or MERGE on a deterministic key; no `datetime.now()` anywhere; retries that are safe because side effects carry idempotency keys; and a defined failure mode for every sensor rather than an infinite wait. The acceptance test I'd actually run: pick any task, execute it three times, assert the output is identical and no external effect fired twice.

**1.11 — "How do you handle multi-tenancy at the platform level?"**
Namespace per team with a resource quota and a queue quota — guaranteed nominal capacity plus borrowing from a cohort, so research bursts into idle production capacity and gets preempted first. Tags are mandatory and enforced at admission: an untagged workload is unschedulable, because retroactive tagging never happens. That one design answers "how do we stop the research team eating production GPUs" without buying more GPUs.

**1.12 — "Explain point-in-time correctness."**
Each training row must see only feature values knowable at the moment the prediction would have been made. Mechanically it's an as-of join taking the greatest feature *arrival* timestamp less than or equal to the *decision* timestamp minus the real pipeline lag. Two timestamps, not one, and the anchor is the decision timestamp — not the label timestamp, because in a lending model the label matures sixty days after the decision, so anchoring the join on the label leaks the entire horizon into every training row. The label timestamp's only job is to supply the outcome. The other half people miss is that you join on when the value *landed*, not when the event *occurred* — a value that arrived six hours late was not available for serving, and joining on event time silently leaks it into training. The label horizon is a separate concern, handled by ending the training window one horizon in the past (see 6.3).

**1.13 — "Give me a point-in-time violation that passes every unit test."**
A dimension maintained as SCD Type 1, so `customer.risk_segment` is overwritten in place. The training join picks up today's segment for a decision made eight months ago, and today's segment already reflects the default you're trying to predict. Offline AUC jumps, online is flat, and nothing fires because schema, row counts and null rates are all fine. The structural fix: no mutable dimension enters a training join — capture it as SCD Type 2 with valid_from/valid_to, or reconstruct it from the event log.

**1.14 — "What are your platform SLOs?"**
Three layers. System: fraction of requests served under the latency budget with a non-5xx. Pipeline correctness: fraction of requests scored with a complete, fresh feature vector — the layer most teams don't have, and where the silent failures live. Model quality: a rolling metric on delayed labels, with proxies where labels lag. The error budget ties them together, and I'd extend the usual policy — a model promotion is a change that consumes error budget, so a team burning budget can't ship a new model either.

### 2. Model deployment and packaging

**2.1 [TOP-25] — "How do you package a model for production?"**
A thin runtime container plus an externally-referenced weight artefact — never weights baked into the image, because a 2 GB runtime plus 140 GB of weights becomes a 142 GB image that is unpullable at autoscale and unversionable independently of the code. Separating them means a code fix ships a 2 GB pull, not a 142 GB one. The container is pinned by digest, not tag. Alongside it go the model signature, the feature contract, the dependency lockfile hash and the manifest. At TrueBalance the serving path is ARM64 Docker images in ECR behind Lambda and SQS with S3-versioned artefacts and a fork-based CI/CD flow; ARM64 was a cost decision that held because every wheel in the tree had an aarch64 build — which is the thing to check before you commit to it.

**2.2 — "'Reproducible and interpretable' is in the JD. How do you deliver both?"**
Reproducible means the manifest is sufficient to rebuild: commit, container digest, lockfile hash, data snapshot id, feature hashes, config hash, seeds. Interpretable is two different things and I'd separate them — global interpretability (feature importance, a model card, documented constraints) versus per-decision explanation (the feature vector, score, threshold and rule applied, written to a decision log). For a regulated lending decision the second is the legal requirement; I built that shape at Sopra Steria with an explainable-AI layer over a loan-risk model so decisions were auditable.

**2.3 — "Do you chase bit-identical reproducibility?"**
No, and I'd say why. Bit-identical needs deterministic kernels, fixed data ordering, fixed world size and no atomics-based reductions; it costs roughly 10–30% throughput and forbids some ops outright. The right bar is statistically reproducible plus forensically explainable: full pinning always, determinism flags only for debugging or under regulatory scrutiny, and a CI rebuild test that retrains on the pinned snapshot and asserts the primary metric lands inside a pre-agreed tolerance.

**2.4 — "What goes in a model signature and why does it matter?"**
Input schema, output schema, params schema. It matters because it's the enforcement point at predict time — type coercion on dataframes, strict on tensors — and because without it you cannot detect a serving payload that has drifted from what the model was trained on. In MLflow you infer it with `infer_signature`. Signatures are also a hard requirement for registering into a Unity Catalog registry — I know that from the docs, not from running it; on the MLflow registry I have used, the equivalent failure is a signature-less model that only breaks at predict time, which is worse because it breaks in production rather than at registration.

**2.5 — "Pickle-based artefacts — what's the risk?"**
Pickle is a program, not a data format: `__reduce__` lets a pickle specify arbitrary callables executed at load time, so `torch.load` or `joblib.load` on an untrusted artefact is remote code execution with your service's credentials, inside a container that has database and cloud access. Mitigations in order: safetensors for weights; `weights_only=True` on torch loads; scanning artefacts before load; signed artefacts with a registry that refuses unsigned or hash-mismatched models; pin by digest not a mutable tag; and do any untrusted conversion in a network-isolated job with no credentials.

**2.6 — "Real-time, async, batch, streaming — how do you choose?"**
From the decision latency and the failure semantics, not from the model. Real-time when a synchronous caller blocks — fail fast, degrade, never queue indefinitely. Async when the contract is a completion SLA rather than a latency SLA, which unlocks spot, aggressive batching and scale-to-zero. Batch when the trigger is a schedule or data arrival. Streaming when the event itself is the unit of work. I push async hardest, because half the "we need more GPUs" requests are actually an online workload that should have been async.

**2.7 — "How do you serve two hundred low-QPS models?"**
Not with two hundred deployments. Multi-model serving with an LRU-loaded shared pool — the shape I actually ran was multi-container SageMaker endpoints at ResMed — or for LLMs multi-LoRA, which I know as a design rather than an operated system — one base model resident, per-request adapter ids, batched-gather kernels so different adapters batch together, costing roughly 5–20% throughput against a single-adapter batch versus N full replicas. The landmine is the cold-model miss: the first request for an evicted model pays the load, so it shows up in your p99 and has to be bounded by a resident-set policy and an adapter registry keyed on the base-model digest.

**2.8 — "Where's the line between preprocessing in the model and preprocessing upstream?"**
Anything derived purely from the request payload belongs in the serving path inside the predict wrapper, versioned with the model — ratios, time-since-request, string lengths. Anything precomputable belongs upstream. The rule: if the input includes a value that only exists at request time, precomputing it is an error, not an optimisation. The catch is that the on-demand transform is now a new skew surface, so it needs a test that exercises the same code object used at training time.

**2.9 — "Multi-container endpoints — when and why?"**
At ResMed I ran multi-container SageMaker endpoints on the internal MLOps platform so several models shared infrastructure, cutting inference cost while holding per-model SLAs. It's right when you have several models with modest, uncorrelated traffic and compatible runtimes. It's wrong when one model is latency-critical and the others are bursty, because you've coupled their fate — a noisy neighbour on a shared endpoint is a p99 problem you can't fix from outside.

**2.10 — "How do you deploy a model that needs a GPU but only sees business-hours traffic?"**
Scale to zero, with the caveat that GPU cold start is 5–15 minutes end to end — node provision, DaemonSets, image pull, weight load. So scale-to-zero is only acceptable if first-request latency is tolerable or you pre-warm on a schedule; otherwise keep a floor of one replica and move the rest to async. And check whether it needs a GPU at all: a sub-100M-parameter encoder at modest QPS on ONNX Runtime with int8 on CPU is usually cheaper to run and much cheaper to operate than an idling accelerator.

**2.11 — "What's in your rollback plan?"**
Rollback is a config change, not a rebuild: target under sixty seconds, one action, no CI run. That requires the routing decision to live in a flag or config service, N-1 kept warm through the bake, and every artefact immutable and content-addressed so "roll back to v3" is unambiguous. The catch worth volunteering: rolling back a model does not roll back the decisions it already wrote downstream, so there has to be a compensating re-score path or a documented, accepted smear.
