*The gate list here is the same one as 3.2 and 6.2 — the answer to this question is the **framing**, so lead with that and compress the list.* The framing matters more than the timeline: the defect is not "the model was worse", the defect is that it shipped silently. So the action items are gate changes — a frozen golden set the pipeline cannot regenerate, per-segment non-inferiority checks, a score-distribution check, a train-versus-previous-train data diff as a reviewable artefact, mandatory shadow with auto-rollback, and a named approver. I'd also quantify the damage window and the affected decisions explicitly, because if any need reversing that clock is already running.

**9.8 — "How do you bring a team along on a new practice?"**
Ship it as a default rather than a mandate. At TrueBalance I built parts of the internal Claude developer assistant on MCP — the first Slack integration, a Google Docs skill with 34 of 34 tests passing, and a PR skill that writes titles and descriptions from the diff — tying Jira, GitHub, Jenkins, AWS, Grafana and Slack into one plain-English interface with each task in an isolated Git workspace. Adoption came because it removed work people already disliked, not because anyone was told to use it, and the mentoring on prompt and tool-calling patterns followed the adoption rather than preceding it.

**9.9 — "How do you prioritise a platform roadmap against a queue of feature requests?"**
By separating requests that are load-bearing for someone's delivery from requests that are preference, and by making the platform's own reliability debt a first-class line rather than the thing that gets deferred. Concretely I'd run three buckets with a fixed split: keep-the-lights-on and reliability debt around a third; the highest-leverage enabling work — the thing that unblocks the most teams per unit of effort — around half; and a deliberate slice for the small requests, because a platform team that never ships small things loses its users' goodwill and then loses the argument on the big things. The prioritisation question I ask each requester is "what does this unblock, and what are you doing instead today" — a request with a real workaround is a different priority from a request that is stopping a launch, and people answer that question honestly far more often than they'll accept a ranking.

> **Say it like this:** "I'd rather be transparent about the queue than fast at saying yes. Publishing the ranked list with the reason attached converts every disappointed team into a reviewer of my reasoning, and about a third of the time they tell me something that changes the order."

**9.10 — "Describe a disagreement with a manager or a product manager, not a data scientist."**
The honest shape from my own experience is the cost-and-timeline one rather than a dramatic conflict. The pattern I'd describe: a stakeholder wants a capability by a date, and the design that meets the date is the one that accrues the operational debt. My move is to make the trade explicit and quantified rather than to argue about the date — here is the version that ships on time and here is exactly what it will cost us in on-call and rework, here is the version that doesn't, and here is a third option that ships a narrower thing on time. In my experience the third option is what actually gets chosen, and the reason to present three rather than two is that two options is a fight and three is a decision. Where I hold firm is on anything that can fail silently, because a silent failure is not a debt you can choose to carry — you don't find out you were wrong.

> **Say it like this:** "I'll trade scope, I'll trade polish, and I'll trade my own weekend. What I won't trade is the ability to detect that something broke, because that's the one shortcut you can't repay later — you just never learn what it cost you."

**9.11 — "How do you onboard a new team onto the platform?"**
With a working example rather than documentation. A template repository that deploys a trivial model end to end on day one — train, register, gate, deploy, monitor — so their first experience is a green pipeline and not a page of prose. Then pair on migrating *one* real model with me doing the platform half, because the gap between the template and their actual code is where every onboarding stalls and it is different for every team. Then the golden-path docs, which are now written against a case that demonstrably works. I'd measure onboarding as time-to-first-production-deploy and treat a regression in that number as a platform defect. And I'd deliberately capture what they had to ask me — every question that isn't answered by the template is a gap in the template, not a gap in the team.

**9.12 — "How do you say no without becoming the blocker everyone routes around?"**
Never say no to the need, only to the implementation, and always leave with a path. Three moves. First, name what I'm actually protecting — "the reason I won't give you cluster-admin is that it makes the audit story unprovable, not that I don't trust you" — because an unexplained no reads as territorial and gets escalated. Second, offer the constrained version now: self-service with a hard TTL, a sandbox with synthetic data, a manual approval this week and automation next month. Something ships. Third, make the exception path real and logged rather than theoretical — a documented override with a named approver, because a policy with no exception process gets bypassed silently, which is strictly worse than an exception you can see. The failure mode I'd flag as the real risk is being right and slow: if the paved road is slower than the workaround, people take the workaround, and then I have neither the governance nor the goodwill.

> **Say it like this:** "The measure of whether I'm a blocker isn't how often I say no. It's whether the people I said no to still come to me first next time. If they stop asking, I've lost, however correct I was."

**9.13 — "The business wants an AI feature you think is a bad idea. What do you do?"**
Separate the two objections, because they get different treatment. If the objection is feasibility — the accuracy won't be there, the latency won't be there, the data doesn't exist — the answer is a time-boxed spike that produces a number, not an argument. A week of work that says "here's the retrieval recall we can actually achieve on your corpus" ends the debate in either direction and costs less than the meeting series. If the objection is risk — it will leak data across tenants, it will make a claim we can't stand behind, it will produce an unexplainable decision in a regulated context — that's not a preference and I escalate it in writing with the specific failure described, because that's the class of thing where being quietly right is worthless. And I'd be honest that I've been wrong on the first kind before; the spike exists partly to check me.

### 10. Versioning and governance with MLflow

**10.1 [TOP-25] — "How do you promote a model to Production in MLflow?"**
That's a trap in current MLflow, and I'd say so: stages were deprecated in MLflow 2.9 and don't exist in the Unity Catalog registry at all — there is no `transition_model_version_stage` there. You set an **alias** — `models:/catalog.schema.model@champion` — and the recommended Databricks pattern is to promote *code* through dev, staging and prod and retrain in each, because prod is where prod data lives. With a shared registry, alias-based artefact promotion is also viable when retraining in prod is impractical, so the modern answer is code promotion by default with UC aliases making artefact promotion a legitimate option.

**10.2 — "What changed between MLflow 2 and 3?"**
MLflow 2 was run-centric: metrics and params lived on the Run, a model was an artefact inside a run. MLflow 3 makes `LoggedModel` a first-class entity with its own metrics, params, tags and `model_id`, so you can log a model without an active run, search logged models by name, and reference `models:/{model_id}`. It matters because one training run produces many checkpoints and variants, and for GenAI traces and eval metrics attach to the model version, so you can compare versions across experiments and across dev and prod. The breaking changes worth naming: Recipes removed entirely, the fastai and mleap flavors removed, `custom_metrics` replaced by `extra_metrics`, `baseline_model` removed from `evaluate`, and SHAP explainers no longer logged by default. I'd also expect the Deployments Server — the old AI Gateway — to have deprecated out, but I'd check that one rather than assert it.

**10.3 — "What is experiment-tracking discipline beyond 'we use MLflow'?"**
The test is whether someone else, six months later, can take a run id and rebuild the artefact and explain why it was chosen. That requires each run to log code commit, container digest, data snapshot id, full config, environment and the parent/child relationship for sweeps — automatically from the training entrypoint, not by hand. Metrics must be namespaced by dataset — `test_golden_v3/auc`, never bare `auc` — so a metric can never be compared across incompatible eval sets. And runs get promoted with a stage and an approver, with the registry entry linking back to the run.

**10.4 — "How do you stop people logging four thousand junk runs?"**
By making the tracker a place where things are found rather than dumped. Namespaced experiments per project with ownership, a naming and tagging convention enforced by the training entrypoint rather than by etiquette, `log_models=False` by default for sweeps so you don't flood artefact storage with checkpoints nobody will load, and parent/child run structure so a 200-trial sweep is one entry. Then a retention policy on unpromoted runs. The underlying problem is usually that nobody can find anything, and the fix is structure, not scolding.

**10.5 — "How do you version data alongside the model?"**
Use the table format's native versioning rather than copying data: Delta time travel or Iceberg snapshot ids give an immutable zero-copy reference you record in the run metadata, along with the query, because the version alone doesn't tell you which subset you took. Then pin it against garbage collection — VACUUM with a short retention will delete the files your snapshot references, so retention policy must be set by the reproducibility requirement, not by storage cost. If the source isn't a versioned table, materialise an immutable content-addressed artefact and store the manifest hash. DVC is the right shape when the workflow is file-based; lakeFS when you want branch semantics over the whole repository.

**10.6 — "Storage says your four hundred Delta versions cost too much. What's your argument?"**
That the retention window is set by the audit and reproducibility requirement, not by the storage bill, and that I can name the specific models whose lineage terminates in those versions. Then I'd narrow the ask rather than defend everything: retain full history only for snapshots referenced by a production model or a regulatory decision — usually a small subset — and expire the rest on a shorter clock. If they still want it gone, the honest statement is that we lose the ability to reproduce those models, and that decision needs to be made by whoever owns the regulatory exposure, in writing.

**10.7 — "How do you version a feature?"**
Never mutate a definition in place — a changed definition silently invalidates every model trained on the old one and every historical row. The feature name is part of the contract, so `txn_amt_7d_v2` is a new feature, backfilled independently, and models migrate deliberately. The registry records the definition hash, owner, source tables, freshness SLO and the models consuming it, so a proposed change can be blocked by its downstream consumers. Deprecation is a workflow — mark, alert, wait for migration, stop materialising — not a delete, because you still need it to reproduce an old model for an audit.

**10.8 — "A regulator asks you to reproduce a decision made fourteen months ago. What do you need to have kept?"**
Two layers. Model lineage: the model version, code commit, container digest, data snapshot, feature definitions and versions, config, evaluation results, the approver and the deployment record. Decision lineage: for that individual prediction, the model version, the exact input features or a reference sufficient to reconstruct them, the output and confidence, the threshold and business rules applied, and the final decision. Both append-only with integrity protection, retained on the regulatory horizon rather than the storage-budget horizon, and access to the audit log itself logged.

**10.9 — "Full input logging is too expensive at our volume. What do you keep?"**
Keep the identifiers and the reconstruction path rather than the payload: entity key, feature-set version, snapshot id, model version, score, threshold, decision. That lets you rebuild the exact vector from versioned sources, which is cheaper than storing it and is what an auditor actually needs. Then sample full vectors — say 1% plus 100% of any decision that was adverse, appealed or flagged — because the tail is where the questions come from. And be explicit that this trade only works if the underlying snapshots are retained; otherwise you've kept a pointer to nothing.

**10.10 — "What's in a model card and who reads it?"**
Purpose, intended and out-of-scope use, data sources with provenance, model and prompt versions, evaluation results with dates and eval-set versions, per-segment and fairness results where relevant, known limitations, the human-oversight design and the escalation path. Who reads it: procurement and security review at enterprise customers, internal risk, and the next engineer to own it. It's generated from the manifest and the eval artefacts rather than written by hand, otherwise it rots within two releases.

**10.11 — "MLflow Tracing — what is it and where do traces live?"**
It's the GenAI observability layer, OpenTelemetry-compatible, with typed spans for LLM, retriever, tool, chain, agent and parser, and one-line autoinstrumentation across a long list of frameworks plus a `@mlflow.trace` decorator for manual spans. For production the relevant detail is the trace location: traces can land in Delta tables in OpenTelemetry format, which is SQL-queryable and governed, versus the experiment store which had capacity caps. And production monitoring is scheduled scorers running against a sampled slice of live traces, attaching results as feedback — the selling point being that the same scorers run in dev and prod.

**10.12 — "How do you govern prompts?"**
As artefacts, not strings in code: a registry with semantic versioning, diff, peer review, and environment aliases pointing at immutable versions. Every trace records the exact prompt version so any output is reproducible and any regression bisectable. A prompt change goes through the same pipeline as a code change — eval suite in CI against the golden set, blocked on a regression beyond a stated margin, then canary at 5% watching quality, latency, cost and error rate. And prompts must be versioned as a *pair* with the model, because a prompt tuned on one model is not portable.

### 11. Security and compliance

**11.1 [TOP-25] — "Walk me through PII handling across an ML pipeline."**
Start with a classification at column and field level with an owner, a legal basis and a retention period, because you cannot protect what you haven't mapped. Then minimise: most models don't need raw identifiers, so direct identifiers are dropped, hashed or tokenised at ingestion and only derived aggregates cross into the feature layer. Enforce with column-level access control and dynamic masking in the catalog so the control lives on the data, not on each pipeline's good behaviour. Then the boundaries people forget: logs and traces, which capture feature values and prompts under a different retention policy; notebooks and ad-hoc exports; error messages; model artefacts, since embeddings and training samples live in checkpoints; and eval datasets copied into a Git repo. A deletion policy that covers the warehouse but not the feature store, the vector index, the logs and the backups is not a deletion policy.

**11.2 — "Tokenisation, masking or redaction — when do you use each?"**
Redaction removes irreversibly and is correct for free text going into an LLM prompt or a log, at the cost of any downstream analytical use. Masking preserves shape for display and is a poor privacy control, because a small value space plus auxiliary data makes re-identification easy. Tokenisation substitutes a surrogate — vault-based when you need controlled reversibility, deterministic or format-preserving when you need joins to keep working, accepting frequency-analysis and linkage risk within the token domain. The legal point that distinguishes a senior answer: pseudonymised data with a recoverable key is still personal data under GDPR Recital 26, so tokenisation reduces exposure, it doesn't exit the regime.

**11.3 — "You mask a clinical field before sending text to an LLM and the answers become useless. What's the trade-off?"**
That masking identity fields and masking substantive fields have completely different effects on task performance. I ran that benchmark myself on a side project, so I'll be clear it's not ResMed work: identity-masking preserved task performance almost as well as raw text, while masking the substantive clinical content collapsed it, because the model no longer has the thing it needs to reason about. So the design move is to tokenise the identifiers and keep the clinical content, with the authorisation boundary enforced at retrieval rather than by mutilating the text. And measure it — task accuracy under masking is an empirical question, not an assumption.

**11.4 [TOP-25] — "GDPR right-to-erasure against a trained model and a vector index."**
Split it into three layers because they have genuinely different answers. Source and derived data is straightforward engineering: delete from the operational store, propagate via CDC — and deletes really must propagate, since upsert-only pipelines are the classic bug — then bronze, silver, gold, the feature store's offline *and* online layers, caches, logs, traces and training snapshots, with backups covered by a written, tested policy of not restored and re-deleted on restore. Vector indexes are the layer people underestimate: you must delete the chunks and understand your engine's delete semantics, because HNSW implementations typically soft-delete and keep the vector in the graph until compaction. So you need a deletion SLA, a compaction schedule and a reconciliation job that proves the id is gone. Model weights is the contested layer: there's no accepted general method to remove one person's contribution, and the defensible position is to argue the parameters aren't personal data because the individual's data isn't reasonably extractable, *test* that with memorisation probes and record the result, bound exposure with a scheduled retraining cadence so persistence has a stated maximum, and add output-level suppression as a compensating control. What you must not do is claim erasure is complete while the vector index and online feature store still hold the data.

**11.5 — "Tenant isolation in a RAG system — how do you actually guarantee it?"**
The strongest form is physical: a namespace or index per tenant, so a query cannot address another tenant's vectors even with a bug in the filter. Where a shared index is used, the filter must be a pre-filter inside the search, not a post-filter, both for recall and because a post-filter skipped on a fallback path leaks. The tenant id must be derived server-side from the authenticated session's token claims and never read from the request body, the conversation or the model's output — anything the model can influence is attacker-controllable. Then a deny-by-default client that refuses to execute a query with no tenant predicate, so a coding error raises an exception rather than leaking. And prove it continuously: log the tenant label of every returned document with an automatic mismatch alarm, plant honeypot documents in a canary tenant that page on retrieval, and keep an integration test asserting cross-tenant retrieval returns zero.

**11.6 — "Prompt injection — how do you actually mitigate it?"**
Start from the correct premise: it's an architecture problem, not a prompt problem, because the model has no reliable way to distinguish trusted instructions from untrusted content in the same context, and neither RAG nor fine-tuning mitigates it. Indirect injection arrives via retrieved documents, tool outputs, file contents and email bodies. So close the exfiltration channels — markdown images whose URL fires a fetch, clickable links, any tool making an outbound request, and writes to shared stores — with an egress allowlist. Then scope every tool's permissions to the *end user's* authorisation rather than a broad service account, require human confirmation for destructive or outbound actions, separate the planner from the executor so untrusted content influences data but not control flow, and run an injection red-team suite in CI on every prompt and model change.

**11.7 — "What's the RAG-specific version of that threat?"**
In a multi-tenant work-management product, a document *is* an injection vector: any user who can put text into a shared sheet or a comment can attempt to steer another user's agent. Combine that with permission-aware retrieval and the real threat is injected instructions in attacker-controlled content, executed with the victim's permissions and the victim's tool scope. That's why input filtering on the user's message is insufficient — you have to scan retrieved context too, and more importantly you have to assume the scan fails and rely on tool scoping and egress control.

**11.8 — "Secrets in ML systems — what's different?"**
The blast radius is larger and the hygiene is worse, because ML workflows are full of interactive environments. Notebooks print environment variables, experiment trackers log whole config dicts including credentials, training scripts run with long-lived personal cloud keys, and model artefacts sometimes contain configs with tokens baked in. So: workload identity and OIDC federation instead of static keys, short-lived scoped tokens for interactive work, secrets injected at runtime, a CI scanner that covers notebooks and artefacts as well as source, and per-environment scoping. Rotation with a tested revocation path — where the test isn't "can we rotate" but "we rotated and we know what would have broken".

**11.9 — "SBOM and provenance for ML — what's different from a normal SBOM?"**
A conventional CycloneDX or SPDX SBOM covers Python and system dependencies, which is necessary but misses the ML-specific components: the base model with its digest and licence, the datasets, the adapters and the inference engine. CycloneDX's ML-BOM extension exists for exactly that. Pair it with signed in-toto or SLSA attestations from the build system so the registry can enforce "only models built by the approved pipeline from an approved base with a recorded dataset hash may be promoted". The point isn't the document, it's being able to answer "which deployed models are affected by this CVE, this poisoned dataset or this revoked licence" in minutes.

**11.10 — "DPDP for an India GCC — what changes for an ML platform?"**
The structural differences from GDPR are the ones that bite. Consent is the dominant basis — there's no legitimate-interests catch-all, the Act enumerates legitimate uses instead — notices must be standalone and plain-language, and breach notification to the Board and to affected principals has **no materiality threshold**, so every personal data breach is reportable, which is a far heavier operational burden than GDPR's risk-based test. If the entity is designated a Significant Data Fiduciary you inherit an India-resident DPO reporting to the board, an annual DPIA, an annual independent data audit, and **algorithmic due diligence** — an explicit obligation to verify that algorithms and trained models used in processing don't pose risks to data principals' rights. That last one is the ML-platform item, and it maps directly onto model lineage, documented evaluation including fairness slices, and a registry that can say what was deployed when and on what data. On timing I'd say the phased ramp runs to roughly mid-2027 and I'd verify the current dates rather than quote them precisely.

**11.11 — "Legal says we've been designated an SDF. What are your first three builds?"**
One: a lineage and registry spine that can answer, for any deployed model, what data it was trained on, what evaluation it passed, who approved it and when it was deployed — because you cannot perform algorithmic due diligence or a DPIA on a system without that. Two: a decision log with per-prediction inputs-or-references, model version, threshold and outcome, append-only, because rights requests and audits are per-individual. Three: the deletion fan-out — a tested path that reaches the warehouse, feature store online and offline, vector index, caches, traces, checkpoints and eval datasets, with a published SLA. Everything else — fairness slicing, model cards, the independent audit evidence pack — is assembled from those three.

**11.12 — "Adversarial risks specific to a model in production?"**
Model extraction, where an attacker distils your model through the API — mitigate with rate limits, per-account cost budgets, output granularity limits like returning a label rather than a full probability vector, and anomaly detection on query patterns. Membership inference and training-data extraction for generative models — mitigate with training-data deduplication, which is the single most effective control, output filtering and memorisation testing before release. Data poisoning where an attacker influences training data through user-generated content or a feedback loop — mitigate with provenance on training data, anomaly detection on new batches, and never auto-retraining on unfiltered production feedback. And evasion for fraud and moderation, where the adversary is adaptive and offline benchmarks decay, so the answer is a retraining loop driven by observed evasions.

### 12. SQL and Python for a platform engineer

**12.1 — "What Python does a platform engineer write that a data scientist doesn't?"**
Long-lived, concurrent, failure-tolerant code. Async I/O for serving and for fan-out to feature stores and vector indexes; Pydantic contracts at every boundary so a malformed payload fails at the edge rather than three layers in; structured logging and OpenTelemetry instrumentation; retry and circuit-breaker logic with idempotency keys; and packaging — wheels, entry points, pinned lockfiles, reproducible containers. The mental shift is that a notebook can fail loudly and be re-run, whereas a service has to degrade predictably.

**12.2 — "How do you make feature fetching fast?"**
Batch the lookups. A model needing 200 features across six entities should issue about six multi-get calls, not 200 gets — feature fetch is usually a larger share of p99 than inference for classical models. Then measure feature-fetch latency separately from model latency in the traces, or you optimise the wrong half. Beyond that: connection pooling sized to concurrency, a timeout shorter than the caller's, and an explicit degraded path returning a default the model was trained to handle plus a flag feature marking it missing.

**12.3 — "asyncio versus threads versus processes for an inference service."**
Async for I/O-bound fan-out — feature store, vector DB, downstream model calls — where you're waiting on the network and one event loop handles high concurrency cheaply. Threads for blocking library calls you can't make async, accepting the GIL. Processes for CPU-bound work, which for CPU inference means one worker per core with the threading env vars pinned. The operational trap that actually bites: numeric libraries default to using every visible core, so inside a container with a CPU quota you get massive context-switching and destroyed tail latency — set `OMP_NUM_THREADS` and the intra-op thread count to the actual cgroup quota, and benchmark at production concurrency rather than single-request.

**12.4 — "Your CPU model is fine at 10 QPS and falls apart at 40. What's happening?"**
Almost certainly thread oversubscription plus queueing. Each request spawns a numeric library thread pool sized to visible cores, so at 40 concurrent requests you have hundreds of threads fighting over a two-core quota and the kernel spends its time context-switching. Confirm it by checking cgroup throttling counters and by pinning threads to one and re-running — if p99 improves dramatically at lower thread counts, that's it. Then the fix is one intra-op thread per worker process, worker count matched to the quota, and admission control so you shed rather than queue into overload.

**12.5 — "How do you test a data pipeline in Python?"**
Pure transformation functions with tiny hand-built fixtures covering the boundary cases — nulls, empty groups, duplicate keys, timezone edges — because those are where pipelines actually break. Property-based tests for invariants like idempotency and row-count conservation. Contract tests at each stage boundary asserting schema and value domains. And a small-sample end-to-end run in CI on the real code path. What I avoid is tests that pass without testing anything — asserting a job returned zero rather than asserting the output is correct.

**12.6 — "How would you write a drift monitor as a library rather than a script?"**
A metric computation separated from the alerting policy separated from the transport. Compute produces a typed record — feature, window, statistic, value, sample size, reference id — written to a metrics table; policy reads that table and decides warn or page from thresholds and persistence rules held in config; transport routes to the right audience. That separation is what lets you backfill a new threshold over history to see how often it would have fired, which is the only honest way to set one. At ResMed the equivalent utility ingested data-scientist-authored thresholds and slice definitions and provisioned the Datadog dashboards and alerts from Snowflake feature statistics.

**12.7 — "What's your position on Pandas versus Spark in a pipeline?"**
Use the smallest tool that fits, and be explicit about the crossover. Pandas or Polars for anything that fits comfortably in memory on one machine, because the debugging loop is seconds and the failure modes are obvious. Spark when the data genuinely doesn't fit or you need the cluster's parallelism — and then write DataFrame API or SQL rather than Python UDFs, because UDFs break the vectorised engine and, on Databricks specifically, aren't accelerated by Photon at all. The wrong answer is Spark by default for a hundred-megabyte table, which I've seen cost more in cluster startup than the work.

**12.8 — "Write a health check for a model endpoint. What's in it?"**
Not a 200 from an HTTP handler. Readiness runs a real inference on a canary input and asserts the output shape and a known score within tolerance, so a model that failed to load fails the check. It also asserts that the loaded model version matches the expected version from config, which catches a silent deploy mismatch. Liveness is separate and deliberately dumb — process responsive — because gating liveness on a twelve-minute weight load produces a restart loop. And the health endpoint reports model version, feature-contract hash and weight digest, so an operator can answer "what is actually running" without a shell.

**12.9 — "SQL you'd expect a platform engineer to write?"**
Window functions for anything sequential — as-of joins, sessionisation, first-and-last-per-group, running aggregates — because those are the shape of most feature and monitoring queries. Set-based comparisons for reconciliation between a source and an index. Anti-joins for orphan detection. And cost-aware SQL: partition pruning predicates, avoiding a cross join hidden behind an unqualified condition, and knowing what your engine does with a `DISTINCT` over a wide table. See the SQL subsection below for the five I'd expect to be asked live.

**12.10 — "What's the most common SQL bug you see in ML pipelines?"**
A silent join fan-out. A join intended as one-to-one is actually one-to-many because the right-hand key isn't unique — often because it's a slowly-changing dimension with multiple versions per key — and your row count triples, your aggregates inflate, and nothing errors. The detection is a row-count assertion at the transformation boundary comparing input and output cardinality against the expected relationship, which is a one-line check that catches more real defects than any distribution monitor.

### 13. Databricks lakehouse specifics

**13.1 [TOP-25] — "How much Databricks have you done?"**
About a year and a half, on **Azure** Databricks, and it was data-quality and ETL work rather than Lakehouse platform ownership. Concretely: large-scale data-quality checks with Deequ on Spark, and drift-detection jobs orchestrated through Azure Data Factory. I have not used Unity Catalog, Mosaic AI Agent Framework or Databricks Vector Search, and I haven't worked at petabyte scale — I want to be precise about that rather than have it come out later. What does transfer is the substrate: Spark, Delta semantics, data-quality constraint frameworks, and the metrics-repository-plus-baseline pattern that Databricks' data profiling implements as a product.

> **Say it like this:** "My strongest bridge is data quality. Deequ's `Check` and `Constraint` map onto Lakeflow expectations; Deequ's `AnalysisRunner` and metrics repository map onto the profile metrics table; and Deequ's anomaly detection over a metrics repository is the same idea as the drift metrics table with a baseline. The difference is that expectations are inline in the pipeline with an `ON VIOLATION` policy, whereas Deequ is a separate verification pass — and that difference changes where bad data can reach."

**13.2 — "What's Unity Catalog for, in one answer?"**
A governance layer over a three-level namespace — catalog, schema, object — where the governed objects are not just tables but volumes, functions, models, and now agents and MCP services. Above it sits a metastore per region, and metastore-level objects like storage credentials, external locations, connections and shares sit *outside* the three-level namespace, which is a common depth probe. Privileges inherit downward from `USE CATALOG` and `USE SCHEMA`. I'd be clear I know its model rather than claiming operating experience.

**13.3 — "What does Unity Catalog not do?"**
Speaking from its documented model rather than from operating it — it's not a data quality engine — there are no constraints beyond Delta CHECK and NOT NULL, so quality is pipeline expectations plus data profiling. It's not a transformation or orchestration engine. It governs *through Databricks compute*, so a process reading the underlying cloud files with its own credentials bypasses it entirely. Lineage is per-metastore and doesn't cross regions, and it's broken by path-based reads and obscured by UDFs. And there are no cross-metastore joins, so multi-region means multiple metastores bridged by federation or sharing.

**13.4 — "Delta transaction log — how does it work?"**
An ordered set of JSON commit files under `_delta_log/`, each containing actions — metaData, add, remove, protocol, commitInfo, txn — with a Parquet checkpoint every ten commits by default so readers don't replay everything. ACID comes from optimistic concurrency: a writer reads a snapshot, writes files, then atomically claims the next version, and a conflict either retries or raises. Data skipping uses min/max/null-count statistics on the first thirty-two columns by default, which is why reordering a wide table so filter columns come first is a real tuning trick. And log files are cleaned on their own clock — `delta.logRetentionDuration`, thirty days by default, and only once a later checkpoint covers them. What people get wrong is thinking VACUUM governs that; VACUUM removes unreferenced *data* files on `deletedFileRetentionDuration`. Two retentions, two clocks, and the reproducibility question depends on both.

**13.5 — "We ran VACUUM. Can we roll back to last month?"**
No. VACUUM removes files no longer referenced with a default retention of seven days, so it destroys time travel past that window; going below seven days requires disabling a safety check and can corrupt concurrent readers. History retention is a separate property — `logRetentionDuration`, defaulting to thirty days — and in recent runtimes it must be at least the deleted-file retention. The practical consequence for ML is that a training snapshot referenced by a production model must have its retention set by the reproducibility requirement, or your "reproducible" pipeline breaks silently in a month.

**13.6 — "Z-order or liquid clustering?"**
Liquid clustering for all new tables. It's incremental rather than a full rewrite, and you can change the clustering keys without rewriting the data, with `CLUSTER BY AUTO` letting the platform pick keys from query history. The constraint to name: it's mutually exclusive with both partitioning and ZORDER. Z-order isn't formally deprecated but it's legacy guidance. Alongside that, predictive optimization now runs ANALYZE, OPTIMIZE and VACUUM automatically on managed tables, which is the "you shouldn't be hand-scheduling OPTIMIZE any more" answer.

**13.7 — "Partitioning and file sizing."**
Target 128 MB to 1 GB per file — smaller and you pay listing, metadata, planning and per-file open overhead that dominates on object storage; larger and you lose parallelism and pruning granularity. Partition on a low-cardinality column that appears in most predicates, usually a date, and never on something like user_id, which creates millions of tiny directories and destroys planning time. For within-partition skipping use clustering rather than more partitions. Streaming writes are the main source of the small-file problem, one file per micro-batch per partition, so schedule compaction — and remember compaction rewrites files, which interacts with time travel retention and with readers holding an old snapshot.

**13.8 — "What's the default behaviour of a failing expectation in a declarative pipeline?"**
From the documented semantics rather than from having run declarative pipelines: warn — and the important part is that warn still **writes the invalid records to the target** and merely flags them in metrics. Only `ON VIOLATION DROP ROW` discards them and `ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE` stops the update. Most candidates assume expectations quarantine by default; they don't, and the quarantine pattern is something you build with an inverted-condition expectation routing to a separate table. The metrics land in the event log, which is queryable as a table, and that's how you build data-quality dashboards and alerting on top.

**13.9 — "How would you do data quality on Databricks given your Deequ background?"**
Expectations inline in the pipeline for the blocking checks — schema conformance, row count within a band, primary key uniqueness at the ingestion boundary; referential integrity, null-rate bands and join fan-out at the transformation boundary — with `FAIL UPDATE` only where publishing bad data is worse than not publishing. Then data profiling for the statistical layer: profile metrics per column, per window, per slice, and drift metrics against both the previous window and a baseline table. For an inference profile the right baseline is the training or validation set, which is how you detect drift relative to what the model was trained on. The tiering decision — which failures are allowed to publish — matters far more than the tool.

**13.10 — "What drift metrics does the profiling layer compute?"**
For numeric features, Wasserstein distance plus deltas in mean, median and standard deviation; for categorical, Jensen–Shannon divergence, a chi-squared statistic and p-value, total variation distance and L-infinity distance; plus null-count and row-count deltas. Two limits worth naming: time-series and inference profiles compute over the last thirty days, and snapshot profiles have a table-size cap. I'm confident on the metric set; I'd verify the exact column names in the metrics table rather than quote them.

**13.11 — "Deploy code or deploy models?"**
I haven't run asset bundles in anger, so this is their documented pattern plus my own view of the trade. Databricks' recommended pattern is to promote *code* across environments and retrain in each, because prod is where prod data lives. With a shared registry you can also promote artefacts by alias, so the modern answer is code promotion by default with alias-based artefact promotion where retraining in prod is impractical — for example when the training run is expensive or the production data is a superset that doesn't change the model materially. Asset bundles are the packaging: one `databricks.yml`, targets per environment, and a development mode that prefixes resources and pauses schedules so a developer deploy can't collide with production.

**13.12 — "Biggest Databricks cost mistake you've seen?"**
I haven't run a Databricks cost review myself — my Databricks was Azure, Deequ and ETL, and cost wasn't my surface there. So let me answer as what I'd look for, in order. First, scheduled jobs pinned to all-purpose compute rather than jobs compute, at roughly three to four times the DBU rate for identical work; I'd verify the current ratio, but the direction isn't in doubt and it's the largest single line item I'd expect to find. Second, no auto-termination on interactive clusters. Third, Photon left on Python-UDF-heavy jobs, where it costs two to three times the DBUs and accelerates nothing, which is a real trap because Photon reads as a free speedup. And before any of that I'd want to know whether `system.billing.usage` is even joinable to a team — sliced by `custom_tags` and `usage_metadata`, joined to `list_prices` on the effective date range — because tags are set at cluster creation, so if tagging isn't enforced at admission the report simply can't be built and the first deliverable is the tagging policy, not the savings.

> **Say it like this:** "I'd rather tell you the method than borrow a war story I don't have. The method is: make it attributable, then rank by spend, then attack the top three — and 'make it attributable' is usually the part that takes a month."

**13.13 — "Serverless changes the cost model how?"**
I haven't run Databricks serverless, so this is from the pricing model. For serverless the DBU rate already includes the VM cost, so serverless DBU rates look higher than classic rates but aren't comparable line for line. It also removes the cluster you would have tagged, which is why serverless usage policies exist — they inject tags per user into the billing records so spend stays attributable. Operationally serverless mostly removes a class of cost mistake (idle clusters, slow starts) and adds an attribution problem you solve with policy rather than with tags on infrastructure.

**13.14 — "Do you know about Lakebase / Lakeflow / the 2026 renames?"**
Enough to not sound like I read a 2024 tutorial. Delta Live Tables is now Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines, Workflows are Lakeflow Jobs, Lakehouse Monitoring is surfaced as data profiling under data quality monitoring, Mosaic AI Vector Search is Databricks AI Search, and Online Tables became Online Feature Stores on Lakebase, which is the managed Postgres-compatible OLTP layer. The trap I'd flag is Lakewatch — their agentic SIEM, announced this year and since backed by the Panther Labs acquisition — which is security, not model monitoring. Confusing the two would be a tell. I'd use both names in conversation: "Delta Live Tables, which I think is now Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines".

### 14. LangChain and LangGraph

**14.1 [TOP-25] — "Where do LangChain and LangGraph fit in an ML Ops pipeline?"**
LangGraph is a state machine with persistence and good ergonomics for human-in-the-loop interrupts, and that's genuinely the useful 20% of it. LangChain is glue and integrations. For a platform I'd use LangGraph where the workflow has real branching, needs to resume after a restart, or needs an approval step; and I'd own the loop directly for single-purpose agents, because most of the reliability I need — cost budgets, idempotency, replayable traces — is not something a framework gives you. At TrueBalance the internal developer assistant is built on MCP rather than a framework, with each task running in an isolated Git workspace, which is the same instinct: own the boundary, borrow the plumbing.

**14.2 — "What does the LangGraph checkpointer actually give you, and what's the operational cost?"**
It checkpoints state at every node transition, which is what makes `interrupt()` durable across a process restart — that's the real reason teams pick it. Three operational details that signal experience: `checkpointer.setup()` creates the schema and belongs in a CI/CD migration step, not application startup, or every replica races to create tables on deploy; checkpoint tables grow without bound and need a TTL and retention job; and checkpoints contain full message state, which means customer data in your Postgres, subject to the same retention, residency and deletion obligations as everything else — so in a multi-tenant product those rows need tenant scoping and row-level security.

**14.3 — "How do you stop an agent looping and burning money?"**
Bounds, all of them, enforced at the gateway so no code path can bypass them: max steps per run, max calls per tool, max retries with exponential backoff and jitter, wall-clock timeouts per tool and per run, and hard token or dollar caps per run, per user, per tenant and per day. Then two rules that catch the specific failure: a repeated-failure rule terminating when the same tool with the same arguments fails twice, and no-progress detection hashing the tool-and-arguments tuple so three repeats break the loop. And when budget is exhausted, fall back or escalate to a human — never silently return a partial answer.

**14.4 — "Why do agents loop in the first place?"**
Most often because a tool fails without signalling failure — it returns an empty result set on error, the agent reads that as "no results", rephrases and retries forever. So tools must return structured errors with a code, a message and a retryable flag, never an empty success. The other causes are no valid stopping condition, two nodes that undo each other, and context rot where history grows until quality degrades and cost explodes. Documented cases include an agent calling the same broken tool four hundred times in five minutes before a platform rate limit stopped it.

**14.5 — "Retries in an agent — what's the catch?"**
That a retried step re-executes a non-idempotent tool, so you've now created two tickets or sent two emails. Every mutating tool needs an idempotency key generated once per logical intent, so a retry is a no-op at the sink. And retry budgets matter: three retries at each of three layers is twenty-seven times the load on a service that's already struggling, which turns a slow dependency into an outage. Exponential backoff with full jitter, because without jitter retries synchronise into a thundering herd.

**14.6 — "How do you evaluate an agent?"**
Three levels, and you need all three. Final task success against a rubric — what the business cares about and the least diagnostic. Trajectory — the sequence of steps, either matched against a reference or judged, which tells you *how* it failed. And single-step tool accuracy decomposed into tool selection, schema validity, argument correctness and side-effect correctness, because the fixes for those four are completely different. Alongside those, the operational metrics people forget: steps versus the minimum, loop rate, recovery rate after a tool error, cost per successful task, p95 wall clock and human-escalation rate.

**14.7 — "MCP — what's the ops view?"**
It's a protocol, not a framework, and its value is avoiding N×M tool integrations across clients. The ops view is that it's a supply-chain surface: pin server versions, review tool descriptions as code because a tool description is untrusted text that lands in the model's context — that's the tool-poisoning vector — scope OAuth tokens narrowly per server, and log every tool call with arguments and results. The spec hardened authorization by making MCP servers OAuth resource servers and requiring RFC 8707 resource indicators, so a token is bound to the specific MCP server it was issued for. That is what kills token passthrough and the confused-deputy problem you get the moment one client talks to many servers — without it, a token minted for a low-trust server is replayable against a high-trust one.

**14.8 — "How do you version prompts, tools and models together?"**
*Extends 10.12 — the new material here is the tool schema and the trace triple, so lead with those rather than re-stating prompt versioning.* As one deployable unit. A prompt is versioned against a specific model, because a prompt tuned on one model isn't portable; a tool schema is an API contract with a deprecation window; and the trace records prompt version, model version and tool versions so any production run can be replayed offline. Then the change pipeline is the same as code: eval suite in CI gated on a regression margin, canary at 5% watching quality, latency, cost and error rate, automatic rollback. Pin model versions to dated ids and never point production at a floating alias, because a provider rotating a model behind an alias changes behaviour with no deploy on your side.

### 15. High availability, disaster recovery and multi-region

This maps to the JD's *first* "You Have" bullet — "Enterprise SaaS software solutions with high availability and scalability" — and it is the likeliest design prompt in the round that isn't about models at all. Answer it as a SaaS engineer who happens to serve models, because that is what they are hiring.

**15.1 — "Design the serving tier for high availability. What are your RTO and RPO, and how do you get them?"**
I'd refuse to design before the numbers are agreed, because RTO and RPO are the entire design. RTO is how long the feature can be down; RPO is how much recent state you can afford to lose. And the useful move for an ML feature specifically is to set them *per component*, because they differ wildly: the model artefact has an RPO of effectively zero cost — it's immutable, content-addressed and replicable to every region in advance, so losing a region loses nothing. The online feature store has a real RPO, because it holds recent state you cannot regenerate instantly. The vector index sits in between: it's derived, so it's rebuildable, but the rebuild takes hours and costs embedding spend, which means you replicate it rather than plan to rebuild it. Prediction and decision logs have the strictest RPO because they're an audit obligation, so they stream to durable cross-region storage synchronously.

| Component | Rebuildable? | Realistic RPO | Failover approach |
|---|---|---|---|
| Model artefact + manifest | Immutable, pre-replicated | Zero | Cross-region object replication; each region pulls by digest |
| Container image | Immutable | Zero | Replicate to a registry in each region; never pull cross-region at scale-out |
| Online feature store | No — recent state | Seconds to minutes | Async replication; accept staleness, expose it as a feature |
| Vector index | Yes, but hours + embedding cost | Minutes | Replicate the index; rebuild is the *third* option, not the second |
| Offline lakehouse | Source of truth | Minutes | Cross-region table replication on a schedule matched to retrain cadence |
| Prediction/decision log | No — audit obligation | Near zero | Synchronous durable write, cross-region, before the response returns |

> **Say it like this:** "The thing people get wrong on ML disaster recovery is treating the model as the hard part. The model is the *easy* part — it's an immutable blob, I can have it in every region before the incident. The hard parts are the online feature store, because it holds state I can't regenerate, and the decision log, because losing it is a compliance failure rather than an availability one."

**15.2 — "Active-active or active-passive for an inference service?"**
Active-active for stateless scoring, and inference is closer to stateless than most services think — the model is read-only, so two regions serving the same immutable artefact behind latency-based or weighted routing give you both HA and lower latency for free, and you get continuous proof the second region works, which is the failure mode that kills active-passive. Active-passive is the honest choice when the state is the problem: a single-writer feature store, a strongly-consistent decision ledger, or a regulated data-residency constraint that forbids serving EU traffic from another region. The trap in active-active for ML specifically is *model version skew* — during a progressive rollout the two regions can be running different model versions, so the same customer gets different answers depending on routing. That has to be either accepted explicitly and documented, or prevented by pinning a user to a region for the duration of a session and rolling out region-by-region rather than globally.

> **Say it like this:** "Active-passive fails on the day you need it, because nobody has exercised the passive side. If I have to run active-passive for a state reason, then I'm running a scheduled failover drill in production, or I don't actually have a second region — I have a bill."

**15.3 — "A region goes down. Walk me through what happens to a RAG feature."**
Health checks fail, the global router shifts traffic, and the interesting question is what the surviving region *has*. Model and image: present, because they were replicated by digest ahead of time. Vector index: present if replicated, and if it wasn't, this is the moment you discover that a four-hour rebuild is your RTO. Feature store: present but stale by the replication lag, so scores are computed on slightly old features — which is usually acceptable and must be *declared* rather than discovered, because a silently stale feature is exactly the failure mode from 1.6. Then two second-order effects people miss. First, the surviving region now carries double the traffic, so if it was sized at 60% headroom it is now saturated and you have converted a regional outage into a global latency incident — capacity for failover has to be pre-provisioned or the autoscaler has to be able to get instances in a rush, which is precisely when GPU capacity is scarcest. Second, in-flight async work: SQS-style queues and any partially-completed batch need idempotent replay, or failover produces duplicate side effects.

**15.4 — "What does a degraded-but-available AI feature look like?"**
This is the most valuable HA question for an AI product and most teams have no answer, so having one is a differentiator. The principle is that the feature degrades in defined steps rather than returning a 500, and each step is a product decision made in advance, not an engineering improvisation at 3am. A ladder for a RAG-backed assistant, from healthy to worst:

```text
  L0  full     retrieval + rerank + generation + citations          normal
  L1  reranker down       fusion order, skip cross-encoder          quality dip, invisible
  L2  index stale         serve + surface "last updated <time>"     honest, still useful
  L3  generation degraded smaller/cheaper model, shorter answers    slower, still grounded
  L4  retrieval down      no answer; keyword search results only    obviously narrower
  L5  hard down           deterministic UI path, feature hidden     no wrong answers
```

The rule that makes the ladder safe is that a degraded AI feature must never silently produce a *lower-quality answer that looks identical*. L2 surfaces staleness. L4 stops answering rather than answering ungrounded. For a classifier the equivalent ladder is: full feature vector → a documented default plus a missing-flag feature the model was trained to handle → a rules-based fallback → refuse and route to a human. And the fallback path needs the same monitoring as the primary, because a fallback nobody watches becomes the permanent state after an incident nobody closed.

> **Say it like this:** "The worst outcome for an AI feature isn't downtime, it's confident wrongness during a partial outage. So my degradation ladder is designed so that every step down is either invisible or visible — never a quiet quality drop that users only detect three weeks later."

**15.5 — "How do you test DR, and how do you know your RTO is real?"**
By failing over on purpose, on a schedule, in production, with the business informed. An untested DR plan is a document, and I'd say that plainly. The progression I'd run: first a game day on paper to find the missing runbooks; then a failover of a non-critical read path; then a full regional failover during a low-traffic window with a pre-agreed abort; then unannounced. Measure the actual RTO rather than the planned one — the gap is always instructive and is usually somewhere nobody modelled, like a DNS TTL nobody lowered, a secret that only existed in one region, a Terraform state that can only be applied from one place, or an IAM role scoped to a single region. For ML specifically, three checks that generic DR drills miss: can the surviving region pull the current model *by digest* without the primary registry; is the feature-store replication lag actually within the RPO you claimed, measured rather than configured; and does the decision log survive the cut with no gap, because that's the one where a hole is a compliance finding rather than an outage.

**15.6 — "Scalability, not availability — how do you know the platform will hold at ten times the load?"**
Load-test the *shape*, not the volume. Ten times the requests against a synthetic uniform load tells you almost nothing, because the failures at scale come from distribution, not from count: the p99 prompt, the tenant with a hundred times more documents, the hour when every customer's scheduled report fires simultaneously. So I'd replay captured production traffic amplified, preserving the arrival burstiness and the input-size distribution, and I'd look for the knee rather than the ceiling — the point where latency stops degrading linearly, which for LLM serving is KV-cache exhaustion and preemption, and for classical serving is usually connection-pool or feature-store saturation rather than the model at all. Then the three structural questions: what is the per-tenant blast radius when one tenant scales anomalously (quotas and admission control, not capacity); which component has a hard ceiling that can't be scaled horizontally (usually a single-writer store or a rate-limited third-party API); and what breaks *first* — because the correct answer to a scale question is naming the first bottleneck and its number, not asserting that everything scales.

### 16. Ingesting structured and unstructured data at scale

The JD says "Solution handling large scale structured and unstructured data from varied data sources" as its own line. Section 7 covers RAG document ingest as a retrieval problem; this covers it as a *data platform* problem, which is what the bullet is asking.

**16.1 — "Design ingestion for structured and unstructured data from varied sources."**
One landing zone, two paths after it, and a medallion structure over both — the design mistake is to build two parallel platforms because the data is shaped differently.

```text
   SOURCES                    LANDING                 BRONZE            SILVER              GOLD
   ┌──────────────┐
   │ App DBs      │──CDC────┐
   │ SaaS APIs    │──poll───┤
   │ Event stream │──stream─┤          ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │              │         ├─────────▶│ raw, immutable, partitioned by arrival date,      │
   │ Files/S3 drop│──notify─┤          │ payload kept verbatim + source + ingest_ts + hash  │
   │ Attachments  │──notify─┤          └───────┬───────────────────────────────┬───────────┘
   │ PDFs/scans   │──notify─┘                  │ structured                    │ unstructured
   └──────────────┘                            ▼                               ▼
                                        ┌─────────────┐                 ┌──────────────┐
                                        │ parse/typed │                 │ extract:     │
                                        │ schema      │                 │ text, layout,│
                                        │ evolution   │                 │ OCR, tables  │
                                        └──────┬──────┘                 └──────┬───────┘
                                               │                               │
                                               ▼                               ▼
                                    ┌────────────────────┐        ┌────────────────────────┐
                                    │ conformed entities │◀──id──▶│ doc records + chunks   │
                                    │ (typed, deduped,   │  keys  │ (text + metadata +     │
                                    │  SCD2 dimensions)  │        │  ACL + embeddings)     │
                                    └─────────┬──────────┘        └───────────┬────────────┘
                                              │                               │
                                              ▼                               ▼
                                        features / marts              vector index + KG
                                              └───────────┬───────────────────┘
                                                          ▼
                                                   models & retrieval
   DEAD LETTER  ◀── anything that fails parse/extract/validate, with the raw payload,
                    the error, the parser version, and a replay handle.  Never dropped.
```

The four decisions that make it work. **Land raw and immutable first** — every parser you write today is wrong in some way you'll discover in six months, and if you didn't keep the original payload you cannot reprocess. **Schema-on-read for the unstructured leg, schema-on-write for the structured leg** — you cannot enforce a schema on a PDF, but you *can* enforce a schema on the *record you extract from it*, and that extracted record is where the contract lives. **The join key is the point** — the value of having both legs on one platform is that an attachment can be attributed to a row, a project and an owner, and if the unstructured leg has no foreign key back to the entity model, you have built a document search engine next to a warehouse rather than one system. **Everything fails to a dead letter with a replay handle**, never to a log line.

**16.2 — "PDFs, scans and attachments at scale — what actually breaks?"**
Cost and variance, in that order, and neither is the parser. Cost: OCR and layout models are per-page and they are not cheap, so the first control is a content hash so you never re-extract an unchanged document, and the second is tiering — cheap text extraction first, and escalate to OCR or a layout model only when the cheap path yields too little text or the document is detected as scanned. That routing decision is worth more than any accuracy improvement in the expensive parser. Variance: a real corpus contains password-protected files, corrupt files, forty-thousand-page files, files whose extension lies about their type, embedded spreadsheets, and rotated scans, so every stage needs a per-document timeout and a size cap, and one pathological document must not be able to stall a batch — which means per-document isolation and a bounded retry, not a monolithic job. Then the two quality traps: tables lose their meaning when flattened to text, so tables get extracted as structured records rather than as prose; and extraction quality has to be *sampled and measured* per source type, because a connector that silently returns empty text for one document class is invisible in aggregate metrics and shows up months later as "the assistant doesn't know about contracts".

**16.3 — "Mixed-schema connectors — how do you keep twenty sources from becoming twenty pipelines?"**
By separating the connector from the conformance. A connector's only job is to land the source's payload verbatim plus a standard envelope — source id, source version, ingest timestamp, arrival partition, payload hash, and a delete tombstone flag — so every connector is small, mechanical and independently testable. Conformance to the entity model happens once, downstream, in one place with one set of rules. That's what stops twenty sources becoming twenty bespoke pipelines. On schema evolution: additive changes auto-evolve and are recorded; type changes and drops are *breaking* and must fail the pipeline rather than silently coerce, because a silent int-to-string coercion is how a feature becomes constant. And the practical detail that pays for itself is a schema registry with a compatibility mode enforced in the producer's CI, so a breaking change is rejected at their pull request instead of discovered in my 3am page.

**16.4 — "What happens to a record you cannot parse?"**
It goes to a dead-letter table — a table, not a queue and not a log — carrying the raw payload, the source and envelope, the failure reason, the parser version, the attempt count and a replay handle. Three properties matter. It's **queryable**, so "what fraction of source X is failing and since when" is a SQL question; a dead-letter queue you can't aggregate is a hiding place. It has an **owner and an SLO** — dead-letter volume and age are monitored SLIs, because the real failure mode is not the parse error, it's the dead-letter table nobody has looked at for four months while 3% of a source silently vanished. And it's **replayable by partition** after a parser fix, idempotently, which is only possible because the raw payload was kept. The one nuance: distinguish *malformed* from *unsupported*. Malformed is a defect and should alert. Unsupported — a new document type nobody has written an extractor for — is a backlog item, and mixing the two means the alert is noise within a week.

> **Say it like this:** "The number I'd want on a dashboard from day one is the fraction of each source that reaches gold. Not the row count, the *yield*. A pipeline that succeeds while quietly discarding 3% of one source looks perfectly healthy on every metric except that one."

### 17. Cloud choice — AWS, Azure, GCP

**17.1 — "You've used AWS and Azure. How do they differ for ML platform work, and which would you pick here?"**
This is the one JD line I can answer with no hedge at all: about five years of cloud with AWS as the primary, and roughly a year and a half on Azure — Databricks, Data Factory, ML Studio and Azure OpenAI. The differences that actually matter to a platform engineer are not the service lists.

| Dimension | AWS | Azure |
|---|---|---|
| ML platform centre of gravity | SageMaker as a broad, somewhat sprawling suite; you compose | Azure ML plus a very strong first-party Databricks relationship; more opinionated |
| Identity | IAM — fine-grained, powerful, easy to get subtly wrong | Entra ID + RBAC — coarser, but enterprise identity is genuinely better integrated |
| Data platform | Composed: S3 + Glue + Athena + Redshift/Iceberg | More cohesive: ADLS + Databricks/Synapse/Fabric, tighter defaults |
| Orchestration | Step Functions, MWAA, or you run Airflow | Data Factory as the default, which is strong on connectors and weak as a code-first orchestrator |
| Foundation models | Bedrock as the multi-vendor front door | Azure OpenAI, deeply integrated, with enterprise networking and residency stories |
| Kubernetes | EKS, with Karpenter as a real differentiator for GPU fleets | AKS, competent, less of a GPU-scheduling ecosystem |
| Where it bites | IAM complexity and service sprawl | Fewer escape hatches when the opinionated path doesn't fit |

For this role the JD says "AWS hosted data platform preferable", and I'd agree with that for a serving-heavy ML platform — EKS plus Karpenter for the compute fleet, S3 and Iceberg or Delta for the data plane, and the maturity of the spot and instance-family ecosystem matters more than it sounds when accelerator cost is a line item. Where I'd push back on a pure-AWS answer is if the analytics estate is already Databricks: then fighting the existing gravity to move the lakehouse costs more than it saves, and the right architecture is AWS-hosted Databricks rather than a migration.

> **Say it like this:** "My honest position is that the cloud is rarely the decision. The decision is where the data already lives and where the governance is already enforced, because moving those is a year of work and moving compute is a quarter. I've worked both and I'd rather inherit your constraints than argue for mine."

**17.2 — "Where does GCP win, and what would you lose by not picking it?"**
I'd be straight that I haven't run GCP in production — my cloud is AWS primary and Azure secondary — so this is comparison from documentation and from what colleagues have run. Where it's generally acknowledged to win: BigQuery as a serverless warehouse with a genuinely different cost model, GKE as the most mature managed Kubernetes with Autopilot and Image Streaming, and TPU access if that's ever relevant. What you'd lose by not picking it is mostly BigQuery's operational simplicity for analytics, and for an ML platform that's a smaller loss than it looks, because the ML serving and governance surfaces are where the work is and those are comparable across all three.

**17.3 — "Multi-cloud — would you?"**
Not as an architecture, only as a fact you inherit. Deliberate multi-cloud for an ML platform buys portability you will almost never exercise and costs you the managed services on both sides, egress on every cross-cloud byte, two identity models, two on-call knowledge bases, and a permanent lowest-common-denominator constraint on design. The version I *would* defend is portability at the layer where it's cheap and real: containers and Kubernetes as the compute substrate, an open table format so the data isn't hostage, MLflow or an equivalent open registry so the artefacts aren't, and Terraform so the infrastructure is describable. That gives you a credible exit without paying for one every day. And I'd distinguish that from the case where multi-cloud is imposed — an acquisition, a customer's residency requirement, a vendor concentration policy — where the correct response is to pick one primary and treat the other as a bounded, explicitly-scoped satellite rather than pretending to symmetry.

### CODERPAD ARTEFACTS — what you will actually type in the pad

The round ships a CoderPad link and is titled "AI/ML Ops Design and Domain". In a design round the pad is a shared scratch surface, so the artefact is almost certainly one of four things: an architecture sketch, a manifest or config, a schema or contract, or a small query. Rehearse drawing these cold, because a diagram you have drawn before takes ninety seconds and one you're inventing takes six minutes of silence. Ch.54 covers the pad's mechanics; this covers what to put in it.

**Drawing rules for a shared text pad.** Boxes and arrows only — no ASCII art you have to be careful about. Left to right for data flow, top to bottom for control flow. Label every arrow with what crosses it, because the arrows are where the interview questions live. Keep it under fifteen boxes; if it needs more, you're drawing implementation, not architecture. Type the box labels first and the connectors last, so a half-finished diagram still reads. And narrate while you type — silence in a pad is the worst thing in the round.

#### A1 — The reference ML platform (draw this for any "design us a platform" prompt)

```text
   DATA PLANE                TRAINING PLANE           ARTEFACT PLANE
  ┌──────────────┐          ┌───────────────┐        ┌────────────────┐
  │ bronze       │ snapshot │ containerised │ model  │ registry       │
  │ silver       │─────────▶│ training job  │───────▶│ + signature    │
  │ gold         │   id     │ (pinned deps) │ +evals │ + manifest     │
  │ feature layer│          └───────────────┘        │ content-addr.  │
  └──────┬───────┘                                   └───────┬────────┘
         │                                                   │
         │ online features                        promotion  │ GATE CHAIN
         │                                        event      │ G0 build   G4 behaviour
         ▼                                                   │ G1 data    G5 parity
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐                   │ G2 offline G6 perf/cost
  │           SERVING PLANE              │◀──────────────────┘ G3 slices  G7 shadow
  │  online (sync)  async(queue)  batch  │   digest              G8 canary
  │  3 SLA classes, not 1 endpoint type  │
  └──────────────┬───────────────────────┘
                 │ predictions + feature vectors + decision log
                 ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐     ┌──────────────────────┐
  │ OBSERVABILITY PLANE                  │     │ GOVERNANCE PLANE     │
  │ data monitors | model monitors|traces│◀───▶│ lineage | ACL | audit│
  │ one place, so an incident traces to  │     │ retention | approvals│
  │ a TABLE, not just to a model         │     └──────────────────────┘
  └──────────────────────────────────────┘
```

The line to say while the last box lands: "What makes this a platform rather than a collection of scripts is that the arrow from artefact plane to serving plane goes through a gate that can say no without a human's permission."

```text
  request ──▶ authn/authz ──▶ tenant_id + principals   ◀── FROM TOKEN CLAIMS ONLY
                  │              (never from body, never from model output)
                  ▼
            ┌───────────┐
            │ query     │
            │ embed     │──── assert: query embedder version == index version
            └─────┬─────┘
                  ▼
     ┌────────────────────────────┐
     │ HYBRID RETRIEVAL           │   PRE-FILTER inside the search:
     │  dense (HNSW) ─┐           │   tenant_id AND principals ⊇ caller

     │  BM25 ─────────┘           │
```

```json
{

  ],

    "ci_gate": "serving_payload_keys ⊇ required_names",
    "emit_metric": "per_feature_missing_rate"
  }
```
