#### Story 5 — The MCP developer assistant: agent operations and blast radius

**Design lesson:** *"An agent's tools are its blast radius. The interesting engineering in agent platforms is isolation, permission scoping and evaluation — not prompting."*

This is your bridge to every agent and GenAI-platform question on the JD, including the Mosaic AI Agent Framework one. Use it deliberately.

> **Say it like this:**
> "At TrueBalance I built core parts of the team's internal Claude-based developer assistant on the Model Context Protocol. It ties Jira, GitHub, Jenkins, AWS — Athena and EC2 — Grafana and Slack into one plain-English interface. I built the first Slack integration, the Google Docs skill, and a PR skill that writes the title and description from the diff, and I mentored the team on prompt and tool-calling patterns.
>
> The part that's actually a platform problem: every task runs in an isolated Git workspace. That one decision does most of the safety work — two concurrent tasks can't corrupt each other's tree, a bad tool call is contained, and you can throw the workspace away. The generalisation is that for an agent, the tool surface is the blast radius. So the design questions are the ones you'd ask of any privileged service: what identity does the tool call run as, what's the smallest permission set that lets it work, which operations are read-only versus mutating, and which mutating ones need a human confirmation.
>
> The second thing I'd emphasise is evaluation, because that's where agent systems actually fail. Unit tests on skills get you determinism — the Docs skill has thirty-four tests and they pass — but they don't tell you whether the agent is *useful*. For that you need a fixed golden set of tasks, a rubric per dimension, and the bit people skip: human calibration of the judge itself. An uncalibrated LLM judge silently drifts your quality gate and you find out months later."

| Drill-down | Your answer |
|---|---|
| "How do you stop it doing something destructive?" | "Three layers. Scope the credential — the agent's role can't do what it doesn't need. Classify tools read-only versus mutating and require confirmation on irreversible mutations. Isolate execution so the worst case is a discarded workspace. And log every tool call with arguments, because after an incident 'what did it actually do' has to be answerable." |
| "How do you evaluate it?" | "Fixed task set with expected outcomes, scored per dimension, run on every change to a skill or a prompt. Judge calibrated against human labels on a sample. And I'd wire the eval into a promotion gate, not a report — a report gets read once." |
| "Prompt injection, given it reads Jira and PRs?" | "Assume every piece of retrieved content is untrusted input, not instruction. The mitigation that works is authorisation, not filtering: the agent shouldn't have a tool that can do the damage the injection would ask for. Output-only filtering doesn't help once the injection has reached a tool call." |
| "How does this map to a managed agent framework?" | "The transferable concepts are agent-as-versioned-artifact — prompts, tools, retriever and model version pinned and promoted together — traces as first-class data, and evaluation wired into promotion. What I'd need to learn about a specific framework is where its opinionated seams are." |

| Numbers | Verdict |
|---|---|
| **34/34** tests on the Google Docs skill | Safe. "The Docs skill has 34 tests and they pass." |
| First Slack integration; PR skill writes titles/descriptions from the diff; isolated Git workspace per task; mentoring | Safe. |
| Adoption, time saved per developer, number of users, PRs generated | ⚠ Do not invent. |
| Any claim to have built the whole assistant | ⚠ He built **core parts**. Say "core parts" — the precision buys credibility. |

---

#### The knowledge-graph bridge — the JD names it twice, so make sure you do

The JD says "RAG stacks (Vector DBs, **Knowledge Graph**)" and lists Knowledge Graph again under what you have. This is the rare case where a literal JD keyword maps to production work of his with hard numbers, so it must not be left as a clause at the end of the intro. Have this ready as a thirty-second block and deploy it the moment retrieval, RAG or graphs come up.

> **Say it like this:**
> "On the knowledge-graph line in the JD — I have a production one. At TrueBalance I replaced a brittle regex SMS parser with a domain knowledge graph: seven entity types, twenty-nine predicates, and eighty-five-plus canonical field mappings. On a hundred-thousand-message production sample it gets a hundred per cent field coverage — a hundred and sixty-nine thousand, eight hundred and seventy-nine fields out of the same number — with a hundred and seven tests, and I migrated it into a standalone CI-guarded ML repo. To be precise, that's field *coverage*, not accuracy; accuracy is a separate measurement.
>
> Why it matters next to a vector index: an embedding can tell you two messages look alike. It can't tell you they're the same lender under two spellings, and it can't answer 'which tradelines belong to this entity' without making something up. The graph carries identity and constraints; the vector index carries unstructured similarity. In a RAG stack I'd use the graph for entity resolution and to decide what is *allowed* into the context window, and the index for the span retrieval inside that permitted set."

| Drill-down | Your answer |
|---|---|
| "How do you do entity resolution?" | "Concretely, on the bureau side: ninety-eight per cent of tradelines hide the lender name, so I built a seven-strategy confidence-ranked evidence matcher — each strategy proposes a candidate with a confidence, and they're ranked rather than short-circuited, so a weak strategy can't overwrite a strong one. That took the match rate from 29.7 to 68 per cent across a hundred and nine thousand tradelines with zero previously-matched tradelines lost, which was the hard constraint: a matcher that improves recall by breaking existing matches is a regression. The successor design uses temporal clustering and is *projected* at four-to-six-times precision — projected, not measured." |
| "When does a graph beat a vector index?" | "Three cases. When the question is a join — 'everything connected to this entity two hops out' — because that's a traversal, not a similarity. When correctness depends on a constraint the embedding doesn't encode: a lender is one entity even under six spellings, and no amount of cosine similarity makes that a fact. And when you need to explain the answer, because a path through a graph is an audit trail and a nearest-neighbour list isn't. Vectors win on unstructured recall over text nobody has schematised. Most real stacks want both, with the graph deciding scope and the index doing retrieval inside it." |
| "GraphRAG then — have you built that?" | "Not as a named pattern, no. I've built the graph and I've built production RAG, at ResMed, over medical reports with hybrid vector-plus-metadata retrieval. Wiring the graph in as the retrieval scope rather than as a separate store is the step I haven't shipped, and I'd rather say that than claim the pattern." |

---

### 10.3 The gap playbook

This is the part of the hour most likely to decide the outcome. The JD lists five tools he has not used and one scale he has not worked at. He has already disclosed all of it in writing. That converts the gaps from a liability into a demonstration of calibration — **if** he answers each one the same way every time.

#### The three-beat pattern, used for every gap without exception

1. **Name it flatly.** "I haven't used X." No hedging verbs. No "much", no "directly", and no trailing "…in production" unless not-in-production is literally the precise truth for that one tool.
2. **Map to the nearest primitive he *has* run** — the category, never the brand. "What I have built is the same job by hand: …"
3. **Show depth by naming what you would need to verify**, and how fast. The specific unknowns you can name are the proof that you understand the tool class. **Then ask a question back** — every gap script below ends on one, with no exceptions.

The question back matters. It turns an interrogation into a design conversation and gets the interviewer explaining their stack — which is both information for you and a better use of the clock.

| Gap | Nearest thing he has actually run | The one-line bridge |
|---|---|---|
| Unity Catalog | Hand-built governance: owner per dataset, PII classification, role-based grants, lineage for downstream blast radius; HIPAA-class data handling at ResMed | "Governance as a control plane, not a spreadsheet" |
| Mosaic AI Agent Framework | MCP developer assistant: versioned skills, tool scoping, isolated execution, LLM-judge evaluation with human calibration; ResMed GenAI query router | "Agent as a versioned artifact; the hard part is evaluation" |
| Databricks Vector Search | pgvector, FAISS, Chroma, Pinecone; hybrid vector + metadata retrieval at ResMed; RAG evaluation harnesses | "A managed index over a source table that must stay in sync and must inherit the source's ACLs" |
| Monte Carlo | Deequ checks on Azure Databricks; freshness/volume/schema/null checks in-pipeline; the Datadog drift utility | "Freshness, volume, schema, distribution, lineage — built by hand" |
| AWS Bedrock | SageMaker endpoints, Azure OpenAI, provider-API LLM workloads, production RAG | "A managed regional endpoint reached over PrivateLink; guardrails as platform, not app code" |
| Petabyte scale | Spark/Deequ on Azure Databricks; Snowflake feature stores; 100K-message and 109K-tradeline production workloads | "I've hit the *shape* of these problems, not that volume — here's what I'd expect to break first" |
| Databricks as the primary platform | ~1.5 years Azure Databricks for data quality and ETL, alongside AWS | "Databricks as a Spark tenant, not as the Lakehouse control plane" |

#### Unity Catalog

**Expected follow-up:** "So how would you do governance without it?" or "What would you need from a catalog?"

> **Say it like this:**
> "I haven't used Unity Catalog. What I have done is the same job by hand: one catalog of tables and features with a named owner per dataset, column-level classification for sensitive fields, access granted by role rather than per person, and lineage captured well enough to answer 'which downstream model consumed this table' when something upstream breaks. At ResMed the data was HIPAA-class, so classification, masking before anything reached a model, and an audit record of who saw what were platform requirements, not features.
>
> My read of Unity Catalog — and I'll flag that this is reading, not operating — is that it collapses those into one control plane across tables, models, features and functions. The consequence I find interesting is that it then becomes the *same* permission boundary that scopes what an agent's tools can reach, which is exactly the problem I've been solving with hand-rolled policy, and hand-rolled policy drifts.
>
> What I'd need to verify in week one against a real workspace: whether `USE CATALOG` and `USE SCHEMA` traversal is granted separately from `SELECT`, because a grant can look present and still not resolve; how ownership differs from privilege, since an owner bypasses a lot of what you thought you'd locked down; how row filters and column masks compose with grants; how external locations and path-based access behave, because that's where the boundary usually leaks; and what actually breaks in a Hive-metastore-to-Unity-Catalog migration. Those are the places I'd expect theory and practice to diverge.
>
> How are you using it today — as the governance boundary, or mostly for lineage?"

⚠ Note the correction embedded there: privileges in Unity Catalog are **additive and inherited downward** through metastore → catalog → schema → object, and there is **no DENY**. So do not offer "how grants conflict and what the precedence rules are" as a thing you'd investigate — there is no conflicting-grant precedence problem, and asking about one signals a generic RBAC article rather than the actual model. The traversal, ownership and masking questions above are the real gotchas. *(Verify against current docs if you have five minutes; this is the fastest-moving product on the list.)*

#### Mosaic AI Agent Framework

**Expected follow-up:** "How would you evaluate an agent, then?" Take this one; it is the strongest ground he has.

> **Say it like this:**
> "I haven't used the Mosaic AI Agent Framework. I have built and evaluated LLM systems — a production query-routing assistant at ResMed with RAG over a clinical knowledge base, and an internal MCP-based developer agent at TrueBalance.
>
> The concepts I'd expect to transfer: an agent is a versioned artifact — prompts, tools, retriever and model version pinned together and promoted as a unit, because changing the retriever without changing the version is how you lose reproducibility. Traces have to be first-class data rather than logs, because your evaluation set comes out of them. And the hard part isn't building the agent, it's evaluating it. I've done LLM-as-judge evaluation with a fixed golden set and a rubric per dimension, and the piece people skip is calibrating the judge against human labels — an uncalibrated judge drifts your gate silently, so the metric goes up while the product gets worse.
>
> What I'd need to learn is where the framework's opinionated seams are: what the built-in judges actually score, what the trace schema captures, and — the one that matters — whether an eval result can be wired into a promotion gate or whether it only produces a report. A report is a document; a gate is a control.
>
> Is the agent work here a platform other teams build on, or an application team shipping one agent?"

#### Databricks Vector Search

**Expected follow-up:** "What would you look for in a vector index?", or a recall/latency question.

> **Say it like this:**
> "Not used it. I've built retrieval with pgvector, FAISS, Chroma and Pinecone, and a hybrid vector-plus-metadata retrieval pipeline in production at ResMed over medical reports.
>
> My mental model of a managed vector index is: an index over a source table that has to stay in sync with it, with an ANN structure trading recall for latency, and it must inherit the source's row-level permissions or you've built a data-leak machine. So my questions are the ones I'd ask of any index — what's the sync lag on updates *and deletes*, because deletes are where managed indexes usually disappoint and that's a compliance problem, not just a correctness one; is it HNSW or IVF and what are the tunables; how do I measure recall@k against an exhaustive baseline; and does filtering happen before or after the ANN search, because pre-filter versus post-filter changes effective recall a lot at high selectivity.
>
> Where I do have depth is the evaluation side: in every RAG system I've worked on, chunking strategy and retrieval quality drove more of the output quality than the choice of model did, and I measured that rather than assuming it.
>
> What's your source of truth behind the index here — tables that change under it, or a mostly static corpus? The sync-and-delete behaviour is the first thing I'd want to understand, and the answer changes completely between those two."

#### Monte Carlo

**Expected follow-up:** "What did you build instead?" and, if they are sharp, "What's wrong with hand-rolled checks?"

> **Say it like this:**
> "No hands-on with Monte Carlo — I haven't used it. I've implemented the same function in-pipeline: freshness per feed, row-volume anomalies, schema-change detection, null and distribution checks per column, and enough lineage to tell you the downstream blast radius of an incident. At Tiger I did large-scale data-quality checks with Deequ on Azure Databricks with drift jobs orchestrated through Data Factory; at ResMed I built the self-service drift utility that generated Datadog monitors from a config. Freshness, volume, schema, distribution, lineage is the standard framing and it's the same set.
>
> What I'd expect a tool like Monte Carlo to add over my hand-rolled version is monitor generation across thousands of tables without me writing each one, and lineage I don't have to maintain by hand — which is the part that always rots first.
>
> And the trap I'd watch for is the one I hit with my own checks: thresholds that generate alerts nobody owns. My first question on day one would be what fraction of alerts are actioned and who's on the routing rule, because an observability tool with a ten per cent action rate has made things worse, not better — it's spent the team's attention budget.
>
> Is it deployed across everything, or on a critical subset?"

#### AWS Bedrock

**Expected follow-up:** "How would you choose between Bedrock and self-hosting?" Answer with a decision boundary, not a feature list.

> **Say it like this:**
> "I haven't run Bedrock in production — and to be exact, I haven't run it at all beyond reading about it. What I have run is LLM workloads through provider APIs and through Azure OpenAI, and I've served smaller transformer models — BERT-class — on SageMaker endpoints. I have not operated a self-hosted LLM fleet, so take my build-versus-buy view as reasoning from the cost structure rather than from having run one.
>
> The primitives as I understand them: a managed, regional model endpoint that I reach over PrivateLink from my VPC, with IAM as the auth boundary and CloudWatch or S3 invocation logging — so the data-residency conversation is about which region and how logging is configured, not about it running inside my account. Then guardrails applied as a platform-level filter rather than in application code, managed retrieval over an object store, and provisioned throughput as the commitment-versus-burst pricing decision.
>
> The design questions I'd ask are the same ones I'd ask anywhere: what's the p99 under real concurrency rather than in the docs; what's my fallback when a model version is deprecated, because deprecation is a scheduled outage you get told about late; do I get token-level logging so I can attribute cost per tenant and build an eval set; and is the guardrail evaluated on inputs, outputs, or both — output-only filtering doesn't stop a prompt injection that has already reached a tool call.
>
> On build versus buy I'll commit: managed, until either steady-state token spend clearly beats reserved capacity, or I need a model or a fine-tune the managed service won't host. Below that line, self-hosting buys you a GPU fleet to operate and a 24/7 on-call surface, and most teams underprice that.
>
> Is Bedrock the serving path for the AI work here, or is it behind an abstraction of your own? That changes how much of the vendor's opinion I'd actually be inheriting."

⚠ Two things in that script depend on facts only he can confirm. **(a)** The BERT-class-on-SageMaker clause: only say it if a BERT-class model was genuinely served on an endpoint he ran. If not, cut the clause and say *"I've run LLM workloads through provider APIs and through Azure OpenAI, and I have not operated a self-hosted model fleet."* **(b)** The "not at all beyond reading" clause: say it only if true. Do not describe a POC that did not happen — there is a documented prior incident of GPU-sizing claims that were not real reaching a recruiter, and this is the same failure mode.

#### Petabyte scale

The JD says "large Petabytes of data". This is the gap most likely to be probed *without* being named, so handle it proactively the first time volume comes up. Never let a "large-scale data" sentence imply petabytes by omission — and equally, do not substitute a different magnitude claim you also can't support. "Terabyte-class" is not on the approved numbers list either.

**Expected follow-up:** "What's the largest dataset you've worked with?" Answer with the sizes you actually measured, decline the rest, then move to shape.

> **Say it like this:**
> "I should be precise here: I have not worked at petabyte scale. The concrete sizes I can stand behind are the ones I measured myself — a hundred and nine thousand tradelines in the lender-matching work, a hundred thousand production SMS through the knowledge graph, and Snowflake feature tables at ResMed. For the Spark and Deequ jobs at Tiger I'd be guessing at total volume, so I'd rather describe the shape than quote a size I can't verify.
>
> What I'd claim is that I've hit the *shapes* that break at scale — skewed joins, small-file explosion, point-in-time-correct joins over long histories, and the point where a full scan stops being an option and partitioning and file layout become the design rather than a tuning step. I've used Iceberg as a table format and I understand why compaction and metadata management become an operational job rather than a setting.
>
> If you put me on a petabyte-scale table tomorrow, the things I'd expect to bite me first are partition and clustering design, the cost of a naive shuffle, and the fact that a mistake costs real money rather than five minutes. I'd want to shadow someone who has operated it for the first month rather than pretend the difference is only a config value.
>
> What's the actual working set on the tables an ML platform here touches — is the petabyte the archive, or the training input? Those are very different problems and I'd rather solve the one you have."

#### Databricks as the primary platform

This gap is quantitative rather than binary, and it needs the sharpest wording — "1.5 years of Databricks" on a CV sounds like considerably more than it is.

**Expected follow-up:** "So how long is your ramp?" and, more pointedly, "We're Databricks-first — does that worry you?"

> **Say it like this:**
> "Let me be exact about the Databricks experience, because it's easy to overread. About a year and a half, on Azure Databricks, and it was Spark work — large-scale data-quality checks with Deequ, drift-detection jobs orchestrated through Azure Data Factory. I was a tenant on someone else's Lakehouse, not the person who owned the Lakehouse platform. I haven't used Unity Catalog, Vector Search or Mosaic.
>
> On the arithmetic, so it reconciles against whatever the sourcing recruiter sent you: about five years of cloud, AWS primary throughout, with the year and a half of Azure Databricks running *alongside* that at Tiger rather than after it. My platform ownership is the AWS side — SageMaker, Lambda, ECR, SQS, S3, CodePipeline — and that's where I've built training, serving, drift and CI/CD as one system.
>
> The honest read is that the platform concepts transfer directly and the Databricks-specific operational knowledge doesn't. On ramp, I'd expect to be productive on the pipeline and serving side immediately and slow on Databricks-native operations for something like a quarter — job clusters and cost behaviour, the catalog model, and whatever your deployment seams are. Does that worry me? Only in one direction: I'd be learning the platform while being expected to have opinions about it, which is uncomfortable but not risky, because the failure modes I'd be guarding against — silent skew, ungated promotion, unowned alerts — are the same ones regardless of vendor.
>
> How much of your platform is Databricks-native versus your own abstraction on top of it? That ratio decides my ramp, so what's the split today?"

#### "Your profile says X, but you're telling me Y"

The most dangerous version of a collision is not about years — it is about tooling. The CV and the the recruiting agency-forwarded profile carry a tooling list; a list is read as a claim of use. When the interviewer holds up a line from it, the *only* safe move is to make the precise version the one you volunteer, immediately, without defending the CV.

> **Say it like this:**
> "Fair — and I'd rather you have the precise version than the CV version. On a CV that line means the tool was in the stack I worked in. What I've personally operated is the Spark and Deequ side. If the CV reads stronger than that, that's on me and I'd rather correct it here than have you find out in month two."

| If they point at | The precise version, said flat |
|---|---|
| "Databricks" | "Azure Databricks, Spark and Deequ, data-quality and ETL, about a year and a half, as a tenant. Not Lakehouse platform ownership, and no Unity Catalog." |
| "MLflow" | See the branch below. Default to the conservative one. |
| "Vector databases" | "pgvector, FAISS, Chroma and Pinecone. Not Databricks Vector Search." |
| "GenAI / LLMs on AWS" | "SageMaker endpoints and production RAG on AWS; the LLM calls went through provider APIs and Azure OpenAI. Not Bedrock." |
| "Petabyte / large-scale data" | "Large-scale in shape, not in petabytes. I have not worked at petabyte scale." |

Never say "the recruiter must have written that" or "the CV was auto-generated". Own it and correct it in one sentence; the correction is the signal, the blame is noise.

#### The grammar rule: never let a mapping sentence become an implied claim

The most common way an honest candidate accidentally lies is a **dangling comparison**. "It's basically like what I did with X" is heard as "I have effectively done X." The fix is grammatical, not moral: keep the subject of every sentence honest, and mark every statement about an unused tool with an explicit epistemic verb — "my read is", "my mental model is", "I'd expect".

| ❌ Never say | ✅ Say instead |
|---|---|
| "I've worked with Unity Catalog-style governance" | "I haven't used Unity Catalog. I've built role-based access and lineage by hand." |
| "It's basically the same as what I built, so it'd be easy" | "The concepts overlap. The operational detail is where I'd expect to be slow for a few weeks." |
| "I'm familiar with Bedrock" | "I haven't used Bedrock. My understanding of the primitives is …" |
| "We used Databricks for our ML platform" | "I used Azure Databricks for Spark data-quality work. Our ML platform was on AWS." |
| "I've touched Monte Carlo a bit" | "No hands-on. I've built the same five pillars in-pipeline." |
| "We processed petabytes" / "terabyte-class" | "I have not worked at petabyte scale. The sizes I measured were 109K tradelines and 100K messages." |
| "Our vector search…" (next to a Databricks sentence) | "pgvector and FAISS in my case — I haven't used Databricks Vector Search." |
| "I've self-hosted LLMs" | "Provider APIs and Azure OpenAI. I have not operated a self-hosted LLM fleet." |

Three phrases to delete entirely: **"I'm familiar with"**, **"I've touched"**, **"it's basically the same"**. All three are heard as claims of use, and all three collapse under one follow-up. The recovery line if he catches himself mid-sentence:

> **Say it like this:**
> "Let me correct that — I said 'we used', and what I mean is the team's stack included it. The part I personally ran was the Spark data-quality side."

Self-correcting in real time is a positive signal. Being corrected by the interviewer is not.

#### ⚠ The MLflow trap — two branches, and the conservative one is the default

There is a live inconsistency to resolve before the call. MLflow appears on his tooling list and may appear on the CV the recruiting agency forwarded; the round-1 guidance and a prior resume audit both say **do not claim hands-on MLflow**; and the JD names MLflow explicitly, so it will very likely come up.

**Default to Branch A.** Under time pressure at 14:30 you will read whichever script is in front of you, so the safe one is written first and the other is fenced.

**Branch A — conservative. Use this unless Branch B's test passes.**

> **Say it like this:**
> "MLflow is on my tooling list from experiment tracking on team projects, but I wouldn't describe myself as having *operated* it. My systems of record have been the SageMaker-native registry on the NatWest platform, and on my current stack S3-versioned artifacts plus a serialized feature contract shipped in the artifact bundle and a CI promotion gate. So on MLflow specifically, treat me as knowing the problem class and learning the operations."

**Branch B — claiming. Use ONLY if you can name, out loud and without hesitating, the project, the tracking server and what you logged to it.** If any of those three is fuzzy, you are in Branch A.

> **Say it like this:**
> "I've used MLflow for experiment tracking on [project], logging [runs/params/metrics/artifacts] to [tracking server]. I haven't operated it as the central registry for a multi-team platform — my registry experience is the SageMaker-native one — so if that's what the role needs, treat it as somewhere I'd be learning the operations rather than the concepts."

Under no circumstances expand either branch into a claim of MLflow-based lineage, model-stage transitions, registry administration or aliasing. And note the trap inside the trap: legacy MLflow stage vocabulary — "none / staging / production" — is the wrong lifecycle to draw for SageMaker (§10.2 Story 2), MLflow has moved to aliases, and Unity-Catalog-registered models don't carry stages at all. Saying those words implies exactly the operational experience Branch A is disclaiming.

Same rule for GPU fleet sizing: he may do the arithmetic live as a **labelled estimate**, never as recall.

#### The years reconciliation: "your CV says 8 years, the sheet says 4.5 in ML titles"

Answer in one confident breath, with a rising arc. Do not say "only". Do not sound like you are conceding something.

> **Say it like this:**
> "Yes — eight years of building production software, of which about four and a half in explicitly ML-titled roles. The first stretch was backend and data engineering, and honestly that's where the platform half of this job comes from: pipelines, contracts with upstream teams, on-call, and what happens when a nightly job fails at two in the morning. The ML years are where I own the model lifecycle end to end.
>
> I'd rather have them in that order than the reverse. Most production failures I've seen in ML are data and operations failures wearing a model costume — and I'd already been on the wrong end of those before I trained anything."

#### The 6-versus-4.5 bridge — they are both on the recruiter sheet

The sheet the sourcing recruiter sent carries **AI/ML ~6 years** *and* **MLOps ~4.5 years**. Ch.54's advice was to avoid putting the two numbers in one sentence; that is not sufficient here, because the interviewer is holding the sheet and will put them in one sentence for you. Have the bridge ready and say it without flinching — it takes twelve seconds and it makes the sheet look deliberate rather than inflated.

> **Say it like this:**
> "Both numbers are on that sheet and they measure two different things, so let me split them. AI/ML work starts around 2020 at Sopra Steria — the CNN, YOLO and OCR identity-verification system, and a loan-risk model with an explainability layer for auditable decisioning. That's the six. Explicitly ML-titled roles start December 2021 at Tiger Analytics, and MLOps specifically tracks those same years. That's the four and a half. If you want one number to level me on, take four and a half and judge the scope rather than the arithmetic."

| If they push | Say |
|---|---|
| "So you're really a 4.5-year ML engineer." | "For levelling, judge me on scope and what I've owned rather than title history. The right test is to hand me an ambiguous production problem and watch where I take it — which is roughly what we've been doing for the last forty minutes." |
| "This is a platform role — is that enough ML?" | "For an ML *platform* role the split is the point. The people who build good ML platforms are usually the ones who did infrastructure before they did models, because the platform's users are engineers, not notebooks." |
| "What would more ML years have given you?" | "More reps on large-scale training infrastructure specifically. That's the gap I'm deliberately closing, and it's a reason this role is interesting rather than a reason it's risky." |

One more precision move worth making once, unprompted, if credit modelling or LLM evaluation comes up — state a boundary on your own work before they find it:

> **Say it like this:**
> "To be precise about scope on that one — I *reviewed and evaluated* the logprobs-to-credit-risk approach and killed it on AUC evidence. I didn't fine-tune the model."

Volunteering a boundary buys more credibility than any claim.

### 10.4 The consistency sheet

Everything below is either already in writing with the recruiter or already published on the CV. Deviating from any of it — even upward — reads as carelessness at best.

Ch.54 §54 carries the full version of this sheet and the honesty guardrails; do not re-read both. What follows is the delta this round stresses: the rows most likely to be cross-checked live, plus the two reconciliations Ch.54 didn't need.

#### The rows that get cross-checked

| Item | Say exactly | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Total experience | **8 years** engineering | Preferred phrasing: "eight years engineering, about four and a half of them in ML engineer titles." |
| AI/ML experience | **~6 years** | Pairs with 4.5. **Use the bridge in §10.3** — from roughly 2020 at Sopra (CNN/YOLO/OCR, loan-risk with XAI); ML-titled roles from Dec 2021. Do not dodge the pairing; explain it. |
| MLOps experience | **~4.5 years** | Tracks the ML-titled years, Dec 2021 onward. |
| Python | **8 years** | |
| Cloud | **~5 years**, AWS primary throughout | ⚠ Always add the overlap clause: *"with roughly a year and a half of Azure Databricks running alongside it at Tiger rather than after it."* Without that, AWS 5 + Azure 1.5 = 6.5 against a stated total of 5, and the interviewer does that subtraction instantly. |
| Azure | **~1.5 years** | Inside the cloud window, not additional to it. |
| Databricks | **~1.5 years**, Azure Databricks, Spark/Deequ, data-quality and ETL, as a tenant | ⚠ Always attach the qualifier. Never say "one and a half years of Databricks" bare. |
| Current tenure | **Joined TrueBalance February 2026** — seven months as of this interview | ⚠ Expect the question. Script in §10.5. Do not round it up, do not volunteer "only". |
| Current CTC | **[current CTC — private]** | Fixed only. Do not add variable or ESOP numbers. |
| Expected CTC | **[expected CTC — private]** | Do not soften it in this round. |
| Notice period | **60 days**, buyout discussable | |
| Offer in hand | **None** | Answer plainly. Do not manufacture leverage. |
| Location | Bengaluru; hybrid Infantry Road is workable | |

#### Technical numbers from his own work

| Number | Where | Safe to state? |
|---|---|---|
| ROC-AUC **0.84**, out-of-time | TrueBalance withdrawal-propensity model | ✅ Safe. Always "out-of-time", never "test". |
| **~4,001** offline features vs **28** payload keys | The parity collapse | ✅ Safe as the *diagnosis*. ⚠ Do **not** quote 28 as the post-fix required count — see the VERIFY note in Story 1. |
| **7** entity types, **29** predicates, **85+** canonical field mappings | TrueBalance knowledge graph | ✅ Safe. |
| **169,879 / 169,879** fields — 100% field coverage on **100K** production SMS | Knowledge graph replacing the regex parser | ⚠ Caveat required: "100% *field coverage* on a 100K-message production sample." It is coverage, not accuracy. If asked "100% accurate?": *"Coverage, not accuracy — every field the schema defines got populated. Accuracy is a separate measurement."* |
| **107** passing tests | Knowledge-graph repo, CI-guarded, standalone ML repo | ✅ Safe. |
| **29.7% → 68%** match rate over **109K** tradelines, zero lost matches, **7** strategies | Lender identification for bureau tradelines | ✅ Safe. "Zero lost matches" = no previously-matched tradeline was lost; say it that way. |
| **4–6x** precision from temporal clustering | The successor design | ⚠ **Projected, not measured.** If you cannot say it with the word "projected" attached, do not say it at all. |
| **34/34** tests | Google Docs skill in the MCP assistant | ✅ Safe. |
| **300** locations, planning **7 days → 5 days** | Sopra Steria OR-Tools route optimisation | ✅ Safe, and now doubly useful: it is one of the pieces of evidence behind the "AI/ML from ~2020" bridge. |
| "AWS showcased the architecture at re:Invent" | Tiger Analytics / NatWest | ✅ Safe in exactly that form. ⚠ Never "I presented at re:Invent". |
| "SageMaker Model Registry on the NatWest platform" | Tiger Analytics / NatWest | ⚠ **VERIFY BEFORE CALL** — not a settled fact in the record. Unconfirmed, describe the mechanism, not the brand. |
| ResMed multi-container endpoints "cut inference cost" | ResMed IHS | ⚠ Qualitative only. **No percentage exists.** Highest fabrication risk in the deck. |
| "Terabyte-class", or any TB/PB figure | — | ❌ Not an approved number. Use the measured sizes (109K tradelines, 100K SMS) and decline the rest. |
| Any uptime, QPS, p99, cost saving, user count, teams onboarded | — | ❌ **None of these exist.** If asked, say so and offer the measurement you would build instead. |

The universal fallback — and the rule that makes it land:

> **Say it like this:**
> "I don't have a number for that I can stand behind, and I don't want to invent one. Here's how I'd measure it if I owned it — and here's one I did measure: …"

**Never use the fallback bare.** Every refusal is immediately followed by a number he *does* have. Refuse-and-pivot reads as calibration; refuse-and-stop, three times in a sixty-minute round, reads as a CV with nothing measured in it. The pairings, memorised: cost question → 0.84 out-of-time AUC; scale question → 109K tradelines and 100K SMS; adoption question → the six fields of the drift spec and 34/34 tests; quality question → 29.7% → 68% with zero lost matches.

### 10.5 Tenure, motivation, compensation and logistics

#### "Seven months at your current job — why are you moving already?"

This is the single most certain non-technical question in the loop, and it comes before or after the design work, never during. Answer it in two sentences, unprompted-calm, with no criticism of TrueBalance in it (see §10.6 rule 23).

> **Say it like this:**
> "Seven months, yes — I joined TrueBalance in February. I joined to own a model end to end and I've done exactly that: the propensity pipeline is mine from features through real-time serving, plus the knowledge graph and core parts of the internal developer assistant. What that role doesn't have underneath it is a platform other teams build on — it's a small team where I *am* the platform. This job is the thing I did at Tiger and at ResMed, at a scale where it stays interesting for years, which is the only reason I'd move this early."

**The follow-up, which will come:** *"So won't you leave us in seven months too?"*

> **Say it like this:**
> "Reasonable question — look at the pattern rather than the last row. Three and a half years at Sopra Steria, about a year and a half at Tiger, two and a half at ResMed. The short one is the outlier and it's short for a scope reason, not a company one: the next thing I want to own isn't the shape of that role. If you hire me to own an ML platform, the thing that would make me restless is the scope shrinking — which is precisely the thing I'd want us to be explicit about in this loop, so I'd rather ask you now: what does this role own in twelve months that it doesn't own on day one?"

Do not say "only seven months". Do not explain the move by anything wrong with the employer. Do not mention any engagement that is not on the CV as part of the reason.

#### Why Smartsheet — make it about the product, not about "enterprise SaaS"

A generic "large enterprise SaaS" answer fits any company and scores nothing. Use the object model from the Ch.54 primer; it is the reason this is an interesting ML-platform problem rather than a big one.

> **Say it like this:**
> "Two reasons, and the second is the real one. The first is that this is an ML *platform* role in a company where the platform has actual internal users, which is the scope I'm moving for.
>
> The second is the data shape. Smartsheet's content is customer-authored — sheets with typed columns, rows as a hierarchy, cross-sheet references and cell links — so it's structured enough to reason about and completely heterogeneous across customers, sitting next to attachments, comments and update requests that aren't structured at all. That's the JD's line about structured and unstructured data from varied sources, but the part I find genuinely hard is the permission model: owner, admin, editor, commenter, viewer, plus row-level scoping through things like Dynamic View. Any retrieval layer over customer content has to inherit that sharing model exactly, per row, or the feature is a data-leak machine. That's the same problem I described on the vector-index side — an index that doesn't inherit its source's ACLs — except here it's the core constraint rather than an edge case. I'd rather work on that than on a bigger but blander pipeline.
>
> And the India GCC being built out means platform ownership is real here rather than a slice of someone else's roadmap. Is that how you'd describe the scope of this team?"

⚠ Awareness, not a talking point: Smartsheet has been **privately held since the Blackstone/Vista take-private closed in January 2025** *(verify if you have a minute — this is the kind of fact that dates)*. So do not reference stock price, public quarterly metrics, or equity upside, and do not ask about ESOP or RSUs. If comp structure comes up at all, route it to the sourcing recruiter.

#### Compensation and logistics, if it comes up

It usually does not in a technical round. If the interviewer raises it, they are checking for a clean, non-anxious answer — not opening a negotiation. One sentence each, then hand it back to the recruiter.

| Topic | Exact wording |
|---|---|
| Expected CTC | "I've shared [expected CTC — private] fixed with the sourcing recruiter and that's the number I'm working with. Current is [current CTC — private]." |
| If pushed on flexibility | "I'd rather keep the number consistent with what I gave the recruiter and let you and the sourcing recruiter shape the structure." *(Do not negotiate in a technical round. Do not say "flexible".)* |
| Notice period | "Sixty days. Buyout is discussable — I'd want to agree that with HR rather than commit to a date here." |
| Earliest start | "Realistically sixty days from resignation, earlier if a buyout works. I won't quote a date I can't hold." |
| Hybrid / Infantry Road | "I'm in Bengaluru and hybrid at Infantry Road works for me. No relocation, no constraint on office days." |
| Offer in hand | "None currently." *(Flat. No embellishment, no implied timeline pressure.)* |
| Equity / ESOP | Do not raise it and do not ask. If they raise it: "Happy to take the structure conversation with the sourcing recruiter and HR." |
| Anything outside the CV — other engagements, side work, consulting | **One posture, no improvisation, in every section of this document: do not volunteer it, do not allude to it, do not use it as evidence in a technical answer.** If asked directly: *"Happy to go through anything on that with HR as part of the process."* Then stop talking. This round is recorded; an unnamed "compliance product I've worked on" invites "which company?", and that question has no good answer on camera. |
| "Why leaving / why Smartsheet?" | Tenure script and Smartsheet script above. Answer tenure first, motivation second — in that order the move sounds chosen rather than forced. |

### 10.6 The things he must not say

Read this list last, out loud, five minutes before the call.

**Fabrication — instantly disqualifying if probed**

1. Any percentage or dollar figure for the ResMed cost reduction.
2. Any latency, QPS, uptime or volume number for any past system. He has none.
3. "Petabytes", "petabyte-scale", "hundreds of terabytes" — **or "terabyte-class"** — about his own work. The approved sizes are the ones he measured: 109K tradelines, 100K SMS.
4. "I presented at re:Invent." AWS showcased the architecture; he did not speak.
5. "4–6x precision" without the word **projected** in the same breath.
6. "100% accuracy" for the knowledge graph. It is 100% **field coverage** on a 100K-message sample.
7. GPU fleet sizing from experience. Live arithmetic labelled as an estimate is fine — *"back-of-envelope, and I'd want a single-replica load test in week one to check it"* — recall is not.
8. "I've self-hosted LLMs." He has run provider APIs and Azure OpenAI. He has not operated a self-hosted LLM fleet.
9. MLflow as the central registry of a multi-team platform. Branch A in §10.3 is the default.
10. "SageMaker Model Registry on the NatWest platform" as settled fact, unless he confirmed it before the call. Otherwise: the mechanism, not the brand.
11. Any claim to have built the *whole* MCP assistant. Core parts.

**Written artefacts — the pad is a recorded document**

12. Real model names, feature names, table names or statistics from a former employer, typed onto the shared pad. Generic placeholders, every time, with the spoken line *"names and numbers here are illustrative"* before he starts typing.
13. Any date on an illustrative artefact that collides with his own timeline — a 2026 baseline on a ResMed example is spotted by anyone holding the CV.
14. "none → staging → production" as a registry lifecycle. Wrong for SageMaker, legacy for MLflow, non-existent under Unity Catalog. Use the two-box shape in §10.2 Story 2, or label the box "registry state (product-specific)".
15. A contract sketch whose required count equals the number of keys the payload already had — that makes the CI gate tautological and it is the first thing an architect will notice.

**Overclaim by implication**

16. "I'm familiar with" / "I've touched" / "I've read about" — all heard as claims of use.
17. "It's basically the same as X, so it'd be easy." The worst sentence available: it insults the tool and signals he will underestimate the migration.
18. "We used Databricks for our ML platform." He used Azure Databricks for Spark data-quality work; the ML platform was AWS.
19. Unity Catalog, Mosaic AI Agent Framework, Databricks Vector Search, Monte Carlo or Bedrock **in any affirmative sentence about his own use**. (Negative disclosures — "I haven't used Unity Catalog" — are exactly what this document wants; it is the affirmative that is banned.)
20. One "in production" qualifier stretched across all five tools. Four are never-used; only Bedrock takes that framing, and even there the flat version is safer.
21. Letting "vector search" stand unqualified next to a Databricks sentence. Name pgvector / FAISS / Chroma / Pinecone every time.
22. AWS-five-plus-Azure-one-and-a-half without the word "alongside". Five plus one and a half is not five.

**Design-round anti-signals**

23. "It depends" without immediately committing to a boundary.
24. "We can figure that out later" about the hard part — especially skew, cache invalidation or multi-tenancy, which is exactly why they asked.
25. Twenty seconds of product names in a row. If he catches himself: *"Concretely, the mechanism is…"*
26. Solutioning before requirements. Nothing goes into the pad as a design before the REQUIREMENTS and NUMBERS blocks exist.
27. Defending a design after the interviewer has shown it is wrong. Correct move: *"Let me steelman that — yes, that beats mine because…"*
28. Instant capitulation on every push, which reads as no conviction. If he still believes it: *"I'd keep mine, but I'd want to test Z before betting on it."*
29. A refusal with nothing after it. Every "I don't have that number" is followed in the same breath by a number he does have.

**Career and tone**

30. "Only four and a half years in ML." Never "only". Same for "only seven months".
31. Apologising more than once for a gap. One disclosure, then move.
32. Criticising a current or former employer, a client, or whoever wrote the previous system — including as the reason for a seven-month tenure. Describe defects mechanically — "the transform imputed defaults", not "someone wrote this badly".
33. Volunteering any engagement that is not on the CV, named or unnamed, as evidence in a technical answer.
34. Anything about compensation or equity beyond the single scripted sentence in §10.5.
35. Filling silence. After "I don't know that", **stop**. The next thing out of his mouth should be how he would find out, not speculation dressed as fact.

> **Say it like this (the line that covers the whole list):**
> "I'd rather be the person who says 'I don't know' on the third day of an incident than the one who guessed on day one."

### 11.2 The reference architecture you draw from memory

One diagram answers roughly 80% of "design an ML platform / design a serving system / how would you productionise this model" prompts. Draw it in the pad **before** you talk about it; type the section banner first, then fill.

#### The pad version — this is the one you actually type

Twelve lines, under 90 seconds, fits a split pane at 76 columns. Everything else in this section is elaboration you speak, not draw.

```text
====== DESIGN v1 ==========================================
 client -> gw -> [ INFER ] -> [ MODEL SVR ] -> resp  p99 __ms
                   | ^
                   v |
       [2] ONLINE STORE (Redis) <- [3] stream+batch feat jobs
 [4] LOG raw req/resp -> object store (replay set = train set)
 |
 [5] LAKEHOUSE -> features (PIT) -> train -> GATES
 |   gates: contract | offline+CI | slices | parity | $/1k
 [6] REGISTRY (alias @champion) -> shadow -> canary -> champ
 |
 [7] OBS: infra | freshness | drift | business | $/1k
     rollback trigger  <--->  retrain trigger
===========================================================
```

**Legend — type it under the drawing if there is any doubt, otherwise read it out while drawing:**

```text
[1] request path      - the millisecond loop; the p99 budget lives here
[2] online store      - the feature values serving actually reads
[3] feature jobs      - the stream and batch writers into [2]
[4] log               - raw request/response; replay set = training set
[5] lakehouse + gates - point-in-time features, training, promotion
[6] registry          - versioned artefact + alias; the deploy trigger
[7] observability     - infra / data / model / business, plus $ per 1k
```

#### The full reference drawing — read at 16:30, do not type it in the room

```text
=============== DESIGN (v1) ================================
 [1] REQUEST PATH        p99 budget: __ms
                         (network / features / model / headroom)
  client -> [ gateway ] -> [ inference svc ] -> [ model server ]
                 |               |     ^        (dyn. batching, pool)
                 |               |     | features p99 ~10ms
                 |               v     |
                 |     [2] [ ONLINE STORE: Redis / DynamoDB ]
                 |               ^  upsert, lag < 60s
                 |     [3] [ stream + batch feature jobs ] <- events
                 v
      [4] [ req/resp + feature LOG -> object store ]
                 |     same payload = replay set AND training input
                 v
  [5] LAKEHOUSE:  raw -> curated -> feature tables (PIT joins)
                 |   train -> candidate -> GATES:
                 |   contract | offline+CI | slices | parity | perf/$
                 v
      [6] [ REGISTRY: version, manifest, lineage, alias @champion ]
                 |  registry event -> GitOps commit -> shadow 24h
                 |  -> canary 1% -> 10% -> 50% (guardrails, auto-
                 |     rollback) -> champion
                 v
      [7] [ OBSERVABILITY: infra | freshness | drift | biz | $/1k ]
            +--- rollback trigger ---+--- retrain trigger ---+
============================================================
```

**The seven sentences, one per element, said while you draw:**

> **Say it like this (1, request path):** "Three loops with different clock speeds live in this picture: inference in milliseconds, retraining in days, governance in quarters. I'll draw the serving path first, then the pipeline that feeds it, then the controls around both."

> **Say it like this (2–3, features):** "The online store is the thing I'd put on the critical-path risk list, not the model. In my current role the failure that mattered wasn't the model — it was 4,001 offline features against 28 keys actually present in the live payload, and the transform silently imputed defaults, so we served a near-constant vector at 200 OK. It never paged, because it never errored. That's why the control I shipped was a serialised feature contract and a hard-fail on a missing required feature, not a better alert."

> **Say it like this (4, logging):** "The rule I hold to is: log the raw request payload, not the computed features, because that same log is the replay set, the training input and the incident evidence. If you log only the features you can never re-derive what actually happened. In my case what exposed the parity gap was diffing the offline feature list against the live payload keys — a raw log turns that diff into a query instead of an archaeology project."

> **Say it like this (5, gates):** "Let me split what I've shipped from what I'd build. What I shipped after the parity failure was a serialised feature contract next to the artifact, a hard-fail when a required feature is missing, a CI subset assertion as a promotion gate, and a per-feature missing-rate metric emitted by the scorer. The way I'd extend that to a platform is five gates: the data contract; an offline metric where the confidence interval on the improvement has to clear a margin we agreed before we trained; no material slice regression; train/serve parity scored through the real container; and latency plus cost per thousand. That makes promotion evidential rather than binary."
>
> *(Only if they push on the metric gate: "concretely, bootstrap the delta against champion and gate on the lower bound of that interval." Do not lead with that sentence — said cold it costs a clarification round-trip you cannot afford in sixty minutes.)*

> **Say it like this (6, registry):** "Design-wise, the registry stage or alias change is the event that triggers the deploy — a human doesn't run a pipeline. And rollback should be a config revert rather than a pipeline run, so it's seconds rather than a CI cycle. I'd target well under a minute. I haven't measured that on a system I've owned, so treat it as a target rather than a benchmark."

> **Say it like this (7, monitoring):** "Four layers — infra, data, model, business — but I only page on three things: serving availability, feature-freshness SLO, and a guardrail breach during a canary. Everything else is a ticket, because a paging drift alert trains people to ignore drift alerts."

#### Bridging the generic architecture to Smartsheet

The round is "Design **and** Domain", and the domain is enterprise SaaS collaboration. If the prompt turns out to be "design AI for the work graph" or "add a model to Smartsheet", overlay these three lines on the same seven elements rather than starting a second drawing. Fuller treatment: `01_smartsheet_delta.md` §(d) and `08_rag_agents_primer.md` §8.3.

1. **The tenant is the top-level isolation boundary**, sitting above everything in the diagram. Every box acquires a tenant dimension: the online-store key, the log partition, the feature table, the index, the cost metric. Per-tenant cost attribution is a design input, not a reporting afterthought.
2. **Row-level permissions have to survive into features, retrieval and logs.** The product grants at workspace and sheet level and then narrows per row (Dynamic View, WorkApps). A feature aggregated across a sheet, a retrieved chunk, or a logged payload is a covert copy of rows the requester may not be entitled to. The control is: resolve the requester's visible row set first, filter at query time, re-check at render.
3. **The sheet/row structure is a forest, and a forest is a graph.** Rows carry a `parentId`; cell links and cross-sheet references make edges between sheets. That maps directly onto the knowledge-graph work — entity types, predicates, canonical field mappings — so entity resolution over user-defined schemas is the same problem as replacing the regex SMS parser, not a new one.

> **Say it like this:** "Before I draw, one thing about your shape specifically: in a multi-tenant collaboration product the hard part isn't the model, it's that the tenant boundary and the row-level permission have to survive all the way into the feature store, the retrieval index and the request log. Any aggregate, and any retrieved chunk, is a covert copy of rows somebody may not be entitled to. So I'd put tenant and visible-row-set on the diagram as first-class dimensions rather than bolting them on later. Does that match how you think about it, or is isolation handled somewhere I can't see from outside?"

#### If the pad plan breaks

Two derailments are likely enough to have an answer ready for.

- **"Skip the diagram, just talk."** Keep the same seven-part spine verbally and narrate the numbers instead: request path and its budget → online store → feature jobs → log → lakehouse and gates → registry and rollout → observability and triggers. Open with "I'll walk it in the order I'd draw it: serving path, then the pipeline that feeds it, then the controls." The structure is what is being scored, not the ASCII.
- **They take over the pad.** Stop typing immediately, watch what they write, and narrate against *their* artefact. Ask one orienting question — "should I assume that box is the online store?" — then attach numbers and failure modes to their boxes. Reclaim the keyboard only for a numbers block or the drift stub, and ask before you do.

#### Variant A — RAG / GenAI service

```text
=================== RAG SERVICE =============================
 query
   -> [ authz + tenant/ACL resolve ]
   -> [ retriever ]   BM25 + vector ANN (HNSW), RRF fuse
   -> [ rerank ]
   -> [ LLM ]         <- prompt-prefix cache feeds the LLM
   -> [ output guard ] -> response

 ACL: the tenant filter is applied AT QUERY TIME -- the index
      does NOT enforce the source's permissions on its own.
      pre-filter vs post-filter changes recall: say which.

 INGEST: docs -(CDC)-> chunk -> embed (content-hash dedupe)
         -> index   (what is the sync lag, and who watches it?)
 EVAL:   golden set (versioned) + judges (human-calibrated)
         -> promotion gate
 OBS:    traces (spans: retriever / tool / LLM)
         -> quality, TTFT, tok/s, $ per resolved task
=============================================================
```

> **Say it like this:** "Two things dominate RAG quality and neither is the model: chunking-plus-retrieval, and whether the index respects the same permissions as the source. My understanding is that a vector index generally carries index-level grants rather than row-level ones, so multi-tenant isolation lands on a query-time filter or on separate indexes — though some managed stacks do document-level filtering at retrieval, Bedrock Knowledge Bases and Azure AI Search among them. My own vector work has been pgvector, FAISS, Chroma and Pinecone rather than a Databricks index. The failure mode of that class of tool is the same either way — retrieval that outruns the source's permissions — and that is what I'd design against whichever product we're on. Tell me which model yours uses and I'll design to it."

#### Variant B — retraining loop

```text
=============== RETRAINING LOOP =============================
 trigger: schedule | drift alarm (PSI) | volume | manual
    |
    v  snapshot data with a PINNED version id
       (retention must outlive the model)
 [ train ] -> [ eval vs champion: same held-out snapshot,
    |          same slice code ]
    |          +-> parity test: score N rows THROUGH the
    |              real serving container
    v
 [ register: commit, image digest, lockfile hash, data
   snapshot id, seeds, metrics ]
    |
    +-> shadow (24-72h, mirrored traffic, distribution diff)
    |     -> canary -> champion
    |
 LABELS arrive after delay D -> cohort/vintage curves, not
   weekly aggregates
 eps-random hold-out slice (1%) keeps labels unbiased and
   guards against a degenerate feedback loop
=============================================================
```

> **Say it like this:** "Auto-train yes; auto-promote only where the label loop is fast and unbiased. Anything where the model gates its own training data — credit, fraud, approvals — I auto-train and require a named approver, and I keep a small random hold-out so I still have unbiased labels at all."

---

### 11.3 The twelve clarifying questions

Ask six to nine of them, in this order, in under four minutes. Best form is an assumption with an exit: *"I'll assume X unless you'd rather I design for Y."*

1. Is this **one model or a platform serving N teams**? (Ask first — it changes everything.)
2. Who is the user — an internal ML team, or an end customer inside the product?
3. **Batch, online, streaming, or agentic** multi-step?
4. **QPS** average and peak, how spiky, and payload size?
5. **Latency budget end to end**, and how much of it is mine versus the caller's?
6. **Freshness** — of features, and of the model itself? Minutes, hours, or "monthly retrain is fine"?
7. **Availability target, and what does degraded mean** — stale prediction, heuristic fallback, or hard fail?
8. Where do **labels** come from and how delayed are they?
9. Is **cost a first-class constraint**, and cost per what — request, tenant, or month?
10. Am I **living inside an existing stack** (cloud, lakehouse, orchestrator) or is this greenfield?
11. **Compliance and tenancy**: PII in features, residency, retention, per-tenant isolation, and do we have to reproduce a decision after the fact?
12. **Who operates it** — team size, and who gets paged when the model is wrong?

Close the block with: *"Anything I've assumed that you'd like me to change?"*

### 11.4 Tradeoff phrase bank — 20 stems

Say these. Tradeoff reasoning that stays in your head scores zero. The blanks are deliberate: fill them from what they told you, never from what you assumed about their business or their team.

1. "That buys us ____ at the cost of ____, and the way I'd decide is ____."
2. "The reason I wouldn't start there is that it adds an on-call surface before we have evidence we need it."
3. "I'd take the staleness — if the business metric moves on ____ cohorts, then ____ of lag costs almost nothing and saves us a streaming pipeline. Is that the right cadence?"
4. "I'd change this decision if ____ crosses ____ — that's the revisit trigger."
5. "Cheapest-first: I'd check the data before the code and the code before the world."
6. "Let me steelman that … yes, that beats mine, because ____. Let me redo the feature path."
7. "I'd still keep mine, because ____, but I'd want to test ____ in week one before I bet on it."
8. "That's the boring option and I'd pick it deliberately — a team of ____ can carry ____; it cannot carry ____."
9. "I'm about sixty percent confident in that number. The way I'd de-risk it is a single-replica load test on day two."
10. "Concretely, the mechanism is ____." (Use whenever you catch yourself listing product names.)
11. "The failure mode of that class of tool is ____, which is what I'd design against regardless of which product we buy."
12. "That's the same dial pointed in opposite directions — throughput and interactivity. Pick the SLO first, then derive concurrency, then replicas."
13. "I'd put the human exactly here, at the promotion gate, and automate everything on either side of it."
14. "The thing I'm not going to build now is ____, because there's no evidence we need it. I'd revisit at ____."
15. "The cost here is dominated by ____, so the single biggest lever is ____ — everything else is rounding."
16. "Let me zoom into the feature path for three minutes and then come back up to the whole picture."
17. "The most likely way this fails in production is ____, so the control I'd add first is ____."
18. "Below ____ I'd use B; above it, A. The boundary is where the extra machinery starts returning more than it costs in on-call."
19. "That optimisation is real but second-order — I'd rather fix the duty cycle first, because idle dwarfs instance choice."
20. "I don't want to over-fit the design to a number I invented, so tell me if your real ____ is very different from what I assumed."

Two phrases banned for the hour: **"it depends"** (without immediately committing) and **"we can figure that out later."**

### 11.5 Numbers to have in the head

Every figure below is **approximate and order-of-magnitude** — the point is to enable arithmetic out loud, not to be quoted. If challenged, say "that's a rough figure I'd verify." Where a number has two defensible bases, both are given: **say which basis you are using before you divide**, because being corrected on your own basis is worse than being 2× off on the answer.

#### Latency (approximate, p50 unless stated)

| Thing | Rough number |
|---|---|
| Redis GET, same AZ | 0.2–1 ms; p99 1–2 ms |
| DynamoDB single-item read | single-digit ms; p99 ~10 ms |
| Postgres point query (indexed, warm) | 1–3 ms |
| S3 GET, small object | **~100–200 ms first byte** — that is AWS's own published performance guideline for S3 Standard, so quote that one to an AWS-heavy room. In-region GETs of small objects are often tens of ms in practice; say which of the two you mean. Throughput ~90 MB/s per stream, parallelise for more. (S3 Express One Zone is the single-digit-ms tier if latency is the actual requirement.) |
| Same-AZ network RTT | 0.1–0.5 ms |
| Cross-AZ RTT | ~0.5–2 ms (and it is *billed*) |
| Cross-region RTT (e.g. Mumbai↔Frankfurt) | ~110–140 ms — a hard floor, no design fixes it |
| Vector ANN top-10, ~1M vectors, in-memory HNSW | 2–10 ms; add network for a managed service |
| Embedding call, hosted API, single short text | ~30–100 ms; batch to amortise |
| LLM TTFT, hosted API | ~200–800 ms; self-hosted small model 50–200 ms |
| LLM decode, per user | 20–80 tok/s typical; below ~20 feels slow in chat |
| Kafka produce with ack | 5–20 ms |
| Container cold start, ML image on K8s | 3–15 min end to end (pull + weights + warmup) |
| Lambda container cold start, ML image | seconds, not ms; assume 2–10 s |

#### Cost shapes (approximate, list price, verify before quoting)

| Thing | Rough number |
|---|---|
| H100 (SXM), on-demand | ~$7–12/GPU-hr list, depending on cloud. AWS p5.48xlarge is 8×H100 at roughly $55/hr following the 2025 price reduction, so ≈ $6.9/GPU-hr; Azure and GCP list higher. ~$2–3/GPU-hr on a neocloud or committed. |
| A100 80 GB | ~$3–5/GPU-hr |
| A10G / L4 | ~$0.7–1.5/GPU-hr |
| T4 | ~$0.35–0.5/GPU-hr |
| AWS Inf2 / Trn | **Name the instance size or don't quote a price** — a family price is meaningless and gets corrected in the room. inf2.xlarge ≈ $0.76/hr, inf2.8xlarge ≈ $2/hr, inf2.48xlarge ≈ $13/hr; trn1.2xlarge ≈ $1.3/hr, trn1.32xlarge ≈ $21/hr; trn2 nodes are tens of dollars an hour. The durable point, and the one you actually say: **the real cost is Neuron compiler coverage for your model architecture, not the hourly rate.** |
| Frontier-API blended | ~$5 per 1M tokens as a planning figure; output tokens cost ~4–5× input, so an output-heavy workload sits nearer $15–20 per 1M *output* tokens |
| Prompt caching | cache read ≈ 0.1× input, cache write ≈ 1.25× input → **it pays for itself on the first re-read**. Break-even ≈ 1.3 uses of the prefix: one write plus one read is 1.35 against 2.0 uncached. |
| Async/batch API tier | ~50% of standard price |
| Self-hosted 4×H100 at list, ~3,400 tok/s, 100% utilised | ≈ **$2–3 per 1M output tokens**. Show the arithmetic: 4 × $6.9/GPU-hr = $27.6/hr; 3,400 tok/s × 3,600 s = 12.2M tokens/hr; ≈ $2.25 per 1M. On cheap committed GPUs ≈ $0.8. |
| Self-host break-even | **State the basis before you divide.** Break-even ≈ (self-host $ per 1M output) ÷ (API $ per 1M **output**). At ≈$2.25 against a ~$20/1M frontier *output* price that is ~11% sustained utilisation. Measured against the $5 **blended** planning rate above it is ~45%. Half an ops FTE pushes both up materially — derive that live from whatever salary you assume rather than quoting a memorised figure. And say the caveat aloud: a self-hosted open-weights 70B is not the same product as a frontier model, so this is a floor, not a like-for-like. |
| Databricks DBU ordering | The ordering is by **DBU rate**: jobs compute cheapest → pipelines → all-purpose (~3–4× jobs) → SQL serverless. But serverless folds the cloud VM cost into the DBU rate, so on spiky BI it often wins on **total** cost. Photon ≈ 2–3× DBUs and does nothing for Python UDFs or RDD work. ⚠ Attach the disarming half-sentence every time you say this: *"that's from the pricing page and the `system.billing` tables, not from owning a Databricks bill."* |

#### Model memory (weights only; add ~10–20% for activations and framework overhead)

| Model | FP16 (2 B/param) | INT8 (1 B) | INT4 (~0.5 B) | Full fine-tune, Adam (~16–20 B/param) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 7B | ~14 GB | ~7 GB | ~3.5 GB | ~112–140 GB (multi-GPU) |
| 13B | ~26 GB | ~13 GB | ~6.5 GB | ~210–260 GB |
| 70B | ~140 GB | ~70 GB | ~35 GB | ~1.1–1.4 TB |

**LoRA:** base weights stay frozen and can be int8/int4; the trainable adapter is typically ~0.1–1% of params (a rank-16 adapter on a 7B is tens of MB). Practical effect: a 7B QLoRA fine-tune fits on a single 24 GB card; a **70B QLoRA fits on a single 80 GB card** — the QLoRA paper fine-tuned a 65B on one 48 GB GPU — and 2×80 GB buys headroom for longer sequences and larger batch rather than being the minimum. Serving many tenants = one base in HBM plus many adapters swapped per request, which is the modern multi-model endpoint.

#### KV cache — the concurrency ceiling

```text
KV bytes/token = 2 (K,V) x n_kv_heads x head_dim x n_layers x bytes_per_elem

70B-class (GQA, 8 kv heads, head_dim 128, 80 layers):
  FP16: 2 x 8 x 128 x 80 x 2  = 327,680 B  ~= 320 KiB/token
  FP8 :                        ~= 160 KiB/token

N_concurrent ~= (total HBM - weights - overhead) / (KV_per_token x ctx)
  4xH100 = 320 GB; weights FP8 = 70 GB; overhead ~20 GB -> 230 GB free
  FP16 KV @ 4k ctx: ~1.34 GB/req (327,680 x 4,096) -> ~170 concurrent
  FP8  KV @ 4k ctx: ~0.67 GB/req                   -> ~340 concurrent
```

⚠ If you write the multiplication on the pad, write **1.34 GB** — or just say "about 1.3". 327,680 × 4,096 = 1.34 GB decimal, 1.25 GiB. Do not write 1.31: the arithmetic on the pad will not agree with the number you said.

> **Say it like this:** "Note what that means for a product ask: moving from 4k to 32k context cuts max concurrency by eight. That's a capacity-planning conversation, not a product one."

**Decode roofline**, the same family of arithmetic: `max steps/s ≈ aggregate HBM bandwidth ÷ total weight bytes read per step`. On that same 4×H100 box it is ~13.4 TB/s aggregate against 70 GB of FP8 weights, so **~190 steps/s theoretical**. Real batch-1 decode lands nearer 30–50 tok/s, because tensor-parallel all-reduce and kernel-launch overhead consume most of the roofline. Say both numbers: the gap between 190 and 40 is exactly where the serving engineering lives, and it is why batching — not FLOPs — is the lever. (Note the box: 70 GB of weights does not fit on one 80 GB card alongside a KV cache, which is why the arithmetic is aggregate bandwidth across four cards, not one card's 3.35 TB/s.)

#### Drift thresholds — the near-certain "what would you alert on?"

The JD names data drift verbatim and the round is tagged Domain, so this will be asked. The full implementation with the edge cases handled is in `06_bedrock_and_observability_primer.md` §B5; this is the version you carry in your head.

| PSI | Conventional reading | What I'd actually do |
|---|---|---|
| < 0.1 | no material change | nothing |
| 0.1 – 0.25 | moderate shift | ticket; look at the top contributing bins, not the aggregate |
| > 0.25 | material shift | ticket and investigate; page **only** if a guardrail or business metric moves with it |

Say the caveats in the same breath — they are what separates a memorised band from somebody who has run this:

- **PSI is bin-count dependent.** Ten fixed quantile bins taken from the *training* snapshot is the convention. Change the binning and the number changes, so a threshold is only meaningful against **frozen reference bins** shipped alongside the model.
- **Empty bins send PSI to infinity**, so you need an epsilon floor (1e-6 is typical) or Laplace-style smoothing. Say which you used, because it moves the number.
- **Categoricals need an explicit unseen-category bucket.** Without one a brand-new category silently vanishes and PSI looks healthy while the model is being fed something it has never seen.
- **Alternatives:** two-sample KS for continuous features — report the D statistic, not the p-value, because at production sample sizes every p-value is zero; chi-square for categoricals; and for multivariate drift, train a domain classifier to separate reference from current and read its AUC (≈0.5 means indistinguishable, above ~0.7 means the two periods are trivially separable).
- **Rank order matters.** Prediction-distribution drift and feature null-rate move earlier and cost far less to compute than full input drift. Label drift is the only one that proves harm; everything else is a leading indicator.

> **Say it like this:** "I'd alert above 0.25 PSI against frozen reference bins, ticket between 0.1 and 0.25, and I wouldn't page on any of it. Drift is a ticket; the page is a guardrail breach or a freshness SLO miss. And I'd say out loud that the threshold is meaningless without the binning and the epsilon floor pinned next to the model — otherwise PSI moves purely because somebody re-binned."

#### Standard conversions

| From | To | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| Daily volume → RPS | **Pick one and say which**: ÷100,000 for the fast estimate, ÷86,400 for the exact | Fast: 1M/day ≈ 10 RPS; 100M ≈ 1k; 1B ≈ 10k. Exact: 1M/day ≈ 11.6 RPS; 100M ≈ 1.16k; 1B ≈ 11.6k |
| Average → peak | ×3–5 for consumer diurnal; ×10 if event-driven | state which you assumed |
| Words → tokens | ×1.3 (≈ 4 chars/token) | 1,000 words ≈ 1,300 tokens; one A4 page ≈ 700 tokens |
| Concurrency | Little's Law: `N = λ × T` | 500 RPS × 200 ms = 100 in flight |
| Rows → bytes | 2 KB/feature row | 5M hot users × 2 KB = 10 GB → fits one Redis node |
| Spot checkpoint interval | `sqrt(2 × checkpoint_cost × MTBF)` | 2-min checkpoint, 6 h MTBF → ~38 min |
| Cost per 1k predictions | `(GPU $/hr ÷ (RPS × 3600)) × 1000` + store reads + logging | compute it, then challenge your own design with it |

### 11.6 The "I don't know" ladder

Five rungs. Pick one **before** you start the sentence; the failure mode is starting on rung 1 and discovering mid-sentence that you're on rung 4.

**Rung 1 — I know this cold.** Answer with mechanism, then a number or a failure mode, then check in.
> "Yes — concretely, the mechanism is ____, and the thing that bites is ____. I've hit that on ____. Want me to go deeper on any of those?"

**Rung 2 — I know the concept, and I've operated the equivalent, not this product.**
> "I know the category and I've run the equivalent with different tooling. Concept-level it's ____; the failure modes of that class of tool are ____. What I haven't done is this specific product, so if its behaviour differs from what I just described, tell me and I'll adjust."

**Rung 3 — I know the concept, I have not run anything in the category.**
> "I know the concept, not the product's behaviour. Concept-level: ____. Product-level I'd be guessing, so I'll stop there rather than invent detail."

**Rung 4 — I know the problem it solves, nothing more.** Name → bridge → mechanism → ramp → question back.
> "I haven't used it. I know what problem it exists to solve — ____ — and I've solved that problem by hand with ____. The questions I'd want answered in week one are ____."

Then the tail question. **The generic tail works for all five items** and is the one to memorise verbatim:
> "What does it actually buy you here — is it the governance boundary, the cost lever, or mostly convenience?"

If you have one more sentence to spend, the per-item tail is sharper:

| Rung-4 item | Tail question |
|---|---|
| Unity Catalog | "Is it the boundary you actually enforce access on, or mostly lineage and discovery with the real enforcement somewhere else?" |
| Mosaic AI Agent Framework | "Are you using it for the evaluation and tracing loop, or is it serving agents in production too?" |
| Databricks Vector Search / AI Search | "Is the index doing your tenant isolation, or are you filtering above it in the application?" |
| Monte Carlo | "Does it own the alerting, or does it sit alongside expectations you've already written into the pipeline?" |
| AWS Bedrock | "Is it the gateway for everything, or one route among self-hosted models and direct vendor APIs?" |

**Rung 5 — I have never touched it and I can't usefully reason about it.**
> "I don't know that. Here's how I'd find out in ten minutes, and here's what I'd expect the answer to be and why — but that's an expectation, not knowledge."

Then **stop talking.** Silence is fine. Speculation dressed as fact is not.

**If they push:** *"Fair. I'd rather be the person who says 'I don't know' on the third day of an incident than the one who guesses."*

**Never say:** "I've read about it", "I'm familiar with it", "I've touched it a bit", "it's basically the same as X so it'd be easy."

**Rung-4 list for today, memorised:** Unity Catalog, Mosaic AI Agent Framework, Databricks Vector Search, Monte Carlo, AWS Bedrock. Also: petabyte-scale Lakehouse ownership, and GPU-fleet sizing at scale — you have the arithmetic, not the operating scars, and say so if pressed. Databricks experience is **Azure Databricks + Spark + Deequ, about 1.5 years, data-quality and ETL work** — say that sentence exactly, and offer Deequ→expectations as the honest bridge.

⚠ The ladder cuts both ways. Rung 2 forbids confident universals about products you have not run. "Every vector database behaves like X" is a rung-2 sentence wearing rung-1 clothes. End at the honest edge and hand the question back.
