### 11.7 The first five minutes and the last five minutes

#### Opening (say this in roughly this shape, 90 seconds, then hand back)

> **Say it like this:** "Thanks — quick framing so you can steer me. Eight years of production engineering, about four and a half of them in ML-engineer titles. Currently senior ML engineer at TrueBalance, consumer lending, where I own an XGBoost propensity pipeline end to end — feature engineering through real-time serving on Lambda and SQS, ARM64 images in ECR, versioned artifacts in S3 — plus a domain knowledge graph that replaced a regex parser, and part of our internal MCP-based developer assistant. Before that, ResMed for two and a half years: RAG and GenAI over clinical data on AWS, feature-store schemas in Snowflake, Airflow pipelines, and multi-container SageMaker endpoints sharing infrastructure across models on the internal MLOps platform. Before that, Tiger Analytics, where I designed an end-to-end MLOps platform on SageMaker for a UK bank — training, inference, drift detection, CI/CD, automated retraining — under FCA constraints. The through-line is that most of the production failures I've seen in ML are data and operations failures wearing a model costume, which is why I gravitate to the platform half of this work."

Then, unprompted, in minute three — or the moment the first product name appears:

> **Say it like this:** "One thing I flagged to your recruiter in writing and want to repeat directly: I haven't run Unity Catalog, Mosaic AI Agent Framework, Databricks Vector Search, Monte Carlo or Bedrock in production. My Databricks experience is Azure Databricks with Spark and Deequ, about a year and a half, and it's data-quality and ETL work rather than Lakehouse-platform ownership. I've built the equivalent layers with other tooling — governance and lineage, retrieval, data-quality monitoring, managed model serving — so when those come up I'll tell you what I know about the category and where my knowledge stops. I'd rather do that than guess. Where would you like to start?"

Then, before you design anything:

> **Say it like this:** "Let me spend about five minutes on requirements and rough numbers, then sketch a high-level design, then go deep wherever you want. Stop me any time and I'll re-prioritise."

Paste the pad skeleton immediately:

```text
======== 1. REQUIREMENTS ========
======== 2. NUMBERS =============
======== 3. DESIGN ==============
======== 4. OPTIONS / PICK ======
======== 5. DEEP DIVE ===========
======== 6. FAILURE MODES =======
======== 7. ROLLOUT / NOT DOING =
```

#### The fifteen lines you can type cold

Round 1 was a live coding round on this same pad, so the interviewer already knows you can type. In a design round the highest-value use of that is a *monitor*, not an algorithm: it lands the JD's drift bullet and its observability bullet inside ninety seconds, and it converts an abstract answer into an artefact. Rehearse it at 17:10 until you can produce it without thinking. Narrate what it is while you type — "this is a pad stub, not production code; the real one lives in a library with tests."

```python
# drift monitor stub: frozen reference, epsilon floor, unseen bucket
REF_EDGES, REF_PCT = ref["edges"], ref["pct"]   # frozen at train time
EPS = 1e-6

def psi(values, name):
    idx  = np.digitize(values, REF_EDGES[name])       # unseen -> edge bin
    cnt  = np.bincount(idx, minlength=len(REF_PCT[name]))
    cur  = np.maximum(cnt / max(cnt.sum(), 1), EPS)
    refp = np.maximum(REF_PCT[name], EPS)
    return float(((cur - refp) * np.log(cur / refp)).sum())

for name, col in features.items():
    v, tags = psi(col, name), {"feature": name}
    emit("feature.psi", v, tags=tags)
    emit("feature.nulls", float(np.isnan(col).mean()), tags=tags)
    if v > 0.25:
        open_ticket(name, v)      # ticket, not page — see the drift table
```

The three things to narrate while typing, because they are the whole reason this is worth typing: **the reference bins are frozen and shipped with the model** (otherwise the threshold means nothing); **the epsilon floor** (otherwise an empty bin gives infinity); and **`np.digitize` folds out-of-range values into the edge bins**, so an unseen category or a new range cannot silently vanish. Then close it:

> **Say it like this:** "And the missing-rate metric sitting next to it is the one that would have caught my train/serve parity failure on day one instead of after the fact — that's why it's in the same loop as the drift metric rather than in a separate dashboard."

**Optional second artefact, six lines** — only if cost attribution comes up and you still have the pad. Preface it honestly, because it is Databricks-specific and you have already disclosed the limit of that experience:

```sql
-- which job burned DBUs last week (from the docs, not from a real bill)
SELECT u.usage_metadata.job_id, u.sku_name,
       SUM(u.usage_quantity)                       AS dbus,
       SUM(u.usage_quantity * p.pricing.default)   AS approx_usd
FROM system.billing.usage u
JOIN system.billing.list_prices p ON u.sku_name = p.sku_name
WHERE u.usage_date >= current_date() - INTERVAL 7 DAYS
GROUP BY 1, 2 ORDER BY approx_usd DESC LIMIT 20;
```

> **Say it like this:** "Price rows in `list_prices` are time-ranged, so on a real bill you'd also join on the validity window — I'm writing the shape, not something I've run against your account. The reason I reach for a query rather than a dashboard is that per-tenant and per-model cost attribution has to be something somebody can run and argue with, or nobody ends up owning the number."

#### Closing (last five minutes)

Ask three questions, in this order. Do not ask about salary, notice or process — that is the recruiter's lane.

1. "When a model behaves badly in production, who gets paged — the platform team or the model-owning team — and how often does the wrong one get paged?"
2. "How do you gate a model into production today — machine-checked promotion gate, or review-based? And has it ever blocked something that should have shipped?"
3. "How much of the platform is Databricks-native versus your own abstraction on top, and how do you feel about that ratio?"

Spares if one is answered pre-emptively: cost per prediction and who owns it; what's on the paved road and why teams go off it; the last data incident that reached customers and the control that came out of it.

Then close it yourself:

> **Say it like this:** "Last thing — is there anything about my background that gives you pause? The Databricks-native tooling gap is already on the table and I'd rather address it now than leave it unanswered."

If they name a gap, respond with the ladder (rung 4), a ramp, and **no apology**. One sentence, then stop.

Sign-off:

> **Say it like this:** "Thanks — this was genuinely useful. If it helps, I'm happy to send a short written version of the design I sketched, including the parts I'd cut. The coordinator has my details."
